channel.title: Personal News Feed — Other
channel.description: Personally scored travel, food, and lifestyle articles curated by news-filter

item.title: Traditional gumbo, kettle-boiled bagels, Chelsea buns: What do ‘endangered dishes’ tell us about the world today?
item.description:
Source: Adventure Score: 4.70
Globalization, overtourism, climate crisis, and social change can all contribute to the loss of beloved cultural practices—including what we eat. But what does this mean for cultural and food heritage? And how can travelers help preserve the flavors that make our experiences so much richer?

item.title: Thousands of African birds are missing from sound libraries. A massive grassroots effort hopes to change that
item.description:
Source: Adventure Score: 4.50
Thousands of African bird species remain missing from the sound libraries that train AI-powered research and conservation tools. Now, the Cornell Lab of Ornithology and BirdLife South Africa are leading an ambitious continent-wide grassroots effort to fill in the gaps. Alexandra Owens reports.

item.title: On a yoga mat, this Irish writer rediscovers the language of her motherland
item.description:
Source: Adventure Score: 4.05
The Irish language—Gaeilge—is experiencing a cultural revival in Ireland. Éalú Aran is one of a wave of retreats and courses that teach the language in an informal setting outside the classroom, keeping it alive for generations to come. “Up onto the toes. Na méara coise, as they’re called. The ‘fingers of your feet’.” Weaving between Irish and English phrasing, Áine Seoighe is directing a yoga and breathwork session. We’re on Inis Oírr, the smallest of the Aran Islands off Ireland’s western coast. This is a Gaeltacht region, where Irish, or Gaeilge, is the dominant language. We’re a few hours into an Éalú Aran day retreat, a bilingual wellness program run by native islander Seoighe since 2023. Through activities such as meditation, nature walks, basket-making and sea swimming, participants are gently immersed in the language. It’s one of many Irish-language-focused events cropping up all over the country, propelled by a resurgence of interest in the vernacular. Now a mandatory subject in the Irish education system, Gaeilge is Ireland’s first official language, followed by English. It seems more people are embracing this aspect of Irish identity that was historically marginalized under British colonial rule. However, despite enjoying it in school, I rarely had cause to use it in my hometown, Dublin, afterwards. But when I recently returned to Ireland after living overseas, I realized attitudes to the language had shifted. Peers are doing re-immersion courses, Irish-speaking cafés have opened, and I’ve started to hear more families speaking ‘as Gaeilge’, a colloquial turn of phrase that means ‘in Irish’. A short ferry ride from Doolin village brings us to the island, with the Cliffs of Moher looming in our rearview as we sail west. On the approach, Inis Oírr’s waymarks emerge: The rusting MV Plassy shipwreck, striped Fardurris Point Lighthouse, O’Brien’s Castle. By the pier, horse-drawn carriages and bicycle rental shops await visitors—the few cars on the island belong to its population of roughly 340 residents. Meeting us by the harbor, Seoighe launches into a welcome ‘as Gaeilge’ before guiding us on a walk around the island’s wind-whipped perimeter. Limestone forms Inis Oírr’s foundations, ground down into white-sand beaches along the shore. Generations of islanders spread seaweed across the land to render it tillable. Miles of dry stone walls crisscross the island’s 2.3-square-mile (5.9 square kilometer) expanse. “The language is such an important part of the island, of the community, of our past and present. Doing anything here on the island has to incorporate the language.” - Áine Seoighe, Éalú Aran retreats An ancient Celtic language, Irish was gradually excluded from legal proceedings, classrooms and state affairs when Ireland was under British rule. Clandestine educators (known as ‘hedge schools’) and rural communities quietly kept the language alive, but it was threatened with extinction by the Great Famine of the 1840s, when Irish-speaking rural areas were plagued by high death rates and mass emigration. When the Irish Free State was founded in the 1920s—giving independence to 26 of Ireland’s 32 counties—its status was restored. English nevertheless remains more widely spoken, but 40 percent of the Republic of Ireland’s population reported that they could speak Irish in the latest census, recorded in 2022. Gaeltacht regions are pivotal to the language’s survival. Seoighe, now 36, was raised speaking Irish at home on Inis Oírr. “When I was growing up, island life was still quite slow,” she tells me. “Irish was very much the only language really spoken in the community.” Though still fluently spoken on Inis Oírr, its use on the island has waned somewhat in recent decades for a number of reasons, including societal changes, social media and TV, Seoighe admits. Bringing Gaeilge into Éalú Aran retreats, which vary in length from a day to a week, was instinctual. “The language is such an important part of the island, of the community, of our past and present,” she says. “Doing anything here on the island has to incorporate the language.” Fionnuala Ní Uallacháin, multimedia officer for Scéal.ie, which catalogues Irish-language events around the country, confirms there has been a surge in their number and variety, from “ciorcal comhrá” (conversation circles) and park runs to stained glass workshops and hillwalking meet-ups. Language courses are “increasing in popularity exponentially,” she says. High-profile Irish artists such as Kneecap, the Belfast group that lyricize in Irish, are partially to credit for the resurgence, and widely seen as a “cool band doing new things with Irish,” Ní Uallacháin tells me. A fresh wave of Irish-language podcasts, such as How to Gael and Beo Ar Éigean, and content creators (among them, Cúán de Búrca and Mollie Guidera) is also driving renewed interest. This grassroots revival is something Declan O’Connor, who teaches surfing through Irish and English at Tonn Nua Surf School in County Mayo on Ireland’s west coast, has observed. “There’s definitely been a resurgence. I’ve noticed it with the surf school, but also I’ve noticed it outside at festivals and in random meetings with people.” This year, he started hosting bilingual surf and yoga retreats on the Mullet Peninsula in the northwest of the county, in collaboration with Irish-language surf group Surfála. “The informal setting, it just loosens [people] up and gives them the opportunity to give it a try,” he says. On the yoga mat, the vocabulary I studied in classrooms of my childhood resurfaces. I’m surprised by how much I remember. A recent study by Irish language course provider Gaelchultúr found nearly 70 per cent of adults want to improve their grasp of the language while almost half of those aged under 25 reported using Irish when socializing. Its research also showed that close to half of people under 44 would send their child to a Gaelscoil, where subjects are taught through Irish—a 20 percent increase on a similar 2015 study. Older generations feel a “wistfulness” for the language, Fionnuala observes. “You see a lot of people going back to [learn] Irish when they retire,” she says. Éalú Aran retreats are open to Irish-language novices, as well as experienced speakers. Attendees have visited from wider Europe, North America and Australia. My British partner finds he can follow along without any basis in the language. Participants are “surprised at how much communication isn’t vocal,” says Seoighe. During one of our hikes, Seoighe forages sea beet, an ancient plant often called ‘wild spinach’, for us to taste and points out currachs stacked on the sand, the traditional Irish boats that once were the only way to access the island. Alternating between Irish and English as we go, she translates Gaelic turns of phrase without interrupting the conversation’s flow. Eventually, we reach a ‘garraí’, a walled plot overlooking a freshwater lake, Loch Mór. Inside is a yurt, the setting for our yoga class. “I’ll go in and out of Gaeilge, but you’ll follow that, I’m sure,” Seoighe tells us, as we begin. The tent is open to the elements. Currachs move across the lake, while a sleepy calf is feeding in the adjoining garraí. “Learning a language keeps the mind active, curious and engaged,” she says. “So for me, wellness and language-learning are a very natural combination: We are looking after the body, the mind and our connection to our culture and the world around us.” For Seoighe, movement facilitates learning. “When we move, we are focused mainly on the movement, not the words. We hear the language repeatedly and naturally, and over time the sounds and words begin to become familiar.” This is certainly my experience. On the yoga mat, the vocabulary I studied in classrooms of my childhood resurfaces. I’m surprised by how much I remember. “Dún na súile … weʻll close the eyes here,” Seoighe says, encouraging us to think of the “gaineamh agus an fheamainn, the sand and seaweed that made the land” as we stretch out on the “talamh” (ground). Lunchtime arrives. A picnic of cheddar cheese, homemade bread and potato salad has been prepared by the island’s Teach an Tae café. It’s been spitting rain all morning, but suddenly the sky brightens and the water glitters; we enjoy lunch on the rocks overlooking the lake. Later, on the island’s main beach, Seoighe fires up the sauna, and we join locals and holidaymakers in the icy water. By the shore, the words snámh (swim) and fuar (cold) come back to me. My time on Inis Oírr has proven I haven’t fully lost my Irish, but I’ll have to put in some work to find it again. It’s a beautiful language to rediscover and we owe so much to its custodians, like Seoighe, who are safeguarding it for future generations. “Keeping the language living is about much more than preserving words,” she says. “It is about preserving a different way of seeing and understanding the world.” ** The writer was a guest of Éalú Aran. Retreats are priced from EUR€95 ($110/AUD$155) per person. Transport and accommodation were arranged by the writer. **** Adventure.com strives to be a low-emissions travel publication. item.title: Are hikes, homestays and conservation-first tourism an alternative to Cancún’s heady nightlife and sprawling hotels?
item.description:
Source: Adventure Score: 3.42
In the 1960s, the Mexican government backed mass-market tourism with its development of Cancún, but a 2026 directive by President Scheinbaum now puts the focus on regenerative tourism. What does that mean for the region? The Yucatán Peninsula is a dichotomy. You only need to look out of the airplane window as you start your descent into Cancún to see the contrasts. One moment, you’re looking at a 12-mile-long (20-kilometer) spit of sand lined with huge hotel resorts. The next, as the plane drops further, an impenetrable carpet of dark-green jungle rolls out as far as the eye can see. Cancún’s Hotel Zone sprung up in the 1970s and since then, has cultivated its reputation for all-inclusive resorts, high-energy nightlife and out-of-the-box holiday experiences. Overdevelopment has placed a strain on natural resources; the demand for fresh water is draining the region’s ancient cenote (sinkhole) network, while sudden demand for workers is creating overcrowded, unplanned inland neighborhoods. But you don’t have to go far to find pockets of low-impact, community tourism. And this year, for the first time ever, the Mexican government has recognized the importance of the latter. In March 2026, Mexico’s National Fund for Tourism Promotion (Fonatur) and the government signed an agreement to encourage its tourism industry—which represents nearly 10 percent of the country’s GDP—to serve as a tool for social justice, allowing local communities to become active participants in a region’s economic growth. While the Mexican government’s focus was on resorts like Cancún several decades ago, President Claudia Sheinbaum’s current vision is different. They want to support destinations where local communities are the protagonists, ensuring the conservation of natural resources under the stewardship of people who have lived there for generations. The government has named three community tourism projects—Pueblos Mancomunados in Oaxaca, and Maya Ka’an and Camino del Mayab in the Yucatán Peninsula—to receive support during 2026. For the latter, the investment will fund better water and wastewater management, trail maintenance, project equipment, public space maintenance and signage. With the Maya Ka’an and Camino del Mayab within 180 miles of Cancún, it appears to show a change of focus. “Maya communities are not treated as attractions or objects of observation. Instead, they’re recognized as active participants, storytellers and custodians of their own culture and territory.” - Fernando Sarvide, local guide This summer, I hiked the Camino del Mayab in Yucatán with local guides José Luis Bé and Fernando Sarvide. The Camino is a 68-mile (110-kilometer) trail through the jungle just south of Mérida, in the northwest of the Yucatán Peninsula, which connects 14 Mayan communities. The terrain on this route, which opened in 2020, is flat and undemanding, but the high temperatures add challenge to the distances, which average around 14 miles (23 kilometers) per day. My hike began with a short opening ceremony in which our guide Fernando reminded the group that we were guests in the jungle, walking through a place that had existed long before us. The three-mile (five-kilometer) walk from X‘Matkuil to Molas, two of the communities on the Camino, runs along the disused railway that once transported henequen (sisal) from haciendas to the coast for export. In Molas, we learnt more about the Mayan way of life, the history of the haciendas, and the surrounding jungle from community members, before finding refuge in the home of Doña Norma for lunch; we enjoyed traditional pibil chicken and refried beans alongside jugfuls of ice-cold horchata (white rice with milk or water, sweetened with cinnamon and sugar). I soon learnt that mornings start early in these communities, with most activity is done and dusted by lunch. Afternoons are set aside for cooling off with a dip in a cenote or taking a siesta in a hammock in the shade. Camino del Mayab was founded by EcoGuerreros, an initiative that promotes community development, environmental conservation and sustainable tourism. One of the project’s greatest achievements is creating opportunities for local people to earn a living within their communities, instead of having to relocate to Yucatán cities such as Mérida or Cancún for work. Doña Norma is a case in point. She had no way of earning money in her community before but now, she loves cooking lunch for trekkers, welcoming them in her home as part of the Camino del Mayab ‘package’. “It opens the door to new experiences for everyone,” she told me. “Visitors learn about our culture, and we learn from them as we share stories, traditions and perspectives. These meaningful connections go far beyond a shared meal.” Chatting to José Luis, who grew up in the Tzacalá community, he said he believed the Camino has had a positive impact. “It’s helped diversify the local economy while strengthening our cultural identity. It’s encouraged us to value and preserve the traditions, knowledge and heritage that make our community unique.” Thanks to the Camino del Mayab and EcoGuerreros, the community now has a library in a previously disused building. As well as distributing books and keeping local stories alive, it’s also a place where young people can get help applying for university, and other life and work opportunities. For Fernando, a guide from Mérida and former teacher of Mexican history, the hike has changed the relationship between visitors and local people. “Maya communities are not treated as attractions or objects of observation,” he told me. “Instead, they’re recognized as active participants, storytellers and custodians of their own culture and territory.” During the afternoons, we bathed in cenotes, the sinkholes scattered about the Yucatán Peninsula. Now a welcome respite from the merciless heat for hikers and locals, they were once believed to be doorways to the Mayan underworld and are still seen as sacred spaces by many. The hike had been an enriching experience. I had gone hoping to learn more about Mayan culture and met many passionate locals keen to share their way of life with me; particularly memorable was learning to play pok da pok, an ancient Mayan ball sport still played in seven Latin American countries, and sees players hitting the ball with only hips, knees and elbows with the aim of getting it through a hoop suspended from the ceiling. “Those of us who live here have fallen back in love with it, thanks to our visitors. Seeing someone’s eyes light up in wonder… that’s the most powerful thing I’ve experienced.” - Manuel Enrique Galindo Triay, guide and biologist It was the more recent history of the haciendas and henequen dictatorships that struck home the most. Haciendas in Yucatán operated as dictatorships until the 1980s, taking land from Indigenous communities and small farmers. José Luis told me part of the Camino’s mission is to change the mindset in the communities: “You work hard, you accept your lot and you have no power.” I’d met old men who’d worked in the hacienda regime as young boys, while the grand buildings, many of which now lie in ruins, are an ever-present reminder of the injustices of the past and of how life once was in those communities. I was heartened to know that 80 percent of what I’d paid to hike the Camino del Mayab would go directly to local people. Mariana Ramos, commercial coordinator for Camino del Mayab, was optimistic about the impact of government support: “It will help improve infrastructure and signage,” she told me, “and fund safe places where visitors can obtain information, eat, shower and stay overnight, supporting the expansion of our self-guided hiking experiences.” The other initiative in the Yucatán Peninsula to receive support from the government is Maya Ka’an, a large sustainable tourism project that encompasses the Sian Ka’an Biosphere Reserve 16 miles (25 kilometers) south of Tulum, created in 2012 to protect the area’s tropical jungle, wetlands, mangroves, freshwater canals and coastal marine environments while prioritizing community leadership in tourism. Like Camino del Mayab, Maya Ka’an focuses on nature-based and cultural experiences and it’s hoped that government support will help improve infrastructure as well as visibility. Román Caamal Coh, general manager of Community Tours Sian Ka’an (CTSK), led by a 100 percent Maya cooperative and one of the projects within Maya Ka’an, explained why he thinks it was chosen by the government. “It’s a low-impact model, managed by communities and community-based enterprises, and it’s one of the most mature and representative examples in Mexico of conservation led by the communities that live there.” Maya Ka’an’s jungle walks, kayaking, birdwatching, cooking and handicraft workshops are a far cry from the pools, beach bars and snorkeling boats that line the Mexican Caribbean coast. And its accommodation offering—intentionally limited to eco-lodges, rustic cabins or guesthouses—contrasts with the large chain hotels that lie behind gated perimeters along Highway 307 from Cancún to Tulum. I met the team behind Community Tours Sian Ka’an to see how the initiative has been transforming the lives of locals. For its treasurer Lucía Pacheco May, her work has enabled her to pay for her children’s education. “I’m happy, because I never had the chance to study,” she told me. “Where I’m from, there’s only a primary school.” Boat captain Ricardo Caamal Aban, who takes visitors on the project’s Ancient Canal tour through Mayan lagoons and mangrove channels, told me: “I’m proudly Maya… I’m passionate about being in contact with nature and sharing what I know with the people who visit us.” It’s a similar story for guide and biologist Manuel Enrique Galindo Triay: “Those of us who live here have fallen back in love with it, thanks to our visitors,” he said. “Seeing someone’s eyes light up in wonder… that’s the most powerful thing I’ve experienced.” For the Camino del Mayab and Maya Ka’an, recognition by the national government as a worthy alternative to the mass tourism and private investment of Tulum and Cancún has been a significant gamechanger. As CTSK’s Román told me, “”The Maya Ka’an tourism model translates into dignified employment, less migration to the cities, and a community that values its own culture and natural resources.” ** The writer traveled with her family and self-funded this trip including their time with Community Tours Sian Ka’an. Her own spot on the Camino del Mayab was hosted by environmental conservation organization, EcoGuerreros. **** Adventure.com strives to be a low-emissions travel publication. item.title: This Indigenous-led tour in BC is part of a Canada-wide initiative to put First Nations tourism in the spotlight
item.description:
Source: Adventure Score: 3.12
Seven in 10 Canadians say they’d enjoy learning about Indigenous cultures on their travels, but many don’t know how or where to find a tour. Indigenous-owned Talaysay Tours and B Corp tour operator Intrepid Travel are hoping to fix that. “We are on the unceded territories of the Squamish and Lil’wat people,” says Talaysay Campo, whose name translates to ‘ocean breeze’, ‘wind blowing on the water’ or ‘whispering winds’. “There’s one thing I want to share, and that’s that the land is absolutely everything.” We’re just outside Whistler Village in British Columbia about to embark on a forest trail walk to Lost Lake (Sḵwiḵ), a critical stopping point for Indigenous communities to gather resources and fish when traveling between the coast and the interior. Today we’re on a preview of Campo’s new ‘We Are The Land’ tour. “The reason we chose this name for the tour is something my Aunty Talaysay would tell me when I was a little girl: ‘We are the land’. It means that we are the caretakers of the land,” she says. Campo is co-owner of Talaysay Tours, an Indigenous, women-owned tourism company offering Indigenous-led experiences across British Columbia. Founded by her mother Candace Campo, in 2002, the company is rooted in the traditions and knowledge of both the Shíshálh (Sechelt) and Sḵwx̱wú7mesh (Squamish) Nations, of which the women are members. Walking beneath a canopy of towering old-growth Western Hemlock trees, Campo points out the Devil’s club, a woody shrub used by her ancestors for pain relief. “It’s important to have Indigenous tourism so our local guests and out-of-town guests can build a stronger relationship with the land,” says Campo as we pause by a babbling brook, where glimmers of sunlight dance on the slow-moving creek. “There’s so much going on with logging, global warming—one thing I’ve realized is that if (people) don’t have a relationship with the land, how are they going to take care of it or know how to take care of it?” It’s a question that sits at the heart of a growing conversation about what responsible travel in Canada should look like. As part of this conversation, Talaysay Tours has partnered with B Corp tour operator Intrepid Travel on this new ‘We Are The Land’ experience. It’s aim is to help bring place-based learning, cultural ecology, stewardship and storytelling to Intrepid’s 10-day Grand Canadian Rockies itinerary beginning in 2027. “For us, it’s at the cornerstone of everything that has to do with responsible tourism. We think it’s also just an amazing experience for our customers to really understand the real Canada, and the only way to do that is to partner with an Indigenous-led company.” - Christian Wolters, Intrepid Travel Canada President The Talasay partnership is part of a broader initiative by Intrepid to include more Indigenous tourism across its Canadian itineraries, with the goal to have an Indigenous-led experience on 75 percent of Canada tours by the end of this year, and one on every Canadian itinerary by the end of 2031. According to new research from non-profit foundation Angus Reid, commissioned by Intrepid Travel in July this year and surveying a group of 1,507 Canadians, 57 percent say they are interested in participating in an Indigenous-led tourism experience within Canada, yet fewer than one in five have ever done so. Part of the problem may be visibility. Among Canadians who have never participated in an Indigenous-led experience, 42 percent say they have not encountered one while planning a trip, while another 30 percent say they don’t know where to find one. According to the survey, seven in 10 Canadians would enjoy learning about Indigenous cultures, while more than four in 10 would be more likely to choose a Canadian trip that includes an Indigenous-led tourism experience. The appetite is certainly there. For Intrepid Travel Canada President Christian Wolters, who has joined us on the walking trail, making these experiences easier to access is more than a business opportunity. “For us, it’s at the cornerstone of everything that has to do with responsible tourism,” he tells me, after stopping to taste a few reddish salmonberries, native to the Pacific Northwest. “We think it’s also just an amazing experience for our customers to really understand the real Canada, and the only way to do that is to partner with an Indigenous-led company.” Intrepid is also working closely with the Indigenous Tourism Association of Canada (ITAC) and has committed over USD$350,000 over five years to support the growth and promotion of Indigenous tourism in Canada. This includes adding Indigenous experiences to existing tours, as well as developing new, bespoke experiences alongside Indigenous tourism operators. “Partnerships like this create tangible opportunities and ensure communities gain direct economic and cultural benefits, while supporting our vision of Canada becoming a world leader in Indigenous tourism by 2030,” said Keith Henry, chief executive officer and president of ITAC in a press release. Coming up in 2027, a Huron-Wendat experience in Wendake, Quebec, will be added to Intrepid’s Eastern Canada by Rail itinerary, which will include a guided visit to the Huron-Wendat longhouse at the Huron Traditional Site. This addition will see Intrepid reach its goal of an Indigenous-led experience on 75 percent of their Canada itineraries—a significant milestone on the road to integrating Indigenous-led experiences across every Canada trip. “When it comes to Indigenous tourism in Canada, we only take up five percent of tourism and that’s such a small percentage,” says Campo, as we stand before the lovely Lost Lake with its mountainous backdrop. “So this partnership with Intrepid and other Indigenous companies throughout Turtle Island—these are the partners I wanna work with.” As she distributes traditional ‘hush’ tea made with soothing raspberry leaf, refreshing mint sweet licorice root and vibrant rose hips, we talk of the importance of stories. “When it comes to a lot of Indigenous history and our government, they try to write our story for us,” she says. “We’re redirecting that chapter so we can write and share our stories ourselves.” The writer was hosted by Intrepid Travel **** Adventure.com strives to be a low-emissions travel publication. We are powered by, but editorially independent of, Intrepid Travel, the world’s largest travel B Corp, who help ensure Adventure.com maintains high standards of sustainability in our work and activities. You can visit our sustainability page or read our Contributor Impact Guidelines for more information. Journalist and wanderluster Charmaine Noronha is a travel writer with a penchant for adventure, culture and chocolate. She started her career as a reporter with The Toronto Star before becoming the EIC of Vervegirl Magazine for five years then reported on Canadian news for The Associated Press for 11 years. Most recently, she was a Lifestyle reporter/editor at HuffPost Canada.

item.title: It’s Spider Season. Read This Before You Get a Big Faceful of Web.
item.description:
Source: Backpacker Magazine Score: 5.48
An Apache jumping spider in Golden, Colorado (Photo: Adam Roy) I was running on my local trail system one warm September morning when something caught my eye. On the concrete wall of a pedestrian overpass sat a large spider, legs stretched out from its glossy black body. It was probably an inch and a half across from the tip of its back legs to its front. I recognized it without even having to see the red hourglass on its stomach: a mature female western black widow. It was the latest of about a half-dozen widows I had spotted in the two weeks prior—more than I had seen in the rest of the year leading up to it. Across the U.S. and the rest of the Northern Hemisphere, it’s spider season—the time of year around late summer and early fall when arachnids suddenly seem to be everywhere. For hikers, the change is especially notable: You may have noticed wolf spiders scuttling across the forest floor or picked silk out of your hair after walking face-first one of the many webs festooning the trail. What’s behind the boom? In a word: love. Or sex, anyway. “At this time of the summer in Colorado, that’s when the males start wandering and looking for females,” says Jackie Billotte, a research associate at Westminster, Colorado’s Butterfly Pavilion and PhD candidate at Colorado State University. “Mating becomes the primary goal. So, you’re just bound to run into males that are out looking for a good time, for lack of a better term.” According to Billotte, there aren’t actually more spiders during spider season: Arachnid populations stay fairly steady year-round, with hatchlings of some species overwintering in their egg sacs. It’s just that for most of the year, we don’t notice our eight-legged neighbors. Spiders, by their nature, don’t spend a lot of time in the open. Most are ambush predators: They either stay in their webs or hunt within a very small range. When males go through their final molt and reach sexual maturity, however, their priorities change. After charging up their palpal bulbs—two swollen reproductive organs mounted on their pedipalps, near their faces—with sperm, they go on the hunt for a partner, prioritizing their reproductive urges over food and safety. Once they’ve found and coupled with a female, the males of some species, like black widows, will damage her web to prevent rival males from accessing her. After that, their time on earth is limited: While female spiders may survive a few years—and some, like tarantulas, can hang on for decades—Billotte notes that the mature males of most North American species will either end up as prey or succumb to cold temperatures. Others may even end up as food for their mate. “The Tinder scene for spiders is a little rough,” says Billotte. “The term is sexual cannibalism, and it’s exactly what it sounds like. It’s not an all-the-time thing, and it varies by species…but it does happen, and it makes sense evolutionarily because it’s a free meal.” We’re also more likely to notice both male and female spiders in late summer and early fall just because they’ve had more time to grow. Newly-hatched spiderlings tend to be tiny—sometimes nearly invisible to people. By September, however, they’ve bulked up, aided by access to plentiful food and good weather. “During the summer, they have more prey availability,” Billotte says. “It’s warmer, so their metabolisms are up, so they can grow faster. It’s just a good condition for them, and that’s when the males are going to go through that last growth spurt. We’ve established that by the beginning of fall, spiders are giant and horny. But that doesn’t mean hikers need to be worried about them. Billotte says that spider bites are far rarer than most people think. (‘People’ includes physicians: One 2016 study in the journal Toxicon concluded that nearly 80 percent of spider bite diagnoses by physicians may be wrong.) While almost all spiders have venom, their bites evolved to capture prey, not harm people. Venom is metabolically expensive to produce: Spiders spend a lot of energy to make it, and can’t afford to waste it, so they generally only bite as a last resort to avoid being crushed. Confronted with a giant mammal thousands of times their size, they’ll usually freeze or run away instead. Here in Colorado, Billotte says, hikers are likely to run into wolf spiders, orb weavers, and roly-poly hunting woodlouse spiders, none of which have a venom powerful enough to harm a human. Even bites from North America’s two most potent varieties of spider, the recluses and black widows, rarely do real harm. While Billotte says that hikers who are suffering serious pain or swelling, nausea, or other symptoms after a bite should go see a doctor, she notes that most bites resolve on their own without treatment. (According to data from America’s Poison Control Centers, there has not been a death from a confirmed black widow bite in the United States since 1983.) “I would never tell anyone if you get bit and it’s getting red and angry, don’t go to the doctor,” Billotte says. “But are you immediately going to die? No, probably not.” While it may not feel like it to the spider-averse, getting to see North America’s roughly 4,000 species of spiders hunting, courting, and mating in their natural habitat is an opportunity that Billotte says she hopes hikers of all ages can learn to enjoy. “I had the privilege to get taken out as a kid and go hiking and camping,” she says. “I had parents that encouraged me to investigate when I was out there, and that became my job.So, you never know. Your kid could be some weird girl…that’s obsessed with bugs, like all of us are.”

item.title: Forget the Camino: Europe’s Newest 191-Mile Thru-Hike Features Wilderness Wine Bars and Zero Crowds
item.description:
Source: Backpacker Magazine Score: 4.16
Logar Valley (Photo: Mediaspeed, foto: Jan Godec) The trail passes through the 3,000-foot-high Logar Valley cinematic as a Peter Jackson sequence: Gnarled apple trees and wildflowers line long, narrow fields of bright green grass, and forests of knobby conifers sweep toward a horizon of snow-capped peaks. Historic stone and plaster homes with low-slung shake roofs huddle near the woodline. The path follows the upper Savinja River, which flows clear and aquamarine over a bed of off-white rock. It passes into silvery linden and elm forests as the valley narrows. A tiny, log cabin-style pub offering wild-fermented wines, žganje (berry liquors), and Carniolan sausage plates overlooks the entry to the cirque. Stairs climb toward a high, bowled ridge. The sound of crashing water echoes off stone. Another bend and Rinka Waterfall erupts from a notch in the sheer cliffside, plunging 300 feet into a bright blue pool. Trekkers can admire the action from the deck of a cantilevered, hike-in bar and café that clings to an escarpment about halfway up the falls, or walk another half-mile to take in the view from an alpine meadow where villagers once summered sheep. A Scandinavian-style mountaintop lodge operated by the Alpine Association of Slovenia offers cheap and comparatively luxe overnight accommodations for thru-hikers. The walk and stay are part of the nation’s newly designated Kamnik-Savinja Alps Water Trail (KSAWT). The 191-mile route connects numerous preexisting paths in a loop that showcases the aquatic resources of Slovenia’s second largest mountain range. The trek is divided into 11 stages that link more than a dozen historic villages and towns, and features three lakes, four rivers, numerous waterfalls, and more than 200 springs and streams. “The international backpacking community has started to call Slovenia Europe’s hidden gem,” says hiking enthusiast and Trail Angel Central (TAC) founder, Scott Vanderlip. The retired software engineer and serial entrepreneur operates a seasonal hiker camp on the Pacific Crest Trail. He’s traveled the world to connect with trekking communities for the TAC and logged miles on many of Europe’s most notable long routes—including the new water trail. “To me, Slovenia is a treasure trove for long-distance backpackers,” says Vanderlip. Particularly those who prefer their alpine views with a hardy side of cultural history and traditional foods, yet want to avoid big crowds. Europe’s most popular long trail, the Camino de Santiago, attracts more than 530,000 thru-hikers a year. The Alpine Association of Slovenia, meanwhile, says just 10,350 people have completed the nation’s cross-country Mountain Trail since it was founded in 1953. What’s more, Slovenia—which borders Northern Italy to the west and Austria to the north—is about the size of Massachusetts and home to some 6,200 miles of hiking trails. That gives its 1.7 million annual trekker tourists plenty of room to space out. The notoriously tough Mountain Trail features more than 23 miles of cumulative elevation gain and 14 peaks above 7,000 feet. The KSAWT, however, is a more laid back adventure. Stages average 10.6 miles a day, inviting hikers to soak in the views and indulge in picturesque swimming holes. The route climbs to high points like the overlook above Rinka Waterfall, but forgoes tough-to-reach peaks like 8,392-foot Grintovec in favor of more accessible alpine valleys, meadows, and the banks of the pristine waterways that flow through them. Mountain huts and lodges pepper the route with affordable places to sleep. Electric shuttle vans patrol nearby roads and make it easy to slackpack to and from amenity-packed stopovers like the Medieval fortress town of Kamnik. Points of aquatic interest like Lake Črnava—which is backed by a 16th century castle and bowl of 7,000-foot peaks—are showstoppers. But the trail was actually inspired by less visible resources. The loop was the outgrowth of a 2022 project to map and raise awareness around the region’s abundant springs. Local stakeholders and conservation groups joined forces with the Slovenian Tourist Board and European Union Common Agricultural Policy Network to map and analyze the most productive natural founts. The group identified fifty-four pristine watering holes, including carbonated iron and mineral springs. Infrastructure like hardened treads, stone headwalls, spring boxes, and outflow pipes were added to both invite and protect sites from hiker visits. Annual drinking water festivals were organized to showcase the aquatic wealth and how it influences local products like wine, beer and spirits. “Then we thought, why not connect these amazing resources in a network that provides a very different kind of experience than your usual mountaineering trail,” says Slovenian Tourist Board spokesperson, Maša Puklavec Polutnik. The KSAWT linked trails to the 54 springs and some of the most scenic portions of the waterways they feed into in 2023. Signage provides insight into their geology and historic importance. “These mountains have acted like a natural water tower that supplies clean, potable water to settlements and villages for millennia,” says Polutnik. Hikers are encouraged to challenge their palates and try to distinguish the subtle differences between springs. They can then compare their own observations to scientific breakdowns with exact mineral compositions and taste-notes for each. “It’s a really cool side quest to do as you’re passing through these astoundingly beautiful and historic areas—and unlike anything that I’m aware of in the U.S.,” says Vanderlip. He encourages trekkers to up the culinary ante by immersing themselves in local foodways. “Every town and village you pass through has its own version of popular regional dishes and drinks,” says Vanderlip. “And they all take deep pride in those differences and traditions.” Wines, for instance, feature unique and often much older grape varietals compared to those typically found in western Europe and the U.S. That and ancient techniques like whole-cluster fermentation (where the stems are left on) or the use of native yeasts brings wildly different flavors than your typical chardonnay or merlot. Pair them with traditional cured meats like zgornjesavinjski želodec—a mix of fresh pork leg and shoulder meat, cubed bacon, sea salt, pepper, and garlic water that’s pressed flat during curing—and iconic cheeses like Trnič, which shepherds on the high-elevation Velika Planina plateau craft from cottage cheese, cream, and salt. “There’s just so much to love,” says Vanderlip. “On one hand, the hiking is world-class and filled with scenery that would more than justify a visit without any of the other perks.” But when you factor in refreshing spring water, historic villages, delicious eats, and nifty cultural traditions? That elevates the KSAWT to a bucket list walk.

item.title: Dale ‘Grey Beard’ Sanders Fell 71 Times and Quit Once Before Setting His Latest Appalachian Trail Record
item.description:
Source: Backpacker Magazine Score: 3.42
Dale "Grey Beard" Sanders on his 2026 thru-hike of the Appalachian Trail. (Photo: Courtesy of Dale Sanders) Dale ‘Grey Beard’ Sanders, 91, was about two tenths of a mile from the top of Mount Katahdin when he took a hard fall. Just steps away from becoming the oldest person to thru-hike the Appalachian Trail in a calendar year, he hit the ground for the 71st time on his 12-month journey. Two days later, he told Backpacker, “I’m a little sore on both legs from that, but it’s simply just small contusions and no bones or anything is broken or damaged.” Out of the 71 falls that Sanders took, the vast majority were “soft falls,” which meant that he quickly got up, brushed himself off and kept walking without pain. But seven of those falls left him in a daze. “I laid down on the ground, and I didn’t care who saw me,” he said. “I was all moaning and groaning for a while.” Sanders says his balance was noticeably worse than in 2017, when he had set a previous Appalachian Trail age record by hiking the trail at 82. “When you get older, it seems that our body starts to deteriorate, and we simply do not physically have the abilities that we had when we were under 40 and below,” Sanders said. “The older you get past say 50 or 60, it starts going down.” In order to claim the age record for a thru-hike of the Appalachian Trail, hikers have to tackle the whole 2,200-mile trail within a 12-month period. They must also hike past every white blaze (“in some cases, crawl by,” said Sanders, alluding to his experience on Mount Katahdin). Neither the Appalachian Trail Conservancy (ATC) nor Guinness currently differentiate between supported, self-supported, and unsupported age records on the trail. Prior to Sanders’ record, M.J. ‘Nimblewill’ Eberhart last claimed the title at age 83 in 2021, taking the record from Sanders. To Sanders’s knowledge, no other 90-year-old has attempted to thru-hike the Appalachian Trail. Compared to his 2017 thru-hike, Sanders had to significantly dial down his mileage. As an 82 year old, he hiked many 20-mile days, but averaged closer to 11 miles per day this year. It was also tough on his mind, which occasionally wavered at the sight of a steep climb. While he trained for six months before setting out on his latest thru-hike, he still underestimated the difficulty of the Appalachian Trail. “I realized quickly that my ceiling of physical ability was much lower than it was at 82 years old,” he said. Most AT thru-hikers blaze through the route, tackling it in four to six months. Sanders nearly took the entire 365 days to complete his trek, hiking for 200 of those days. On one occasion, he even quit the trail. He was in Maine when it happened: A hard fall 142 miles short of the northern terminus landed him in the hospital, where doctors checked for internal bleeding and ran tests to see why he was experiencing numbness in his left arm. One doctor suggested that it was time to hang up his hiking poles to head home and talk to his primary care physician and neurologist. “I didn’t want to go home because it was so close to the end,” he reflected. But after receiving a call about his mother-in-law’s death, his fate was decided: He was going home to Tennessee. After attending the funeral, resting, and scheduling new doctor’s appointments, his neurologist determined that Sanders had experienced bleeding in his brain, but it wasn’t active and it appeared to be old. His numb arm was due to a pinched nerve. Both that doctor and his primary care provider cleared him to hike. Given the short window of time that Sanders had to finish the final stretch of trail, he knew it was unlikely that he’d finish before time ran out. But he decided he wanted to see Katahdin, even if it meant he’d only land the age record for a section hike instead of a thru-hike. With a bit of luck and sheer determination, Sanders ultimately made it to the northern terminus of the Appalachian Trail with 5 days to spare. When asked why he was so determined to get back on trail, Sanders explained that the record felt bigger than he was. “I hold several age records in several different venues, most of them hiking and paddling, and in each and every one of those, it seems that I’ve given people hope. [It’s when] people have hope that they have inspiration,” he said. “Hope is really important.”

item.title: Plastic Is Poisoning the Earth—So This Designer Made a Backpacking Kit Without It
item.description:
Source: Backpacker Magazine Score: 3.35
Transcript My name’s Tom Bonamici, I’m an assistant professor of product design at the University of Oregon , and I teach in general product design for undergraduates and also our master’s program in sports product design. So, my research is about lightweight backcountry travel, and I am particularly interested in backpacking, been doing it since I was a kid, and I’m also really interested as an Oregonian in sustainability issues. As we all know, backpacking is just rife with synthetic materials, and they’re really awesome. They’re super lightweight and waterproof and strong and badass, and they’re also made out of petrochemicals, which, you know, on the in end is a problem, on the out end it’s a problem. I was just curious to explore academically what it would mean to use a full backpacking kit without any petrochemicals at all, not to say that everyone should, but just to explore what compromises we’d make if we did that. And going in, I kind of anticipated it was going to be heavier, it was going to not perform as well, it might be weaker, but how cool to make a collection that could actually completely compost. I thought that would just be an interesting experiment and exploration. I think to start with, we can start with the backpack because we’re backpacking, and that’s one of the more more fun things to talk about. Generally throughout this collection, certainly with this backpack, I was using pretty normal ultralight backpacking designs and just adapting materials to be completely petrochemical free. So, this is a really kind of standard issue frameless lightweight backpacking pack. There’s no suspension at all. The sleeping pad forms the back panel and adds some rigidity when it’s all packed together. You know, we’ve got the normal big side pockets, the big back pocket, thick shoulder straps. I keep my pack light enough that I don’t typically use a waist strap, but I could certainly have added one. But the materials are what makes this compostable. So, I used a Ventile material. It’s basically a super strong, densely woven cotton material, and this one especially is ripstop. Same thing for the side pockets, it’s a Ventile, but a much lighter weight version. We’ve got cotton cord forming the drawstring in those side pockets and aluminum toggles with a metal spring, so that’s all plastic free. The back pocket is a stretch 100 percent Merino jersey, and we’ve got some more metal hardware holding that in place, another metal hook for the top closure. And the shoulder straps are lined with that same Merino jersey, Ventile on the outside, cotton webbing, and then I used a thick Merino felt as the padding for that back strap. And it’s a little on the stiff side. The more it gets used, the more it’s going to kind of conform. Felt is really good at that. But the challenge throughout this whole collection, and especially in something like a pack that needs to be really strong, is the thread. So, I used 100 percent cotton thread. This is kind of a super heavy-duty thread that is meant for sewing on buttons, for like a fancy suit coat. I ended up with a lot of formal wear overlaps with the materials I was using here. So, the thread I think is pretty strong, but it’s, you know, I can break it if I really yank on it, this very heavy-duty thread. And that’s not a great sign because with a synthetic, you know, typically backpacking packs are sewn with polyester thread, and I can’t break that, you know, like a Tex 80, Tex 100 thread. So, that’s a pretty heavy gauge. And this stuff I can totally break. So, I did adapt by, you know, sewing several times over some seams. If you sew too many times, you’re just going to over-perforate a fabric, and then it can tear like a check out of a checkbook. But we’ll just see how it goes. As as throughout the whole collection, it’s an experiment. But I’m quite excited about the pack. And again, I wasn’t getting weird with the design of it, just with the materials. For the sleeping bag, I did a sleeping quilt. This is the same quilt design that I’ve done in the past with synthetic materials, which is super light and super comfortable. I use my homemade quilt all the time. It’s the kind of usual idea where you have a somewhat tapered rectangle, and then it forms a footbox, and you can kind of tie up that footbox and cinch it at the bottom, and it works great. Instead of a zipper, although I could use a cotton taped, metal-toothed zipper, I just went ahead and used some little ties because I’ve done quilts with zippers in the footbox and I’ve also done quilts with just snaps across, and they both work just fine. This is for summer backpacking, so I don’t need like full Arctic enclosure. The shell material is a silk-cotton blend. This is meant for the lining material of a formal suit. So, again, one of those like formal wear overlaps with this collection. Cotton tape and cotton cord for the ties and the draw cord, and cotton thread. And then the material on the inside is a wool material. It’s called Lavalan, and it’s this puffy wool batting. Got a scrap here. That’s kind of very, very cleaned from how wool comes off the sheep, and then kind of spun and matted into this lighter weight and fluffy material. It’s really nice, it’s really warm. I used kind of a layer and a half. This is their almost heaviest weight and then I used a little bit more very lightweight quilt batting in there that was Merino quilt batting. This material is nice because it’s a little bit more resilient than some of the synthetic options. It is heavier. This quilt weighs a little under 2 pounds, and my homemade quilt weighs a little over 1 pound. So, it’s definitely heavier, but I think it’s going to be plenty warm. The feeling of that fabric is so nice, and totally compostable as with everything else. So, I’m excited about this one. It’s quite bulky. That’s one of the downsides of using the wool instead of a synthetic and certainly a down. But it actually compresses pretty well once you jam it into the backpack, then it holds its form, and it’s actually kind of nice when you’re backpacking with a frameless pack to let the pack be full because then you don’t have any flopping or shifting. You might wonder why didn’t I use down? Because down is natural. When you make something with down, it needs to use downproof fabric. And typically what that is is a really, really lightweight synthetic material that’s calendared. So, calendering means that you’re taking that material and putting it through these heated rollers, and it’s almost melting it, but it’s just like smushing the the yarns of that woven textile together and closing up all of the gaps in between the warp and the weft fibers, bringing those gaps together. And that means that those little stems on the down puffs can’t work their way through and pop out like they do on your pillows at home. So, there are there are certainly natural materials that could fit the bill. In fact, the Ventile materials that I used are probably dense enough to be downproof or like functionally downproof. And there are some upholstery materials that are all cotton that are meant to be downproof. But they’re super heavy. So, it would end up tripling maybe the weight of the of the quilt and adding to the bulk, too. One of the hardest challenges in this whole collection was doing a sleeping pad . And this is the one, the sleeping pad and the shoes, man, are just, that’s that’s the tough one. So, this, I know this is just kind of a punishing sleeping pad. It’s super narrow. It is full length, and I’m 6’2″, so it’s nice to have, you know, enough length. And it’s so flat. It’s not providing any cushion at all. This is just a thermal break. But I wanted a sleeping pad that could function as a back panel in the backpack, and I needed that thermal break. If you’ve ever had a inflatable pad that deflated during the night, we all know that the ground is just so cold. Imade this with, again, some of that Ventile material, the super lightweight, and then a really thin layer of cork, which is not going to hold up long term, I know it, because it kind of crumbles. And that’s sandwiched in with some Melton wool. And Melton wool is a a very dense, almost felted thick woven wool material. Sometimes it’s made with a Merino, usually it’s more of a strong wool because it’s just felted in so much, you don’t need that softness and kind of luxurious hand of Merino. And then the whole thing is bound with cotton twill tape and, again, cotton thread. And then I sewed across in some channels just to try to hold that cork into place long term. This is something where, as I said, the collection is about exploring compromises, and it’s a big compromise in comfort. I was backpacking last weekend and just loving my big plush, Big Agnes pad, you know, just like sprawled out on that and sleeping like a baby. And this isn’t going to be like that. It’s also heavy. This is just under 2 pounds, which is pretty painful because that’s well over double a Z Lite. So, if I’m going to be less comfortable, I’d rather have a Z Lite. But, you know, that’s just straight petrochemicals, so it didn’t work for this project. So, again, the the collection was about exploring compromises, and I’ve definitely found some compromise area with the sleeping pad. And that’s okay. I did look into whether or not it’d be possible to do inflatable natural pads and also just like thicker, squishier materials, you know, wool felt. I looked into kapok, which is this kind of tree seed pod husk material that was used for insulation and also for life jacket flotation before petrochemicals. It’s not as good as foam for a life jacket, so don’t get any ideas. And all this is possible. Like with natural latex rubber, it would theoretically be possible to make an inflatable pad, but roughly running the numbers, it would be much, much heavier than this, like 5 to 8 pounds for just the pad. They were available, you know, you look in old Abercrombie & Fitch catalogs from the early 1900s, and they had inflatable pads, and they weighed 10 to 15 pounds. So, you know, if you’re horse packing, maybe that’s a good option, but for the purpose of this project, again, I was trying to keep everything as light as possible. For trekking poles, I knew I wanted to use trekking poles, and I need them for my 40-year-old knees, and also to set up the tarp. And I looked into making them out of aluminum because metal was allowed in the confines of this project, but to make them extendable, adjustable, I think it could be done. You know, if I were a really amazing machinist, I’m sure I could make all those parts out of aluminum and have it be fine. I’m not an amazing machinist, and I didn’t want to use those plastic adjusters, which are so great and so good at what they do, but again, for the confines of this project, I wanted to keep it original. So, I ended up using Calcutta bamboo. And this is a species of bamboo that’s insanely strong. It’s still used for ski poles and for fishing gaffs, that’s the like big hook that you use to yank that 200-pound tuna in the boat. It’s way stronger in flexion than aluminum, which is pretty sweet, and not too heavy at all. It has a really thick wall. So, this is a little chunk of it, and it’s got this thicker, denser wall, and it’s just a lot tougher than normal bamboo. And then in Slovenia, of all places, I found a ski pole DIY supply house. With the tariffs, I paid a phenomenal amount of money to get these ferrules, which are meant to be used with bamboo poles. So, these are all aluminum with a carbide tip, just like a normal trekking pole. So, we’ve got a really durable way to hit the ground. I used a suede grip. I made a wrist strap, adjustable with an aluminum buckle, Merino wool lining, Ventile outer shell. And then I even found some I put in a brass threaded insert in the top of the pole and a really nice bolt to hold the whole thing in place. So, it’s super comfortable, it’s super strong, I think stronger than my carbon fiber poles, which I’ve broken, just crossing a river and I don’t think these are going to have that issue at all. And then in order to avoid, you know, I didn’t want this project to look too hippy-dippy or Ren Faire or like, you know, Civil War reenactor or anything, so while the bamboo is beautiful naturally, I just coated the whole thing in some ink, some Sumi calligraphy ink. I had that for woodworking marking, and it applied beautifully. I had to just sand the outside of the bamboo to remove that natural waxy finish, and then the ink went on, and it’s staying on, and it doesn’t rub off or anything. So, these poles I think are going to be maybe the the strongest part of this collection, like physically strongest. I think a lot of the textiles have to be a little bit weaker, mostly because of using a natural thread, but these poles are going to be stronger than the aluminum or carbon fiber equivalents that are at REI. I’d say the only bummer or compromise about these is that they’re not height adjustable. No problem to just make them appropriate for my height for use, but I wouldn’t then be able to adjust it even taller to use with a a tent, for instance. And it’s possible to lash two poles together, but it’s a lot easier with like a Voile strap, or something, you know, synthetic. So, it’s it’s just interesting how the the confines of this project, the rules of the project, just put a lot of constraints on the decision making all throughout. For the tent or shelter, I did a tarp, and I usually sleep under a tarp when I’m backpacking, and they work great. I live in the West, and am blessed to have pretty predictable stretches of good weather and fewer bugs. For the situation we get to backpack in out West, it’s nice to not need to worry about the bugs so much. So, I did this very lightweight tarp design. Again, it’s very similar to tarps that I’ve made in the past. So, it’s basically a 9-foot long tarp, and it’s, you know, catenary-cut curves so that the tension is really even on the seams and on the sides, and tensioning lines, and I use trekking poles to set it up. The difference about this tarp, being petrochemical free, is that it’s made out of oiled silk. And this is a really unusual material nowadays. I found a lot of references to it in literature from over 100 years ago, but almost nothing since then. And that’s probably because synthetics are a lot stronger and a lot more predictably waterproof, and that’s okay. But given the confines of the project, I needed to find something lightweight and waterproof enough. So, this is waterproof enough. I haven’t done a hydrostatic head test on it, but I can fill up a embroidery frame with this material on it with water, and it doesn’t drip through even over 24 hours. And, you know, with a rough garden hose test, it’s managed to just kind of bead that water off really, really nicely. What is oiled silk? It is a silk taffeta, so it’s a really, really lightweight almost a ballgown type material, and then I soak it in a blend of linseed oil and natural turpentine. Turpentine is basically distilled pine tar or pine sap. You distill it like you would distill whiskey and you end up with turpentine. That’s the same stuff that artists use to cut their paints. And I use the turpentine to cut down the linseed oil so that it can flow through the fabric more easily and that I can wring it out more easily. If there’s too much in there, it’ll end up getting really sticky and like, yeah, too too sticky and gross. Ugh. But with with the right blend and the right amount of kind of wringing out and careful drying, I can get it to where it’s this really nice, predictable hand and waterproof enough without being too sticky. You can see that it’s yellowed, and some of my older samples have yellowed a lot more. This is a kind of interesting anecdote because what we read about as oilskins, that’s what fishermen wore, like in Captains Courageous or something, you know, those books from 150 years ago about people fishing in the North Sea, they’re all wearing oilskins. Oilskins are basically a canvas smock soaked in linseed oil. And as it ages and oxidizes, it turns yellow, and that’s why Paddington Bear and, you know, all those traditional raincoats are yellow, because it’s kind of an inheritance from the oilskin. Kind of an interesting detail. When I first made this tarp, it was this like just ivory off-white, and that was 2 months, 3 months ago, and it’s already turned started to turn yellow, and the older it gets, the more yellow it’s going to get. So, I did use some reinforcements at important areas, like the the main seam attachment point of the tarp. I used a kind of a Ventile patch in some areas and just a self-fabric patch in other areas. I used cotton tape to reinforce those attachment points. I did a lot of kind of repetitive straight stitching, but again, not too close together, so it doesn’t get perforated and just rip out. We’ll see how this holds up. This is not nearly as strong as synthetics, but this is one where I’m pleased to say it’s actually lighter weight. I used, due to the width of the fabric, this tarp is even a little bit smaller than the one I usually use, that’s sil- sil-coated polyester. And this is this is 440 grams, so that’s just under a pound. It’s like about, I don’t know, 14 ounces or something, the the weights that we expect out of ultralight shelters.

item.title: Three Hikers Used AI to Plan Their Mount Shasta Climb—and Ended Up Needing Rescue
item.description:
Source: Backpacker Magazine Score: 2.75
Mt. Shasta (Photo: Mimi Ditchie Photography via Getty) In what rescuers called a “mentally challenging” operation, a team of three young climbers safely descended Mt. Shasta over the weekend after spending an unplanned night on the peak with no warm sleep systems or shelter. The group had hunkered down off trail in a potentially dangerous location after running out of food and water—and rescuers say their reliance on an AI chatbot to plan some aspects of their trip contributed to their ordeal. From going too light on food and water to camping in a prohibited location, virtually on top of a mountain headspring, rangers said the three college students came ill-prepared to meet the challenges of the mountain. “These were smart guys,” said Nick Meyers, program manager for the Forest Service’s Mt. Shasta climbing rangers and avalanche center. “But they just missed the mark. It led to spending all day, all night, and all day again walking up and down off the mountain.” The three men, college students in their early 20s, arrived at the Clear Creek Trailhead to climb 14,179-foot Mt. Shasta on Saturday, August 29. They ascended that night to a well-known base camp area at 8,600 feet, arriving around 8 p.m. The next morning, they launched their summit bid with an alpine start at 3 a.m. They advanced very slowly. Ten hours later, they had managed to ascend another 2,600 feet, covering only about one mile. The summit of Mt. Shasta was still another 3,000 feet up and well over a mile ahead. While their slow pace didn’t signal any specific problem, it was becoming a downstream hazard, because their AI-assisted food and water planning had only fueled them for an 8-hour round trip. “We don’t know why they were as slow as they were,” Meyers said, noting that the group did have a conversation at this point about whether to turn around. By 3 p.m., they had reached a distinctive waypoint at 12,800 feet called Mushroom Rock. According to rangers, the group again debated going up or down, consulting two other parties. One said up, one said down. At 7 p.m., they finally summited Mt. Shasta, 16 hours after they had departed base camp. The climbers turned around quickly, reaching Mushroom Rock again by 8, but ran into another problem right away: the phone they had been using to navigate via AllTrails was dead, and the portable charger they’d brought along refused to charge it back up. The men dialed 911, asking for directions. But they mis-navigated nonetheless, wandering significantly off route to the south. After several more hours, they had proceeded in the dark over a neighboring ridgeline into Mud Creek Canyon, an area with dangerously loose rock where there is no established route up or down the mountain. The group had already called rescuers again to report hypothermia and a knee injury when one of them slipped after dark with no headlamp on. “One thing was leading to another on these calls, and we knew they needed help,” Meyers said. Teams reached the group the next morning, Aug. 31, after an exposed bivy near 11,000 feet. A helicopter rescue—often the standard on the steep, uneven and rocky terrain above treeline on Shasta—was unfeasible due to the location. “They were exhausted, but we had to hike them out,” Meyers said. He added that their condition was less than desperate: They had avoided serious hypothermia, and the injured party member was ambulatory. After some food, water, and a pep talk, all three walked down under their own power. Passing their campsite, rangers found the group’s tent pitched damagingly close to the headspring of Clear Creek, among scattered food wrappers and cookware. They reached Clear Creek Trailhead at 6:30 p.m, concluding the planned 8-hour trip after 39.5 hours. Meyers attributed the incident to lapses of information and mentorship. The group said they knew about the robust Mt. Shasta information website, shastaavalanche.org, but didn’t use it to prepare. They also had suitable gear—a solid tent, headlamps, and snow travel equipment, as well as summit passes—but lacked other equipment that would have supported their plan, like a reliable charging system for their phone or a backup method of navigation.. “Our objective is always to give people information,” Meyers said. “We don’t try to influence what people do, but instead give them the knowledge and resources they need to make good decisions in the mountains. “We know people are going to use AI to prepare themselves, and it’s happening more and more – especially with educated young people. But there’s no excuse for ignoring the information when it’s freely available. We just try to encourage everyone to talk to a real person first. We’re here to help.”

item.title: An Ultralight Expert Shares What’s Worth Your Money Now—and What You Should Skip
item.description:
Source: Backpacker Magazine Score: 2.10
For five years, Nathan Pipenberg has covered ultralight gear for Backpacker, writing about everything from new fabrics to radical new concepts in backpack design. Alas, all good things must come to an end, and this month, Nate is leaving his post as chronicler of the lightest and brightest. For his final column, he took a look back at some of his favorite gear he’s covered, as well as a few things that missed the mark. Here, Nate wraps up half a decade of research by rounding up what lightweight gear he thinks is worth spending money on now, and what he thinks backpackers should skip. —Adam Roy, Editor-in-Chief I’m out on a quick evening hike tonight, and it’s a little bit of a bittersweet moment because tomorrow I’m writing my final installment of my ultralight column for Backpacker Magazine. I’m Nate Pipenberg, and I have been Backpacker Magazine‘s ultralight columnist for the past five years or so, and I’ve had a great time doing it. So with my final story coming up, you know, rather than attempting to wax poetic, which I don’t think anyone wants to hear, I figured I would return to every ultralighter’s favorite topic, which is, of course, gear. As a gear writer, I’ve had access to dozens, if not hundreds of products: you know, sleeping bags, pads, tents, backpacks, you name it, I’ve been able to test it. You know, I thought it would be fun to talk about some of my favorites, some of the stuff that, you know, if I was not a gear writer, the stuff that I would actually buy, the stuff that I love, that I use all the time, as well as the stuff that I would never spend my own money on. So when I get off trail and go back home, I’m going to sit down and walk you through some of my favorite pieces of gear. The first thing is a frameless backpack. Frameless packs have had their own innovations, and one is vest-style straps. This pack here doesn’t even have fully vest-style straps, they’re kind of more of a hybrid. But the important thing, at least for me, is that the bottom of the strap is a little bit wider than a traditional strap. With a pack like this, the load of your backpack really is spread across your back, your shoulders, and your chest, instead of just creating pressure points on your shoulders, and it’s just a far more comfortable way to carry a load without a hip belt. I love the kind of freedom of movement, you don’t feel constrained by having the hip belt around you, and if the load is light enough, I really think they are very comfortable to use. And while we’re on the subject of backpacks, one thing I definitely would not spend my money on is an Ultra backpack, a Dyneema backpack, or a Graphite backpack. The same actually goes for a Dyneema tent or any sort of stuff sack or accessory made with any of these kind of high-tech composite fabrics. These fabrics are billed as being super strong, but in my experience, most of them come with some sort of drawback or downside of their own. Some of them have a tendency to delaminate, and some of them, especially Dyneema tents, are so thin and lightweight that the super strong and durable characteristics of the fabric are kind of undercut by just how light and fragile the fabric is. In the case of a backpack, I’m a big fan of a simple ripstop or Robic nylon, which is the fabric used here on this Gossamer Gear Skala 38. In general, I’m not a big fan of expensive rain gear. I’m someone who, for years, used the $25 Frogg Toggs ultralight jacket, including on long thru-hikes, but recently, I found this jacket. It’s the Showers Pass Cloudburst, and even though it is $260 and 10 ounces, I’m actually a pretty big fan of it. You know, just saying those stats out loud, $260, 10 ounces, it’s not very cheap, it’s not even all that lightweight, but I still like it. And the main reason for that is that this is a stretchy rain jacket, which is not something that I’ve seen very often. Compared to your average ultralight rain shell, this thing is basically dead quiet, it’s super comfortable, and so far I’ve found it very breathable as well, which is always an important consideration for a rain jacket, especially if you’re using it in hot weather. I find myself pulling this out even if it’s dry out, just as another warm layer, and paired with, you know, something like an active insulation layer, which I’m going to get into next, this basically forms my ideal softshell jacket. Another thing I wouldn’t usually spend my money on is hiking-specific clothing. That might sound a little bit crazy, but in general, I think anything that’s made of nylon or polyester or wool is probably going to work out okay if you’re going on a hike. You know, gym shorts, running tops, wool sweaters, they all work great. If there was one specific item for hiking that I would buy, that would probably be either an Alpha Direct or TecnoWool hoodie or shirt. This is the TecnoWool crewneck from FarPointe Outdoor Gear, which is really just my absolute favorite active insulation layer. It’s almost like, you know, it’s really almost like magic, just how warm and breathable this thing is. Pairing something like this as your insulation layer with, you know, a wind shell, or in my case I bring this rain shell to cut wind, combined, those two work great to tackle all sorts of, you know, wet, rainy, windy conditions for a very, very low amount of weight. Another thing I would buy is a winter sleeping pad. This is the Therm-a-Rest NeoAir XTherm NXT. This is the one I would buy, and it’s pretty simple. There’s three good reasons why. The first is durability. Of all of the kind of mainstream popular inflatable pads, the XTherm has the most durable floor with a 70-denier nylon on there. That’s in comparison to a lot of 20, 30, and 40-denier options. The second is its warmth. This is with an R-value of 7.3, a very warm, four-season, winter-ready pad. And most importantly, the third reason I would buy a winter pad is because there’s really no good reason not to. You know, this XTherm might be two or three ounces heavier than the NeoAir XLite, or the Rab Ultrasphere 5.5, or the Exped Ultra 6.5R, but you know, it’s only a couple ounces heavier, and it has more durability to boot. Using a winter pad in the summer isn’t going to be too hot. The extra reflective insulation doesn’t really work that way in the summer, in my experience. Just buy one pad, buy a winter pad, you’ll save yourself, you know, the $200-$250 versus buying dedicated air pads for winter and summer use. And finally, the last thing that I think every ultralight backpacker should splurge on, if they have the means to do so, is a true summer-weight sleeping quilt. A summer quilt is incredibly light, they pack down so small, and once you’re used to the weight and the pack size and everything of a summer sleeping quilt, it is pretty hard to go back. The one I’ve got here is a fairly new quilt from Cumulus. This is called the Neo Quilt 150. This is basically the lightest one they offer. It really is amazing, you know, how much smaller and lighter your pack can be when you’re not lugging around a 15 or 20-degree sleeping bag. And it’s also really nice waking up and you’re not sweating in the middle of the night because you have way too much insulation on top of you. So yeah, those are a few of the pieces of gear that I’ve come to love after testing, you know, dozens, if not hundreds, of gear items over the past five years here at Backpacker, as well as a couple of my hot takes about what I don’t actually like all that much. Thanks for watching.

item.title: Hiking Norway's heavily monitored Russian border
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel Score: 5.47
Hiking Norway's heavily monitored Russian border A series of scenic paths trace the Norwegian-Russian border. But as you trek through the tundra and forests, you may notice watchtowers and cameras hanging in trees. I'm standing at a hillside clearing in the tundra along the Russian-Norwegian border, watching the Pasvik River ripple and writhe below. Maybe it's the rustle of birch leaves overhead or the buzzing sound of mosquitoes circling all around me, but I have an unshakeable feeling that I'm being watched. Then again, those hairs on the back of my neck could be triggered by the nearby military watchtower, and the fact that this public hiking trail is under constant surveillance. Located in the far reaches of north-eastern Norway on a jagged fjord close to where Finland, Russia and Norway meet, the small town of Kirkenes is best known among travellers as the final turnaround port for a number of small Arctic cruise lines. But increasingly, local operators are leaning into another opportunity: leading cruisers on wind-whipped treks along Nato's northernmost land border to the unfenced-but-heavily-monitored 198km-long line separating Norway and Russia. Here, surrounded by taiga forest, travellers can explore a network of public trails where cameras hang in the trees, watchtowers dot the horizon and military patrols ensure visitors are abiding by the periodic pillars (yellow for Norway, red for Russia) marking the international boundary between the two nations. Drawn by the prospect of exploring the Arctic's most closely watched frontiers, I've set out on a three-hour trek through a birch forest strewn with boggy puddles. The trail runs parallel to the Pasvik River for roughly 1km before it reaches the "border corridor": an 8m-wide (26ft) strip of cleared forest that's a veritable no-man's land where travellers can't go. From there, the trek culminates in a scramble up Russehøgda, a hillside overlooking the Storskog border crossing that is the only legal land border between the countries. But as we enter the forest, my guide, Henrik Hoffmann, switches off his mobile to avoid connecting to Russian data networks. He instinctively taps a satellite phone in his pocket, and I'm reminded that this is no ordinary walk in the woods. The lure of Russia's land border Hoffmann has been leading these border-trek trips since 2025 but relocated to Kirkenes in 2021, just before Russia's invasion of Ukraine a year later. Since then, he says that both Russia and Norway have increased security along their respective borders here. Now, seemingly minor offences, like throwing stones towards Russia, risk heavy fines and wandering beyond the marked international boundaries has resulted in detainments. Still, he says that after travelling along Norway's coastline, many passengers who arrive in Kirkenes on Hurtigruten and Havila cruises are eager to escape the confines of ships and shuttle buses and get an up-close look at where these two nations meet. "Many older travellers are particularly interested because they remember the Cold War and have followed relations between Europe and Russia over many decades," Hoffmann explains. "The hike allows them to experience the landscape for themselves while learning about the history and present-day realities of living beside Russia." More like this: While Kirkenes Tours is the newest operator to offer border excursions, it's not the first. Havila Voyages has been leading visitors to this area since 2000, while Hurtigruten told the BBC that its Norwegian Border tour – which also leads travellers through a WW2 atomic bomb shelter – recently became the most popular of its eight Kirkenes excursions. "Interest in the border has definitely increased over the past few years," says Hoffmann. Despite an initial reduction in tourism following Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022, he explained that understanding the border is now a driving motivator for those visiting Kirkenes.
