Be sure to pop your Champagne into the fridge for at least 4 hours before assembling to keep everything cold. And don’t skip the lemon twist: It perfumes this elegant cocktail as you sip. French 75 FAQ Isn’t a French 75 made with cognac? It can be. Gin is common in modern versions, including this recipe, but cognac does have historical precedent. Making the drink with gin gives the French 75 a crisper, more botanical flavor; using cognac makes one that tastes richer and more warming. Feel free to substitute cognac here for the gin in equal measure. Can I use prosecco instead of Champagne? Yes. Cava, prosecco, or another dry sparkling wine can stand in for Champagne. Look for a bottle labeled “brut” to keep the finished French 75 from becoming overly sweet. Read more about buying Champagne: What if my French 75 is too sweet? If you prefer a drier cocktail, reduce the simple syrup to ½ or ¼ oz. You can always add more to taste. Why is it called a French 75? The cocktail takes its name from the French 75-millimeter field gun used during World War I—a reference to the drink’s considerable kick. Its precise origins are debated, but, according to Chris Hannah, head bartender at Arnaud’s French 75 Bar in New Orleans, allied French and American military celebrated with cognac and Champagne, toasting the French 75 cannon for keeping them safe. Today, you’ll more often see the drink made with dry gin. Can I make French 75s ahead? Not entirely. It’s best to keep the Champagne chilled and sealed until you’re ready to serve, but you can mix the gin, lemon juice, and simple syrup up to 6 hours ahead. For 8 servings: Stir 1½ cups gin, ¾ cups fresh lemon juice, ¾ cups simple syrup, and ½ cup water (the water replaces the dilution caused by shaking) in a pitcher to combine. Chill until ready to use. To serve, pour 3½ oz. of your chilled gin mixture into a flute glass and top with 2 oz. Champagne as directed. Recipe information - Total Time 5 minutes - Yield Makes 1 Preparation - Step 1Combine 1½ oz. gin, ¾ oz. fresh lemon juice, and ¾ oz. simple syrup in a cocktail shaker. Fill shaker with ice, cover, and shake vigorously until outside of shaker is very cold, about 20 seconds. Step 2Strain cocktail through a Hawthorne strainer or a slotted spoon into a large flute. Top with 2 oz. Champagne and garnish with long spiral lemon twist. Editor’s note: This French 75 recipe was first published in our May 2016 issue; it has been updated for style. Head this way for more of our favorite gin drinks →

item.title: What Is Half-and-Half, Exactly?
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 5.52
Despite the promise of its name, the half-and-half you buy at the supermarket isn’t actually equal parts heavy cream and whole milk. While the dairy-aisle staple does fall somewhere between the two, and you can get away with substituting it for one part milk and one part cream in most cases, the truth is slightly more complex. By law, half-and-half must contain between 10.5% and 18% milkfat. Most commercial products land on the lower end of that spectrum, at around 11.5%. The result is dairy that’s richer and more luscious than whole milk, but more fluid than heavy cream. Whole milk, meanwhile, has a fat content of about 3.25%, and cream contains at least 36%. Mix the two in equal measure, and you’ll end up with something considerably richer than most store-bought half-and-half. For a closer substitute, combine two parts milk to one part cream (~14%) or three parts milk to one part cream (~11%). What about shelf-stable half-and-half? Your first interaction with half-and-half might have been those tiny cups that get tossed on the table at diners, fast food joints, and other less-than-fancy places. One or two of them does the trick to make even the cheapest, most burnt coffee taste better—or, at the very least, creamier. To keep these thimble-sized cups shelf-stable, manufacturers use ultra-high-temperature processing and may add stabilizers. Similar-looking cups labeled “creamer” may contain little to no actual dairy. What is fat-free half-and-half? Fat-free half-and-half is typically made from skim milk that’s been amended with thickeners and other stabilizers. While the cartons might look similar, the taste and texture aren’t quite the same (not creamy like melted ice cream, but creamy like melted shaving cream). Some manufacturers claim the cooking properties of their fat-free products are equal to those of regular half-and-half, but we generally don’t recommend swapping one for the other. How to cook with half-and-half Half-and-half is an ideal ingredient for soups, sauces, mashed potatoes, and custards when you want richness without the heft of heavy cream. Because it contains less fat, it’s more likely to curdle when added directly to high heat or acidic dishes (such as tomato sauce or lemon desserts). For added insurance, you can temper the cold half-and-half with some of the hot liquid, then add it back in. More often than not, though, you can add half-and-half straight to the saucepan, like in our creamy cauliflower soup, where the dairy is added to hot broth and vegetables and simmered before blending, or our coconut cream pie, where it’s added to reduced coconut milk and cooked. Half-and-half also works well in quiche and other egg bakes, chowders, panades for meatballs or meatloaf, and custardy desserts like our Caramelized Banana Pudding and panna cotta. How to store half-and-half Keep half-and-half refrigerated and generally follow the manufacturer’s guidance for how quickly to use it; recommendations vary by brand. Once opened, some cartons can last up to 10 days. Ultra-pasteurized dairy generally has a longer shelf life when unopened than conventionally pasteurized half-and-half. Unused half-and-half can be frozen for up to 2 months, but may separate upon thawing—shake well and blend into soups or mix into batters. You can also freeze half-and-half in an ice cube tray and add a few cubes straight to a pan sauce. What can you substitute for half-and-half? If you’re out of half-and-half, combine ¾ cup whole milk with ¼ cup heavy cream for a substitute similar to most supermarket half-and-half, or ⅔ cup whole milk with ⅓ cup heavy cream for a slightly richer version. Homemade half-and-half won’t behave exactly like the homogenized stuff you buy in stores and may separate a little. Just give it a shake or stir before adding it to your coffee, sauce, or stew. No heavy cream? Whole milk can stand in for half-and-half in many recipes, though the result will be less rich. For hot dishes, you can compensate by adding a few pats of butter. Going the other direction, heavy cream can generally replace half-and-half 1:1, though the result will be richer (you could also thin it somewhat with water, if desired). If dairy isn’t a requirement, a barista-style plant-based milk works well. Canned evaporated milk can also work in a pinch, but its richness falls somewhere between whole milk and half-and-half, and it has a cooked flavor that may not suit every application. And what if you have half-and-half but the recipe calls for milk or cream? Half-and-half can generally replace whole milk 1:1 in savory dishes like soups, sauces, and mashed potatoes; expect a richer result. It can also replace heavy cream when the cream is primarily there to add richness (like in chowder or custard), though the finished dish will be lighter. Just remember, unlike heavy cream, half-and-half doesn’t contain enough fat to whip, no matter how vigorously you agitate it. Editor’s note: This story was originally published in 2018; it has been updated for style with additional reporting by Anna Hezel and Joe Sevier.

item.title: Pommes Dauphine
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 5.05
Pommes dauphine (classic French potato puffs) are part of the vast lexicon of potato dishes rarely seen outside of the country. Think of the bite-size clouds as fried mashed potatoes, only lighter and more magical. Chef Alexia Duchêne of Le Chêne in New York City sticks to the traditional method, mixing equal parts pâte à choux with a purée of roasted potatoes. You’ll spoon the mixture into hot oil to create golden, crisp yet airy puffs. Serve as a chic appetizer or party snack paired with aioli or whatever dipping sauce your heart desires—or, in true French fashion, alongside a hearty steak or roast chicken as an impressive side. For more French classics, check out the following recipes: Bistro-Style Croque Monsieur; Poulet Rôti; Ratatouille; and Dover Sole Meunière. Ingredients 1 4 1 ⅔ 2–3 Special Equipment Need to make a substitution? Preparation - Step 1Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 350°. Sprinkle coarse salt over a rimmed baking sheet to cover (aim for a ¼"–½" thick layer). Nestle 1 lb. large Yukon Gold potatoes (2–3) into the salt and roast in oven until a knife pierces through flesh with little resistance, about 30 minutes. Step 2Remove from oven and, working quickly so potatoes remain hot, peel with a paring knife and halve. Pass potatoes through food mill into a medium bowl; set aside. Step 3Bring 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ⅔ cup water to a simmer in a medium saucepan over high heat, stirring with a stiff heatproof spatula or sturdy rubber spatula to help melt butter and dissolve salt. Immediately reduce heat to medium; add ⅔ cup all-purpose flour all at once and stir quickly until most of the flour is absorbed. Cook, stirring vigorously and breaking up pockets of flour as needed, until a thin film forms on bottom and sides of pan and dough comes together into a single mass, 2–3 minutes. (It should look glossy and feel buttery and smooth.) Remove from heat and let sit in pan until no longer hot but still warm, about 3 minutes. Step 4Add 2 large eggs to mixture one at a time, mixing until incorporated after each addition. Pâte à choux should be thick, glossy, and fall off spatula in a V-shape. If it’s too thick, stir in another 1 large egg. Add dough to reserved potatoes and stir to combine; season with kosher salt. Step 5Pour peanut oil into a medium Dutch oven or large heavy saucepan fitted with thermometer to come 3" up sides (about 8 cups). Heat over medium-high until thermometer registers 360°. Reduce heat to medium (you want to maintain the temperature). Using a spoon lightly coated in oil and working in batches of 6–8, spoon irregular amounts of batter into pot. Fry, turning often, until golden brown all over, about 4 minutes. Using a spider or slotted spoon, transfer to a rimmed baking sheet lined with paper towels to drain and immediately season with kosher salt. Repeat process with remaining batter, adjusting heat as needed to maintain temperature. Transfer pommes dauphine to a platter to serve.

item.title: Pumpkin Chili
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 4.95
This pumpkin chili gets an entire can of pumpkin purée—but you’d hardly know it. Rather than making the chili taste like pumpkin, the purée gives it velvety richness, body, and an autumnal hue. (Be sure to buy pure pumpkin purée, not pumpkin pie filling.) Best of all, it comes together on the stovetop in just 35 minutes, making it an easy weeknight dinner that’s equally at home on game day or Halloween. One unusual step makes this quick chili work: Instead of browning the ground beef separately, you’ll cook it directly in the spiced pumpkin mixture. This keeps the meat tender during the short cook time while a vigorous stir breaks it down into chunky, satisfying bits. Worcestershire sauce brings in plenty of savory depth. Top each bowl with sour cream, sliced jalapeño, and crunchy toasted pepitas. Pumpkin chili FAQ Can I use a different ground meat? Yes. Ground turkey and chicken both work well, but ground pork makes an especially rich, savory chili. Swap an equal amount of any of these for the beef and otherwise follow the recipe as written. Can I substitute butternut squash purée for pumpkin purée? Yes. Canned butternut squash or even sweet potato works well here—just make sure it’s 100% purée, not pie mix or otherwise sweetened. How should I store leftover pumpkin chili? Let leftover chili cool, then refrigerate it in an airtight container for up to 5 days or freeze it for up to 3 months. Reheat it gently on the stovetop or in the microwave, adding a splash of broth or water as needed to loosen it. Recipe information - Total Time 35 minutes - Yield 4 servings Ingredients 2 1 1 4 1 2 1½ 1 2 3 1 1 4 Need to make a substitution? Preparation - Step 1Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a medium Dutch oven or other heavy pot over medium-high. Add 1 onion, coarsely chopped, and 1 medium jalapeño, coarsely chopped; cook, stirring often, until slightly softened, 3–4 minutes. Step 2Add 4 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and cook, stirring often, until fragrant, about 1 minute. Add one 15-oz. can pumpkin purée, 2 tsp. smoked paprika, and 1½ tsp. ground cumin and cook, stirring often, until some of the liquid in purée has evaporated, 3–4 minutes. Step 3Add 1 lb. ground beef, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 2 Tbsp. Worcestershire sauce; season generously with freshly ground pepper. Cook, breaking up beef with a wooden spoon and stirring often, until meat is cooked through and incorporated into purée to create a thick paste, about 5 minutes. Step 4Add one 15-oz. can black beans, rinsed, one 15 oz. can pinto beans, rinsed, and 4 cups low-sodium chicken broth. Increase heat to high and bring to a boil. Reduce heat so mixture is at a simmer and cook, stirring occasionally, until thickened to the consistency of chili, 15–18 minutes. Stir in remaining 1 Tbsp. Worcestershire sauce. Step 5To serve, ladle chili into bowls and top each with a dollop of sour cream; scatter unsalted, roasted pumpkin seeds (pepitas) and thinly sliced jalapeños over.

item.title: Pommes Purée (French Mashed Potatoes)
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 4.56
Pommes purée is France’s answer to mashed potatoes. But instead of simply mashing the spuds, they get passed through a food mill and a tamis (a large fine-mesh drum) to make them as smooth as satin sheets. Think of them as the fancier, more luxe version of the comfort food classic. Here, chef Alexia Duchêne of Le Chêne in New York City, takes inspiration from chef Joël Robuchon’s famous version, adding a wealth of milk and butter to the potatoes for a truly decadent result. You can serve them as a comforting side next to roast chicken or seared steak, elevating any dinner into a bistro-worthy affair. For more French classics, check out the following recipes: Bistro-Style Croque Monsieur; Poulet Rôti; and Ratatouille. Ingredients 2 1 1 Special Equipment Need to make a substitution? Preparation - Step 1Place 2 lb. 4 oz. large Yukon gold potatoes (5–7) in a large pot and pour in water to cover by about 2". Season generously with kosher salt and bring to a boil. Cook until potatoes are fork-tender, 20–25 minutes. Step 2Meanwhile, heat 1 cup whole milk in a small saucepan over low heat and keep warm. Step 3Drain potatoes. Working quickly so they remain hot, peel potatoes with a paring knife and cut into pieces. Pass potatoes through food mill into a medium bowl, then pass through tamis onto a sheet of parchment paper, pressing with a heatproof rubber spatula. Step 4Transfer potato purée to a small pot or large saucepan and cook over medium-low heat, stirring constantly, until dried out a little and steaming, about 3 minutes. Gradually pour in warm milk, stirring constantly until smooth and spoonable (you might not need all of the milk). Remove from heat and add 1 cup (2 sticks) chilled unsalted butter, sliced, a few pieces at a time, whisking after each addition until melted and combined before adding more. Taste pommes purée and season with salt as needed.

item.title: Saucy Pork Chops With Coconut Crisp
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 4.52
If the only pork chops you’ve encountered are dry and leathery, give this recipe a try. Thick-cut pork chops are more forgiving of extended cook times and the generous pour of sauce makes up for any mistakes, should they occur. The buttery pan sauce takes a page from Chris Morocco’s Steak for One, gaining its silky texture from a bottle of oyster sauce. Anything with the word “premium” on the bottle is preferred for flavor, and avoid any oyster-flavored sauces—they are too salty. The coconut crisp is the star of the show. For the best visual effect, you want big shards of coconut flakes rather than shredded here. Doubled up and stored in an airtight container, the crisp will be good for up to five days. Use it over seared tofu or chicken breasts, or buttered white rice with a drizzle of soy sauce. Find more great pork chop recipes here: Green Chile Puttanesca Pork Chop; Rosemary and Dried Cherry Pork Chops; and Mustardy Cider-Braised Pork Chops. Recipe information - Total Time 45 minutes - Yield 2 servings Ingredients Coconut Crisp 1 1 3 ½ 1 1 ½ Pork Chops and assembly 2 2 1 2 2 Need to make a substitution? Preparation - Coconut CrispStep 1Cook 1 bunch scallions, thinly sliced, one 2" piece ginger, peeled, cut into matchsticks, and 3 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large cast-iron or other heavy skillet over medium heat, stirring often, until scallions and ginger are barely golden and wilted, 6–8 minutes. Add ½ cup unsweetened coconut flakes and cook, stirring often, until coconut is golden, about 5 minutes. Transfer to a medium bowl; reserve skillet. Stir 1 Tbsp. sugar, 1 tsp. garlic powder, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt into coconut crisp. Do Ahead: Coconut crisp can be made 5 days ahead. Store airtight at room temperature. - Pork Chops and assemblyStep 2Sprinkle two 1"-thick bone-in well-marbled pork rib chops all over with 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt and a generous amount of freshly ground pepper. Heat 1 Tbsp. vegetable oil in reserved skillet over medium-high. Cook pork chops, undisturbed, until browned underneath, about 5 minutes. Turn and continue cooking, turning every 2 minutes or so, until pork chops are deeply browned on both sides, 10–12 minutes (an instant-read thermometer inserted near the bone should register 145°). Transfer pork chops to a cutting board and let rest while you make the sauce. Step 3Reduce heat to medium and cook 2 Tbsp. unsalted butter in same pan, swirling occasionally, until it foams then browns, about 1 minute. Pour in ½ cup water and bring to a simmer, scraping up any browned bits. Stir in 2 Tbsp. premium oyster sauce and cook sauce until it thickens enough to lightly coat a spoon, about 2 minutes. Step 4Thinly slice pork chops and transfer to a platter; spoon sauce over. Top with coconut crisp and thinly sliced jalapeño.

item.title: A Really Big Chicken Parm
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 4.05
When Senior Test Kitchen Editor Jesse Szewczyk first came across Chef Skyler's giant chicken cutlet that went viral on TikTok, he knew he wanted to put his spin on it. His take? This supersized chicken Parmesan topped with marinara, melted mozzarella, and fresh basil. (Turns out Chef Skyler also had the same idea; check out her version here.) To make it, you’ll start by rolling out ground chicken between two sheets of parchment paper until it’s as thin as a ruler. You’ll coat the top of it with flour, eggs, breadcrumbs, and Parmesan—just like you would a typical cutlet. The next step is the only one that takes effort, and one that requires a burst of confidence to pull off: You’ll flip the entire disk in one swift move, exposing its undressed underbelly so you can bread the other side. If this process does not go as planned, don’t fret: A misshapen “cutlet” will bake up just as delicious (and hidden underneath all the toppings, no one will see its flaws). Serve it as is, tuck it between slices of crusty bread for a filling sandwich, or serve it alongside a simple salad for dinner. Check out more winning weeknight dinners here: Pad Kra Pao; Sheet-Pan Feta With Tomatoes and Chickpeas; and Spaghetti With So Much Zucchini. Recipe information - Total Time 1 hour - Yield 4 servings Ingredients 1 2 3 1 4 1½ 8 Need to make a substitution? Preparation - Step 1Place a rack in lower third of oven; preheat to 425°. Place 1 lb. ground chicken in the center of a large sheet of parchment paper cut to fit a rimmed baking sheet. Place a second sheet of parchment paper (the same size) on top, then roll out chicken until very thin and it covers parchment, leaving 1"–2" border around sides. Carefully and slowly peel off top sheet of parchment; set aside. Step 2Whisk 2 large eggs in a small bowl with a fork to combine. Mix together 3 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (½ cup), 1 cup panko, a pinch of kosher salt, and a pinch of freshly ground pepper in another small bowl. Step 3Generously season top of chicken with salt and pepper. Scatter 2 Tbsp. all-purpose flour over and rub into an even layer to completely coat surface. (It’s easiest to use your hands for this.) Brush half of eggs on top with a pastry brush or your hands. Scatter about half of panko mixture over, pressing in with your hands to adhere. Generously coat entire surface with nonstick vegetable oil spray. Place reserved sheet of parchment on top of chicken, then hold both sheets together and turn over in a swift, confident motion. Peel away top layer of parchment and discard. Generously season top of chicken with salt and pepper. Scatter remaining 2 Tbsp. all-purpose flour over and rub into an even layer to completely coat surface. Brush half of egg on top. Scatter remaining panko mixture over, pressing in with your hands to adhere. Generously spray entire surface with nonstick spray. Step 4Transfer chicken with parchment paper onto a rimmed baking sheet. (It’s easiest to hold baking sheet flush against the counter and drag parchment paper with chicken onto it.) Bake chicken, rotating baking sheet front to back halfway through, until deep golden brown all over, 28–35 minutes. Remove from oven, turn cutlet over with tongs, and spread 1½ cups homemade or store-bought marinara sauce over. Scatter 8 oz. mozzarella, coarsely grated (1–1½ cups), on top, then bake just until cheese is melted and browned in spots, 14–18 minutes. Remove from oven and top with basil leaves and drizzle with extra-virgin olive oil if desired.

item.title: Pommes Anna
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 3.94
Pommes Anna is a French potato cake made of thinly sliced potatoes cooked in nothing more than butter. While humble in its ingredients, the cake is as dramatic as can be. Baked in a skillet, it gets turned out to reveal a graphic spiral of spuds on top. Chef Alexia Duchêne of Le Chêne in New York City, keeps things classic in her recipe, layering paper-thin slices of potatoes with plenty of butter to create a multilayered potato cake that’s crisp on the outside and tender in the center. For more French classics, check out the following recipes: Bistro-Style Croque Monsieur; Poulet Rôti; and Ratatouille. Ingredients 5 1¼ ½ Special Equipment Need to make a substitution? Preparation - Step 1Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 400°. Slice 5 lb. large Yukon gold potatoes (10–15), peeled, lengthwise on a mandoline set to 1-mm thickness. Step 2Brush a large high-sided skillet with some of 1¼ cups clarified butter to coat. Cut a round of parchment paper to fit bottom of pan and place in pan. Brush parchment with more clarified butter. Using cutter and working with a few slices stacked together at a time, punch out enough rounds to fill bottom of pan. Arrange slices around sides of pan, overlapping slightly, to create a circle (make sure slices are compact and tight). Repeat process, creating concentric circles, until you have an even layer covering entire bottom of pan. Drizzle with some clarified butter and generously season with kosher salt. Repeat process (no need to cut potatoes into rounds), creating more layers, until all of the potatoes slices and clarified butter have been used. Dot ½ cup (1 stick) unsalted butter, sliced, over final layer of potatoes. Step 3Cover pan with a lid or foil and bake potatoes until tender, 50–55 minutes. Uncover and bake until deep golden brown in spots, 45–55 minutes more. Let cool slightly, then place a plate upside down over pan. Holding plate and pan together, carefully turn over in one swift motion to invert pommes Anna onto plate. Remove pan.

item.title: Crispy Potato Kugel
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 3.76
When many people hear “kugel,” visions of a sweet egg noodle casserole first come to mind, delighting many and confusing others. Savory potato kugel, however, is almost universally pleasing. Landing in between a latke and a Spanish tortilla in flavor and texture, potato kugel is, like all kugels, a baked casserole common in the Ashkenazi Jewish culinary tradition. Filled with grated potato, onion, and egg, it’s a no-brainer side dish for high holidays, like Rosh Hashanah and Passover, or weekly shabbat, but it’s welcome on the table any day alongside meaty mains such as braised brisket or roast chicken. Where latke mixture must be squeezed extremely dry to fry into crisp pancakes, potato kugel’s creamy texture comes from leaving some of that liquid in the mix. Using mayonnaise in the filling—and to grease the pan—instead of traditional schmaltz or olive oil helps ensure the kugel bakes off moist, rich, and crisp—never dry or greasy. Fat wedges of potato kugel are excellent topped with a dollop of sour cream and a sprinkle of chopped chives (but, of course, if you’re keeping kosher and serving meat alongside, you’ll want skip the dairy). Recipe information - Total Time 2 hours - Yield 10–12 servings Ingredients 4 3 1 3¼ 3 3 1 1 Need to make a substitution? Preparation - Step 1Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 400°. Brush bottom and sides of a 9"-diameter springform pan, metal cake pan, or cast-iron skillet with 2 Tbsp. mayonnaise. (If using a springform pan, place a baking sheet underneath rack to catch any drips.) Fill a medium bowl with water. Peel 3 lb. russet potatoes (about 4 large) and quarter; place in bowl of water. Quarter 1 medium onion. Using a food processor fitted with a coarse grating disk, grate potatoes and onion. (Alternatively, grate on the large holes of a box grater.) Step 2Transfer potato mixture to a large colander or fine-mesh sieve set over a large bowl. Sprinkle with 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt and toss to combine. Let sit 5 minutes to allow excess liquid to drain. Step 3Using your hands, press out more liquid from potato mixture (it should not be totally dry). Transfer colander to a plate. Gently pour out liquid from bowl, leaving behind any white starch accumulated at the bottom. Step 4Add 3 large eggs, 3 Tbsp. potato starch or cornstarch, 1 tsp. garlic powder, 1 tsp. freshly ground pepper, remaining ¼ cup plus 2 Tbsp. mayonnaise, and remaining 2¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1½ tsp. Morton kosher salt to starch left in bowl and whisk to combine. Add potato mixture and mix with your hands to coat completely in egg mixture. Scrape into prepared pan and move around with a fork to fill pan and create some surface texture without compressing mixture. Step 5Add 3 large eggs, 3 Tbsp. potato starch or cornstarch, 1 tsp. garlic powder, 1 tsp. freshly ground pepper, remaining ¼ cup plus 2 Tbsp. mayonnaise, and remaining 2¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1½ tsp. Morton kosher salt to starch left in bowl and whisk to combine. Add potato mixture and mix with your hands to coat completely in egg mixture. Scrape into prepared pan and move around with a fork to fill pan and create some surface texture without compressing mixture.

item.title: 3 Best Bread Knives, After Testing 35 Blades (2026)
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 2.70
Serrated bread knives may seem like specialized kitchen tools, but you’d be hard-pressed to slice that beautiful loaf of sourdough you brought home without one. Unlike standard kitchen knives, serrated knives have, well, serrations—a line of individually sharpened teeth along the edges that dig into whatever you’re cutting with each stroke. This sawing action easily cuts through a soft bread crumb without smooshing it, and it’s also helpful for slicing delicate tomato skin or peeling a watermelon. Our top picks - Best bread knife overall: Mac Superior Bread Knife - The best cheap bread knife: Mercer Culinary M23210 10" Bread Knife - A worthy splurge: Shun Classic 9" Bread Knife For years, the common thought was that a good serrated knife didn’t have to be expensive, and we generally agree—you can find an affordable bread knife that’ll do the job well and free up more of your knife budget to invest in the rest of your knife set. Some of that is because part of what makes a chef’s knife expensive, the high quality steel forged to hold a fine, sharp edge for a long time, isn’t as much of a thing for serrated knives. The design of the teeth makes it so that the blade can still function even if it isn’t that sharp; that’s not really the case for straight edge knives. And, because sharpening a serrated knife is a much more involved process than sharpening a a straight edge knife, some people think it’s better to replace a serrated knife after several years rather than try to maintain it. However… After testing over 35 bread knives over the last few years, I think it’s worth investing in a higher-end bread knife that’ll stay sharper longer, with blade geometry that makes slicing as easy as possible. And so I recommend one of those along with a variety of more affordable picks below. Regardless, the best bread knives at any price point are sharp, long enough for large loaves of bread, and sturdy in the hand. The top picks below all aced that criteria even with long-term testing. New in this update: We adjusted replaced the top pick in this piece after long-term testing of our favorite knives, and because of pricing and availability issues with a longtime favorite brand Tojiro. We also updated additional reviews, including on knives from Made In, Winco, and Mac after more testing. Finally we added a section on serrated knife sharpening and tested a well-liked serrated knife sharpening rod. Best bread knife overall: Mac Superior Series 10.5” bread knife Pros and cons Pros: - Long blade makes slicing through wide bread loaves easy - Curved shape offers extra leverage Cons: - On the pricier end of the spectrum Specs Knife length: 15.38" Blade length: 10.75" Weight: 6.6 oz. What we love: Mac’s Superior Series bread knife features an extra-long curved blade that makes slicing bread a breeze. Even the crustiest, oversized miche loaves were no match for this knife. It features rounded teeth that cut easily into the crust without snagging, making each stroke smoother and more deliberate. It also sliced neatly through tomato skin and glide effortlessly through the pulp, delivering perfectly uniform tomato slices. The Mac is made from high-carbon stainless steel that will keep an edge longer—a plus because serrated knives are so labor-intensive to sharpen. The curve to the blade is another excellent design choice. That curve adds cutting force to the knife because the belly extends about half an inch beyond the handle, creating immediate leverage with each stroke. In long-term testing, I found that Mac’s Superior Series offered sustained performance that cheaper knives just couldn’t match, bumping this knife into our top-pick slot. What we’d leave: My biggest gripe about this knife is the price point and handle construction. While the blocky handle scales are comfortable, it seems reasonable to expect a $100 knife to have an integrated bolster and nicer finish. For those looking for a nicer handle and are willing to spend money, you can check out the Mac Professional Series below. NOTE: The Mac Superior series is sometimes listed as the Mac Professional series on Amazon and other large marketplaces. It is not! The Professional series has a metal bolster between the blade and the handle. No bolster, not Professional. The actual Professional series knife should also cost about 50% more than the Superior series model. A cheap (but very good) bread knife: Mercer Culinary M23210 10" Bread Knife Pros and cons Pros: - Great value knife Cons: - Not full tang - Plastic handle Specs Knife length: 15.5" Blade length: 10" Weight: 5.9 oz. What we love: Premium bread knives have their perks, but a good one doesn’t have to break the bank. The Mercer Culinary Millennia 10" bread knife is less than $20, and it’s the one we use most frequently in the Bon Appétit Test Kitchen. “This bread knife came in the kit bag I got in culinary school, and I am still using it today,” food director Chris Morocco says. “It won’t split atoms, but it is dependable, and for this price, you will love it all the more.” It has deep, wide serrations, also known as a wavy edge, as opposed to the pointy teeth you see on the Wüsthof or Tojiro. Instead of a wooden handle, the ergonomic handle of the Mercer is made from a combination of rubber and plastic. While this knife isn’t full-tang (no knife at this price is), it still feels stable and comfortable to hold. Our editors have used this knife for every slicing task you can imagine: crusty bread, pineapple, ripe tomatoes, overstuffed BLTs—and it always gets the job done. What we’d leave: This knife performed admirably for its price point, but it was the least sharp of our other two winning bread knives, requiring a bit more effort to cut crustier loaves. Some people also didn’t like the Mercer’s plastic handle, which wasn’t as comfortable as our other picks. A beautiful bread knife splurge: Shun Classic 9" Bread Knife Pros and cons Pros: - High carbon steel will stay sharper longer - Beautiful knife Cons: - Pricey Specs Knife length: 14" Blade length: 9" Weight: 6.8 oz. What we love: While chef’s knives are often praised for their steel quality and appearance, bread knives are typically prized for their functionality. While you don’t need to spend as much on a bread knife to get top-tier performance, we really loved the total package from Shun’s Classic line bread knife. It’s made from Damascus steel with a VG-MAX core, which is a much higher-carbon-content steel than most bread knives. This means that the serrated edge of the knife is less likely to dull over time—key for a knife that needs to be maintained professionally to keep sharp edges. In testing, it sliced tomatoes beautifully thin, and even the crustiest sourdough provided almost zero resistance. We also appreciated the height of the blade, which provided some extra heft and cutting force without adding extra weight. Finally, the Japanese wa-style handle was comfortable to grip when you needed a little extra leverage. Because there’s no palm swell or shape to the handle, it lets the user find the position that’s most comfortable for them. Shun’s bread knife might be pricier than our other top picks, but the price definitely matches the performance and knife quality. If you’re looking for a serrated knife that will stay sharper for longer, then this might be the right pick for you. What we’d leave: The 9" blade was plenty long for most loaves of bread, but wider boules were tricky to cut all the way across without having to angle the knife. It’s hard to ignore how expensive this knife is. While it does have the highest quality fit and finish of our winners, its performance boost over our two budget picks might not quite be enough for some people. Still, if you’re picky about the details of knife construction and steel quality, this knife justifies its price point. How we tested bread knives We spoke with our Test Kitchen editors to find out which blades they’ve relied on throughout their careers. Then we tested more than two dozen bread knives on crusty sourdough and winter vine tomatoes—ideal examples of that tricky firm-outside, soft-inside texture that serrated knives handle so well. We also conduct long-term testing on our top picks to evaluate how they hold up with daily use, noting whether the blades retain their sharpness and if the handles show any signs of cracking. What makes the best bread knife We focused on evaluating the following factors when it came to making our selections: How effectively it cuts The ideal knife practically does the work for you, creating clean cuts with minimal downward pressure. In our testing, we found that thin knives usually got the job done best. Weight Your knife should have enough heft to cut through foods that have a firm exterior and a delicate interior. A too-heavy knife, however, will be cumbersome to wield. Shape of teeth A serrated knife is defined by its toothlike edge, but there are a few variations on the design. A serrated knife can have rounded, scalloped teeth; pointy teeth; and even double serrations that feature a combination of the two. While scalloped teeth might seem like the least effective option, our testing proved that this is not always the case. In fact, knives with teeth that were too pointy risked snagging and tearing on bread interiors or tomato flesh. How it feels to hold We considered the knife as a whole—from the tip of its blade to the end of the handle. We looked for knives that had ergonomic handles that fit the natural contours of our hands and paid attention to the balance of weight between the handle and the blade. We wanted a knife that felt hefty enough to give us proper leverage when slicing hardier loaves, but not so heavy as to become unwieldy. The ones we picked above were the most stable and comfortable to hold, the easiest to work with, and they made the cleanest cuts. Other bread knives we like Dexter Russell Basics 10" Scalloped Bread Knife This knife from Dexter-Russell was a top contender for the best budget spot thanks to its super sharp scalloped blade, which made easy work of slicing through tough sourdough crusts and delicate tomato skin. In the end, the Mercer edged out the competition because of its grippy, more comfortable handle, slightly sturdier construction, and (just barely) lower price tag. That said, this would be a good option if the Mercer is ever out of stock. Hedley & Bennett 8.6" Bread Knife Senior test kitchen editor (and Bon Appétit’s resident baking expert) Shilpa Uskokovic loves this bread knife from Hedley & Bennett because it’s sleek and light. While it has a smaller 8.5" blade, its angled, serrated edge becomes more pointed at the tip, making it easier to maneuver and offering heightened precision for more fragile slicing tasks. It’s relatively affordable at $90 at the time of writing, and it comes in a variety of colors. However, for all those positives, the Hedley & Bennett doesn’t offer quite the force you get from a longer blade. MAC Professional Series 10.5" Bread Knife After long-term testing, this knife is a personal favorite of Bon Appétit writers and editors—but the price makes recommending it tricky. With nearly the exact same blade as MAC’s Superior series, MAC’s Professional Series bread knife is also a high performer. The slight curve on the spine gives you tons of leverage to get through crusty bread with little effort, and the sharpness of its rounded teeth lets it slice without snagging. The big thing that sets this knife apart is its fit and finish. With a full bolster that has enough room for a pinch grip, full tang construction, and three handle rivets, this knife is built to withstand heavy-duty wear and tear. Is it overkill for a bread knife? Absolutely. But for knife aficionados, the high price tag might be worth it. Performance-wise, the MAC Professional bread knife easily sliced through the crustiest loaves and glided through tomatoes. It also felt great in the hand, even if it was a little heavy. Overall, the price-to-performance ratio kept this bread knife from the top picks, but if you want an upgrade on our top pick, it is a great option to consider. Wüsthof Classic 9" Double Serrated Bread Knife This German-made knife is another pricey blade, but it justifies that price tag with its interesting and super-effective design. While this one has a shorter 9" blade, it’s double serrated, which means it has mini teeth within the larger, scalloped serrations. All those extra sharp points give it a better grip on waxy surfaces like the exterior of a tomato or watermelon and make for fast, easy slicing. It’s also a knife that asks very little of you—during testing, the double set of serrations cut through hard crust with very little exertion from the tester and produced such thin slices of tomato that we could see right through them. One final advantage of a double-serrated blade: because there are more of them, each individual serration will wear less, so the knife stays sharper for longer. The shorter blade did make it tricky to cut wider loaves straight across, though it was an adequate length for most batards and pan loaves. Mercer Culinary 8" Züm Bread Knife Sharp and with a comfortable handle, the ZüM knife from Mercer Culinary excelled in our testing. It neatly sliced through the tomatoes, piercing the tough skin easily without smashing the delicate flesh. It also perfectly sliced through the sourdough crust and crumb without snagging. The only thing we didn’t like was the 8" blade length, which was a little short for bigger sourdough loaves, but for around $50, it’s an effective budget option with high-end handle construction and a full bolster. Not quite our favorite budget pick, but a good alternative, and a good option for people who want a very comfortable handle. Misen 8" Serrated Knife Misen’s bread knife was a mid-tier performer in our tests, cleanly cutting through tomatoes and bread without any notable issues. We also thought the handle was comfortable, and its overall build quality was high. The blade’s taller heel also meant it performed well slicing through larger sourdough loaves. However, its performance didn’t quite match our top picks, and our two budget models performed better at half the cost. We recommend either spending a little more for a nicer bread knife, or saving a bit of cash instead—unless you can find this knife on sale. Bread knives we don't recommend A former top pick, I still stand behind this knife’s performance and build quality. What I don’t love, however, is its spotty availability and fluctuating price. At around $60, I thought this knife was a steal. Now that its price has rocketed up to match Mac’s Superior Series bread knife, I can’t recommend it when the Mac offers better build quality and consistency. Still, if you can catch this knife on a deal, go for it—it’s sharp and nimble, but sturdy enough to tackle most tasks. Like its sturdier cousin, this bread knife from Tojiro is sharp and swift. But when we originally picked this serrated knife, its price was around $40. For that price, this knife was a great pick. But its cheaper build quality, lack of a full tang, and slightly smaller wood handle mean we don’t see much value in recommending this knife now that it’s price has nearly doubled. Bob Kramer is a legendary knife maker, but the Bob Kramer Essential Bread Knife by Zwilling felt like overkill for a serrated knife. Its $400-plus price point is excessive for a tool with such a narrow set of uses (no matter how often you bake homemade bread), and because this knife is made from carbon steel, it'll be prone to corrosion and rust. Does it work well? Definitely; it was one of the better tomato knives we used. But is it worth the sky-high price? In our opinion, no. This knife has a nice weight to it—stable without being heavy—and it's easy to control through longer cuts. However, it wasn't as sharp or efficient as the top performers. Global's great knives have won the hearts of many a BA staffer. That said, their metal handles are divisive—some people think they're comfortable to hold and others find them too thin and slippery. While our testers say this knife is well-balanced and decently sharp, they ultimately disqualified it from our winners list due to its handle shape, short blade length (8.5"), and less-than-perfect performance in the tomato test, where its large teeth snagged just a bit on the tomato's flesh. IKEA's $25 bread knife handled bread and tomatoes competently without excelling at either. The serrations weren't the sharpest we tested, but they cut cleanly enough for everyday use. We were impressed by the sharpness of Kuhn Rikon's serrations, which allowed for precise cuts. Its limitation is its reach; at under eight inches, wide bread loaves demand more back-and-forth. But if you're not into sourdough boules, this will be an impressive performer. This is a beautiful knife (just look at that gorgeously curved handle grip), but the Lamson's teeth weren't sharp enough. The knife snagged on crusty sourdough boules and required a lot of force to make cuts. Its 8" blade was also too short to cut through entire loaves, and it snagged slightly on tomato skin. Lamson does offer complementary sharpening for life, but for this price ($90 at the time of writing), we feel the bread knife should be sharper out of the box. Sharp and well-made, we do like Mac’s Chef’s Series bread knife. But it’s only slightly cheaper than our top pick and doesn’t feature a curved belly. Again, the decision not to recommend it comes to value; you’ll get a much more better slicing experience if you drop an extra $10 on the Mac Superior. Though it was razor sharp, MAC's offset knife was too short to effectively slice bread. At only 7.5", we had to maneuver it to make it through an entire sourdough loaf. We also didn't like its offset blade, which made it hard to intuitively feel where the blade was compared to the handle. It did excel as a tomato slicer, but it would be hard to recommend it at this price point. The first time we tested Made In’s bread knife, we found it lacked sharpness. That’s no longer the case—their slightly updated model has sharper serrations and slices through bread and tomatoes with ease. The big issues are with the weight and the price—the heftier handle does balance well against the blade, but overall it’s a heavy knife. It’s also more expensive than our top pick while having a shorter, straighter blade. This knife is fine, but there are plenty of others that offer better value. A little too flimsy, this knife struggled to neatly slice through sourdough bread. Even though it was sharp, the blade tended to flex when cutting, creating uneven slices of bread. We also didn't like the cheapness of the handle or the offset blade shape, but it did offer solid performance at a very affordable price. For how pricey this knife is, we were disappointed in how dull the blade appeared to be. Since it's difficult to sharpen a serrated knife, initial sharpness is a key factor in picking out the best option for your kitchen. This knife snagged on tomato skin and tore apart the delicate sourdough bread crumb. Though the handle was beautiful and felt nice in the hand, this knife was the most expensive model we tested and had some of the worst performance. Considering it's one of the most expensive bread knives we tested, we were hoping for better performance out of the Miyabi Kaizen 9.5" Bread Knife. Instead, it crushed most loaves of bread instead of cutting them, and it got stuck on tomato cores. The Opinel Intempora fell short—in some cases, literally—in a few areas. Its 8" blade is shorter than we'd like, making it hard to cut through sourdough boules without changing the slicing angle. Its teeth weren't quite as sharp as we'd like either. It didn't mangle the tomatoes (a win!), but we had difficulty keeping the blade straight—the knife typically snagged on the fruit's core, creating wobbly, inconsistent tomato slices. We do like the round polyurethane handle and the high-quality high-carbon stainless steel, but we expect better performance from a knife of this price. The Shun Classic Master Serrated Knife has a unique wavy edge that adds to the overall serration pattern. It excelled at slicing paper-thin tomatoes and was comfortable to hold, but its edge shape didn't consistently cut through bread well. Its blade was also on the shorter side, making this knife less well-suited for large loaves. This knife has a lot going for it: The Shun Ultimate Utility looks almost like a toy shark and, accordingly, has plenty of bite—we loved how sharp its rounded teeth were. Its flat sides and curved tip mean that this knife is able to both slice your sandwich toppings and spread mayo on a piece of soft bread. It also sliced tomatoes perfectly and slid right through the crust of the sourdough boules. But its tiny 6" blade, which is more similar to a santoku than a typical bread knife, made it hard to cut even slices. And when you factor in the price ($140 at the time of writing), we just can't recommend it. This model from Victorinox, the makers of one of our favorite budget-friendly chef's knives, performed pretty well overall. Testers found that while the plastic handle looks flimsy, the knife cut really well and felt sturdy. However, this is an incredibly light knife—so much so that it verges on too light—and at more than double (or triple, at some stores) the cost of our affordable picks, it costs more than we think is worth spending. The Victorinox Swiss Army 8" knife sliced bread okay, but it required more effort than most other models; worse, it crushed tomatoes. It was also too lightweight to maneuver comfortably. Sharp, well-made, and great at cutting, there's a lot to like about the Wüsthof Classic bread knife. It easily sliced through tomatoes, and it cut swiftly through crusty sourdough bread. But its 8" length struggled to span the entire loaf, and then there's the price. As one of the most expensive bread knives we tested, we think there's better performance for less money—or, you can upgrade to the double-serrated version, which was one of our top picks. The double serrations of this Ikon series knife performed as well on waxy surfaces as the Wusthof Classic double serrated knife above, but struggled a bit against crusty bread. The bigger issue is that this knife regularly retails for about $200 (30% more than the regular Classic series knife). You're paying for the Ikon finishes, which are lovely, but if you're interested in double serration, we think the standard Classic offering (listed above) is a better bet at a slightly more affordable price. Although billed as a "13-inch" bread knife, Zulay's blade is only 8 inches. The short blade struggled with thick, wide sourdough loaves. It was also hard to control; the blade wandered during cuts, making it difficult to produce straight, clean slices. Both bread and tomatoes eventually yielded, but the process felt imprecise compared to most knives we tested. We struggled to make clean cuts with Zwilling's entry-level Gourmet series. While it sliced tomatoes just fine, its teeth often caught on crusty sourdough loaves, interrupting the sawing motion and requiring more force to power through. During testing, its handle scales felt clunky, making the knife awkward to hold and even more awkward to wield, and it failed to perform as well as our two budget picks—both of which are significantly less expensive. Zwilling's double-serrated knife is a good slicer, and its double-serrated edge is similar to the Wüsthof model we recommend. It performed well in testing, yielding thinly sliced tomatoes and perfectly straight slices of bread, but ultimately, this knife's overall weight and high price tag kept it from being a winner. A bit heavier than much of the competition, Zwilling's bread knife was trickier to wield comfortably, and its longer handle made it hard to find a good balance point. Offset knives are awkward to cut with because they remove the leverage you can create with the handle. While this knife from Winco slices tomatoes nicely, it struggles with crustier bread and dulls more quickly than other serrated knives we tested. It does have a bargain price tag though, so there’s that. Serrated knives feature dozens of individually sharpened teeth, meaning that, if you do want to sharpen your bread knife, you need to sharpen dozens of edges instead of the single edge most kitchen knives have. While this process can be tricky and is generally best left to professionals, you can pick up a serrated knife sharpener that lets you add more bite to your blade. These sharpeners work best with pointy serrations that create neat half-circle teeth—simply run the diamond-coated rod in the interior of each curve until they’re sharper than they were before. The only issue? The rod is shaped to work best with pointy serrations, so rounded scalloped edges won’t easily sharpen with a tool like this. Also, even the finest diamond surface is still rougher than ceramic—you can sharpen each pointy tooth on a bread knife with this thing, but it won’t be as highly polished and smooth as a professionally sharpened bread knife. Overall, I recommend these tools for budget-tier bread knives that you want to breathe some life into. Since bread knives don’t smack against hard cutting boards the same way as chef’s knives do, they also don’t dull as quickly. And if you have a higher-end bread knife made from harder steel, it’s likely your knife will hold an edge for a long time without any intervention from you. Fill out the rest of your knife block - The best chef's knives to serve as your daily driver - A nakiri knife is a blade you didn't know you needed - How much do you need to pay for a good knife anyway? Get to know the experts Jesse Raub: I’ve been a professional kitchen product tester since 2021, where I tested nearly everything: espresso machines, wooden spoons, bread proofing baskets, pizza stones, garlic presses, and more. My fascination with kitchen knives began in 2003 when the chef at the kitchen where I worked let me use his personal Wüsthof knives during prep work one day. Over the last two years, I’ve tested over 70 different knives for Bon Appétit and written about the best knife sharpeners and how to best sharpen your knives at home. If you’re ever on the phone with me and hear a light scraping noise in the background, just know that I’m likely touching up my kitchen knives on a whetstone and testing their sharpness by slicing sheets of paper. Additional reporting and testing by Alaina Chou and Jamie Thilman.

item.title: “Chicken Shop Date” Ends a Legendary Run
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 2.38
Welcome to Open Tab, a weekly roundup of the news, gossip, and stories that have stayed open in my tabs all week. Last time we covered the restaurants using AI Foodslop images. Welcome back to Open Tab. Can you smell fall in the air? I cannot, but I want to make an apple pie so badly that I’m pretending I do. I’ve spent the week finding creative ways to dress up a rotisserie chicken, but I’ve found that nothing takes the place of a great sauce. My go-to is a zippy, spicy, creamy-cilantro-y green sauce that does not really have a recipe—if you shoot me an email I’ll give you my loose measurements. This week: a tale of two movies centered around beloved restaurant franchises. One, a sci-fi/thriller called The Waffle House Index, about a woman working at a Waffle House as a big storm approaches. The other, a based-on-a-true-story film about the Hooters origin story. That last comes as the chain attempts a family-friendly rebrand. Earth-shatteringly, it was revealed that the AI-loving Gal Gadot did not receive one of the famed Tom Cruise coconut cakes. “He makes cakes?” she asked, confused, on a recent episode of the Armchair Expert podcast. It’s not a big deal for Gadot, who reportedly does not like cake (?!). I’m sure Gadot is actually not that worried, since her mac and cheese company, Goodles, valued at $88 million three years ago, just got acquired. Also in this week’s Open Tab: The end of Chicken Shop Date, the USDA may be changing beef inspection policy, what’s next for Wonder, and why the customer isn’t always right. Breaking up with Chicken Shop Date After twelve years of hosting her incredibly popular shortform talk show, Chicken Shop Date, Amelia Dimoldenberg announced that it would be ending. “I feel like it’s now time to move on from this adventure and onto a new one,” Dimoldenberg shared in a note posted to Instagram. There will be a few more episodes before the series goes dark The show, which premiered in 2014, originally focused on UK-based rap and grime artists. Shows like CSD changed the way celebrities run press tours, giving rise to a slew of new food-based talk shows like Sean Evans’ Hot Ones, Mythical Kitchen’s Last Meals, and Jesse Tyler Ferguson’s Dinner’s on Me. Perhaps she’s tired of poultry, as Dimoldenberg expands her video empire with non-food content like red carpet reporting for Vanity Fair, and Passenger Princess, a series in which she learns to drive. Beef: now less regulated The US is facing two problems (among many): Very high beef prices, and a summer of worsening food safety regulations. One, solution to the problem? Changing regulations around processing beef, which is just what President Trump said he’d do in a post on Truth Social last week. “I am authorizing legal documents to be drawn in order to allow Farmers and Ranchers to be given the right to PROCESS THEIR OWN FOOD,” he wrote in part. Some advocacy groups expressed concern at the proposed change. “Allowing uninspected meat to be sold to unwitting consumers is the wrong approach, and risks undermining this country’s reputation for producing the safest meat products in the world,” The Meat Institute, a trade organization representing beef and poultry processors, said in a statement. What does Wonder want? The food-tech company Wonder focuses on delivery and takeout from restaurants cooked in its ghost kitchens. Its first location opened in 2023, but the company has raised $2.5 billion since 2021. Founder Marc Lore recently announced plans to create AI which would allow anyone to create a restaurant in the blink of an eye. “You type in what kind of restaurant you want to build. It builds the restaurant — AI does — in under a minute,” he said in an interview with Fortune magazine. The company recently acquired viral New York City restaurant Salt Hank’s, and, this week, the company laid off more than 100 staff members. What does Wonder want? To IPO some time next year, we suspect. And, with more than 150 locations in 10 states and a valuation of nearly $10 billion already, it will likely change the country’s food delivery landscape, and like many publicly traded companies that came before it, probably start to enshittify its product and services once it’s eliminated its competition (But who knows, this is just one beautiful genius’s opinion.) Once, when I was working as a server in high-ish end restaurant, a guy asked me if he could substitute fries with some kind of plain greens. I told him I could offer some spinach. “No, I mean greens,” he replied frustrated, with no additional context to what the hell he wanted exactly. This kind of exchange happened, like, six times per shift, and it’s how I came to understand that, actually, the customer is not always right. Sometimes, reader, the customer is annoying and wrong. In his essay for Bon Appétit, James Beard-winning author and writer Adam Reiner explores how restaurant workers tangle with boundaries while remaining hospitable. Read the essay here.

item.title: Best Dutch Ovens for Braising, Baking, and Beyond (2026)
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 2.17
Over the past few decades, I'd argue that the Dutch oven has eclipsed the stand mixer as the most crucial piece of kitchen equipment for making a kitchen feel like a home kitchen. Is it because they're heavy and expensive? It it because couples always put them on their wedding registries? Is it because you can make soup in them and soup is comforting and feels homey and there's something to that? Not entirely sure. I can say though, that setting down one of these colorful, enameled hunks of cast iron onto a stove is akin to dropping an anchor. By committing to making a Sunday braise in a Dutch oven you're saying, “ This is my home, and because it's my home, I'm gonna make the entire place, and my clothes, smell like ragú.” But which to buy? I've spent years and years thinking about this, because the question of what the best Dutch oven is, is a question that requires a lot of caveats and asterisks. Yes, there are certainly some design and quality metrics that help distinguish the Staubs and Le Creusets from Amazon Basics, but the bottom line is: Every Dutch oven on the market will deliver an extremely similar cooking performance. What it all comes down to is quality and design. Our top picks - The best Dutch oven overall: Le Creuset Signature Round 5.5-Quart Dutch Oven - The other best Dutch oven: Staub 5.5-Quart Cocotte - The best budget Dutch oven: Goldilocks Cheap Dutch ovens work just fine, but their affordability comes at the cost of quality control. Budget Dutch ovens consistently feature manufacturer defects, chipping, and thinner enamel layers that can lead to accelerated wear and rusting. As for design, while there are some practical advantages that some have over others, a lot of it comes down to subjective preferences. There are two people who have worked on this test over the years and we have vehemently disagreed with each other over the top spot, though, to be clear both of our choices are great Dutch ovens. I'll get more into the two that always tussle for the top spot, as well as the most well-designed budget picks that also come with lifetime warranties. Keep reading to learn about how I and my team have tested Dutch ovens over the years, how to keep the enamel in tip-top shape, and which brands didn’t make the short list. New in this update: I added reviews for the Crockpot, Goldilocks, and Müeller Dutch ovens, and moved Le Creuset into a clear top spot. A Beautiful, easy-to-handle Dutch oven with a light interior: Le Creuset Signature Enameled Cast-Iron 5.5-Quart Round Dutch Oven Pros and cons Pros: - Heirloom-quality cookware - Even heating - Relatively lightweight - Lots of size and color options - Lifetime warranty Cons: - Expensive - Light interior enamel will show wear more readily than dark enamel Specs Interior enamel: Light and smooth Available sizes: 2-qt., 4.5-qt., 5.5-qt., 7.25-qt., 9-qt., 13.75-qt. Weight (5.5-qt. size): 11.6 lb. Multiple color options: Yes, though availability varies by size and retailer Heat resistance: 500ºF Warranty: Limited lifetime What I love: We’ve been recommending Le Creuset’s Dutch ovens for as long as we’ve been recommending Dutch ovens. So if you have your heart set on one of these iconic pieces and you’re wondering whether it’s still a wise investment, the answer is a resounding yes. Le Creuset’s smooth, sand-colored interior enamel produced a beautiful, even sear—and the light enamel makes it easy to keep an eye on browning and fond development. Le Creuset’s 5.5-quart Dutch oven also weighs about a pound less than Staub’s with thin loop handles that are easy to grip with or without oven mitts. The lighter weight comes courtesy of noticeably thinner cast iron, but it’s still thick enough to offer wonderful heat retention. Le Creuset Dutch ovens typically have a wider cooking surface and lower sides. This means more space for searing meats for braising—an essential Dutch oven task. A few years ago Le Creuset began offering metal knobs on its Dutch ovens, which was a meaningful upgrade as the old phenolic knobs could melt if you tried to do something like use your Dutch oven to bake bread at 450℉, it would melt. Then there is the manufacturing quality. Le Creuset is a century-old French brand, and though some of its cookware and tableware is now made in other countries, all of the enameled cast-iron cookware—including the Dutch ovens—is still made in the original manufacturing facility in Fresnoy-le-Grand, France. And while we know from experience with inherited pieces that the chip-resistant enamel can last a lifetime (with proper care, of course), Le Creuset Dutch ovens do come with a limited lifetime warranty. What I’d leave: When covered at a boil, the Le Creuset may sputter at the edges a little. If you choose a Dutch oven with light-colored interior enamel, and cook in it often, you should expect some gradual discoloration. If you’re intent on keeping it pristine, you may jeopardize the lifespan of the enamel. Abrasive cleaners can wear the seal off of it and lead to even more staining. A gorgeous, top-notch Dutch oven with a dark interior: Staub Round Cocotte Pros and cons Pros: - Heirloom-quality cookware - Even heating - Dark, textured cooking surface browns quicker and hides stains - Lots of size and color options - Lifetime warranty Cons: - Expensive - Heavier relative to its liquid capacity - Lint from some dish towels can catch on interior enamel Specs Interior enamel: Dark and textured Available sizes: .425-qt., .85-qt., 1.25-qt., 1.75-qt., 2.75 qt., 4-qt., 5.5-qt., 7-qt., 8.75-qt., 13.25-qt. Weight (5.5-qt. size): 12.57 lb. Multiple color options: Yes, though availability varies by size and retailer Heat resistance: 500ºF Warranty: Limited lifetime What I love: In terms of craftsmanship and price, Staub’s Dutch oven, which the brand calls a “cocotte,” is in no ways inferior to the Le Creuset. Both are premium enameled cast-iron round Dutch ovens with high-quality chip-resistant enamel, and both heat and sear evenly. Interior enamel is a matter of preference, and the Bon Appétit staff is divided on this matter. The Staub's dark, textured enamel interior does absorb more thermal energy which is helpful for producing an intense sear. The enamel also also has a rougher surface texture, which Staub claims helps distribute fat beneath ingredients to encourage browning and an easier release. While there is some truth to this, the relationship between surface texture and food sticking isn't cut and dry. Many other variables, such as temperature, time, fat volume, technique, and the type of food, have an impact as well. As Robert J. Macfarlane, a materials scientist at MIT pointed out to me, surface texture can increase surface area, which combined with poor technique and inadequate oil can actually make sticking worse. All of that to say: This Dutch oven produces a great sear, but the added benefits of Staub's dark textured enamel aren't significant enough to champion over classic light enamel. One thing that is for sure though—the dark interior won’t show discoloration like a light one will. Looking beyond the enamel, the Staub's lid is well-designed, preventing liquid sputters when shut at a boil. The bumps underneath are supposed to distribute condensation, though we've never observed a difference in the end product between Dutch ovens with bumpy lids and Dutch ovens without. I prefer the flat lid over a curved one, as you can invert the lid and stack the Dutch oven for easy storage. Yes, it’s pricey, but with proper care it will be something your kids fight over once you're gone. Like Le Creuset, Staub is a French cookware brand (now owned by Zwilling), its Dutch ovens are still manufactured in France, and they maintain an exceedingly high bar for what ends up on store shelves. One of the big reasons for the price is the high volume of units they reject along the assembly line (cast-iron is a material that evades easy refinement). This scrutiny means that your Dutch oven will almost certainly be free of surface defects and chips. If you do find any, definitely reach out to them, as Staub also offers a limited lifetime warranty on its enameled cast iron. What I'd leave: The dark enamel makes it a bit harder to monitor browning, which might be intimidating for greener cooks. Also, the Staub is heavier than the Le Creuset and the handles are slightly smaller, but it's a pretty negligible distinction if you're trying to champion one excellent product over the other. The best budget Dutch oven: Goldilocks Pros and cons Pros: - Generous surface area - Large handles - Affordable - Lifetime warranty Cons: - Heavier relative to its liquid capacity - Too young a brand to judge longevity Specs Interior enamel: White Available sizes: 6 qt Weight (5.5-qt. size): 13.7 lb. Multiple color options: Blue, red, green. Heat resistance: 500ºF Warranty: Lifetime warranty What I loved: As a relative newcomer to the cookware space, Goldilocks has consistently produced well-made, affordable cookware. It's clear that they pay attention to design, and that is evident in their Dutch oven. This Dutch oven was a pleasure to cook with, and had no apparent defects in design or performance. The design prioritizes width over height, something we appreciate for searing and browning meat before a braise. In fact is one of the widest round Dutch ovens relative to its height and volume. But rest assured it fits fine over standard burners. Its handles are also nice and large, making them easy to grab and maneuver, even with thick oven mitts on. It is still more expensive than some of the better known and more popular cheaper models made by Amazon and Lodge, and we can't yet speak to the longterm longevity of the enamel coating since this is still a newer product. However, I'd argue that the physical dimensions themselves also make this a superior choice to previous budget picks. What I'd leave: Again, I can't yet speak toward longevity yet so we will update this test in the future. Beyond that, it is slightly heavier than the winners, and also is extremely limited in size and color offerings. However, 6 quarts is the median ideal size for a Dutch oven. How we tested Dutch ovens Steam test We also tested the lids by conducting steam tests and filling each one about halfway with water that we brought to a rolling boil in order to see if the lid would prevent spattering. Ideally, the lid will release some steam at such high temperatures, but contain water in its scalding, liquid form. Form evaluation Most importantly, we evaluated the physical dimensions of each Dutch oven: how much they weigh relative to their size, how large their handles are, and their height-to-width ratio. We also do longterm testing on winning models to evaluate issues with wear and longevity. Both the Test Kitchen team and the product reviews team use Dutch ovens on a regular basis, which helps inform our testing as well. What we looked for in a Dutch oven Durable enamel Without the kind of serious long-term testing we’re able to do with the Le Creuset and Staub Dutch ovens many of us have owned for years, it’s hard to tell just how durable a Dutch oven’s porcelain enamel will be. But sometimes really cheap enamel will have small chips or pinholes right out of the box. You can also look at customer reviews; most will have at least a few reporting enamel damage. If it’s a small percentage of reviews, it’s likely a manufacturing defect, but if a disproportionate amount of reviewers complain about chipped or damaged enamel, it’s likely a durability issue. Comfortable handles Even when they’re empty, Dutch ovens are pretty heavy—hell, the lids alone are heavy—so the handles should be comfortable to hold with your bare hands. They should also be easy enough to hold or grip while wearing oven mitts. Large surface area A larger cooking surface relative to the total liquid volume means more space for browning meat and other ingredients with less risk of crowding, which can cause things to steam rather than brown. If you remember Julia Child's advice for making boeuf bourguignon, do not crowd the meat! A tight-fitting lid A Dutch oven’s lid should fit snugly on the pot and not rattle around when you’re carrying it or boiling water in it. That said, it’s normal for some steam to escape from even a heavy tight-fitting lid when water inside is at a rolling boil. A long warranty Enameled cast iron, in theory, is very durable, and the very best Dutch ovens are heirloom-quality pieces that will last at least a lifetime with proper care. If a manufacturer offers a very short warranty on their enameled cast-iron cookware, it could (though may not always) indicate a lower-quality product. Other Dutch ovens we liked Made In fits in the middle tier here, as it is a great Dutch oven made with a higher standard of quality than budget models. It is heavier than both Staub and Le Creuset, and the handles are divisive among staff. Some like the wide flat handles for holding when full, while others find there to be not as much knuckle clearance, making them more challenging to grasp completely with oven mitts on. This is a good Dutch oven that had a brief run as our budget pick (before Goldilocks became available), as it comes with a limited lifetime warranty not typical for budget Dutch ovens. It performs well, and was lighter than other budget Dutch ovens. The drawback is that the handles are slimmer than I'd like for easy gripping. Amazon Basics’ kitchen gear is really hit or miss, but the Amazon Basics Dutch oven is surprisingly good—especially for something with such an accessible price tag. This was also a former budget pick. Performance wise it gets the job done. Like the Zulay, it has narrow handles. It’s a good option for home cooks on a budget. However, unlike the Zulay Dutch oven, which has a lifetime warranty, this one comes with a one-year warranty, so inspect it for defects as soon as its out of the box. Overall, our testers were impressed with this sleek, stylish 5.5-quart dutch oven from DTC lifestyle brand Kana. The smooth, light interior enamel produced an even sear on both meat and vegetables, and we didn’t experience any cold spots or notice any chips in the enamel out of the box (some customer reviews have complained of chipped enamel). It’s about a pound lighter than the comparably sized Le Creuset, which means it can heat up and cool down a bit quicker, but the thinner cast iron won't retain heat quite as well. If you want a budget pot and like the modern look (or you really want a moderately priced Dutch oven with a gold-toned knob), the Milo by Kana is a good choice. Dutch ovens we don’t recommend This large, oval Dutch oven from Great Jones is gorgeous. We love the color options, and for a 6.75-quart enameled cast-iron Dutch oven from a popular brand, the sub-$200 price tag is nice too. But, with only one rather large size and the oval shape, it’s not the best option for everyday use—or for induction cooktops with round “burners.” But it’s the perfect size for roasting a whole chicken and large cuts of meat, and the large loop handles are easy to grab with or without oven mitts. Great Jones does offer a smaller round Dutch oven, the Dutch Baby but at 3.5 quarts it’s on the small side of the Dutch oven sweet spot. Tramontina’s relatively affordable stainless-steel cookware is often compared to All-Clad, so we had high hopes for the Brazilian brand’s 5.5-quart enameled cast-iron Dutch oven too. Out of the box, we liked the tall sides (great for deep-frying), but unfortunately it just didn't perform well in our testing. Our testers noticed a persistent cold spot that resulted in uneven cooking—and food sticking to the smooth, light interior enamel. We like Cuisinart’s enameled cast-iron skillet, but the Dutch oven is disappointing. Unlike the skillet, which has a dark, textured interior enamel, the Dutch oven has a smooth, light interior that didn’t perform well in our sear test. We also found multiple cold spots even when it was fully preheated, which produced pork that was unevenly cooked. In addition to its popular pottery and ceramic tableware, English brand Denby offers a small selection of enameled cast-iron cookware, including several Dutch ovens—which it calls “casseroles.” They’re moderately priced compared to similarly sized Dutch ovens from other well-known brands. When we tested the round 5.5-quart (listed as a 26-cm size) the performance was adequate, but the handles were small and hard to grab, especially when it was hot. And overall, nothing about it wowed us. But if you like the look and it’s within your budget—and you don’t mind the small handles—you may be happy with the Denby Dutch oven. We love a lot of KitchenAid gear (hello, gorgeous stand mixer!) but in general, we haven’t been that impressed with the brand’s cookware, and that trend continued with the enameled cast-iron Dutch oven didn’t impress us—though we were certainly impressed with its heft. The 6-quart Dutch oven weighs 20 pounds, empty! That’s the only size available, and it only comes in two colors too. The first time we tested Misen’s Dutch oven, we really liked it. It’s large and deep, which is great for deep-frying, and it made a pretty good stockpot too. But then Misen changed some design elements—most notably it did away with the traditional Dutch oven lid and instead offers the choice of either a silicone option or an enameled cast-iron grill pan that can double as a lid (a traditional lid is available on the larger 7-quart model, which, as we've said, is bigger than most people need). Both lid alternatives made this less functional and appealing than it was when it had a traditional enameled cast-iron lid with a metal knob. Also: Our testers have experienced some minimal enamel chipping with long-term use. This 4-quart Dutch oven from Vermicular comes as-is or alongside Vermicular’s Musui-Kamado, a stand-alone induction heating element that holds the pot, sort of like a very high-end, precise slow cooker. The interior enamel is an off-white color and minimally textured, though not as textured as the dark interior enamel of the Staub. The rim is unfinished to provide a “precision seal.” However, this makes it susceptible to rust, and during testing, did not do a better job at sealing in moisture than the Le Creuset or Staub, which do have an enamel coating around the rim. The side handles on the lid were also unnecessary, and made it difficult to grab, especially when removing it from the oven. This is one of the few cast-iron Dutch ovens we've tried without an enamel coating. While this is a beautiful piece of cookware, it’s the sort of thing that only really makes sense for dedicated cast-iron enthusiasts who love to care for and maintenance their cookware. We’ve found that developing a seasoning on this is quite challenging, and that the type of cooking we generally employ our Dutch ovens for (soups, braises, stews) tends to hinder the process. Smithey recommends a just-cook-with-it method for developing the seasoning, and the brand also claims that it’s fine to use when making soups or acidic braises. However, we found that tomato sauce stripped the seasoning and developed a metallic taste. A really robust seasoning would potentially withstand this, but you’d need to do several rounds of seasoning on your own, and with a big pot like this, that isn’t an easy task. We also found that the cast-iron lid is prone to rust spots. This is because (if you’re primarily cooking on the stovetop with your Dutch oven) the lid never gets hot enough as has no direct contact with fat, which means that it will not develop a seasoning as you cook with it. This is a problem especially because moisture condenses on the interior of the lid while cooking. All in all, having an uncoated Dutch oven is a labor of love. If you do a lot of deep-frying, or cooking on open fires, or you just really like to season cast iron as a hobby, you might be able to tame this beast. If you’re just looking for a regular-shmegular Dutch oven, we’d advise against it.
