Over the years, we've have tested both Lodge Essentials Dutch ovens and Lodge USA Enamel Dutch ovens, the latter of which is made in a newer manufacturing facility in North America. Unfortunately, not all Lodge cookware is created equally, and even though the USA Enamel line is clearly a much higher quality than the Lodge Essentials enameled cast iron, customers have complained about chipping with both. On the other hand, a colleague has been using a Dutch oven from the USA Enamel line for more than a year and hasn’t experienced any chipping. The issue here seems to be inconsistency in quality, but we’ll continue to use these Dutch ovens to see if the newer lines prove to be more durable. FAQ What size Dutch oven should I get? The size you get really depends on what you’ll use it for—if you’re cooking every night for a family of six, a 7-quart Dutch oven will make sense. But for most home cooks (and anyone with four or fewer people in their house), the Dutch oven sweet spot size is 5.5 or 6 quarts. It’s big enough to accommodate a pot roast or a whole chicken, but not too big for a loaf of sourdough if you’re the bread-baking type. It’s also a good size for deep-frying and gives you plenty of room for tossing four servings of pasta without overcrowding the pan. What material is a Dutch oven made of? Dutch ovens can be made of various types of metal or ceramic, and they can be enamel-coated or uncoated. For example, Emile Henry makes an enameled clay ceramic Dutch oven and Dansk makes an enameled carbon-steel Dutch oven (er, “casserole”). You can even get high-quality raw cast-iron Dutch ovens from brands like Smithey and Lancaster, but they require seasoning and more maintenance than enameled cast iron. However, its enameled cast-iron Dutch ovens that are ubiquitous. The cast iron offers incredible heat retention and is compatible with gas, electric, and induction cooktops while the durable porcelain enamel protects the cast iron from rust and corrosion caused by water as well as acidic foods like tomatoes. The enamel also eliminates the need for seasoning. Are Dutch ovens nonstick? One of the biggest misconceptions about this kind of cookware is that the cooking surface is supposed to be nonstick. It’s not. Porcelain enamel may look like a ceramic nonstick coating, and it’s far easier to clean and care for than raw cast iron, but it is not a nonstick surface. Its purpose is to protect the cast iron underneath. That said, with the right temperature and enough butter or oil, food releases from enamel pretty easily. How do I protect my Dutch oven from damage? Enameled cast iron can withstand high heat as well as freezing temperatures, but you do want to avoid thermal shock to your Dutch oven. For example: Don’t take it from the fridge and put it straight over high heat on your stovetop. And when you’re preheating it, do it slowly over low to medium heat. Sudden temperature changes can cause the enamel to chip and in some cases damage the cast iron itself (up to and including actually cracking it), and this kind of damage will often be grounds for the manufacturer to void the warranty. Why shouldn’t I use metal utensils in my Dutch oven? Though some user manuals say metal utensils are fine in their enameled cast-iron cookware, it’s best to use wood or silicone. Metal utensils can, over time, damage the protective enamel, especially if you use them in a hot pot. Even minor, cosmetic scratch marks from metal utensils can be an issue because you may be tempted to buff them out with an abrasive cleaner. Doing that once or twice might not cause any major damage, but repeated use of abrasive cleaners will absolutely erode the top layer of the porcelain enamel and eventually make it porous and prone to much worse staining. What’s the deal with braising divots? Many Dutch oven lids are pocked with divots, which supposedly help to evenly distribute moisture when braising—in theory, kind of basting the meat inside the closed pot. That said, in many years of testing, we haven’t seen any clear evidence of this actually happening. How should I clean a Dutch oven? Enameled cast-iron cookware is incredibly durable because the porcelain enamel protects the cast iron from rust and corrosion. And unlike traditional and ceramic nonstick cookware, a high-quality enamel coating can last forever if you take good care of it—which, sorry to say, means never putting it in the dishwasher. While it’s true that some enameled cast-iron pieces, including Le Creuset’s colorful Dutch ovens, are marketed as dishwasher-safe, if you read the manual, you’ll learn that most manufacturers generally recommend hand-washing. That’s because over time, harsh dishwasher detergents can erode the enamel, making it more porous, which can lead to staining and stuck-on food.

item.title: Zucchini Pasta and More Recipes We Cooked at Home This Week
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 2.00
It’s no secret that Bon Appétit editors cook a lot for work. So it should come as no surprise that we cook a lot during our off hours too. Here are the recipes we’re whipping up this month to get dinner on the table, entertain our friends, satisfy a sweet tooth, use up leftovers, and everything in between. For even more staff favorites, click here. September 4 It’s no secret that I love these tofu meatballs from BA alum Kendra Vaculin. This week I made them for a super simple dinner: spaghetti, jarred marinara, and a flurry of grated parm. The recipe comes together in one bowl—with your hands!—just like meat-meatballs, then cooks in the oven versus a splattering pan. Any leftovers make for a great next-day sandwich or snack. —Emma Laperruque, cooking director When watermelon is as good as it is in late summer, you don’t need a recipe to enjoy it. (Of course we have a great collection of watermelon recipes, should you appreciate some inspiration.) This week, I cut a honking melon into big batons, Salt Bae’d them, drizzled them with olive oil, and tore some basil with its little pink flowers on top. I then sat down and ate each of those batons by hand, from the plate I was meant to share with my partner as he puttered around. You snooze, you lose. —Joe Sevier, senior editor, SEO & cooking ’Tis the season for zucchini recipes. When there’s so much of it around (for such affordable prices!), I like to grate as much as I possibly can into my evening bowls of pasta. Like in this spaghetti recipe, which I developed for the 2026 Farmers Market Challenge. It’s like Amatriciana, sort of, thanks to plenty of guanciale and garlic. But instead of tomatoes, there are three whole pounds of shredded zucchini tossed into the pot. I’ll be eating it outside until fall hits. —Rebecca Firkser, Test Kitchen editor Years ago, I was dating a guy who would make cilantro-mint chutney in big batches and freeze it, defrosting it block by block so we could use it as a dip or drizzle over pretty much everything. This week, I found myself with a hankering for that same spicy sauce, so I cast around for a recipe I thought might be similar. I landed on this one, but allowed for adjustments—less spice, no sugar, and I was generous with my salt. I also added in a spoonful of Greek yogurt to make it creamy. I’ve used it all week—as a dip for quesadillas, as a drizzle atop scrambled eggs, and as a secret weapon to juice up rotisserie chicken tacos. —Sam Stone, senior editor It’s not often that I cook for lunch. I’m quite happy scrounging around my fridge for a fistful of baby carrots and a few knobs of cheese. But when Test Kitchen editor Rebecca Firkser published her newest Good for You recipe, she had my full attention. Her Veggie Club Sandwich promises to keep you pleasantly full while supplying a meal’s worth of veggies between three slices of bread. Rebecca makes the point that you hardly need a recipe to make a sandwich, but in this case you’ll be glad to follow her direction. A marvel of edible construction, this sando requires strategic placement of each component to ensure no filling slips out the back when you take a bite. A well-placed toothpick won’t hurt either. —Carly Westerfield, manager, audience strategy

item.title: Airfares Are at Record Highs. Here's How to Find Affordable Flights
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 5.51
To the chagrin of budget travelers everywhere, airfares have continued to climb to new highs throughout 2026. In July 2026, for example, average airfares were nearly 26% more expensive than in July 2025, according to data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics—a significant hit to travelers’ wallets. And unfortunately, due to a complex web of geopolitical and economic factors, prices aren’t expected to drop anytime soon. Historically, fall is the time of year when airfares cool off, but this year, shoulder season deals are harder than ever to find. In fact, airfares for fall are trending about 2% higher compared to summer prices, according to Expedia. Average airfares this autumn for domestic flights range from about $150 to $400 roundtrip, according to data emailed from Going. On international routes, flights to Europe are as high as $800 roundtrip, and airfares to the Caribbean are reaching up to $500. However, while it might sound hopeless to try to scour booking sites for a good deal, rest assured there are tried-and-true strategies that travelers can use for finding reasonably priced fares through the end of the year. “Flexibility is key—both with dates and destination—to find affordable flights this fall,” says Jennifer Yellin, managing editor of Points Path, which shows travelers flight search results priced in points and miles. Here are our top tips for unlocking affordable airfares through the end of the year. Target an airline and airport known for deals Your choice of carrier, airport of origin, and destination can all play a major part in the final cost of your airfare. Aim to fly into or out of an airport that has a strong track record of offering affordable flights. Going analyzed its 2026 flight deal data to find the US airports that have offered the most affordable departing flights so far in 2026. It found the best airports for cheap domestic flights were Denver (DEN), with 150 departing flight deals that cost an average of $219; New Orleans (MSY), which had 166 deals that were about $228; and Orlando (MCO), which offered 146 deals at an average of $211. Other top airports for domestic deals were Fort-Lauderdale (FLL), Los Angeles (LAX), Charleston (CHS), Raleigh-Durham (RDU), Tampa (TPA), Portland (PDX), and Las Vegas (LAS). The best US airports for international flight deals were Boston (BOS), with 415 deals at about $451 roundtrip; New York (JFK), which has seen 404 international deals so far this year at an average of $445; and Newark (EWR), which has had 333 international deals for about $450 each. Other top airports for international deals included Chicago (ORD), Los Angeles (LAX), Raleigh-Durham (RDU), Orlando (MCO), Miami (MIA), Washington Dulles (IAD), and Austin (AUS). Departing from one of these airports can add up to significant savings. If it’s feasible, consider driving or taking a train to one of these to score discounted airfare for your next big trip. Some airlines offer a greater number of deals, too. Going found that American Airlines offers the most domestic deals (646 so far in 2026), and United offers the most international deals (1,850 and counting this year). Looking to these carriers first could help uncover the most affordable fare quickly. Carefully time your trip The timing of your vacation can make all the difference in finding affordable airfare. Shoulder season is traditionally an off-peak stretch with added savings for travelers, but with off-season deals shrinking, fliers need to get even more specific with timing. Specifically, consider pushing back your fall getaway as late on the calendar as possible, and just before hitting the start of the winter holidays. “Summer demand has spilled into fall,” according to Expedia’s fall travel outlook report. Pushing trips later into October or the first week of November could be a sweet spot for fare savings. In most years, the week of Thanksgiving is usually a guaranteed window for international flight deals from the US because domestic travel soars at this time. But 2026 has put a bit of wrench in that convention, too. International flights around Thanksgiving this year are averaging $1,096 roundtrip, according to Going. It’s still the more affordable window compared to December, when the average international fare swells up to $1,695. Travelers on the hunt for an international deal should plan to fly on the Thanksgiving holiday itself to save up to 25% and plan to book their flights by early October, per Going’s guidance. Using search tools that allow you to look over a stretch of several days to find the cheapest fare, like Google Flights, also helps. “You might find shifting your dates by a date or two in either direction can save you a significant amount of money,” Yellin says. As a general rule of thumb, Saturdays, Tuesdays, and Wednesdays tend to be the most affordable days of the week to fly, according to data from Expedia and Going. Leverage your points and miles Put those hard-earned frequent flier miles and credit card points to work for you to unlock airfares. It’s possible to compare the best airfare deal across credit cards and loyalty programs if you use the right search tool. Points Path, for one, plugs into Google Flights to help travelers compare prices. The tool will “tell you if using cash or points is a better deal, without having to search multiple airline websites individually,” Yellin says. Target your flight search to departure airports that regularly offer the greatest number of points and miles deals. In the US those include: New York (JFK), Boston (BOS), Los Angeles (LAX), Chicago (ORD), Dallas-Fort Worth (DFW), Going says. Where to find specific deals this shoulder season Going’s intel shows that a handful of destinations have a better chance of offering flight deals this fall. For international trips “Portugal, Spain, Italy, Greece, the ABC islands, and Scandinavia are seeing nice shoulder season fare dips,” according to Anna LaBrie, Going’s senior PR manager. “Japan and Southeast Asia are worth watching too, along with Mexico, outside of Día de Muertos.” On the domestic side, “Hawaii, Florida, Phoenix, the Pacific Northwest, Atlanta, the Carolinas, and San Diego are showing softer prices this fall," LaBrie says, noting that travelers should avoid ski towns like Jackson Hole and Aspen, where airfares are beginning to spike. Recent fall fare deals from Going include Boston to Madrid for $517 roundtrip—a 49% discount—and Los Angeles to Tokyo for $613 roundtrip, which is 48% cheaper than average. That’s encouraging evidence that there are good flight deals to uncover this fall, if you know the right tactics for finding them.

item.title: A New Museum, Cruise Haute Couture, and Gorgeous Glassware: Here's What's Exciting Us in Travel Right Now
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 5.41
Whether you're on land or at sea, in a bar or in Bahrain, there are myriad reasons for design lovers to get excited about travel right now. In the September/October 2026 issue of Condé Nast Traveler, we went long on a number of these stories—how Como's enduring craft traditions help make it one of the planet's most luxurious destinations, why Fort Worth is the sartorial epicenter of the rise of ranchcore in fashion. But we also collected a few juicy morsels worth sharing in brief. There's a new museum in the Middle East to earmark if you're interested in the intersection of craft and history, and a French cruise line has launched a new itinerary that will bring haute couture to the high seas. Read on for all we think you should know. A gem of a new museum on Bahrain's pearling path “Inside an elegant home formerly owned by a wealthy merchant family in Bahrain's coastal city of Muharraq sits the two-year-old Siyadi Pearl Museum. The space is the latest addition to the Pearling Path, which connects important structures from the city's pearling history. Along its two miles are 17 significant sites; public squares shaded by flame trees; and a pedestrian bridge that reconnects Muharraq with its original shoreline, which has been mostly lost to development. Terrazzo lampposts topped by pearl-shaped light bulbs double as trail markers. Tales of wealth are told in the grand living quarters of merchants and traders; those of hardship in the display of the simple tools pearl divers relied on (nose clips, stone weights, leather finger covers) during arduous months aboard dhows at sea.” —Nicola Chilton High fashion comes to the high seas “In September 2027, French line Ponant will sail a commonly traveled route along Italy's coast with an entirely unique agenda: placing the country's fashion maisons at the center of the passenger experience. Sailing down the coast from Tuscany and then up to Venice, guests on board the intimate Le Boréal will experience five major haute labels. They will chat with a Brioni tailor about making the perfect alterations; observe a master craftsperson cut precious gemstones at iconic jeweler Pomellato; and explore two historic sites in Florence tied to Gucci via the Palazzo Gucci and the 15th-century Palazzo Settimanni, home to the Gucci archives. Think of this as high fashion on the high seas.” —Erin Florio Drinks wear designer around the globe “Striking, artisanal glassware that upstages the concoction it holds is the coolest thing in cocktail culture these days. Here, bars around the world and the gorgeously unique vessels you may just encounter while there.” —Michelle Tchea This article appeared in the September/October 2026 issue of Condé Nast Traveler. Subscribe to the magazine here.

item.title: Where to Stay in Great Smoky Mountains National Park for Mountain Views and Fall Foliage
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 5.11
Frequently named the most visited national park in the US, Great Smoky Mountains have universal appeal—travelers come from all over the country (and the world) to enjoy the natural beauty of this part of North Carolina and Tennessee. Hikers, anglers, photographers, road-trippers, birders, families, and thrill-seekers can all find reasons to make the trek. Whether you want to see the namesake fog blanketing the peaks—many of which tower well over 6,000 feet—breathe in the crisp air, or glimpse the famous wildflowers and fall foliage, there’s plenty to do, and some excellent places to spend the night once you get here. From the historic LeConte Lodge—the only lodging within the park’s boundaries—with its hard-to-come-by reservations and hike-in access to some of the South’s most luxurious hotels—Blackberry Farm and The Swag are legendary in the hospitality world—there’s something for every type of traveler. Whether it’s your first time exploring the park or you’re planning a return trip, you have options for where to set up your base camp. You can opt for a rustic cabin rental, a kid-friendly resort, or a stylish glamping site depending on your mood. Read on for some of the best places to stay near Great Smoky Mountains National Park for your next nature-filled adventure. How to plan a trip to Great Smoky Mountains National Park How do you get to Great Smoky Mountains National Park? Great Smoky Mountains National Park sits along the border of North Carolina and Tennessee. If you’re flying into the area, McGhee Tyson Airport (TYS) in Knoxville, Tennessee, and Asheville Regional Airport (AVL) are among the most convenient options. From TYS, it’s a 30- and 60-minute drive, respectively, to the park’s main entrances in Townsend and Gatlinburg, Tennessee. The drive from AVL to the entrance in Cherokee, North Carolina, will take you a little over an hour. When is the best time to visit Great Smoky Mountains National Park? Undoubtedly, the best time to visit Great Smoky Mountains National Park is in the fall. If you time it right—keep an eye on the foliage reports—you’ll witness the splendor of all the reds, oranges, and yellows. The changing colors typically start to appear in late September, and they peak between mid-October and mid-to-early November, depending on the weather and elevation. This time of year also tends to be the busiest season in the park, so keep that in mind when you’re planning a trip (book early and visit mid-week if possible). How long should you visit the Great Smoky Mountains? Because of the size and plethora of things to do within the park, you’ll want to plan for multiple days of exploration—I’d recommend at least three. That way, you can drive the scenic loops, complete a few hikes, and check off all the major sites without rushing. This gallery has been updated with new information since its original publish date.

item.title: 'The Gentlemen' Season 2 Takes Us From English Country Estates to Italian Palazzos in Mob Territory
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 5.03
On Location peels back the curtain on some of your favourite films, television shows, and more. This time, we ask: where was The Gentlemen Season 2 filmed? The second season of Guy Ritchie’s hit Netflix series, The Gentleman, is here. The first series introduced us to Eddie Horniman (Theo James), a young British aristocrat who had inherited his father’s grand country estate, only to discover that behind the family money was a secret cannabis empire. In Season 2, Horniman, now the Duke of Halstead, is keen to expand the operation, alongside his business partner, Susie Glass (Kaya Scodelario). This will take them out of the English countryside and subterranean criminal worlds of the East End and Liverpool, and thrust them instead into the world of the Mafia, as they attempt to go international and do business with the dangerous Capo dei Capi, Marco Moretti (Sergio Castellito). “The madness of Italy’s beauty, its culture, its history and its traditions was something I felt would fit perfectly into our show,” says Ritchie. “I had wanted to expand the canvas of The Gentlemen in this season. Italy was just an obvious choice. British gangsters colliding with the Italian Mafia just feels so right for our world. Some fruit hangs low and looks so tasty you just can’t resist for very long.” Here are some of the key locations used in the filming of The Gentleman Seasons 1 and 2, from Ritchie’s Ashcombe Estate to Lake Maggiore in Italy. Is The Gentlemen based on a real-life story? Both the film of the same name and the two seasons of The Gentlemen are not based on a true story, though of course, they borrow elements from the criminal underworld and its cast of characters. The situation that Eddie Horniman and his family find themselves in – of having to find new ways to monetise their vast aristocratic estates – is a reality, however. There are no real life examples of aristocrats running cannabis empires that we know of though. The main thrust of the action in Season 2 of The Gentlemen takes place in Lake Maggiore, connecting Horniman and his business partner Katie Glass to Italy’s criminal gangs – the mafia. Historically, the area has not been known as a mafia heartland – unlike regions like Sicily, for example – but it does have a relationship with organised crime. In particular, the ’Ndrangheta, the Calabrian mafia, have reportedly used the area for cocaine and weapons trafficking, thanks to its close proximity to the Swiss border. Where was The Gentlemen Season 2 filmed? The Badminton Estate, Gloucestershire While some scenes of The Gentleman were filmed on stage sets at Alperton Studios in Wembley, London, the exterior of Halstead Manor, the fictional home of the Horniman family, is The Badminton Estate. The real-life home of the Duke and Duchess of Beaufort is a popular filming location and wedding venue in the south Gloucestershire countryside. Viewers with a keen eye may recognise the property from Netflix favourite Bridgerton and movies including Pearl Harbour and 28 Days Later. The sprawling estate has been occupied for thousands of years, and the remains of several Roman villas surround the main home. The medieval property was owned by the Boteler family before Edward Somerset, fourth Earl of Worcester, purchased the manors of Great and Little Badminton in 1612. It’s his son, Sir Thomas Somerset, who made significant alterations to the original house, and the property has captured the imagination of high society and even the royal family over the centuries – Charles II stayed in the house, and the late Queen Elizabeth II was a regular visitor to the annual Horse Trials. “Badminton felt immediately right for Halstead,” says supervising location Manager Iggy Ellis, “because it’s a proper, lived-in home rather than a National Trust museum. So inside, there’d be some walking sticks by the door or a few shotgun rounds from where they’d been out shooting. There were cracks and tired bits, as you’d get in every family home. But there was also oil painting and history and majesty. It felt perfect for our story.” Ashcombe Estate, Wiltshire In episode one, Ritchie made his own country estate, Ashcombe Park, available for filming a shooting party scene. “That was a lot of fun but tricky at times too,” says production designer Martyn John. “You’re in the middle of nowhere with no phone signal or internet. We had to take everything in; so, flowers, food, dogs, guns and also… frozen partridges.” Ashcombe is a working farm set in 1,100 acres of rolling chalk land, and is named after the ash trees and the valleys (‘combes’) that monopolise much of it. It has been the family home of Ritchie since 2001 (when he bought it with ex-wife Madonna for £9 million), and was previously the home of photographer Cecil Beaton. Loseley Park, Surrey Much like in season one, some of the exterior and interior scenes at Halstead Manor were filmed at Loseley Park, a historic home just outside of Guildford that is now used as a wedding venue. “Where possible we tried to maximise every location because when you move around it costs money that could be on the screen,” explains supervising locations manager Iggy Ellis. “So we used a cottage in the grounds of Loseley for the exteriors of gamekeeper Geoff’s cottage and built the interior in the studio because we needed lots of camera space and somewhere for Geoff’s menagerie of animals.” Swakeleys House, Ickenham Another multi-purpose location was Swakeleys House, a 17th-century mansion in Ickenham. “It was a great find because we were able to use it for so many things,” explains Ellis. “From the rehab centre where Freddie is recovering from the cocaine habit he acquired in the first series to the interior of the prison where Bobby Glass is meant to be serving time.” Built in 1638, it is an excellent example of the ‘Artisan Mannerism’ architectural style, a form of Jacobean architecture that features decorative classical flourishes such as gable ends. It was the home of Sir Edmund Wright, Lord Mayor of London, and was visited twice by the famed diarist Samuel Pepys. The Adelphi Building, London The Adelphi Building off The Strand was transformed into an auction house for a scene in which Susie Glass bids millions for a Botticelli painting, which is later snatched by a gang on e-bikes outside. “I wanted to use that network of streets around the Savoy Hotel, including a secret little tunnel that cuts between John Adam Street and the riverside,” explains Ellis of the chase. “It takes at least three months’ notice to get London streets closed for filming, and there were some careful negotiations with everyone from Westminster Council to building owners and the Savoy Hotel itself. But that amazing chase really is one of the things I’m most proud of.” The Grade II-listed Adelphi has retained many of its original 1930s Art Deco features, including its impressive stone facade, classic columns and Gilbert Ledwood sculptures. Today it is predominantly used as an office space, and houses the publisher Condé Nast, whose titles include not only Condé Nast Traveler, but also Vogue, Tatler and GQ. Villa Rusconi Clerici, Lake Maggiore Villa Rusconi Clerici became the glamorous palazzo home of Mafia heiress (and Eddie’s love interest) Contessa Isabella Savanza de Parme, known as Bella. “We spent three full days looking at several amazing palazzos, including one on Lake Como,” shares John. “But as soon as I saw the one at Lake Maggiore, I knew this was the one. It was in a much less touristy area and it had such great light and glittering water. You could point the camera anywhere and it just looked beautiful.” The interiors too were perfect for Bella’s home. “I wanted a house or a villa which reflected the taste – if not the scale – of Eddie’s country estate, Halstead Manor” says Ellis. “I wanted these two aristocratic families to merge, stylistically. So, you have all the antiques and the paintings that reflect tradition and ancestry, but also modern pieces because, despite the centuries-old history of both families, there’s a new generation in charge now.” Villa Rusconi Clerici is a beautifully preserved 19th-century palazzo on the Piedmont shore of Lake Maggiore, and unsurprisingly is popular as a wedding venue. The villa that exists today was built for a Hungarian colonel and revolutionary, Stefano Türr, who was married to one of Emperor Napoleon’s cousins and became intrinsic to the unification of Italy. The interiors are Art Nouveau in style, including a grand staircase featuring a wrought iron balustrade. Grand Hotel Majestic, Lake Maggiore The Grand Hotel Majestic stood in for the fictional The Grand Hotel, where a wedding takes place later in the series. First built in 1870, it was one of the finest examples of luxury hospitality in the area, and was immediately popular with the international elite. Unsurprisingly, considering its location on the shores of Lake Maggiore, it is often chosen as a wedding venue for modern couples, much like in the show. One of its chief assets is the view across the lake to Borromeo Island, with actor Theo James pictured standing on one of the balconies looking out across the water in one scene. While the interiors are French in style, with parquet flooring and chandeliers, the grounds are also particularly lavish, with centuries-old trees and flowers, and there’s even a small private beach. Chiesa San Leonardo, Lake Maggiore The 16th-century church Chiesa San Leonardo also features in the new season. Located in the lakeside village of Pallanza, the church features striking columns of pink Baveno granite, as well as 17th-century wooden sculptures and altars. There’s also a 65-metre high bell tower, as well as access to the lake from a dramatic staircase. Where was The Gentleman Season 1 filmed? Stoke Court, Buckinghamshire The Badminton Estate gets much of the credit for appearing as the exterior of the fictional Halstead Manor, but some of the interior scenes used Stoke Court in Buckinghamshire. Stoke Court is home to the study, where Freddie shoots Liverpudlian drug dealer Tommy after a memorable scene featuring a chicken costume, Halstead Manor’s boot room, drawing room and orangery. The real-life property is best known for its association with mid-18th-century poet Thomas Gray, who holidayed there during his childhood. Wrotham Park, Hertfordshire Wrotham Park in Hertfordshire plays the part of the home of extravagantly wealthy drug lord Stanley Johnson, aka Bridgewater House. The neo-Palladian English country house was designed by Isaac Ware in 1754, and it’s where we see Susie Glass and Stanley engage in a polite-ish war of words over his desire to take over her father’s empire. London The Gentleman’sfilming locations depict two sides of the coin: lavish country houses owned by the landed gentry and hideouts used by the criminal underworld. For the latter, the locations team looked to London. Locations used across the capital include The Reform Club in Pall Mall, which doubled up for Pinky’s Club, and Billingsgate Market, which is mentioned by name in the series as the headquarters of the Liverpudlian drug group. The exterior shots of the Croydon Tower Block were taken at Brandon Estate, while the boxing ring is the now-closed party venue Printworks in Rotherhithe.

item.title: The Best Fall Foliage in the USA: A Guide to Where to Go This Autumn
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 4.51
It’s a rare occasion that vast swaths of the United States experience a season in a similar way—but the sepia-toned mosaic of fall foliage soon to sprawl across the country in a few short weeks proves that fall is the one exception to that rule. Starting as early as late September and extending well into November, you can expect to find some combination of red, gold, yellow, and orange bathing the trees from coast to coast. But anyone well-versed in leaf-peeping—or the colloquial nickname given to any tourist with a proclivity for fall foliage gazing—knows that some states and regions have more colorful and sweeping offerings than others. So for any looking to leaf-peep-maxx this upcoming fall, we took the liberty of rounding up the states, parks, and areas from across the country where you can expect to find the most vibrant fall tableaus come this October. Blue Ridge Mountains, North Georgia Way down on the south of the eastern shore you’ll find a range of mountains absolutely awash for fall. The Blue Ridge Mountain region of North Georgia makes up a smaller enclave of the greater Appalachian Mountains—and though you can’t go wrong with any stop along the Appalachian Trail when it comes to fall foliage, this little corner right on the border between Georgia and Tennessee is especially ideal for the changing seasons. The Southern climate makes things a little milder, without having to sacrifice the fall grandeur. The area skews more towards nature aficionados, with plenty of nature paths and mountain trails to climb. One particular favorite includes Brasstown Bald, where you can catch the best view of the leaves in peak color. Where to stay in the Blue Ridge Mountains: - A charming Victorian B&B: Blue Ridge Inn Bed & Breakfast - A peaceful mountain escape: The Copperhead Lodge The Berkshires, Massachusetts When it comes to the idyllic pastoral regions of New England, Massachusetts’s Berkshires are right up there with the likes of New York's Adirondacks. One look around and you can see exactly how the lush area inspired writers like Edith Wharton and artists like Norman Rockwell (and if you don’t, just take a quick trip to the Norman Rockwell Museum). Other highlights for our Berkshires guide includes shopping at stores like Fluff Alpaca, hiking up Monument Mountain’s three different trails, grabbing some coffee beans from West Stockbridge’s famous No. Six Depot, and ordering a bite off the farm-to-table menu at Prairie Whale. Pair all of that with the area’s bustling boutique hotel scene in Lenox, Massachusetts, and you’ve got one must-see stop on your Great American leaf-peeping tour. Where to stay in the Berkshires: - For an artistic flair: 33 Main - A motor-lodge-turned luxury hotel: Life House Stowe, Vermont Nestled in the embrace of Vermont’s Green Mountains, Stowe might be known for its slopes and skiing—but it’s also one of the best places to catch a verifiable sea of fall foliage come October and November. This is your quintessential idyllic northern New England escape. While it’s had its fair share of development, there are plenty of locals who reside in the town year-round. Pre-game leaf-peeping by exploring the microbrewing scene or shopping for some top-of-the-line maple products at Shaw’s General Store. It’s also something of a hikers paradise, with absolutely no small shortage of trails for the ambitious explorers and gentler strollers alike. No matter what you choose, there’s sure to be one fantastic view. Where to stay in Stowe, Vermont: - For a hygge vibe: Field Guide - A spa-retreat: AWOL Stowe - A traditionally intimate ski lodge: Edson Hill Great Smoky Mountains, Tennessee and North Carolina The Great Smoky Mountains that trail up the border between Tennessee and North Carolina earned their name from the natural, gauzy fog that often drapes across the region. It gives the area an ethereal, almost otherworldly quality during any time of year. Add in a mosaic of fall foliage and it's no wonder why this spot is home to some of the best fall foliage in the USA. See the sights from the famous Cades Cove loop or hike the Laurel Falls Trail or any of the many paths along the mountains. You’ll also find a range of different lodging options in the area—including glamping experiences, cabins, farms, and more. Where to stay in the Great Smoky Mountains: - An irreverent farm getaway: Blackberry Farm - A sprawling ranch: Cataloochee Ranch - A one-of-a-kind glamping stay: Under Canvas Great Smoky Mountains Aspen, Colorado Aspen is one of those cold weather destinations that’s spoken of with an undeniable air of prestige—the same way you would speak of Lake Como in the spring, or the French Riviera in summer. Like Stowe, it’s most famous for its skiing, but it’s got its fair share of foliage to show off around fall. Especially ideal for those who have a taste for the finer things in life, Aspen’s also a prime luxury shopping destination. Shop high end designer brands like Prada or Gucci, and grab a chic cowboy hat from Kemo Sabe. And you can’t forget the decadent fare available at eateries like Bosq, White House Tavern, Matsushia, and more. Where to stay in Aspen, Colorado: - An Aspen mainstay: Hotel Jerome Sun Valley, Idaho Another skiing staple, Sun Valley has long charmed celebrities and nature-lovers alike. It’s renowned for its skiing but offers golden escape during the shoulder season of fall. Sun Valley’s especially great for any leaf peepers who happen to also be fans of Ernest Hemingway. The famous Lost Generation author loved the region and even finished his book For Whom The Bell Tolls in the Sun Valley Resort’s suite 206. Hemingway’s admiration of and attachment to the area is immortalized with with a memorial and free audio walking tour. Where to stay in Sun Valley, Idaho: - A historic ski resort: Sun Valley Resort - For a laidback lodging: Limelight Ketchum North Cascades, Washington New England often takes the cake when it comes to fall foliage, but don’t write off the Pacific Northwest. One drive along the Cascade Loop will show that this craggy region has its own verdancy amid the snow dusted mountains. Often referred to as the American Alps, there are plenty of peaks and summits to see the leaves—such as the Washington Pass overlooking the Liberty Bell Mountain—while hiking trails like the Maple Pass Loop and Blue Lake offer some of the best opportunities for leaf-peeping. Where to stay in North Cascades, Washington: - A floating cabin: Ross Lake Resort Laurel Hill, Pennsylvania There are plenty of trails and state parks you can take advantage of to gaze at the Pennsylvania foliage. There’s Mount Davis, Ohiopyle State Park, Laurel Hill state park, and so much more. You really can’t go wrong with any of them. But we’d recommend conducting your leaf peeping from inside, specifically inside one of famous architect Frank Lloyd Wright’s most well-known works. Dubbed Fallingwater, this quintessentially mid-century modern structure sits atop a waterfall and is entirely ensconced in a forest of trees—making its airy interiors the ideal framing for the lush colors of fall. Where to stay in Laurel Highlands Pennsylvania: - A sprawling estate: Nemacolin Franconia Notch State Park, New Hampshire Rounding off the New England stops, this nature reserve is nestled in the middle of New Hampshire’s White Mountain National Forest. Here, you’ll find parts of the larger Appalachian Trail, as well as hikes up well-known peaks like Artist Bluff—which afford panoramic views of the area’s famous Echo Lake. The body of water sits at the base of Cannon Mountain and perfectly reflects the prism of color around it, even more so when those colors are the rich reds, golds, yellows, and oranges of fall. Where to stay in Franconia Notch State Park, New Hampshire: - A mansion inn: The Franconia Inn Adirondacks, New York You just need to watch one episode of Gilmore Girls to know that New England is one of the top best places to see fall foliage, and the Adirondacks is one of the region’s best fall exports. Located just about four hours outside of New York City, this mountain area encompasses much of New York’s storied “upstate” region—where people escape from the city to ensconce themselves in the privacy of cozy cabins, lake houses, and more. Here, you’ll find over 3,000 lakes and ponds—such as the famous Lake Placid—and the Adirondack High Peaks. Grab a quick drink at Raquette River Brewing or fill up on French-Canadian comfort dishes at Woodshed on Park, before heading out to take in the vivid leaves. Where to stay in the Adirondacks: - For a luxurious lake island resort: The Sagamore Resort - A rustic log cabin experience: The Point - A Lake Placid classic: Great Adirondack Hotel Columbia River Gorge, Northern Oregon Just above California and below other fall foliage fave Washington, the Northern Oregon region similarly offers plenty of mystically foggy places to peep some leaves. What’s even better is you get the best of both worlds with forests and beaches colliding to make up this scenic coast. Travel through the Columbia River Gorge to see all the leaves, then take a road trip out to Cannon Beach to top the adventure off. Where to stay in Northern Oregon: - A water-front property: Cannery Pier Hotel & Spa Shenandoah National Park, Virginia Just off the Blue Ridge Parkway, and not too far from the border of West Virginia, Shenandoah National Park extends about 197,439 acres across Virginia’s Blue Ridge region. It’s got breathtaking views and nature, making it ideal to catch some of the best fall foliage in the USA. After all, there's a reason we named it one of the best national parks to enjoy during the fall. Shenandoah is mostly visited for hiking, with over 500 miles of trails—many of which you can find along the area’s Skyline Drive—that offer ample opportunity to take in nature, no matter the time of year.

item.title: On California's Central Coast, an Indoor-Outdoor Museum Connects Visitors With Centuries of Chumash Heritage
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 4.32
The Chumash Heritage Marine Sanctuary was featured on Condé Nast Traveler's Bright Ideas in Travel 2025. Read the full list of winners here. I am greeted by cast iron doors, engraved with spiraling pictographs and cool to the touch, even in the morning heat of June. I grip the handle—shaped, I'll learn, like a clapper stick, a traditional Chumash percussion instrument—and push it open. The sounds of birdsong, layered and ambient, rise toward a curved ceiling where light moves like cloud shadow. Here, what lies indoors simulates the beauty of the natural world. I have entered an 'Ap, the Chumash word for home, reimagined at monumental scale. The traditional version would have been made of willow branches and tule reeds, but this one is steel and stone with the same circular, embracing shape: This is the 14,000-square-foot Santa Ynez Chumash Museum and Cultural Center, which opened on May 15, 2025, after 20 years in the making. Every detail has been designed with intention by Native American architect Johnpaul Jones. The ancestral home of the Chumash, the Indigenous Native American people who have lived along California's central coast for more than 13,000 years, spans from Malibu to Paso Robles, including the Northern Channel Islands. In 2024, Chumash stewardship of more than 4,500 square miles of sea and coast in this region was formalized on the federal level as part of the Chumash Heritage National Marine Sanctuary, the first-ever Indigenous-led marine sanctuary in the US. The new museum is the most visible piece of a broader, sustained effort to connect visitors to California's central coast with Chumash culture. The tribe's Culture Department runs a state-credentialed language program—two of its teachers hold the specialized credential that California created in 2008 for Native language instruction—alongside basket weaving classes, an archery club, a youth camp, and a cultural resource management team that protects tribal sites and artifacts. "The circular shapes of the buildings, the model of the oak tree where the coyote lives in the Maria Solares Discovery Center, and the west-facing direction of the buildings represent important symbolism to our people," says Kenneth Kahn, Chairman of the Santa Ynez Band of Chumash Indians. The museum faces the Western Gates, or Point Conception—a spot on the cliffs overlooking the Pacific Ocean, which tribal beliefs describe as the place one departs this world and enters the spirit realm. Felicia Cogorno, Education Programs & Volunteer Manager and tribal member, tells me that if I stand in exactly the right place in the center of the museum's main room, I'll hear my own voice come back to me. I find the spot—a subtle seam in the floor's inlaid pattern—and say something small and ordinary. For a moment, my voice and the birdsong, and the fire and the Sʰamala (Santa Ynez Band native language) words floating from a nearby speaker, are all one sound, indistinguishable from each other. Cogorno grew up on the reservation, on whose lands the center now stands, and manages its education programs and volunteers. She points to the ring of painted figures along the upper walls, each mid-movement, each representing a different animal, each placed at a different ancestral village along the central California coast. "If you were being welcomed to our village," she says, "you would be welcomed with singing and dancing." I wave my hand near the fire. The movement activates the walls where animals light up—deer, bear, condor—each one accompanied by a voice pronouncing its name in Sʰamala, the language of the Santa Ynez Band. The polished stone floor, meanwhile, is inlaid with a seasonal round: concentric rings mapping harvests and hunts and gathering times, labeled in Sʰamala and English, with a bit of Spanish woven in. As Cogorno explains, the arrival of the Gregorian calendar required new words for things that hadn't needed naming before. Before going further into the museum, I stop at a photograph of a woman hanging on the wall. I continue to see her image, reappearing throughout the galleries like a thread you keep finding in the weave. Her name is Maria Solares, I learn. In the early 1900s, she was one of the last fluent speakers of Sʰamala. Between 1914 and 1915, she worked with linguist John Peabody Harrington, sitting for sessions that produced wax cylinder recordings of the languages and more than 100,000 pages of notes. The language survived because she sat in that room and spoke. "She's my five-times great-grandmother," Cogorno says, matter-of-factly. "Many of our volunteers are also descendants of Maria." The permanent galleries are accessed off the ‘ap lobby area through a set of iron doors whose design, Cogorno mentions, was made by her aunt. Inside, the ceiling rises and the light changes, cooler, darker. The exhibit moves through the Chumash cosmology of three worlds—Upper, Middle, and Lower—stacked like basket trays. Most of what surrounds me is the Middle World, the et ya shoop ("here world") display. Cases hold stone tools, hunting materials, and abalone ceremony regalia. Paintings that line the walls show figures fishing, gathering, and paddling. The objects in the cases mirror what the figures carry. I stop at a case of abalone shells, cut into jewelry and adornments, and polished to a high shine, almost iridescent under the gallery lights. "My cousin made those," Cogorno says. Nearby, there's a swordfish headdress with intricate shell work—her aunt, who cast the door handles at the entrance, made that, too. In the Upper World gallery, a taxidermied California condor has her own case, her own story. In 1986, when only 27 California condors remained on earth, she was the last wild female of her species before she was captured, then put into a breeding program. Because of this, she raised the next generation and was released with them, teaching the young birds, somehow, to be condors in a world that had nearly erased them. Nearby, a painting depicts the Condor dance, one of the newer dances in the Chumash tradition. "To me, [the condor return] represents a cultural resurgence," Cogorno says. "We're still here. We're still thriving. We're not static." Outside, the Culture Park opens wide across the landscape. Native plantings—dogbane, yerba mansa—border brooks and pools that are fed by greywater, which the tribe recycles on-site. The limestone underfoot came from a quarry twenty minutes away. Further down the path stands the Tomol House, an open-slatted building that holds its namesake: a 950-pound plank canoe known as a tomol. It is not a relic, but a vessel that regularly hits the water. This very tomol has made what is known as “the crossing”—a culturally significant journey across 26 miles of open Pacific water from Ventura to the Channel Islands—multiple times. The crossing takes 10-13 hours, with 6 people sitting on their knees to paddle. Moving by feel and tradition toward an island they could reach in twenty minutes by motorboat. Jennifer, one of the museum's volunteers and one of the only women to captain a tomol, joins me inside. She talks about the crossing the way any athlete talks about a journey that changed them. "You really connect with past ancestors," she says. I continue on, following an audio narration, drawn from the voices of tribal leaders, that guides me through the middle of the museum, chronicling the mission period—a traumatic era that involved the boarding schools, the forced silencing of language, and the cutting of hair. A time when children were taken away and conditioned into believing their heritage shameful. But as I walk further, the room shifts to contemporary photographs. Ceremonies, children, laughter, a tomol coming into shore. A collection of moments that show the Chumash thriving. On my way out, I pass the seasonal round again—the acorns of fall, the fishing of summer—and I grip the clapper stick door handle one more time. The birds still sing overhead. I push through into the heat and the light, back into the valley the Chumash never left. The Santa Ynez Chumash Museum and Cultural Center is located in Santa Ynez, California, and is open Thursday through Sunday from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m.

item.title: RF Kuang's New Novel Takes On the Angst of a Diaspora Kid on a Study-Abroad Trip to Taipei
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 4.28
In RF Kuang’s latest book Taipei Story, the genre of the campus novel outgrows its name. The novel follows Chinese-American college freshman Lily Chen, who leaves the pale, male, and Yale environs of New Haven, Connecticut, for an intensive Mandarin-language program in Taipei for the summer. While her own family has never stepped foot in Taiwan, Lily holds onto the belief that perfecting her Mandarin will finally reconcile the shortcomings of being a diaspora kid. And when it came to choosing a place to study the language, traveling to Taiwan conveniently didn’t require her to apply for a visa. But on this quixotic mission to achieve total fluency, she finds that the gulf between her and her complicated family history won’t simply mend itself through diligent study. Her presumptions quickly unravel as she seeks answers in the gaps between economy seats on the flight from Boston to Taipei; in the uncertain, stilting words of Chinese heritage speakers; and in arthouse cinemas and concert halls she’s drawn to for the promise of blending in. From the seasonally inappropriate hot springs of Beitou to the glossy, souvenir-flogging halls of Taipei Taoyuan International Airport, the plot of this coming-of-age story doesn’t shy away from the uncomfortable realities of traveling abroad. Compounded by the sudden passing of Lily’s grandfather—which renders her initial motivation to study Mandarin moot—these follies only deepen beneath a veil of complicated mourning. And yet, they are also softened and forgiven with a grace that comes uniquely from allowing ourselves to be vulnerable in foreign places. Condé Nast Traveler recently spoke with Kuang about how home, identity, and being split between two places inspired Taipei Story, which is available in bookstores now. This interview has been edited and condensed for length and clarity. Walk us through your research itinerary for Taipei Story. The first place I looked was personal experience. When I started jotting down notes for what would become this book, I didn't know what it was going to be. I was just trying to make legible a tough time in my life when my Gong Gong passed away and I was in Taiwan. I was also in an intensive language program where I was wandering aimlessly around Taipei, meditating on [concepts of] home and cultural alienation. I wasn't walking around with a research agenda. I was just following crowds into places to see what they were seeing. If a long line of people was swarming, I would just join it. I would end up at screenings of movies I'd never heard of, or bookstores that I didn't know existed because I felt so blank, confused, and empty. I wanted somebody else to show me the answer to, “what is your city?” and if I became a ghost in its wake, was there a way I could totally erase myself? A lot of the descriptions in the novel where Lily ends up going to a place by accident, like the National Concert Hall, are places I also encountered by accident. Then, I started thinking about turning all those notes into an exaggerated, fictionalized version of what this experience would be—like if I were even younger and more dim-witted about how the world works. I read a lot of the major modern Taiwanese authors [like Kaori Li, Bai Xianyong, Chen Yingzhen, Wu Ming-yi, and Yang Shaung-zi—all mentioned in the author’s note and available in English translation] and wondered how they were thinking about home, identity, and being split between their mainland cultural heritage, and what it meant to be Taiwanese. How does this novel interface with—the sometimes impossible—expectations of homecoming? I'm fascinated with fantasies of homecoming and the narratives we buy into about how certain cultural experiences can return you to the fold. A lot of Chinese heritage speakers end up getting these flattened experiences in the US that feel like touch points, but are actually silly ways to reconnect—distilled cultural simulations such as Lunar New Year, red envelope parties, and film screenings. I say this not to mock diasporic kids; it makes total sense. You get so little, so you take whatever you can have, even if it's not region-specific or what your parents experienced. In Lily's case, I'm fascinated by the promises of heritage speaker-study abroad programs (editor’s note: these are linguistic immersion programs designed for students who grew up in households speaking a second language) because they hold so much promise and meaning for many people attending them. With Taiwan in particular, if you think about it just on the logical level, every step of this premise that you could, as a Chinese-American, go to Taiwan, to study Mandarin, to feel closer to your family on the mainland—is crazy. Lily's family has never been to Taiwan. She's the only person who's ever stepped foot there until her mom has a layover. When she finally gets there, she starts learning all the ways in which she is so wrong and how her experiences of Chineseness and the trajectory of her family history has absolutely nothing to do with Taiwan. In the end, she is a little more aware of this complexity and moves towards a more genuine, honest encounter of a strange place. She's like, I'm a foreigner, this is a weird summer, and maybe that's okay. In what ways does foreignness, or a lack of fluency, act as a source of fuel for travel and exploration in this novel? I definitely think [feeling out of place] is generative because I’ve felt like an outsider culturally for most of my life. My family immigrated [to the US from Guangzhou when Kuang was four-years-old], and I never felt like I quite belonged in the world of Dallas, Texas. I was a pretty happy kid, but when you're on the periphery, observing how people behave, I think you just get more perceptive. When I go back to China, that’s also not home, which is not a unique perspective. I think almost every immigrant kid feels this way. When I'm in China, I am looking at my family, and I observe cultural codes that they're following, and I have to figure out how these rules work because I didn't grow up understanding them innately. Being reflective about all of this makes you a good writer. In Lily's case I don't think she perceives her bumbling and ignorance as virtues. For her, it’s a barrier between her and the rest of the world. Because she's so afraid of getting things wrong, she never asks for help and never willing to embarrass herself. The ethical argument that the book is making is that embarrassment is really good for you. To admit, “I don't know what's going on,” and also “somebody helped me,” is an attitude I wish we all embraced more, not just when we're traveling, but in our entire lives. I find it a strength, and Lily finds it a weakness, and by the end of the book, she's at least accepted that she's gonna mess up, and she might as well own it. From the Poppy War trilogy to your last novel Katabasis, you often take on the perspective of being a student. Why return to the eyes of an undergraduate for this story? This book was very different because it's the first book of mine where the protagonists weren't growing up with me. When I was working on the Poppy War trilogy, I was a teenager, and they're teenagers, then they're undergrads, grad students, and in their late-20s. I was writing very reflexively to try to understand the world from my vantage point in life, but I had a couple of life changes in the past few years that made me more interested in going back. With the maturity of turning 30, I have more comfort in making fun of the person I used to be. When I was writing Taipei Story, it was like, I could write a memoir of what I experienced, or I could make things even more ridiculous, even more embarrassing, and reach back to the person I was when I was 18 going to Beijing for the first time and overwhelmed with everything I didn't know. The key to writing from the point-of-view of adolescence is not from this position of condescension that the youths are so silly, but to be kind to your younger self and recognize that all of your insecurities, all the things that you were failing at, everything that you got wrong, are deeply hilarious and also a really shared experience. There's a lot of humanity in cringe. By setting a story in modern-day Taipei, the narrative acknowledges Taiwanese-Chinese geopolitics, and beyond that, the country’s past with Japanese colonialism, the Chinese Civil War. How did you want to depict Taipei as a city with those layered histories? I wanted to be really cautious here, because I'm not Taiwanese. I'm not an expert in Taiwanese history or literature. As I pointed out in the author's note, this is not a voice from the inside but the very filtered perception of an American teenager who’s learning about all of this for the first time. I did want to poke gentle fun at the way that people generally take Western ideological frameworks that are very binary and project them onto local histories with no attention to what locals are actually saying. There's the first chapter where her little cohort of friends are running around the city, and there’s a pecking order based on assumptions about race. People would ask her where should we go? What should we eat? And she’d always pretend to know the answers and go Google them in the bathroom. They do the same thing when they're at Chiang Kai-Shek Memorial Hall trying to understand, is he a good guy or a bad guy? Is he like George Washington? Should we be taking selfies with him? I wanted to give the experience of somebody who feels like they ought to be an expert by virtue of the ethnicity that they were born into, but who’s actually totally detached from genuine knowledge of the place or history. How did grief form your characterization of Taipei? [When Lily’s grandfather passed] it was a snapping moment for her. Up until that point, she is trying to slot all of her experiences into this predetermined narrative that this is getting her closer to the person she could have been if her family had never left China. After her grandfather passes, she is thrown into this weird grief and confusion, and she gives up on that goal altogether. She recognizes the futility of trying to go back and becoming a version of herself that never existed. Paradoxically, this frees her up to take in the things she closed her mind off to before. Now, she's okay with being a tourist. She goes on these Klook experiences [to Pinglin Tea Museum and Yehliu Geopark]. She’s on a bus with American families from Philly doing all the canned, predetermined activities just thinking, “oh, this is fun,” and learning a lot. Despite all the complex grief that is in this novel, it’s also very funny. Is Taipei a place that is particularly funny to you or has its own language of humor that you wanted to capture here? I think every place has surprising, inexplicable quirks if you know how to pay attention to them. One in particular I'm obsessed with is Taiwan English. I was inspired by a blog post by Tao Lin, an author who also wrote a novel called Taipei. It was just a series of pictures that he took walking around of ridiculous translations, and some of them are accurate on a very literal, character-by-character level, and some of them, I can't believe you would get this result if you ran it through any translation app. But it's not just in Taiwan either. You see it on the mainland. For instance, my mom was wearing a shirt, that just said, “GO FUCK” in repeating block letters. She bought it at a clothes market with her sister when she was in China, and she was only paying attention to the fabric, and she was like, “Oh, it's so lovely. Does this color look good on me?” and didn't register the text at all. I said, “Mom, do you know what that says?” She turned it inside out and wore it that way for the rest of the day.

item.title: The Best Beaches in Miami, From Nature Reserves to Sceney Beach Clubs
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.97
Miami has always known how to turn a day at the beach into a scene. This rings especially true along the sandy patches belonging to Miami Beach’s top hotels, which have been upping the stakes with cushy amenities and experiences designed to warrant hefty membership fees for locals—and generate enough revenue to keep their beach clubs at the top of their game. The good news for travelers? Book a room at such hotels—think CNT Triple Crown Winners 1 Hotel South Beach and Faena Miami Beach or the new and improved Delano Miami Beach—and many of those same privileges typically extend to hotel guests, no membership required (though nightly rates will cost ya!). Of course, you don’t need a hotel key, annual dues, or an impending inheritance to experience Miami’s best beaches. Miles of public shoreline remain gloriously democratic, whether you want to join the beautiful bodies and colorful lifeguard stands of South Beach, bike beneath the palms of Key Biscayne, kayak through mangroves at Oleta River State Park, or ditch your swimsuit altogether at liberating, clothing-optional Haulover Beach. Consider these 18 picks less a ranking of sand and more a guide to Miami’s many ways of doing the beach, popular year-round thanks to a balmy climate that makes summer feel seemingly endless. Read our complete Miami travel guide here, which includes: - The Best Things to Do in Miami - The Best Restaurants in Miami - The Best Things to Do in Wynwood - The Best Hotels in Miami How we choose the best beaches in Miami Every review on this list has been written by a Condé Nast Traveler journalist who knows the destination and has visited that activity. When choosing things to do, our editors consider landmarks and experiences that offer an insider’s view of a destination, keeping authenticity, location, service, and sustainability credentials top of mind. This gallery has been updated with new information since its original publish date. This gallery has been updated with new information since its original publish date.

item.title: 7 Best Places in Costa Rica for Surfing, Sloth Sightings, and Tico Cuisine
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.71
Costa Rica is one of those special places where the opportunities for exploration and adventure are nearly as diverse as the flora and fauna (which is arguably the most diverse on the planet). Whether you’re going for the yoga, to birdwatch, to surf, to explore the rainforest, dip in a hot spring, scuba dive, or climb a volcano, you’ll find it all there, along with delicious, healthy food, and accommodations to suit every taste. It’s rare for people to just visit just once. Instead, most people seem to fall in love with it and return over and over, either to old favorite spots, or to sample a new flavor of the experiences to be had. While a full book couldn’t do justice to all you can see there, here are a handful of highlights which you can use as a jumping off point for your exploration of this incredible land. Arenal & La Fortuna It’s hard to picture a better-balanced combination of adventure and relaxation. The town of La Fortuna makes an idyllic base for your exploration of Arenal volcano. Here you will find hot springs galore, white water rafting, rainforest canopy tours, paddling or windsurfing in Lake Arenal, and La Fortuna Waterfall (a 200-foot cascade you can swim right up to). La Fortuna has plenty of restaurants to keep your energy up, too. Where to stay nearby: The original hot springs resort with a natural river of thermal water running through it: Tabacón Thermal Resort & Spa. Eighteen thermal pools terraced into a hillside, plus an on-site wildlife rescue center: The Springs Resort & Spa. Nosara Where surf culture and wellness don’t so much as collide but coexist, Nosara is a laid-back beach town, full of yoga retreats, healthy and delicious restaurants, and plenty of waves. Playa Guiones is one of the most consistent beach breaks on the planet, and there are dozens of surf schools, camps, and a variety of waves for beginners to experts. Read our full guide to Nosara here. Where to stay nearby: For stunning views and one of the best restaurants in the country: Tierra Magnifica. For quick access to the beach and the heart of town: Sendero Nosara. For half hotel, half condo, featuring luxe rooms with an eye toward families: Silvestre Nosara. Manuel Antonio While much of the wildlife in Costa Rica requires going way off the beaten path, Manuel Antonio National Park is a major exception. It boasts some of the most dense populations of sloths, squirrel monkeys, toucans, white-faced capuchins, and many, many more. It’s laced with mellow coastal trails and absolutely jaw-dropping beaches, and the nearby town of Quepos has all the amenities one could want, plus nearby Tico cuisine at Rico Tico Jungle Grill's outdoor deck overlooking the treetops. Where to stay nearby: For luxury, views, and direct beach access: Arenas del Mar Beachfront & Rainforest Resort. For a romantic, adults-only, design-forward, boutique hotel: Makanda by the Sea San José Don’t treat the capital city as a mere layover. San José and the surrounding Central Valley will reward your curiosity, especially if you’re a coffee lover, as this is the region some of the world’s best beans come from. There are plenty of plantation tours around the still-active Poás and Irazú volcanoes, just a short daytrip away. The city itself is bursting with arts, culture, and one of the best and most innovative food scenes in Central America. You can walk off your meals exploring the Gold Museum, the resplendent 1897 National Theater, and plenty of public art and murals. Where to stay nearby: For a luxurious converted mansion in the heart of downtown book Hotel Grano De Oro. For quick access to the best restaurants and shopping in the city there’s InterContinental Costa Rica. For an only-in-Costa-Rica experience at a working coffee plantation with gorgeous architecture outside of the city; Finca Rosa Blanca Monteverde A stunning, green realm where the clouds seem to get caught in the canopy of the giant trees, Costa Rica’s premiere cloud forest is truly a thing to behold. It’s the birding capital of Costa Rica (which makes it one of the birding capitals of the world), and it’s here that you might catch a glimpse of the rare and majestic Resplendent Quetzal. The Monteverde Cloud Forest Reserve, the Santa Elena Reserve, and the Curi-Cancha Reserve (all closely nestled) offer some of the richest wildlife-spotting hiking in the country, and there are some killer coffee tours, too. Where to stay nearby: For a Swiss-style chalet in the middle of the cloud forest, Hotel Belmar. For sustainable luxury with a private wildlife reserve, Hotel Belmar. Puerto Viejo & the South Caribbean Coast A whole different side of Costa Rica from the more-visited west coast, both literally and figuratively. Here you’ll find a mélange of Afro-Caribbean, Bribri indigenous, and Latinx influences, and that really shows up in the mouth-watering food and the local music scene. Puerto Viejo is the central town, full of bars, restaurants, shops, but it’s close to everything from the Gandoca-Manzanillo Wildlife Refuge (a hotspot for nesting turtles), a sloth reserve, a Jaguar Rescue Center, and the absolutely pumping waves of the notorious Salsa Brava surf break. Where to stay nearby: For individually curated Caribbean-Victorian beach bungalows: Hotel Aguas Claras. For a white-washed, design-focused property near the beach: Le Caméléon Boutique Hotel Corcovado & the Osa Peninsula Last but most definitely not least, a visit to Corcovado National Park is on the bucket list of any nature-lover. This rainforest was dubbed "the most biologically intense place on Earth" by National Geographic, and you will see why very quickly upon arrival as your chances are excellent for spotting tapirs, scarlet macaws, all four Costa Rican monkey species, and maybe even a jaguar. Getting there isn’t for the faint of heart, as it typically takes a puddle jumper or a very long drive followed by a boat to get way out there on the Osa Peninsula, and accommodations skew more glamping than luxurious, but if you make the pilgrimage, you will be rewarded by thin crowds and one of the most immersive nature experiences on planet Earth (and there’s good surf, too). Where to stay nearby: The peninsula's flagship eco-lodge on a private 1,000-acre reserve: Lapa Rios Ecolodge. The only luxury property with direct access to the gulf (boat trip required to get there) is Playa Cativo Lodge. Indonesian-style bungalows and beachfront access near Drake Bay: Copa de Árbol Beach & Rainforest Resort.

item.title: 7 Famous Homes From Movies and TV Shows You Can Actually Rent, Including Harry Potter’s Childhood Home and the 'Bachelor' Mansion
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.64
If you’ve ever dreamed of waking up in Bella Swan’s moody Forks home, where a vampire might pop in to say hello at any moment, or planning a Girls-style weekend trip out to Long Island’s North Fork, there’s a world of movie-famous rentals out there for turning your fictional fantasies into a reality. The seven properties on this list span famous homes from film and television, from Harry Potter’s childhood home in Godric’s Hollow to the Bachelor mansion in Agoura Hills. Whether you’re looking to relive your favorite series or cosplay as a main character, these rentals have a certain star quality—after all, it took many professional location scouts to find them. From whimsical lofts in Tokyo fit for solo travelers to Cornwall, England, mansions that double as wedding venues, there’s a recognizable rental below for every kind of travel scenario. Just be sure to book ahead; these famous sets fill up fast. Number of guests: 2 Bed and bath: 1 bed, shared bathroom Why we love it: Courtyard view, wood-burning fireplace, backyard Featured in Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows: Part One, the Vere House serves as Harry’s childhood home in Godric’s Hollow. But its history can be traced back to the 15th century, when the De Vere family built it as a hunting lodge; the front door, with its medieval wooden carvings, is one of the most photographed sites in Lavenham, a village in Suffolk. The house features four en suite bedrooms (another is available to rent here), with access to the shared sitting room, where guests can gather and enjoy a roaring fire (and some crumpets, marshmallows, and sweet chestnuts in the winter months), or the courtyard when the weather’s nice. You’ll also have the option to order a full English breakfast, enjoyed in the communal dining room surrounded by centuries-old objects and artwork. Location: Lavenham, England Things to do nearby: The Crooked House, Six Bells Preston, Great Cornard Country Park Number of guests: 8 Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 1.5 baths Why we love it: Proximity to riverfront, film memorabilia, patio While it’s booked out for months, Bella Swan’s home from Twilight is out there—not in Forks, but St. Helens, Oregon. And it never left 2008: The home is remarkably similar to the way it appears in the film, down to Bella’s purple floral bedspread (while not available for use, it is on display). Though the movie makes it seem like close quarters between Bella and Charlie, the house actually contains five bedrooms for you and your seven closest Twihards to spread out across. One reviewer wrote, “Watching the Twilight movies while staying in the house is every teenage girl's dream, and I can't believe it happened to me!” Location: St. Helens, Oregon Things to do nearby: St. Helens Historic Riverfront District, Historic Columbia Theatre, Crooked Creek Brewery Number of guests: 2 Bed and bath: 1 bed, 1 bath Why we love it: Quirky architecture, indoor fireplace, in-unit washer/dryer Season five, episode three of Girls, simply titled “Japan,” is a world unto itself, and Shoshanna’s cartoon-like home away from home is no different. A jungle gym of sorts, the loft is decked out in primary colors, with bulbous fixtures and a wraparound layout. The bathroom, for instance, is housed in its own circular pod, while the kitchen sits in a central pit. This is a personal unit within a shared residential building, so guests might run into each other along common walkways and staircases. Quirky design lovers, this one’s for you. Location: Tokyo, Japan Things to do nearby: Nogawa Park, Ghibli Museum, Fuchu Art Museum Number of guests: 13 Bed and bath: 6 bedrooms, 4 baths Why we love it: Beach access, pet-friendly, private pool Of the North Fork, Marnie from Girls says, “It’s for people who think the Hamptons are tacky and don’t want to be on a beach that’s near a J.Crew.” Once a Coast Guard lifesaving station built in 1893, the East Marion home that fueled one of the most iconic episodes in the show’s history is available to rent. But that’s not the property’s only claim to fame; the home also appeared in The Undoing, when Grace (played by Nicole Kidman) flees to the beach after her husband (Hugh Grant) goes missing. Right on the Long Island Sound with its own private slice of sand, this spacious home has enough room for up to 13 guests (hopefully your bachelorette weekend is more synchronized dance, less fighting). Location: East Marion, New York Things to do nearby: Orient State Park, Kontokosta Winery, town of Greenport Number of guests: 13 Bed and bath: 7 bedrooms, 8 baths Why we love it: Private pool, hot tub, mountain view Bachelor fans will revel in a stay at Villa de la Vina, the 10,000-square-foot Mediterranean-style mansion nestled within the Santa Monica Mountains of Malibu. You and 12 other guests can spread out across seven bedrooms and get a real-life glimpse of your favorite moments from the show. Whether you compete for love is up to you (may we suggest a bachelorette weekend instead?), but the romantic archways, infinity pool, and Agoura Hills views are sure to make you feel like you’re on a reality TV show. Bonus: Chef-prepared meals, airport transfers, and a chauffeur service are all available upon request. Location: Agoura Hills, California Things to do nearby: Liberty Lane Farms, Ladyface Trailhead, Malibu Wine Hikes Number of guests: 4–6 Bed and bath: 2–4 beds, 1–2 baths Why we love it: Film memorabilia, guided tours, gift shop While the house from A Christmas Story is available for daily tours in Cleveland, real fans of the beloved holiday classic will want to stay overnight in suites styled after the film, including the main house (lovingly restored) or the neighboring Bumpus House. All rooms are decked out in 1940s “hillbilly chic” interiors, and the loft, located in the main house, is where two lucky guests can sleep in Ralphie and Randy’s beds. Be sure to plan ahead, as these coveted rentals get booked up quickly around the holidays, and don’t leave without buying a pair of pink bunny pajamas in the gift shop. Location: Cleveland, Ohio Things to do nearby: Rowley Inn gastropub, Hooper Farm, Lincoln Park Number of guests: 21 Bed and bath: 12 bedrooms, 8 baths Why we love it: Seaview rooms, proximity to beach, grand piano, game room Ideal for an English seaside wedding, the Porthpean House is as romantic as it gets, not least because it was featured in the cult-favorite 2013 film About Time. Overlooking Porthpean Beach, the salt-sprayed home was originally built in 1793 and has belonged to the Petherick family for five generations before becoming a dreamy vacation rental. Sleeping up to 21 guests, it houses several historic rooms, including a drawing room, gaming room, dining room, multiple kitchens, and an office, as well as acres of fresh lawn to frolic around. Location: Cornwall, England Things to do nearby: Porthpean Beach, Porthpean Golf Club, RAF Quadrant Tower

item.title: What Rockaway Film Festival Can Teach Us About Going to the Movies
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.63
Despite its endless appetite for novelty, New York City really is a creature of recursion. Memories never remain too far behind, or rather, too far ahead, before they’re back again wearing a familiar form. One of the city’s finest resurrections in recent memory is moviegoing in the Rockaways. Like the millionaire colonies born of Gilded Age excesses or the Coney Island-rival Rockaways’ Playland that formerly occupied this area of coastal Queens, it’s a stretch of the imagination to conjure up the heyday of movie theaters by the beach. Their near-absence on the peninsula today obscures the foreign era they once thrived in, a few golden decades that spanned from the 1920s to ‘50s earmarked by 25-cent tickets to double features, smoking-friendly cinemas, and faux tuxedoed attendants. A combination of factors ranging from demographic shifts following the Second World War to devastating building fires to general neighborhood decline led to the gradual shuttering of Rockaways’ theaters.
