The last gasp came when Jerry Lewis Cinema closed its doors in 1996, and the Rockaways went without a commercial indoor theater for the next 25 years. The dry spell was finally broken in 2021 by the nonprofit Rockaway Film Festival organization, when it led the effort of building Arverne Cinema, now the only one of its kind. Ever since the festival itself started nine years ago—popping up screens in venues from Fort Tilden to Jacob Riis Park—hope for the return of moviegoing as a neighborhood pastime has abounded, as one might expect following any reported sighting post-extinction. I arrive at this year’s Rockaway Film Festival (RFF9) in local uniform, with swim trunks donned beneath my work slacks and flip-flops afoot in case of any impromptu beach-going. With the day’s storms recently broken, the muggy summer air made way for a preview of the better days of fall to set the stage for an evening at the open-air movies. The outdoor cinema is wrapped by a rough-hewn Brutalist perimeter—half-lined with concrete cubes, the other half enclosed with planks salvaged from the boardwalk destroyed during Hurricane Sandy. Filled with gravel and sand, it’s like we’re on the bottom of a riverbed with the constant stream of smooth-bellied airplanes taking off above us from the nearby JFK airport. The space certainly feels scrappier than the black-and-white photos of its predecessors. For one, the former Arverne Theater—once a venue for Yiddish acts from the Rockaways’ vibrant Jewish community—broadcasted itself with an outsized vertical marquee until its dismantling in 1952. And the Arverne Pier Theater wore its neoclassical inspirations on its sleeve, complete with Corinthian columns and a half-round pediment. The main centerpiece of the cinema that stands today is its screen, and behind it, there’s not much in the way of scenery. Peeping over the horizon, tower cranes hover forever paused in their progress at the defunct concrete facility, leaning over with their trussed necks, a family of mechanical sauropods. The warmth of the space only truly activates once it’s brimming with people: within my earshot, some trade stories on their convoluted commutes to get here; others debate the ethics of documentary-making; but most exchange reports on what they’ve seen recently and the homework they’ve done on what’s about to screen. Though, those conversations might only apply to the crowd for the world premiere of Eternity One, a documentary from Baltimore-based filmmaker Marnie Ellen Hertzler regarding the precarity of Tangier Island, a remote island community in the Chesapeake Bay eroding from the climate crisis. While the film is the first screening of the festival, it’s not necessarily indicative of the programming (or the crowds) to come. The exciting truth is that none of the films quite are, with the RFF9 lineup reading as an eclectic yet affordable menu. Tickets are capped at $10, and a handful of movies are even being shown for free to ensure that everyone who wants a seat can get one. To name but a few of the movies showing, there’s the 1979 Muppets Movie (the one with “Rainbow Connection”), a generational crowd-pleaser sure to work its magic once again with young families in attendance; a collection of animated shorts themed around “Romantasy” for the old school Adult Swim crowd; and a Dabke dance workshop led by El Funoun, a traditional Palestinian dance company braiding celebration with resistance. As the latter item suggests, there’s much more to the festival than just what’s on screen. Most movies are paired with local live acts to fill the air as the crowd mills in or to keep the party going long after the projector shuts off. You might walk into one screening to the processional music of Brooklyn slacker prog and exit the next to a Roots reggae DJ set. Kyp Malone, in all his braid-bearded glory, plays before Eternity One, at times playfully directing us, “now pretend I’m a movie, and pay the fuck attention,” and later offering light conversation starters between straight-from-the-bottle sips of Casamigos like, “did you think fascism was going to feel different?” One particularly inspired pairing comes from the combination of Ridgewood-based documentarian John Wilson’s first feature, The History of Concrete, with a set from Bellerose rapper Heems (of Das Racist fame for any lovers of combination Pizza Hut-Taco Bells). Wilson’s whispering, Kermit-ish cadence juxtaposed with Heems’s audacious bars shorthands the borough’s rejection of one-size-fits-all characterization as one of the most diverse urban centers in the world. Tying a bow on the Queens-ness of it all is the al-fresco setting itself. This might be the one pocket of the city that does sleep. Call it the influence of the local surf culture, or the protected peace of the nearby nature reserves, but the Rockaways are just the kind of place made for prying sticks out of asses. Take it from friendly neighborhood rockstar Patti Smith, who put it simply on her Substack: “Being at Rockaway Beach makes me happy.” It’s long ceased to be a neighborhood that puts on airs, an attitude that liberates us all tonight. Under the darkening sky, I’m oddly comforted by the couple next to me taking advantage of the shifting tenebrism for some drive-in-style PDA. Tucked inside the cul-de-sac of a residential street off of Beach 67, Arverne Cinema is right at home amongst the two-story houses hosting their own celebrations, with one particularly passionate birthday party across the street beating out the volume of Hertzler’s Q&A. While the festival bounced around for its first few years, finding a permanent home in the community had always been the goal. “There’s not much that’s like the joy of sharing a movie that you love very much in a space that was built by friends and neighbors with a full audience,” said RFF co-founder and organizer Courtney Muller, reflecting on the festival’s sixth year at Arverne Cinema. At the risk of sounding like another trite moral about the importance of social gathering post-pandemic, the Rockaway Film Festival is as much about movie-going as it is about movie-watching. Thankfully, the act is not nearly as endangered as it was once reported to be, with chains like AMC boasting booming attendance numbers. But factors such as surging ticket prices and shorter gaps between theatrical runs and streaming releases contribute to the perception that going out to the movies is a luxury, and shrink crowds accordingly. That image is only bolstered by the glamorous superlatives we’ve come to expect from premiere film festivals around the world—the record-smashing standing ovations at Cannes, a bigger and better revamp of Sundance, the making or breaking of Oscar contenders at the Toronto International Film Festival. Between the flimsy baskets of superb beach shack grub and seating reminiscent of a school play, the Rockaway Film Festival is doing the remedial work of bringing movies back to the people by reminding its attendees that a movie theater is not supposed to be a sarcophagus. My favorites in New York, and the ones I’d champion are worth traveling for, are all framed by their own signs of life, from the faint roar of the subways that rumbles through the Angelika to the shoulder-to-shoulder sardine can theaters of Film Forum (though one should never go so far as to condone cellphone use for QR code ordering at an Alamo Drafthouse). That a film festival grows in the Rockaways after more than two decades without a single theater is a feat in its own right, and its longevity for the past nine years speaks to the simple human desire shared by cinephiles and curious locals alike that watching a good movie in a crowd of peers, perhaps even with your toes in the sand, should come at no exorbitant cost. “When this festival began as a four-day experiment in 2018, it was not just about showing movies—it was about saying clearly to this community that it deserves cinema,” shared Rafael Espinal, Commissioner of the Mayor’s Office of Media and Entertainment, to kick off the start of this year’s events, “Rockaway reminds us that cinema belongs everywhere in New York City, not just in the places where people expect them, but right here, by the beach with this community.” In an interview with Hell Gate, Muller described the undercurrent of this year’s programming as the “stories of things coming apart” and what grows in the spaces left after collapse. It might as well be the unofficial motto for the Rockaways, where surfers dropped everything to shovel out sunken homes after Hurricane Sandy, grassroots mutual aid networks opened their doors to displaced New Yorkers after 9/11, and neighbors came together to convert a vacant lot into a movie theater. RFF9 is an exemplary case study that the local flavor of the Rockaways is best appreciated up close. I can’t write about what it was like to taste the salt air seasoned with New York atmosphere and make the flavor materialize on your tongue. A high-budget documentary exclusive to the streaming platform that produced it can’t either. You might have to wait another year for the next festival, take the A train as far down as you’ve ever taken it, come early, and claim one of the beach chairs while you can to feel it for yourself, but the point is that you must. How to Visit Rockaway Film Festival This year's festival runs from September 2-6, and while tickets to the remaining screenings have all sold out online, some have limited capacity for tickets sold at the door, and for others, you can sign up to be on a waitlist at the ticket stand before showtime. For the most up-to-date information on this year's screenings, visit the programming page of the festival here. As far as getting yourself to Arverne Cinema, you have a few options. You could take the Far Rockaway-bound A train to Beach 67 and walk eight minutes to the theater, ride the Q22 bus to the Rockaway Beach Blvd / Beach 73 St stop or the Beach Channel Dr / Beach 71 St stop (and connect to the bus from the LIRR Far Rockaway station), or ride the NYC Ferry, which by and large offers the most scenic views. The festival's website also hosts an extensive Rockaway guide with recommendations ranging from where to get your morning coffee to the best cannabis dispensary in town. Take full advantage of these expert recs by basing yourself directly in the Rockaways. For a weekend stay, the beachy sanctuary of the Rockaway Hotel is the way to go.

item.title: 26-Time US Open Tennis Star Venus Williams on Paris, Partying, and the Perfect Pair of Heels
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.50
If there’s one thing about Venus Williams, it’s that she has stamina. The seven-time Grand Slam singles champion is currently playing in her 26th US Open—making more appearances than any other player in tennis history. The California-born athlete played her first professional match at just 14, meaning she’s been not just a tennis pro, but also a travel pro, for more than three decades. With life constantly on the road, she admits that her idea of vacation is when she gets to relax at her Florida home. But that also means that she prioritizes comfort when it comes to hotels, opting for ones with a homey feel. “I do not compromise on hotels,” the 46-year-old told Condé Nast Traveler during a pre-US Open event at The Langham, New York, Fifth Avenue. “I will compromise on my flight and sit almost anywhere, it doesn’t matter to me. But I just have to be at an amazing hotel.” She admits that when she was younger, she was lured by the “newest, coolest, trendiest” design-forward accommodations. But now, she opts for “extremely established hotels that have amazing service”—plus a "beautiful bed.” While she mused about her favorite city in the world being Hong Kong (she’s contemplating a fall tournament there just to revisit) and her enthusiastic passion for escape rooms (her favorites include The Escape Game, Escapology, and PanIQ, but her goal is to compete in the World Escape Room Championships. which was last in Bulgaria), Williams chose to hone in on a trip to Paris, a city that has helped her redefined her life’s priorities. The trip What trip are you unpacking for us? There have been many trips to Paris Fashion Week, but let’s go back to the one in the winter of 2024, before I was married. I was going to go to one or two shows. Two, for me, is a lot. It involves a ton of getting ready. And on this trip, I took my sister Isha. Can you tell us more about the itinerary? I try to fit in gym sessions here and there, some tennis as well. But most of all, I know I’ll be out every night, so I have to bring clothes to be ready for my nightlife, which is extremely important. Had you been to Paris before? My first time in Paris, I was 16 years old playing the French Open. So in that sense, I go at least once a year. But during this time, I really wasn't working, so I was constantly in Paris. I had this streak where I was there every month for like six months in a row. It finally broke. I was so sad. I just love Paris—it’s such a magical city for me. What makes the city so special? A few years before this, the French Open, which always happens in May, was in October during the pandemic. They put us in a bubble. We were only allowed to have a one-hour walk a day. So once I unfortunately did lose at the tournament. I checked myself into a luxury hotel and started shopping and partying. This was before the second shutdown. Paris became my new favorite city, as it represented freedom and choice. I hadn’t done much in my life out of the court. A friend of mine said, “You should come to the Louis Vuitton show” and I was like, “I gotta get home.” But I went to the show, and it felt like my whole life got started. What she packed What do you usually wear on a flight? It depends on how I feel. If I want to be chic, a cardigan and a turtleneck. I used to always fly in Ugg boots—they’re not that popular now, so I'm like the only one wearing them. Other than that, I love Wolford leggings and definitely a long-sleeved sweater since I'm always cold. Most unusual thing you pack for every trip? A karaoke mic! It’s got to be a quality mic. My family is a karaoke family and you never know when you need the mic. I don't have a go-to song—I have a whole list! The last one was probably “Danger Zone” by Kenny Loggins. My husband loves Michael Jackson, but I’ve learned a few Italian songs from him—we do an Italian duet. [My sister] Serena likes to do The Little Mermaid’s “Part of Your World.” She likes Disney standards. What clothes did you pack? I'll bring two to three workout outfits from Lacoste. I figure I can wash them. I'm probably not gonna be doing cardio. It's most likely going to be strength training, so I could maybe wear it over again. I was more concerned about my evening outfits. I was a single girl. I'm wearing short dresses and preparing for any and every party that I don't even know I'm gonna be at. So then, we have to ask: what shoes did you bring? My heels—the ones that I can dance in and still wear for hours because I love dancing. Christian Louboutin 80 centimeters were my go-tos. They’re high. I’m 6-foot-1 and I love being tall. I’m not afraid of it. What other scenarios did you pack for? I brought one Wilson racquet—that's not a lot of racquets. On another trip, when I was kind of down and out on my own tennis career, I didn't even bring a racquet. Then I suddenly realized I wanted to play tennis and had to get one, which was challenging. I managed to get one of Serena's racquets! Otherwise, I didn't really repeat outfits, so I always had to have something a little bit new. I was also going on dates—many of them not serious at all. But I had to have my date outfits for the daytime, possibly even a lunch date. Which outfit did you wear first? The night we got in, my sister and I were done because we already had to get up in like four hours. We’d taken showers, washed our hair, and put on face masks— all the things. Then a friend texts that there’s a party in so-and-so’s room. I ask my sister if we should go, and she’s awful and says yes. So I grab a Louis Vuitton shift dress. I don't know how I got my hair together so fast, and here's the thing: I didn't take the mask off. It was a clear Tata Harper resurfacing mask—the pink jelly one! So how was the party? The hotel was close, so we ran in the freezing winter night and there was nothing happening at this party! There was one guy there who had a crush on me, but he was not someone you would ever date. Finally we went home and had to wake up two hours later feeling miserable and start hair and makeup for the show. This was my lifestyle and I loved it—I got to live it! I’m not living it now, but that was when you’ve got to have that second outfit ready for that very random moment! What souvenirs did you buy on this trip? Well, I used to have a major shopping addiction. So I took home pretty much everything in Paris. My motto at the time was, "I'm not winning, but I'm spending." I was laughing until the credit card bill came, and then it wasn't funny anymore. I bought watches that I've never worn—that was bad. For the most part, I try to buy timeless things. I don't shop anymore, but deep down I'm just waiting for that moment where I start up again. It's not today. It's not tomorrow. I'm under control…for the moment. Have you found any jet lag cures? If you land at night, stay up on the flight. That rhymes. If you land during the day, go out and play. I'm a rapper now! But if I land in the day, I allow myself an hour or two nap, then I go to practice and stay up. The minimum is 10 o’clock. When you do that, you’ll pretty much be on the time zone. But if you allow yourself to just sleep, you're going to just be miserable. Is there something you bring with you as a piece of home when you're on the road? My dog Harold. He’s a 19-year-old Havanese. On this trip, did you over pack, under pack, or get it just right? Slightly overpacked. When I travel on short trips, I insist on just carry-on. It's very liberating. Packing for tennis is a little challenging because I have to pack my match clothes, practice clothes, and clothes for off the court. There are so many tennis shoes—you need at least two, in case one goes out. It’s happened to me and if you don’t have that second pair on the side, you’re screwed. You also need racquet string, an ice machine, and a bunch of stuff. So I travel with four bags—I give one to my husband, so it’s three, but it’s hard. Finally, what makes the US Open special compared to other Grand Slams? It’s a city that never sleeps. The energy here is so much that people who live here need to get out of the city—that says a lot! And the crowd is just boisterous, but once they're locked in, they're there for you. Then they're not leaving you. It’s just a very special experience.

item.title: Vancouver’s Best Family-Friendly Hotels, From a Local Who Has Tried Them All
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.37
As someone who was born and raised in Vancouver, I’ve seen the city through all stages of life: as a curious teen looking for adventure, as a single twenty-something eager for fun, as a new mom searching for ways to entertain my toddlers, and now as a mom of teens, helping them find new thrills in the city we call home. Regardless of which stage of life you're in, Vancity has something for everyone. When I think of the best family-friendly hotels in Vancouver, I think of spots that make it easy to get around (even without a car) and that have room service or a restaurant with options for picky eaters. With three kids, I also always appreciate some extra space for everyone to settle down after a busy day of exploring. And if there’s a pool, my kids’ trip is pretty much made. For teens, the ability to roam freely on their own is another big perk, so I like a hotel that’s close to the action, with plenty to explore within walking distance. The family-friendly hotels below put you in the heart of Vancouver, with plenty of kid-friendly perks that make it easy to settle in—and hard to leave. FAQ: Where should a family stay in Vancouver? For families, downtown Vancouver is one of the most convenient places to stay, especially around Coal Harbour. You’ll be within walking distance of restaurants, shopping, and major attractions like the Vancouver Art Gallery and the Vancouver Aquarium, with the waterfront and Stanley Park just steps away. Is Vancouver worth visiting with kids? Absolutely. Vancouver packs a lot of family-friendly fun into a relatively compact city, from beaches and bike rides to aquariums and museums. Choose your hotel wisely, and you can walk, bike, or take public transit between many of the city’s top spots. Where should you take kids in Vancouver? Make the most of Vancouver’s mix of nature, culture, and city life, whatever the season. Start in Stanley Park, Canada’s largest urban park, where you can bike or walk the seawall, stop at the Vancouver Aquarium, and cool off with a dip at one of the park’s sandy beaches. Then head to Granville Island for lunch at the Public Market, followed by some shopping and playtime at the Kids Market. For a dose of culture, head to the Museum of Anthropology, where kids can get up close to towering carved poles while learning about the Indigenous cultures and stories of the region. How we choose the best hotels in Vancouver Every hotel review on this list has been written by a Condé Nast Traveler journalist who knows the destination and has visited that property. When choosing hotels, our editors consider properties across price points that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination, keeping design, location, service, and sustainability credentials top of mind.

item.title: The World’s Most Beautiful Libraries Worth Traveling For
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.10
The most beautiful libraries have long been more than places to check out books, though some make a particularly compelling case for lingering. As a demand for third places to gather outside of home or work continues to grow, libraries are having a moment as prime spots for idling, browsing, and simply taking a break from the bustle beyond of their opulent doors. Libraries have taken on an array of forms around the world, as reading rooms that have been tucked into former monasteries, designed as futuristic cultural hubs, and constructed in the heart of the California redwoods. While the books are still the main attraction, it certainly doesn’t hurt to be surrounded by ornate frescoes or unexpected nooks that make you want to stay a while longer. From Colombia to Qatar, these 11 libraries are worth building into your next trip, whether you are architecture-obsessed or longing to sit down in a picturesque setting with a new read. item.title: The 17 Most Beautiful National Parks in the World, From Yellowstone to the Serengeti
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.08
Some places are beautiful for one specific reason: a beach at sunset, a mountain perfectly reflected in a lake, a rainforest humming with wildlife. But national parks offer something broader. By definition, they protect entire landscapes and ecosystems—drawing a line around expanses we’ve collectively decided are too precious to lose. For travelers, having a list of designated wonders is also an easy way to know exactly where (and how) to see some of the world’s most incredible forces of nature. That could mean rafting under waterfalls in Argentina, ballooning over fairy chimneys in Türkiye, ice caving in Iceland, or hiking for three days to reach a wildflower-filled valley in India. There are many thousands of national parks around the world, so the trickiest part is narrowing down the list—but these 17, spanning six continents and encompassing an extraordinary range of scenery, are a good place to start. Lençóis Maranhenses National Park, Brazil At first glance, Lençóis Maranhenses looks like an enormous white desert—but this vast expanse contains multitudes. The park’s sand dunes are striped with turquoise and emerald lagoons (which accumulate during the rainy season), creating the effect of infinitely repeating oases. Book a five-hour bus ride from São Luís for a surreal swim break. Iguazú National Park, Argentina This park protects the Argentine side of the enormous Iguazú Falls (Iguaçu National Park is a hop over the border in Brazil), a system of some 275 roaring cascades deep in the rainforest. The bombastically—but fittingly—named Devil’s Throat is the standout waterfall here. Admire it from one of the walkways, or ride a speedboat right into the spray. Cabo Pulmo National Park, Mexico Who says national parks have to be in the mountains—or even on land at all? Located on the tip of Mexico’s Baja California Sur peninsula, Cabo Pulmo is a coastal wonderland of quiet beaches and rock formations—but its true appeal lies under the surface. Just offshore, the brilliant Pacific waters protect a vast coral reef system teeming with sea turtles and swirling schools of zooming jacks. Yellowstone National Park, United States Choosing just one US park is a near-impossible task, but Yellowstone takes the narrow lead. Not only was it the first designated national park in the country (and, by most accounts, the entire world), but its geological diversity can’t be beat—within its 2.2 million acres, you’ll find mountains, canyons, geysers, rainbow-gradient hot springs, and more. Banff National Park, Canada This one’s no surprise. Banff National Park is one of Canada’s shining stars, beloved for its staggering views of the Rockies and glacial, almost impossibly blue lakes. Lake Louise, Moraine Lake, and Lake Minnewanka are all standouts, equally lovely when reflecting sunshine in summer and frozen over in winter. Namib-Naukluft National Park, Namibia Namib-Naukluft is the Namibia you came for: burnt-orange sand dunes, blindingly white salt pans, and the eerie skeleton trees of Deadvlei. It’s a little bit Mars, a little bit Fury Road, but an absolute original that has no peer. Tsingy de Bemaraha National Park, Madagascar Madagascar is one of the world’s hardest-to-reach countries, which makes its landscapes feel even more immaculate. Case in point: the Tsingy de Bemaraha National Park. Famous for its forest of limestone needles jutting into the sky, the park is almost terrifying in its beauty—though lightened by the fact that the Malagasy word “tsingy” roughly translates to “where one cannot walk barefoot.” Noted! Serengeti National Park, Tanzania The Serengeti occupies an almost mythical space in our collective mind. The Great Migration, in which millions of wildebeest move across the plains, is one of Earth’s greatest natural shows. But even in stillness, the region is magnificent—golden grasslands rolling beneath the open sky, with acacia trees punctuating the otherwise endless horizon. Vatnajökull National Park, Iceland Iceland is known as the land of fire and ice, and no place better encapsulates that dramatic epithet than Vatnajökull National Park. Its eponymous glacier and accompanying ice caves dominate the scene, but active volcanoes simmer beneath the freeze, and rivers of meltwater cut through the terrain. It’s a true study in contrasts, both elemental and chromatic—brilliant blue ice, inky black rocks. Las Salinas de Torrevieja National Park, Spain Yes, it really is that pink. Torrevieja’s salt lagoon gets its hue from microorganisms that release red pigments in saline conditions—an imperceptible process that yields magnificent results. It’s an Instagram darling, sure, but it’s also a place to appreciate nature’s inner workings and see the world through bubblegum-colored glasses. Plitvice Lakes National Park, Croatia Plitvice Lakes National Park may not be hidden, but it sure is a gem. Sixteen interconnected lakes cascade through the forest, linked by a series of waterfalls and natural travertine barriers, and ranging in hue from brilliant turquoise to deep blue and green. Make your way through the selfie-snapping crowds, find an empty spot on one of the wooden walkways, and just stand in awe. Valley of Flowers National Park, India The name pretty much says it all: During the summer blooming season, Uttarakhand’s Valley of Flowers transforms into a huge natural garden, with wildflowers blanketing the alpine meadows in a riot of color. Getting here requires a lengthy trek (we’re talking several days) through the Himalayas, but the effort just makes the visual payoff that much sweeter. Göreme National Park, Türkiye Göreme is defined by Cappadocia’s fairy chimneys, which are about as magical as they sound. The mushroom-shaped rock structures, carved over millennia by volcanic activity and erosion, are best viewed from above—namely in the basket of a hot-air balloon. Set your alarm and time your ride to sunrise, so you can be the first to watch the landscapes awaken for the day. Kelimutu National Park, Indonesia Three lakes, three wildly different colors. Kelimutu National Park’s bodies of water shift at the whims of the minerals and gases beneath the craters, so you never know exactly what shade you’ll see when you arrive—red, blue, green, or black. It’s as if Mother Nature is wearing a trio of mood rings. Zhangjiajie National Forest Park, China Located in China’s Wulingyuan Scenic Area, Zhangjiajie boasts thousands of jagged sandstone peaks that rise dramatically over lush treetops—and when mist shrouds the valley below, they almost seem to float above the clouds. (Look familiar? The park famously inspired the Hallelujah Mountains in Avatar.) Fiordland National Park, New Zealand Fiordland National Park showcases some of New Zealand’s most striking features, all in one space: mountains, rainforests, waterfalls, and deep glacial fjords. Many visitors zero in on Milford Sound, the undeniable star attraction; but there truly are no bad views here. Uluṟu-Kata Tjuṯa National Park, Australia Few landmarks are as recognizable as Uluṟu, a sandstone monolith rising from an otherwise flat and open desert. The rockface changes color depending on the sun’s position—ochre during the day, blazing orange and pink at sunset, and purple at twilight.

item.title: The Most Beautiful Italian Coastal Towns
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 3.01
Most first-time visitors to Italy tend to concentrate on cities like Rome, Florence, and Venice, but if you ask us, off-the-beaten-path Italian coastal towns are some of the most beautiful places in the country. After all, Italy has nearly 5,000 miles of coastline, and some of the country’s coastal settlements predate the Roman Empire. From Liguria all the way down to Calabria, not to mention the Adriatic Coast and the islands, there are charming seaside villages that offer a wide variety of experiences. You might want the glamour of world-famous resort towns like Portofino, Capri, and Taormina, where your dolce vita fantasies can come to life. Or perhaps you’d prefer more under-the-radar towns like Maratea and Carloforte, where you can get an authentic taste of local life. In Italy, most coastal towns come alive in the summer, when visitors from around the world hit the beaches. If you want to avoid the crowds, plan to visit coastal towns in the off-season, but keep in mind that some of them all but shut down in the winter. Spring and fall are usually a good compromise. Read on to learn about 25 of the best Italian coastal towns, with Condé Nast Traveler-approved recommendations of where to stay. item.title: 10 Best Coffee Shops in Seattle
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.72
Seattle could probably coast on its coffee reputation for another half-century, but visitors who equate the Emerald City with the green mermaid miss out on its world-class selection of bright and bold brews. Those live in the independent shops and local roasters that keep Seattle awake for the longest of summer days, and perky through the dark, damp winters. Whether you’re on a pilgrimage to this birthplace of American latte art (at Espresso Vivace), looking to be transported to the cutting edge of specialty coffee (at Slow Day Coffee), or you just want drip and a breakfast sandwich while you get your bike fixed (at Peloton Bicycle Shop & Cafe), this city has the perfect cup for you—here's where to find the best coffee shops in Seattle. item.title: The Best Hotels in Berlin at Every Price Point
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.58
More than three decades after the wall came down, Berlin remains a city in constant flux, where the past and present intertwine in wildly innovative ways. A booming capital brimming with youthful energy and creative ideas, it is reinventing itself brick by brick—and nowhere is this more evident than in its dynamic hotel scene. New life has been breathed into landmark properties, and dilapidated buildings have been rescued and refashioned into chic boutique stays. Famed global brands such as Rocco Forte and The Hoxton have arrived on the scene, joining timeless classics that have stood for the past century. From the splashy west to the grittier east, property choices in every style and at every price point span the city. Here are the best hotels in Berlin that are open for check-in now, as chosen by our local editors. Our top picks: - Best for luxury: Waldorf Astoria Berlin - Best for a central location: Telegraphenamt - Best for families: Michelberger Hotel - Read Full ReviewHoused in a late 19th-century building, Irish lifestyle hotel brand The Dean brings its “vibe first” philosophy to the German capital, pairing bold design with cultural connectivity and a food concept that draws in more than just overnight guests. Interiors channel Berlin’s creative energy and avant-garde spirit from the moment you step inside. Historic architectural details sit alongside saturated colors, sculptural lighting, and a confident, contemporary design language. Room numbers are handwritten on the doors rather than printed—an intentionally imperfect detail that nods to Berlin’s slightly rough-around-the-edges character. In the bathrooms, original black-and-white tiles have been preserved, punctuated by red shower frames and boldly framed mirrors. Toiletries are by D.S. & Durga, lending a subtle spa feel. For food, Benedict is the heart of the hotel—a bakery, restaurant, and bar combined in one lively, open space. Breakfast is served until 4 p.m. on weekdays and all day on weekends. The focus is, naturally, on eggs Benedict in multiple variations: with ham and cheese, avocado, or pulled beef, served on brioche or a buttery croissant. The brand’s Irish roots are also present in the drinks offering: whiskey in every minibar, the Irish cocktail “Ól,” and even a dedicated Guinness tap behind the bar—a small but unmistakable nod to its heritage. —Susanna Gunst - Read Full ReviewThis sophisticated hotel in Mitte’s bustling center, steps from the Brandenburg Gate, features one-of-a-kind guest rooms decorated by local and international artists. The prominent neon sign on the façade is strategically placed above a self-portrait done in bronze by artist Alicja Kwade, and once inside, you’re transported into a moodily lit living room reminiscent of an art patron’s salon. Refined couples, having just finished their cocktails, chat quietly while on their way out to the Staatsoper (German State Opera). It all feels very calm and grown up, like an idealized version of Berlin’s past artistic glories, updated with a buzzy sense of creative present. Bed down in a room with hand-painted wallpaper or a hand-carved folding screen; each is uniquely decorated and may have a one-of-a-kind large-scale painting on the wall, or even a funky video installation. Bathrooms are lined in glazed subway-style tiles and have heated floors and large walk-in showers. The property is an easy to walk to the Reichstag; if you’ve come to shop, Friedrichstrasse is a block away; to run or bike, the large green expanse of Tiergarten is a hop and a skip. —Liz Humphreys - Read Full ReviewWith an exceptional location on Monbijoupark in the Mitte district, this grand neo-Baroque building once housed the city’s vast telegraph office—built between 1910 and 1916, and at one time the most sophisticated postal building in Germany. It has since been meticulously restored and transformed into a posh destination for discerning travelers looking to stay close to a huge selection of trendy restaurants, bars, and shops, as well as beloved Hackesche Höfe's old courtyards-turned-commercial spaces. The 97 guest rooms all have an industrial look, with brick-barrel vaulted ceilings divided by metal beams and exposed brick walls. Art Deco design elements like illuminated glass capsules, which display the room numbers, nod toward the building’s history, and hanging lamps adorn each side of the bed like a movie star’s chandelier earrings. Though occupied by digital nomads during the day, the bar at ROOT buzzes after dark, and a DJ spins techno beats nightly starting at 8 p.m.—this is Berlin, after all. —L.H. - Read Full ReviewFans of the flagship Waldorf Astoria New York will feel right at home in this Berlin outpost, set in an elegant skyscraper in City West and just around the corner from the exclusive shopping boulevard Kurfürstendamm (Ku’damm). Rooms are seriously big—starting at 452 square feet—and designed in a contemporary style, with neutral gray velour furnishings, swirl-patterned rugs, and a statement-making gold wall behind the beds. Large marble bathrooms have separate tubs and showers in every category, and the in-mirror televisions and Aesop toiletries add a luxurious touch. Reached by a separate elevator, the Tower Suites (floors 22 to 31) are worth it for the views—of the city, the Kaiser Wilhelm Memorial Church, or the neighboring Tiergarten park and Berlin Zoo. For a true splurge, the massive 30th-floor Astor Suite (with floor-to-ceiling windows, a balcony, and a separate dining room and kitchen) or the 31st-floor Presidential Suite (complete with a grand piano, open fireplace, and two balconies) boast sweeping city views. —Jennifer Ceaser - Read Full ReviewA neoclassical 19th-century bank houses this five-star Rocco Forte property, which enjoys an unrivaled location on Bebelplatz, right in the historic heart of East Berlin. Many of the building’s original details—graceful marble columns, skylights, an intricate iron staircase—have been retained, most notably down below in the pool area, formerly the bank’s jewel vault. A contemporary design streak runs throughout the lobby, which is dotted with oversized black velvet sofas, towering red-lacquer vases, and dangling globe lights, plus a playful pink neon birdcage as the centerpiece. Book one of the higher-end suites and get perks galore, including personalized concierge service, luggage unpacking, free pressing of one garment, and in-house movies. There's a standard minibar in all rooms, but you can request a bespoke Rocco Forte Nourish minibar in advance, stocked with a selection of healthy snacks and drinks. —J.C. - Read Full ReviewBuilt in 1891 as a private residence and converted into a hotel in 1911, Hotel Zoo has been one of West Berlin’s poshest stays for more than a century. In the 1950s, it served as the VIP hotel for the Berlin International Film Festival and was a haunt for A-listers like Grace Kelly and Sophia Loren. So it’s fitting that the hotel’s glamorous history has been reinterpreted by two Hollywood designers, Dayna Lee and Ted Berner. The cool design aesthetic and location on Ku'damm, Berlin's best shopping street, make it a covetable stay for anyone. —J.C. - Read Full ReviewToday, there’s that sense that Hotel Adlon Kempinski Berlin—having withstood the vicissitudes of a tumultuous century—is armor-plated, as unassailable as the bulletproof floor-to-ceiling windows of the presidential suites. Under the Kempinski aegis since the 1990s, it bottles that sense of timelessness and offers a feeling of security and tradition as something that is as precious as it is soothing. The past is present here, exuding patrician-style grandeur and elegance: the Art Deco floor gauges in the elevators, an old-fashioned bicycle that the bellboys use, the panels of walnut wood in the Michelin-starred Lorenz Adlon Esszimmer restaurant, acres of marble for a grand staircase, and gold flakes even on the lobby lounge’s currywurst. Old-school perfectionism calls for the three types of caviar and Champagne at breakfast, as well as butler-ironed newspapers brought to the table. It all contributes to that illusion that you are in a cocoon, away from the travails of the world. —Catherine Fairweather - Read Full ReviewKPM is the vision of Berlin banker Jörg Woltmann, who helped save the 18th-century Royal Porcelain Manufactory Berlin complex on which the hotel has stood since 2019. The ultra-modern, cube-like building has picked up multiple design and architecture prizes and was nominated as Europe’s Leading Design Hotel by the 2021 World Travel Awards. Rooms are minimalist, chic, and smartly designed, with functional desks, high-tech wall control panels, and clever built-ins that make the spaces seem larger than they are—aided by the floor-to-ceiling windows. If weather permits, take advantage of the rooftop terrace with great views over Berlin—just remember to bring your own drinks, as there is no bar. Major sites like Tiergarten and the Berlin Zoo are 10 and 15 minutes by foot, respectively. —J.C. - Read Full ReviewSet in a restored 1913 Art Nouveau building along leafy Oranienplatz, Orania is one of the few hotels—and the only upscale option—in the edgy, nightlife-filled Kreuzberg. A large, open-plan "Living Room," which functions as a restaurant-bar-lounge, is bookended by two roaring fireplaces (in winter) and surrounded by enormous windows; a raised corner stage sports a Steinway piano (there's classical or jazz most nights). The rooms and suites vary in size and layout, but all are similarly designed: lots of rich woods, deep red textiles featuring the hotel’s signature gold elephant, handmade Persian carpets, and curvaceous lamps from Catellani. If you're a frequent visitor to Berlin and love nightlife, this hotel is ideal for you. —J.C. - Read Full ReviewA renovated 1950s high-rise is home to the Berlin outpost of this hip German hotel chain, which is sandwiched between the Berlin Zoo and the trendy concept mall Bikini Berlin. There's a fun energy as soon as you walk into the third-floor reception area, dubbed Bikini Island, which sports a playful jungle-themed design, with tropical plants, stuffed monkeys, and hammocks perfectly positioned to look out over the zoo’s monkey and bird cages. All rooms, even the ones called XL, are on the smaller side, but the funky Jungle Rooms, many with their own hammocks overlooking the zoo, offer an escape different from others you can find in the city. The hotel is also home to the Monkey Bar, one of Berlin's most popular cocktail spots, and guests can cut the line by taking a private elevator straight to the door. —J.C. - Read Full ReviewThis five-star property, long known for its impeccable white-glove service, has a sophisticated look that nods to 1920s Berlin. Entry-level Deluxe Rooms are plenty spacious, measuring a generous 430 square feet, but it’s worth trading up to a Deluxe View Room for fantastic views overlooking Potsdamer Platz. For even more exclusivity, the 42 Club Level rooms and suites on the 10th and 11th floors offer 24-hour access to a lounge with panoramic city vistas, complimentary food and drink, and a private concierge. The elegant sandstone tower fits right in with the neighboring skyscrapers on bustling Potsdamer Platz, and guests are a short stroll from the Holocaust Memorial, the Brandenburg Gate, and Tiergarten park's 519 acres of tree-lined paths and flowering gardens. —J.C. - Read Full ReviewFrom the outside, the circa-1970s building housing The Hoxton doesn’t look like anything special. But step into the oversized lobby chock-full of comfy places to sit (with your choice of chairs and sectionals arranged around tables of various shapes and sizes, along with one long communal coworking table), and you see why the young (and young at heart) could spend all day here. When the mood strikes for a drink, the sophisticated bar lies right behind the lobby, separated by staggered shelves displaying artfully arranged vases, jars, books, and other design knickknacks. And since the Hoxton also has its own coffee shop (technically a teahouse) and Indian restaurant, it’s truly a place that invites lingering. Each of the 234 guest rooms has a similar look, with scalloped headboards in muted pink and green, speckled terrazzo side tables, Art Nouveau lamps, and hardwood floors. —L.H. - Read Full ReviewBuilt in 1914 in the style of a French palace, this magnificent villa has served as a private residence, embassy, naval officers’ club, and later, a luxury hotel, hosting notable guests such as Romy Schneider and Paul McCartney. In 2014, late Berlin fashion designer Patrick Hellmann acquired the property and began renovations, restoring its glorious historical details while bringing much of the design—previously done by Karl Lagerfeld in the 1990s—firmly into the 21st century. The 43 rooms and 9 suites feature particularly impressive details: A dual-bedroom Kaiser Suite boasts an antique library with original frescoes, and the first-floor Karl Lagerfeld Suite has lovely Art Deco touches and a stone balcony overlooking the gardens. —J.C. - Read Full ReviewVladimir Nabokov, Brigitte Bardot, and Alain Delon have all stayed at this luxury hotel at some point in its history. It opened in 1913 on a quiet, leafy square in posh Charlottenburg and was renovated a century later as part of Marriott’s Autograph Collection. It was just spruced up again in 2025 after its takeover by the Germany-based, design-focused Roomers brand. The boutique property retains its alluring Art Nouveau flourishes, including a sinuous canopy above the entrance, Moorish arched windows, and exquisite stucco work throughout. The flawless redesign integrates historic decorative elements with contemporary touches. The luxurious boutique vibe and ideal location—just a short walk to the shops along Kurfürstendamm and the Berlin Zoo—make it an enduring draw, even after the redo. —J.C. FAQ: What is the best area to stay in when visiting Berlin? For first-timers who want to get a true feel for the city, Mitte is the beating creative heart of Berlin, and where you'll find some of our favorite locally-grown hotels, including Telegraphenamt and Chateau Royal Berlin. Another ideal option is Charlottenburg, in western Berlin, which is home to upscale shopping, the grand Charlottenburg Palace, and hotels like The Hoxton. How do we choose the best hotels in Berlin? Every hotel on this list has been selected independently by our editors and written by a Condé Nast Traveler journalist who knows the destination and has visited that property. When choosing hotels, our editors consider properties across price points that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination, keeping design, location, service, and sustainability credentials top of mind. item.title: Should You Travel to Nepal Right Now? What Locals Want International Travelers to Know
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.54
I arrive in Kathmandu on the last day of August, just five days after devastating flash floods—caused by a glacier and rock collapse along Nepal’s border with China—swept through the Rasuwa district. Entire villages and communities were wiped out, hundreds killed, and thousands more are still missing, including many tourists. It’s an unthinkable tragedy that has unfolded with devastating consequences across parts of Nepal and neighboring Tibet. As I exit baggage claim at Tribhuvan International Airport, one of a tiny handful of non-Nepalis on my flight from Dubai, I see a Flood Related Information & Help Desk manned by police. Outside the airport, the streets are busy, a cacophony of honking horns and motorbikes buzzing between cars, buses, and tuk-tuks as people travel around the Nepalese capital. Here, at least on the surface, things seem normal. I’m welcomed at The Dwarika’s hotel by René Vijay Shrestha Einhaus, owner and CEO of Dwarika’s Collection. After a warm hello, the floods are the first thing we speak of; they’re in the minds and heavy hearts of everyone here. It’s a grave catastrophe that has shaken the nation. But what’s also in the minds of Nepalis is the concern that travelers to the tourism-dependent country, about to come into its peak travel season, will stop visiting. Drinking tea in the courtyard of The Dwarika’s hotel, surrounded by centuries-old Newari wood carvings, the twittering of sparrows, and the chattering of mynahs coming home to roost, feels surreally calm. As we chat, monsoon rains start pouring from the sky, a constant, thunderous downpour that hammers on the rooftops and trees, only letting up in the early hours of the following morning. It doesn’t bode well for those in the areas directly affected by the floods, or for those trying to help them. Look at a map of Nepal and the devastated areas don’t appear all that far from the capital, but the country’s mountainous topography means that there’s no direct route between them, and the roaring rivers have no outlet into the Kathmandu Valley. The Nepal Tourism Board, and practically everyone I speak to on the ground, is keen to highlight that the devastation is concentrated in a specific area, primarily the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli river corridors in Rasuwa, Nuwakot, and parts of Dhading district. The rest of Nepal, from popular trekking areas like Everest and Annapurna, and cities like Kathmandu and Pokhara, remains unaffected and open to visitors. Tourism is a major contributor to the country’s economy, and in 2025 Nepal welcomed 1.16 million visitors. Given the terrifying scenes witnessed on the news and social media, it’s natural that travelers with bookings to Nepal may be concerned about whether they should still come or not. But the message from the Nepal Tourist Board is unequivocal: Nepal is not closed. The country is open and eager to welcome visitors. On September 1, Khadak Raj Paudel, Nepal’s Minister for Culture, Tourism and Civil Aviation, made a heartfelt plea on Instagram for travelers to continue visiting and to stand with the country. “Our airports are still operating, our mountains, trails and trekking routes are still open to you. The hotels are welcoming you with open arms,” he said. “Travelling to Nepal at this time is not just a holiday. It’s a support.” It’s a sentiment echoed by Shrestha Einhaus. His hotels have seen a flurry of cancellations. “Tourism is one of the main economic drivers for Nepal, and is something that breathes life into the country,” he tells me. “That’s why it’s important to share where it’s safe to go, and where it’s not safe to go. The majority of the country is safe.” The best way to support Nepal right now is not to cancel your trip, and to plan your next visit, he says. Namgyal Sherpa, CEO of Sherpa Hospitality, a company operating mountain lodges and trekking expeditions in Everest, Annapurna, Mustang, Chitwan, and Lumbini, is also keen to reassure travelers that there is no need to cancel their trips if they are not going to directly affected areas. “We understand that people may feel overwhelmed by the amount of information and images circulating on social media, but it’s important to remember that these reports do not represent conditions across the entire country,” he says. “Our advice is not to cancel your travel plans, but to review your itinerary carefully and stay informed about local conditions.” Those with imminent travel should refer to the latest information from the Nepal Tourism Board, and coordinate with their on-the-ground hotels and organizers. A number of local and international aid organizations, including the Nepal Red Cross, World Central Kitchen, and Médecins Sans Frontières, are providing urgent relief and recovery operations. Locally, donations are being coordinated by the Government of Nepal’s Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund, operating a “one-door” approach to ensure aid is distributed in an equal and organized manner, and to enable long-term restoration, resettlement, and rebuilding of communities, as well as immediate disaster relief. But in addition to making monetary donations, the message on the ground to those overseas who want to support Nepal in its time of crisis is clear. By visiting Nepal now and traveling in safe areas, you will be supporting the communities, workers, businesses, and families whose livelihoods depend on tourism. “Every person who comes to Nepal is making a contribution and having an impact on the broader community and those who rely on tourism for their income,” says Einhaus. Sherpa agrees. “Responsible tourism can be a powerful part of the recovery, and can provide important support to local communities and the tourism industry at a time when they need it most,” he says. “Nepal has always been a country of resilience, generosity, and community. We believe that with the support of people at home and around the world, the affected communities will recover, rebuild, and emerge stronger.”

item.title: From Kendall Jenner to the Clooneys: This is Where the A-list Stays for the Venice Film Festival
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.48
For over 80 years now the Venice International Film Festival has attracted the world's most glamorous and famous crowd. In the 1950s, it saw Brigitte Bardot pose for paparazzi while sitting on grass, and Elizabeth Taylor take a dip in the lido at Hotel Excelsior Venice. Fast forward to today and it's just as star-studded, with the 83rd Venice International Film Festival hosting an array of actors, supermodels and musicians, from Laura Dern to Robert Pattinson, Irina Shayk and Liam Gallagher. Much of the red carpet action takes place at Hotel Excelsior Venice, which has hosted the main event since 1932. Notably, following a three-year closure, the hotel reopened last year (2025), to reveal a grand renovation and thus many of this year's attendees – Kate Mara, Claire Foy, Maggie Gyllenhaal – have also chosen to stay in the boldly striped suites. It's not the only top hotel in Venice that is known to host film festival attendees. The A-listers that prefer something more private often book into one of the 24 opulent rooms within Aman Venice – not only do the Clooneys love to stay here, they also married in the Palazzo Papadopoli location in 2014. To be even further removed and escape the flashes of paparazzi, Hotel Cipriani, A Belmond Hotel, Venice sits on the eastern tip of the Giudecca island. Its peaceful location has been a long- time favourite for the world's most famous stars, with previous guests including Sophia Loren, Cary Grant, and more recently Jennifer Lawrence and Lady Gaga.

item.title: The Best Airbnbs, Lodges, and Hotels Near Carlsbad Caverns National Park
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.30
Home to jaw-dropping cave formations that look like something out of an H.R. Giger painting, Carlsbad Caverns National Park is hands down one of the most spectacular cave systems in the world. Here, travelers can marvel at jellyfish-shaped rock towers, embark on ranger-guided tours into the caves’ darkest depths, and stand in awe (as I did, for the first time at age nine) as hundreds of thousands of bats emerge to feast on flying insects each evening. However, getting to this remote desert cavern is no picnic—travelers typically road trip to the tiny town of Carlsbad or fly through El Paso to witness these underground wonders. As such, lodging in the area is limited, and finding the right place to bed down after a day of adventure can be a tricky feat, even if you’ve been visiting the park for decades, like me. To find the best of the best, I spoke to park experts and scoured the web for the ultimate vacation rentals, lodges, and hotels near Carlsbad Caverns for your next stay. If you’re looking for an adorable tiny house, a riverside home for the whole crew, or a family-friendly hotel stay, you’re in the right place. How to plan a trip to Carlsbad Caverns National Park How do you get to Carlsbad Caverns? Carlsbad Caverns National Park sits about 20 miles southwest of the town of Carlsbad, New Mexico, via Highway 62/180. Due to the park’s remote location but close proximity to the highway, most travelers opt to road trip. If you're flying in, El Paso International Airport is your best bet, set roughly two hours southwest by car. Nearby, Guadalupe Mountains and White Sands national parks are within a day’s drive, making for an easy three-park combo for the park completionists among us, like yours truly. When is the best time of year to go to Carlsbad Caverns? One thing that I love about cave parks: the interior temperature of the caverns stays the same year-round. This makes Carlsbad Caverns an amazing national park during shoulder season (spring and fall) and winter, when others are covered in snow or inaccessible. Pack a light hoodie and expect a constant 56°F climate inside the caves. Hoping to catch the bat flight program? Head to the park in August or September, when baby bats join hundreds of thousands of adults on their nightly quest to find food.

item.title: The Most Beautiful National Parks in Canada, From the Tourist Favorites to the Hidden Gems
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.30
From the peaks of the Canadian Rockies to the deep woods of northern Ontario to the prairies where bison still roam, Canada’s national parks span some seriously beautiful and ecologically important terrain. Since I moved to the Great White North more than 20 years ago, I’ve wanted to visit all of the country’s protected areas—and I’m now about halfway through the country's 37 national parks and 11 national park reserves. Some of Canada's most stunning parks are well-known, like Banff National Park, where turquoise lakes, natural hot springs, and miles of mountain hiking trails draw more than four million visitors each year. Others, like Auyuittuq National Park in Nunavut’s Arctic wilderness, or Mingan Archipelago National Park Reserve in northeastern Quebec, are harder to reach and less trodden—but just as gobsmacking. Below, I’ve spotlighted 11 of the most beautiful national parks in Canada, from coast to coast, to inspire your own travel wish list. See what speaks to you, and I'll see you on the trails!

item.title: The Last-Chance Tourism of Iceland's Glacier Raves
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.08
Weaving through the crowd, I pause next to Kali Van Horn, a 30-year-old architect from Brooklyn with glitter dripping from her eyes like crystallized tears. We share the moment as strangers, pressing our backs against the frozen wall as two DJs spin house and techno tracks in the heart of Langjökull—Iceland’s second-largest glacier. “It’s healing,” Van Horn says, as rainbow lights illuminate the ice cave’s blue hues. Surrounding us are people wearing winter coats accessorized with light-up scarves, sparkly snowflake-shaped sunglasses, and hoods lined with lavender fur. This is part of Iceland Eclipse, a festival on the Snæfellsnes Peninsula, offering late-night raves, cacao ceremonies, and lectures on whale communication to 3,333 total attendees. There’s a strong Burning Man overlap among the crowd, from longtime Burners to attendees drawn to the festival’s mix of music, spirituality, and spectacle. Most are here to extend their experience of the total solar eclipse one day prior, for which they’ve traveled great distances and invested even more grandly. This experience, an 11-hour, $600-price-tagged excursion called “Into the Glacier”, is perhaps the most exclusive event on the lineup. More than ever, rare natural wonders and phenomena are gaining top billing for luxury travel experiences—and this one, both in ambition and vibe, is a standout, drawing just 100 attendees to commune with this 395 square-mile mass of ice. As we drive from the festival grounds toward Langjökull, the stark landscape is punctuated by the occasional sprig of purple flowers. Spikes jut from the massive tires of our car—a vehicle bearing a Jägermeister sticker and the license plate JAGER—which crunches over gravel as the Red Hot Chili Peppers blasts through the speakers, and ravers in the back seat discuss ketamine and the rise of AI. The cars climb higher on the glacier until they begin to get stuck. Then, when they inevitably do, drivers jump out and release air from the tires, redistributing weight so they can continue. The rocks around us fade into sheets of textured ice as we drive onto the glacier, streams of clear water rushing through jagged indentations. This glacier is thousands of years old, our driver explains, formed from layer after layer of snow compressing into ice. As we exit the vehicle, I notice an entrance in the ice—a portal beckoning us to another dimension. We enter the passage, its walls carved entirely from the glacier. I’m still dangling my crampon—a spiked traction device for walking on slippery ice—in one hand when an Into the Glacier staff member swoops in, gliding it over my hiking shoe in a single fluid motion. “Cinderella treatment,” he says with a grin. I follow a faint beat as I meander through a 1,640-foot labyrinth—the largest manmade ice tunnel in the world—before stepping into a wider, taller space within the ice. It’s designed like a chapel, with wooden benches and faux flowers forming a heart on the wall. Near the exit stands a bearded Into the Glacier tour guide whose name is Hjalamroli Hjalmrsson, I learn, and who tells me his age is “young and old at the same time.” We’re lucky to be partying in the Icelandic Highlands, he impresses upon me: 1,300 meters above sea level, surrounded by “500 billion tons of snow, water, and ice.” The sound dances around us. “It's very echoey. You feel the bass is bouncing off the icy walls,” Hjalmrsson says. “The sound kind of drowns, but that's interesting. It's something that you can compare to a big warehouse.” Just two days ago, when I met with Iceland Eclipse’s co-producer Fridrik Olafsson, 41, he told me that he chose not to haul up large amounts of audio or lighting equipment for the event—“the setting itself does the trick,” he said, spreading his hands on the table. His wife had stenciled a drawing of a moon embracing the sun on his thumbnail. On his other hand, a crescent moon with a face howled. Olafsson took a phone call four minutes into our interview, speaking in terse Icelandic, before telling me that three days of storms had ravaged the festival, damaging three main-stage tents, and ruining 50 glamping tents. He described roaring gusts of nearly 70 miles per hour, desperately tying down tents with heavy machinery, and crew members working for 24 hours to make repairs. “Us Icelanders would call it a windy day, but our foreign counterparts were absolutely shocked,” Olafsson said. Olfasson received permission from local authorities and the mayor for Iceland Eclipse excursions. He had previously collaborated with Into the Glacier—which offers daily tours inside Langjökull—while organizing a music event for Secret Solstice, an Icelandic festival he founded that ran from 2014 to 2019 and offered $1 million ticket packages for groups of six guests, including private jet rides and a personal chef. This post-eclipse event is just the tip of the iceberg when it comes to upscale glacial experiences. Inside Langjökull, I follow the steady pulse of music to a mass of 100 people swaying in a hypnotic trance. Hólmar Thor Filipsson, 52, an Icelandic DJ known as Hólmar (Acid Tourist), is playing back-to-back with Margeir Steinar Ingólfsson, 51, an Icelandic DJ known as Margeir. “Everyone there was experiencing something for the first time ever,” Thor Filipsson tells me, later, back at the camp. “It was like the eclipse in a way, but more concentrated, and it felt a little bit sci-fi.” Ingólfsson operates on the same wavelength. “I even came with a special gift for the glacier from my friend, who is a glacier specialist,” Ingólfsson, 51, says. His friend has collected water from glaciers around the world, and Ingólfsson placed a few drops near the DJ booth. When I ask about the night's song selection, Ingólfsson says they took their cue from the glacier itself. Was the glacier in the mood for house and techno, I ask? “Yes,” Ingólfsson replies. “That was the vibe that the glacier wanted at this time.” As the rave beats on, cans of pink vodka cocktails appear in our gloved hands. The beverage packaging suggests that “Flamingo” is an adequate description for a flavor—apparently, that means something like the nostalgic taste of liquified pink Starbursts. Iceland Eclipse staff members are on task with collecting trash in plastic bags, the goal being to leave the glacier just as it was found. Hours later, our two-drink-maximums met, we exit the glacier and totter down to the Into the Glacier Klaki Base Camp, about 10 minutes from the ice cave’s entrance. I meet Lyndsay Klebba, a 36-year-old writer from Chicago, who is wearing a fluffy yellow hat and a pashmina decorated with spotted mushrooms. She decided to visit Iceland after a 23andMe test revealed her Viking heritage: “To be surrounded by ancient ice and listening to New Age music—it's just a clash of titans,” she says. She spent most of the party tucked behind the DJ booth, her heart against the ice to feel the bass. She also wandered into an icy alcove and stuck out her tongue to catch droplets trickling from the ceiling. “The freshest water I ever tasted.” Klebba is the exact audience that Iceland Eclipse is after—those moved by the specialness of the glacier as a setting. “Ice holds a lot of history,” says Mitch Morales, CEO of IMXP and founder of Iceland Eclipse. “The ice in the glacier is thousands of years old–I think about what was happening in the world when this ice was frozen, all the memory, and thinking about this as being a temple in the same way." Morales, 41, is planning IMXP’s “Eclipse Trilogy” of annual totality events. Just last month, he was scouting for the ideal 2027 Luxor site; he is considering Australia or New Zealand for 2028. His ambitions extend even further, though, he says: He eventually wants to host an eclipse viewing on the moon. “In Egypt, there are stone temples that are dedicated to the things that came before them. In a way, I think that a glacier party is similar to that,” Morales says. Gazing out the window as the car crept down the glacier, Klebba observes small signs showing how far Langjökull’s ice once extended. The glacier has lost an estimated 29 percent of its mass between 1890 and 2019, according to a 2020 study published in Frontiers in Earth Science. “Where we were right now would have been glacier probably 40 years ago,” Klebba says. “The fact that we had to drive up several miles just to get to it makes you think about what's going on today.” Some travelers seek out landscapes threatened by global warming, a phenomenon known as “last-chance tourism.” Langjökull has already outlived nearby Okjökull, which became Iceland’s first glacier lost to climate change in 2014. Its name was shortened to Ok, dropping jökull—Icelandic for glacier. “Knowing that this was the last chance to party inside a glacier because of climate change was a big factor in me deciding to attend,” says Hayley Sharkey, 27, reflecting on the event. Sharkey is a Miami public relations coordinator who has adorned her blue snow jacket with faux-fur cuffs. “Future generations will not be able to understand how it felt to be inside a glacier. The feeling of natural ice surrounding you will be seen as a myth.”

item.title: Where was The Gentlemen Season 2 filmed? The sophomore season expands beyond English country piles to Mafia-held Italian palazzos
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 5.12
On Location peels back the curtain on some of your favourite films, television shows, and more. This time, we ask: where was The Gentlemen Season 2 filmed? The second season of Guy Ritchie’s hit Netflix series, The Gentleman, is here. The first series introduced us to Eddie Horniman (Theo James), a young British aristocrat who had inherited his father’s grand country estate, only to discover that behind the family money was a secret cannabis empire. In Season 2, Horniman, now the Duke of Halstead, is keen to expand the operation, alongside his business partner, Susie Glass (Kaya Scodelario). This will take them out of the English countryside and subterranean criminal worlds of the East End and Liverpool, and thrust them instead into the world of the Mafia, as they attempt to go international and do business with the dangerous Capo dei Capi, Marco Moretti (Sergio Castellito). “The madness of Italy’s beauty, its culture, its history and its traditions were something I felt would fit perfectly into our show,” says Ritchie. “I had wanted to expand the canvas of The Gentlemen in this season. Italy was just an obvious choice. British gangsters colliding with the Italian Mafia just feels so right for our world. Some fruit hangs low and looks so tasty you just can’t resist for very long.” Here are some of the key locations used in the filming of The Gentleman Seasons 1 and 2, from Ritchie’s Ashcombe Estate to Lake Maggiore in Italy. Is The Gentlemen based on a real-life story? Both the film of the same name and the two seasons of The Gentlemen are not based on a true story, though of course, they borrow elements from the criminal underworld and its cast of characters. The situation that Eddie Horniman and his family find themselves in – of having to find new ways to monetise their vast aristocratic estates – is a reality, however. There are no real life examples of aristocrats running cannabis empires that we know of though. The main thrust of the action in Season 2 of The Gentlemen takes place in Lake Maggiore, connecting Horniman and his business partner Katie Glass to Italy’s criminal gangs – the mafia. Historically, the area has not been known as a mafia heartland – unlike regions like Sicily, for example – but it does have a relationship with organised crime. In particular, the ’Ndrangheta, the Calabrian mafia, have reportedly used the area for cocaine and weapons trafficking, thanks to its close proximity to the Swiss border. Where was The Gentlemen Season 2 filmed? The Badminton Estate, Gloucestershire While some scenes of The Gentleman were filmed on stage sets at Alperton Studios in Wembley, London, the exterior of Halstead Manor, the fictional home of the Horniman family, is The Badminton Estate. The real-life home of the Duke and Duchess of Beaufort is a popular filming location and wedding venue in the south Gloucestershire countryside. Viewers with a keen eye may recognise the property from Netflix favourite Bridgerton and movies including Pearl Harbour and 28 Days Later. The sprawling estate has been occupied for thousands of years, and the remains of several Roman villas surround the main home. The medieval property was owned by the Boteler family before Edward Somerset, fourth Earl of Worcester, purchased the manors of Great and Little Badminton in 1612. It’s his son, Sir Thomas Somerset, who made significant alterations to the original house, and the property has captured the imagination of high society and even the royal family over the centuries – Charles II stayed in the house, and the late Queen Elizabeth II was a regular visitor to the annual Horse Trials. “Badminton felt immediately right for Halstead,” says supervising location Manager Iggy Ellis, “because it’s a proper, lived-in home rather than a National Trust museum. So inside, there’d be some walking sticks by the door or a few shotgun rounds from where they’d been out shooting. There were cracks and tired bits, as you’d get in every family home. But there was also oil painting and history and majesty. It felt perfect for our story.” Ashcombe Estate, Wiltshire In episode one, Ritchie made his own country estate, Ashcombe Park, available for filming a shooting party scene. “That was a lot of fun but tricky at times too,” says production designer Martyn John. “You’re in the middle of nowhere with no phone signal or internet. We had to take everything in; so, flowers, food, dogs, guns and also… frozen partridges.” Ashcombe is a working farm set in 1,100 acres of rolling chalk land, and is named after the ash trees and the valleys (‘combes’) that monopolise much of it. It has been the family home of Ritchie since 2001 (when he bought it with ex-wife Madonna for £9 million), and was previously the home of photographer Cecil Beaton. Loseley Park, Surrey Much like in season one, some of the exterior and interior scenes at Halstead Manor were filmed at Loseley Park, a historic home just outside of Guildford that is now used as a wedding venue. “Where possible we tried to maximise every location because when you move around it costs money that could be on the screen,” explains supervising locations manager Iggy Ellis. “So we used a cottage in the grounds of Loseley for the exteriors of gamekeeper Geoff’s cottage and built the interior in the studio because we needed lots of camera space and somewhere for Geoff’s menagerie of animals.” Swakeleys House, Ickenham Another multi-purpose location was Swakeleys House, a 17th-century mansion in Ickenham. “It was a great find because we were able to use it for so many things,” explains Ellis. “From the rehab centre where Freddie is recovering from the cocaine habit he acquired in the first series to the interior of the prison where Bobby Glass is meant to be serving time.” Built in 1638, it is an excellent example of the ‘Artisan Mannerism’ architectural style, a form of Jacobean architecture that features decorative classical flourishes such as gable ends. It was the home of Sir Edmund Wright, Lord Mayor of London, and was visited twice by the famed diarist Samuel Pepys. The Adelphi Building, London The Adelphi Building off The Strand was transformed into an auction house for a scene in which Susie Glass bids millions for a Botticelli painting, which is later snatched by a gang on e-bikes outside. “I wanted to use that network of streets around the Savoy Hotel, including a secret little tunnel that cuts between John Adam Street and the riverside,” explains Ellis of the chase. “It takes at least three months’ notice to get London streets closed for filming, and there were some careful negotiations with everyone from Westminster Council to building owners and the Savoy Hotel itself. But that amazing chase really is one of the things I’m most proud of.” The Grade II-listed Adelphi has retained many of its original 1930s Art Deco features, including its impressive stone facade, classic columns and Gilbert Ledwood sculptures. Today it is predominantly used as an office space, and houses the publisher Condé Nast, whose titles include not only Condé Nast Traveller, but also Vogue, Tatler and GQ. Villa Rusconi Clerici, Lake Maggiore Villa Rusconi Clerici became the glamorous palazzo home of Mafia heiress (and Eddie’s love interest) Contessa Isabella Savanza de Parme, known as Bella. “We spent three full days looking at several amazing palazzos, including one on Lake Como,” shares John. “But as soon as I saw the one at Lake Maggiore, I knew this was the one. It was in a much less touristy area and it had such great light and glittering water. You could point the camera anywhere and it just looked beautiful.” The interiors too were perfect for Bella’s home. “I wanted a house or a villa which reflected the taste – if not the scale – of Eddie’s country estate, Halstead Manor” says Ellis. “I wanted these two aristocratic families to merge, stylistically. So, you have all the antiques and the paintings that reflect tradition and ancestry, but also modern pieces because, despite the centuries-old history of both families, there’s a new generation in charge now.” Villa Rusconi Clerici is a beautifully preserved 19th-century palazzo on the Piedmont shore of Lake Maggiore, and unsurprisingly is popular as a wedding venue. The villa that exists today was built for a Hungarian colonel and revolutionary, Stefano Türr, who was married to one of Emperor Napoleon’s cousins and became intrinsic to the unification of Italy. The interiors are Art Nouveau in style, including a grand staircase featuring a wrought iron balustrade. Grand Hotel Majestic, Lake Maggiore The Grand Hotel Majestic stood in for the fictional The Grand Hotel, where a wedding takes place later in the series. First built in 1870, it was one of the finest examples of luxury hospitality in the area, and was immediately popular with the international elite. Unsurprisingly, considering its location on the shores of Lake Maggiore, it is often chosen as a wedding venue for modern couples, much like in the show. One of its chief assets is the view across the lake to Borromeo Island, with actor Theo James pictured standing on one of the balconies looking out across the water in one scene. While the interiors are French in style, with parquet flooring and chandeliers, the grounds are also particularly lavish, with centuries-old trees and flowers, and there’s even a small private beach. Chiesa San Leonardo, Lake Maggiore The 16th-century church Chiesa San Leonardo also features in the new season. Located in the lakeside village of Pallanza, the church features striking columns of pink Baveno granite, as well as 17th-century wooden sculptures and altars. There’s also a 65-metre high bell tower, as well as access to the lake from a dramatic staircase. Where was The Gentleman Season 1 filmed? Stoke Court, Buckinghamshire The Badminton Estate gets much of the credit for appearing as the exterior of the fictional Halstead Manor, but some of the interior scenes used Stoke Court in Buckinghamshire. Stoke Court is home to the study, where Freddie shoots Liverpudlian drug dealer Tommy after a memorable scene featuring a chicken costume, Halstead Manor’s boot room, drawing room and orangery. The real-life property is best known for its association with mid-18th-century poet Thomas Gray, who holidayed there during his childhood. Wrotham Park, Hertfordshire Wrotham Park in Hertfordshire plays the part of the home of extravagantly wealthy drug lord Stanley Johnson, aka Bridgewater House. The neo-Palladian English country house was designed by Isaac Ware in 1754, and it’s where we see Susie Glass and Stanley engage in a polite-ish war of words over his desire to take over her father’s empire. London The Gentleman’s filming locations depict two sides of the coin: lavish country houses owned by the landed gentry and hideouts used by the criminal underworld. For the latter, the locations team looked to London. Locations used across the capital include The Reform Club in Pall Mall, which doubled up for Pinky’s Club, and Billingsgate Market, which is mentioned by name in the series as the headquarters of the Liverpudlian drug group. The exterior shots of the Croydon Tower Block were taken at Brandon Estate, while the boxing ring is the now-closed party venue Printworks in Rotherhithe.

item.title: What does the EU's new hand luggage rule mean for travellers? Here’s everything you need to know about the updated air passenger rights
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 5.11
