On Tuesday 1 September, Members of the European Parliament confirmed changes to air passenger rights that were first reported earlier in 2026. These rules have been in place for more than 20 years, since 2004, and aim to protect passengers against disruption to their travels. While many of our rights, such as compensation if flights are delayed by a certain number of hours, will simply be upheld by the latest vote, there are some changes due to come into effect, too. Extra costs for hand luggage have been something that’s plagued travellers for decades, but new regulations are set to change that. After more than a decade of negotiations between the Council of the EU and the European Parliament, a landmark agreement has been reached. What is the new rule for hand luggage? New rules will include the right for passengers to carry one personal item such as a small bag or backpack with them onboard without incurring an extra cost. Airlines will also be required by law to display air fares that include carry-on luggage while booking to improve transparency and comparability between airlines and tickets. Airlines may still offer cheaper tickets who travel without hand luggage, MEPs say. A small catch to be aware of, however, is that this regulation applies to EU airlines only. This means that on non-EU airlines, like easyJet and Jet2, passengers may still be bound to the old regulations – except on flights returning to the UK from an EU country. Which other rights have been introduced? Several new rights are set to improve passenger safety and protection. These include rules to make it easier for passengers to claim compensation and access assistance in case of delay or cancellation, as well as new regulations reinforcing rights for persons with specific needs, such as persons with disabilities or reduced mobility and pregnant passengers. Air passenger rights changes to know - The right to carry on board, without extra cost, one personal item, such as a small bag or backpack - Passengers will no longer be charged for correcting spelling errors or for a printed version of a boarding pass if they have already checked in - Passengers will be able to take the return flight of a two-way ticket even if they did not use the first flight - Clearer and quicker reimbursement for flight disruption and travel delays - Passengers with disabilities and reduced mobility will have the right to compensation, rerouting and assistance if they miss a flight due to the airport’s failure to help them reach the gate on time - Any person accompanying a child below the age of 14 will be entitled to an adjacent seat without paying extra. The same right will apply to passengers with disabilities and reduced mobility, and to pregnant women. “I’m proud that, after 13 years of negotiations, we reached a landmark agreement to strengthen EU air passenger rights,” announced Alexis Vafeades, minister of transport, communications and works of the Republic of Cyprus. “This modernised framework will deliver certainty, fairness and stronger protection for millions of European air passengers. The agreement strikes a fair balance for our airlines, helping preserve connectivity that is vital to the EU’s internal market and its citizens.”

item.title: Flying with children is about to get cheaper and easier thanks to new EU rules – here's everything you need to know
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.89
Ever found yourself fuming that in order to ensure you get a seat next to your child on the way to your family holiday, you have to pay extra for a seat for each of you – on top of what's probably an already hefty ticket price? You're not alone. But changes to EU air passenger rights will make this annoyance a thing of the past, as the right for children under the age of 14 to sit next to an accompanying adult free of charge will be protected. In September 2026, Members of the European Parliament approved changes to rules on air passenger rights that have been protected since 2004. There's a slate of changes due to come into force, but the parents among the Condé Nast Traveller team were particularly intrigued by the promise that a free adjacent seat will be guaranteed for a child under the age of 14 and the adult accompanying them. That means airlines cannot split up families at seat allocation, and cannot charge you extra to sit together. Why under the age of 14? For most airlines, children under 14 cannot travel without an accompanying adult on the same flight. The change means that adding extra fees to allow parents and children to sit together – which can quickly add up as they're charged per person – will be a thing of the past. The rules come into effect 12 months and 20 days after their publication in the Official Journal of the European Union – around August 2027, just in time for any end-of-summer holidays. Other rights that will come into practice next August thanks to these include: - Making it easier to claim compensation if your flight is delayed or cancelled - Transparent pricing that displays ticket prices including cabin baggage by default - Personal items stored under the seat should be free of charge

item.title: In London, artisans are keeping hands-on heritage alive – meet the makers championing the craft revival
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.36
There was a moment last year when the penny dropped for Guy Salter, founder of London Craft Week, a citywide celebration of the handmade that marked its 12th edition this May with nearly a quarter of a million visitors. Seeing queues amassing outside the eclectic shows, workshops, installations and talks, he thought to himself, craft is officially a thing. When Salter started the now cult event in 2015, the revival of making was already well underway, but the momentum and proliferation of craft-based practices has mushroomed across London in the decade since. In the face of an increasingly automated, AI-generated world, we are seeking objects that are human, with provenance and a sense of place. Beyond London Craft Week, the Crafts Council’s annual fair for contemporary craft and design, Collect, gathers 300 artists and makers at Somerset House each February, and organisations such as Qest (Queen Elizabeth Scholarship Trust), Cockpit Arts, The King’s Foundation and Heritage Crafts robustly support craftspeople with education, training and awareness. The craft boom has inspired amateurs too: pottery now has a primetime TV show, and basketry and textile weaving are enjoying a widespread revival – the former is celebrated at annual summer festival Tear Up. London’s craft heritage has deep roots stretching back to the 12th century, when artisans and merchants founded guilds to protect their craft and commercial interests. Groups formed for tailoring, furniture making, pewtering and dyeing, and as they got more powerful they built livery halls – in 1515 a hierarchy was introduced, including special recognition for the 12 most powerful guilds. Today 114 worshipful companies remain. Most studios are part of an intricate network of suppliers, complementary trades and outsourced workers, with London particularly well placed to support these connections, as well as provide local, national and international clients with easy access to the myriad makers tucked away in all corners of the city. Creating a new generation of craftspeople is one of the key challenges for the sector. But at a time when arts education is being relentlessly cut in schools, many companies, including the Goldsmiths’ Company and Cordwainers’ Company, actively support apprenticeships and training for their specialisms. “The opportunities for the youngsters into those trades are ever shrinking, and there’s definitely an appetite to create something where there are clearer pathways,” says shoemaker Deborah Carré. “We need to value this time and training, so it becomes part of our economic future. Living heritage is an evolving thing, not a static museum piece.” Clare Coulson Allyson Williams, seamstress Deep in the Yaa Centre, a buzzing arts hub that nurtures the creativity behind the Notting Hill Carnival through costume-making workshops, steel band studios and a central atrium for performances, is the HQ of Allyson Williams, the festival’s matriarch. Williams is lead seamstress at Genesis, one of the UK’s longest-running mas, or masquerade, bands: the collectives whose handcrafted costumes bring the traditions and stories of Afro-Caribbean ancestry and spirit – plus a contagious joy – to west London’s streets each August. The lush, syncopated rhythms of calypso music fill the air, and atelier-style cutting tables bestride deep plastic containers scarcely repressing explosions of sequins, velvet, silk, brocades and Lycra (“I’ve used every material known to man”). Shelves hold fragments of outrageously bejewelled body sculptures. It’s a fashion collection for street theatre; every year Williams creates samples referencing a theme for revellers to order from, and garments are then tailored to their specifications. Some involve wild proportions: one client masquerades as a Moko Jumbie (stilt-walking dancer). Since she established Genesis in 1980 with her late husband and Carnival co-founder, Vernon Williams, their faithful recreations of historical events and civilisations have been superseded, post-noughties, by fantastical themes rendered in meticulously decorated bodysuits. “Learning those techniques was incredibly uplifting, and exacting; there’s nowhere to hide. I’d like to be remembered as the person who brought amazing designs to life…. and made a mean bikini.” Katie Baron Anderson & Sheppard, tailors To step into the high-ceilinged, wood-panelled bespoke tailoring house of Anderson & Sheppard, established 1906, is to take a near-quantum leap into a living slice of quintessential British heritage. It’s wholeheartedly styled like a traditional gentlemen’s club, with a leather sofa, fireplace, crystal decanter and tumblers. Biblically weathered order and measurements books – tantamount to classified documents, in which every client’s details are logged by hand – line upper shelves. “We’re sticklers for tradition,” says front-of-house custodian Martin Crawford. “People like to come in and see their grandfather’s handwriting.” A corridor provides glimpses of the cutters at work, in full suiting, and paper patterns – anatomical blueprints – hanging from metal hooks. The cutters, of whom A&S has trouser and coat specialists, are essentially the architects of the design, measuring, drafting and hand cutting garments ready for construction. Here making a suit is an art form and a vocation, and the experience of buying one is aptly theatrical. A&S developed the “English drape” in the late 1920s: a softer, demilitarised, more glamorous tailoring language made for movement. Popularised by King Edward VIII, it has drawn fans in both business and the arts – including Fred Astaire and Brad Pitt. While men’s styles remain its mainstay (“Other houses are far better at suiting the female form,” says Crawford), A&S also crafted Marlene Dietrich’s famous black tux. Fluidity rules in this perfectionist’s paradise: “The job necessitates being very self-critical,” says senior cutter Leon Powell, “but our work is rooted in feeling, the ‘rock of eye’ [a tailor’s intuition].” KB Ella Merriman, rush basketry artist Cradled among the silk dyers and ceramicists of the labyrinthine Cockpit Arts building in Bloomsbury sits the studio of Ella Merriman, whose experimental twists on traditional basketry have propelled her to the forefront of the conceptual handicraft movement. Eight-foot bolts of rushes, harvested once annually in Somerset and Oxford, and bound with colourful string, line windows garlanded by chains of rush-end offcuts. Prototype works range from vessels to vast circular lighting fixtures. Her métier often involves teasing rush into unfathomably shaped objects using “weird moulds” as diverse as traffic cones and charity shop vases. Merriman works the harvested stems, dried slowly and then dampened to retain their flexibility (thick stems serve as uprights, narrower stalks the weft “threads”), around these structural bases, weaving intuitively by hand. Chairs and footstools in bright pink and yellow rest on dust-sheeted tables. The delightfully dishevelled studio echoes the poetic idiosyncrasies of nature that are central to her work and her feeling that “slight wonkiness is so beautifully human”. Regularity is anathema to Merriman’s practice, which she discovered accidentally via a short course after studying furniture and product design, and a close call with the “too rigid” world of architecture. “It felt like a remembering, rather than a learning. Working with a material like this is a relationship. In design, you’re trained to find repeatable functions, but here every stem is different and must be respected.” KB Lock & Co, hatters “We say that we make heirlooms,” says hatter Awon Golding as she stands in the tiny attic workroom on the top floor of Lock & Co Hatters’ storied shop in St James’s, where the rafters are filled with fedoras and trilbies, and artisans stitch, sculpt and trim summer’s most extravagant headwear. Celebrating its 350th anniversary this year, Lock & Co is the oldest shop in London – and the oldest hat shop in the world – yet very little about the craft has changed in that time. Hats are still made on wooden blocks (carved by Boon and Lane in Luton) and boaters are created with strip straw (where a continuous length of woven straw is handsewn in a spiral), both critically endangered skills. In tiny hushed workrooms each stage of the hat is crafted by an all-female team: hand-dyeing, steaming and finishing with the finest ribbons, feathers and flowers that cover every surface. The shop, a stone’s throw from St James’s Palace, has served countless royals (it currently holds a royal warrant from King Charles), along with politicians (Winston Churchill’s order ledger is in the ground-floor heritage room), authors, actors and icons including Jacqueline Kennedy and Princess Diana. The bowler hat was invented here – it was originally commissioned for the gamekeepers of the Holkham estate – and top hats are among the individual orders fulfilled by an expert team on the ground floor. Many creations use vintage materials: “You’re buying into a little piece of history, and it’s so much more special,” says Golding. CC Mary Wing To, whip and harness maker The smoulderingly musky scent of leather is absorbed instantly on a visit to Mary Wing To’s garden workshop in suburban south London. The material is the cornerstone of a luxurious artisanal practice straddling the rare craft of traditional whip and harness making (she was protégé to the Queen’s master saddler) and fashion design and sculpture. Blankets of it are accompanied by a sumptuous marble cutting slab; Tohiti canes for whip shafts; her favourite awls for piercing, scoring and dyeing; mood boards marrying editorials, equestrianism and erotica; and mannequin heads, both equine and human. Wing To discovered leathercraft during her fashion design and technology MA at London College of Fashion, when she undertook a saddlery course at Capel Manor College as its first-ever fashion student, upskilling to produce her equestrian-inspired final collection. That parlayed into an apprenticeship at the Royal Mews, the working stable that oversees royal ceremonial transportation – she was on duty for the wedding of the Prince and Princess of Wales – and proximity to “leathercraft at its highest level”. Whip making came via the tutelage of legend Denis Walmsley. An obsession with discipline – both in the process and finished pieces – has driven her to deliver numerous competition wins for saddlery and wearable arts, and exhibition honours at the V&A. “For me it’s always been about consistency and discipline, and passing on these skills; these incredible legacies.” KB Maya Njie, perfumer The Shoreditch studio of perfumer Maya Njie – a second-storey hideaway bordered by the rumbling beat of the Tube, where she develops genderless and vegan scents and runs private workshops – is a touchingly intimate echo of her home. More vintage boutique than clinician’s lab, it’s a snapshot of her Swedish Gambian heritage and the hub of a nostalgia-riffing creative practice designing biographical fragrances that encapsulate moments, people and places. A mood board-esque wall of thank-you cards, exhibition flyers and her own photographs dominate the entry. Having studied surface design at London’s University of the Arts, she’s still a prolific image maker – each scent comes with an evocative postcard-sized visual and thumbnail colour palette. Paintings are propped against walls, surrounded by an eclectic mix of furniture (“mostly sourced from eBay and antiques markets”) including a German medicine cabinet housing precious olfactory accoutrements such as resins, essential oils, aroma-compounds, cruelty-free musk and molecules, with which she creates her unique blends. The finessed formulas are left to mature then filtered into small batches of scent. Ten years after launching online, she now has eight core perfumes: a personal archive in olfactory form. “There’s an importance in diverse cultural stories being told [via scent], especially when perfumery dates back millennia, long before France was the epicentre of fragrance,” says Njie. “Everyone can take inspiration from a place, but it’s vital to have perfumers telling stories deeply authentic to who they are.” KB Rian Kanduth, gilder Alchemist’s chamber meets forensic laboratory at Rian Kanduth’s diminutive studio in the City & Guilds of London Art School, like a portal to arcane magic. It’s a sensory sweetshop for the investigative decorative arts, where her projects often demand exacting historical knowledge and a scientifically granular handle on environmental factors including heat, light and humidity. Every inch is surrendered to experimentation: cabinets and refrigerators hold pigments and abrasives including rabbit-skin glue, “dragon’s blood” (a crimson tree resin for vibrant glazes) and “dead bugs’ graveyard” (cochineal dye), and test tubes of gold leaf “bling” are tacked to the wall for eye-level inspection. Sensorial instincts are vital because water gilding – the application of a micro-thin layer of metal or other ornamental substrate to a surface – is an art form of more than 18 steps, some going back 5,000 years. Other techniques include pastiglia (intricate paste work patterns), verre églomisé (reverse glass gilding, creating a shimmering effect), sgraffito (scratching a surface layer to reveal a contrasting underlay), gesso and punchwork (stamping patterns into a gilded surface). It “requires us to use all our senses, including smell, to do the right thing”, says Kanduth. “It’s a constant analytical process where we’re perfecting the recipe.” She normally works “upside down and really high” across private homes, artists’ studios, museums and Unesco heritage sites. Like paramedics for at-risk art, she and her team sometimes undertake emergency conservation, from dealing with damaged carvings to time-pressured archaeological digs. KB Kaori Tatebayashi, ceramicist Kaori Tatebayashi’s airy studio is filled with ceramic flowers. There are towering foxgloves suspended along the walls; primroses, miniature iris and hyacinths arranged in a tableau on the floor; and tables topped with fritillaries and full-blown tulips, as well as an unfurling magnolia flower held on a branch. Hand modelling in warm white stoneware, she captures a fleeting moment of the plant’s life, working directly on her kiln shelf. “Once I start I don’t stop – I have to be so quick,” she says of the time constraints of working with clay. Each piece is fired, then left unglazed and undecorated, so that the focus is on the flower’s form. “When the colour is removed, you see plants with a fresh eye.” Born in Arita, Japan, home of Imari porcelain, Tatebayashi studied ceramics at Kyoto City University of Arts before moving to London to attend the Royal College of Art and then relocating permanently in 2001. Alongside her solo exhibitions at Tristan Hoare Gallery, she takes on private commissions and site-specific installations. Her peaceful Deptford studio, hidden at the back of a modern building right on the banks of the Thames (at high tide the water laps just feet from her door), is decorated with antique furniture, cabinets filled with curiosities, books of botanical drawings and a table of plants that she sources from specialist growers, her shared allotment in south London, and sometimes from clients’ gardens. In spring, when her favourite bulbs begin to emerge, her personal life is put on hold. “When they start flowering, I drop everything.” CC Darren Appiagyei, wood sculptor Anchored in the stoic energy of heavy-duty machinery, the workshop of award-winning wood artist Darren Appiagyei in Deptford’s Cockpit Arts studios is a dusty, spit-and-sawdust hub suited to the slow satisfaction of iterative hands-on experimentation. The room he affectionately calls “the shed” is dominated by a hulking lathe, simple workbench and chrome shelving unit brandishing an array of logs. It’s here that self-taught Appiagyei transforms the raw shafts of felled trees – relishing their grains, knots and imperfections – into receptacles at equal turns robust and exquisitely fragile-looking. They’re so finely honed, often featuring wafer-thin walls, that they sometimes resemble ceramics. During a practice he describes as “very meditative, even therapeutic”, he carves into the trunks (all commandeered within a five-mile radius, aligned with his reverence for nature and focus on sustainability), finessing parts of the exterior and leaving others raw to expose the timber’s unique organic patina. Sometimes he uses a pyrography device to scorch tiny dots onto the surface like a 3D pointillist, rendering them “stylistically primitivist but also very refined”. A decade since he graduated in 3D design from Camberwell College of Arts, where he first learnt wood turning, his obsession with the material remains undimmed “because it has a life of its own. It’s wholly its own organism, which keeps it exciting.” KB Carréducker, shoemakers On the wall behind a workbench at Carréducker, the company founded by Deborah Carré and James Ducker in 2004 to make handsewn shoes, is a pegboard featuring the tools of their trade. There are lasting pliers, feathering knives, burnishing irons and the brilliantly named “fudge wheel”, a stitch-marking tool. Nearby there’s a vitrine of maquettes showing different stitch constructions, from blind welt to Norwegian welting. In all, there are 200 steps in making a shoe, says Carré, and how each is executed affects the final balance, proportions and look. They make everything here, from walking boots and derbies to Oxfords and sneakers. Carré describes their house style as “magpie”, which reflects the fact that each design is led by their client’s tastes and preferences. Not a lot has changed in the craft since the Worshipful Company of Cordwainers was granted ordinances in the City of London in 1272; even the business duo’s preferred oak-bark-tanned leather comes from J & FJ Baker in Colyton, Devon, where there has been tanning on site since Roman times. Alongside making bespoke shoes for private clients, the pair also run workshops and courses for amateurs and wannabe shoe-makers in their studio in the Oxo Tower on the Thames. “Our students are attracted by the mindfulness, the focus, the concentration, the mental health benefits of working with their hands,” says Carré. CC Michael Ruh, glass-blower In the southeast London studio of Michael Ruh, the blazing furnace pushes the temperatures to 50 degrees Celsius in summer, and the air is scented with the distinctive perfume of wood smoke and molten beeswax, used to lubricate the glass-blower’s tools. Transforming cullet, a waste product from the optical glass industry, is a visceral and sensory practice, and one where speed and movement is key: malleable molten glass waits for no one. Ruh originally studied fine art before he began working with glass in Belgium. He launched his eponymous studio with partner Natascha Wahl in 2004, and moved to his current mews location in 2013. Alongside his glassware and private commissions, the space hosts occasional workshops in glass engraving, and open studios. It was the constant motion and the possibilities of this challenging material that first captured the imagination of the American-born maker, whose recycled glassware, lighting and tableware are highly sought-after. He blows and shapes sculptural pieces using innovative moulds made in paper or wood, adding organic curves or impressions in the soft glass. His beautiful, functional objects are distinctive for their subtle markings, created with self-made tools. Tumblers are circled with fine lines, often inspired by the light and landscape or the bracing icy winters of his Minnesota childhood; memories that are frozen in time as the glass rapidly cools. CC Tuesday Riddell, lacquerwork artist Odes to the romance, mysteries and beguiling savagery of nature are abundant in Tuesday Riddell’s studio on the banks of south London’s River Wandle. The space hosts micro mises en scènes of shells, leaves and feathers mingling with jars of richly coloured pigments; booklets of gossamer-thin gold and silver leaf; charcoal sketches depicting black cats and earthworms tumbling from seething soil (“five-minute works to get my creative flow moving”); and weathered copies of Angela Carter’s gloriously dark, folklore-twisting novels. Renowned for the endangered, conservation craft of Japanning (lacquerwork), Riddell has always found inspiration in the natural world’s sublimely lethal majesty: “I’m fascinated by the tension between the fragility and the horror of nature. Anything too pleasant feels stale.” This skill, which she learnt during a Painter-Stainers decorative surfaces fellowship at the City & Guilds of London Art School, involves applying 30 to 40 layers of black lacquer – composed of shellac (natural resin) and pigments – to boards, building intense depth. It’s a long process: sanding in between every five or 10 layers, rendering them flush for the next application. Extended drying times mean Riddell often has up to 30 artworks in progress. The final, pictorial element becomes highly nerve-racking – an incorrect stroke can obliterate months of preparation, but the risk, she says, is worth it: “No other process fully captures what I’m imagining. It’s like subconsciously knowing a language you somehow magically speak.” KB Hand & Lock, embroiderers The Fitzrovia HQ of Hand & Lock, Britain’s oldest and most revered embroidery house, is a treasure trove of decorative artistry inconspicuously enclaved behind glazed double doors. Its four storeys have a palpable air of mystique thanks to a stream of confidential projects with its royal, military, fashion couture and pop culture clientele. There’s a jewel box shop whose wooden drawers cradle glittering gemlike brooches, insignia, cords and coloured fringes; a school; traditional and digital ateliers; and a samples-packed bead room. Key techniques include goldwork, using metal threads and bullion to add volume and texture; couture-associated tambour beading, which has a flawlessly uniform fluidity; and silk shading, where threads coalesce into a painterly breed of realism often used to depict flowers or animals. Work they can divulge: items for King Charles III’s coronation, including ceremonial and regimental garments, plus former House of Commons leader Penny Mordaunt’s cape dress and headband; the winged jacket for Elton John’s Who Believes in Angels? album cover; and work for Guillermo del Toro’s Frankenstein and Emerald Fennell’s Wuthering Heights. According to Sophie Carr, who ran emerging talent incubator The Hand & Lock Prize for Embroidery for eight years after winning it in 2011, they recently embroidered a luxury train carriage’s interior. Hand & Lock also creates two main annual collections, sells YouTube-tutorial-accompanied taster kits, and hosts courses with The National Gallery, V&A and Kew Gardens. Why the booming popularity? “Detail, a satisfyingly slow process and desire for modern heirlooms,” says Carr. KB Bellerby & Co, globemakers The cavernous, corrugated-roof workshop of Bellerby & Co Globemakers in Stoke Newington feels more like a film set than a 21st-century studio. It’s a vivid tableau of the myriad skills that go into making each bespoke globe: sets of gores hang from pegs and string across windows (each globe has 12 or 24 of these panels that are dampened and then precisely applied to the surface of the sphere), and shelves are topped with globes in all sizes awaiting the meticulous hand painting and illustration that is applied by a team of watercolour artists. When Peter Bellerby was searching for a globe for his father almost two decades ago, he couldn’t find anything that fitted the bill. So he went on a two-year odyssey to create one, and launched his eponymous firm in the process. “Globes are a wonderful convergence of the arts and the sciences,” he says of the skills in engineering, geography and artistry required. Each globe takes weeks or even months to make, and is a work of art, customised with family histories, past travels, migration routes and themes. The slow and meticulous process of making by hand is celebrated: apprentices here train for at least a year before producing the 22cm desk globe. The biggest – a show-stopping 152cm diameter model created for the new National Geographic museum in Washington, DC – is the largest hand-painted globe in the world, and smoothly spins on an axis. CC Kyriacos Hadjikyriacou, pleater Secluded in a vast hangar on a Tottenham industrial estate, Kyriacos Hadjikyriacou, the UK’s most revered pleater, is working among a shadowy horde of industrial machinery (“some can create 1,500 styles, others just one”), a towering backdrop of fabric bolts, and two gleaming steel steam boxes that hold court like bonfire-powered beach huts. There are also reams of delicate textiles, artfully gathered, ruched, scored and creased (designs can be machine-birthed and hand-finished, and vice versa). The dichotomy of his work – clients include students, hair academies and high-profile fashion houses such as Alexander McQueen and Victoria Beckham – demands both technical acumen (his career began in hydroponics and agricultural engineering) and a craftsman’s dexterity. “Pleating is geometry. If you don’t know geometry, you’re a folder, not a pleater,” says Hadjikyriacou. Original inventions are key to his success (he’s now in his late 70s), alongside precision replicas. One of his favourite concoctions is a white satin crown-pleated coffin inlay, “a design so unusual it took a year to develop”. Inspiration lies everywhere: honeycombs, mushroom innards, hieroglyphics, “If you can think it, you can do it.” KB Manuel Mazzotti, bookbinder Located in an unassuming east London residential complex, the studio of award-winning bookbinder Manuel Mazzotti is a hive of carefully controlled creative chaos. He is a virtuoso in finding new ways to bind, cover and encase printed material (books, but often in unconventional form), and signs of an impatient mind relentlessly in prototyping mode abound: a sprawling plan chest strewn with mid-assemblage projects; plotters (for precision cutting); bone folders (for creasing); and Japanese stepped rulers beloved by Mazzotti for “their simple effective clarity”. Images from favourite works crowd the walls and a circa-1910 heat press (refurbished to run on electricity) sits majestically in the corner while a pair of Japanese Daruma dolls – talismans of goal setting – keep watch. Both aesthetician and technician, Italian-born Mazzotti studied mechanical engineering then transportation design before going to Switzerland’s prestigious Centro del Bel Libro to learn bookbinding. He famously uses challenging materials (recently, Carrara marble) and wildly proportioned designs – such as the supersized “clamshell” format for artist Hormazd Narielwalla’s Sky in a Box – in his creations. His personal work teases the dichotomy of raw, salvaged materials with pristine detailing, emphasising physical nuance. An avid book collector who scours bookshops for special editions like others hunt rare vinyl, Mazzotti is emphatic about their emotional magnetism, noting a rising appetite from creative agencies, artists and families reimagining heirlooms. “Books are powerful objects. They’ve always represented knowledge and status, but now, as we question what will remain of our digital footprint in 100 years, they also mean continuity.” KB Blenheim Forge, knife makers Aptly for a brand birthed in 2014 as a DIY endeavour in a south London back garden – “We somehow forged a knife in conditions where it shouldn’t have succeeded, then spent years obsessively trying to replicate it,” says Jon Warshawsky, one of the three founders – entering the railway arch home of small-batch knife makers Blenheim Forge is like slipping into a bricolage steampunk dreamscape. After passing through iron gates wrought into organic patterns and a small courtyard amassed with metal ephemera, I clamber through a wooden door-within-a-door camouflaged by a floor-to-ceiling mural of a bull and a jester. Inside, the aroma of maple wood erupts as a knife’s handle is put through its bandsaw paces. The knives are created by fusing multiple bars of steel, a sandwich that’s battered into shape via power hammers or anvil-based hand-forging. They’re then heat-treated and tempered for durability and sharpness, ground down, polished, etched and sharpened. The workshop, separated from the display-based front area by a Crittall glass partition, is packed with machinery for specific procedures to hone high-performance knives for professional chefs and dedicated home cooks. Heavily inspired by Japanese knives, with names including Gyuto, Nakiri and Santoku, each is forged from a combination of steels to be precise, strong and balanced, but adapted for everyday multipurpose Western culinary sensibilities, including being lighter and more comfortable to handle. Constantly innovating, Warshawsky and his co-founders, James Ross-Harris and Richard Warner, flex their creative muscles on a bimonthly special, using new techniques or developing genres such as an oyster shucker or barbecue knife. They recently commissioned their own steel, which will, says Warshawsky, “level up everything we make”. KB Clio Peppiatt, fashion designer Clio Peppiatt’s inaugural Knightsbridge flagship is a boudoir of a boutique birthed with modern showgirls in mind. Seashell cocktail goblets, sumptuous carpets and soft fabric wall drapes in dreamy baby blue evoke silver screen-era Vegas and create a cinematic backdrop for contour-caressing bridal and evening wear embellished head to hem in traditional Tambour beading and hand-embroidery. Modern heirlooms are devoted to the joy of dressing up – “I see my pieces as wearable art that celebrates the wearer,” says Peppiatt. Minidresses contain approximately 250,000 recycled glass beads; long dresses half a million. It’s all steeped in a familial legacy of female entrepreneurialism stretching back eight generations. Peppiatt’s great-grandmother, the first in the lineage to professionalise crafting, was a lacemaker specialising in women’s gloves, and Peppiatt’s grandmother taught her artisanal embroidery skills. Peppiatt hand-draws and paints every design – often playful motifs such as coral reefs and cactus-bearing desertscapes – in her west London studio, and collaborates with a Mumbai-based atelier on everything from prototypes to final pieces, “because their skills are like nothing else”. Those designs become marks on tracing paper via a “tattoo-gun-style holepunch”, are stretched across a table-sized embroidery loom, then worked on from underneath using a hooked needle. “It’s very intuitive,” she explains, “because you can’t see your hands while working.” Has her label’s sensibility changed since its 2015 inception? “It still has a maximalist spirit, but with joy and a sense of femininity that is felt not performed.” KB

item.title: UK flight delays after NATS technical failure hits Heathrow, Gatwick and other airports
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.22
Several major UK airports have experienced delays due to an air traffic control technical failure. The National Air Traffic Services (NATS) has identified the issue, but there is no certainty in whether air traffic will go back to normal today. The national air traffic control service (NATS) warned in their latest statement on X: “We have identified that the issue was in our flight processing system. Our engineers are on site and working urgently to resume normal operations as quickly as possible. We recognise the ongoing disruption to travel, for which we sincerely apologise.” The statement continued: “Flights are still departing and airspace is open, but recovery will take some time. We will provide further updates as soon as possible.” Heathrow Airport shared an update on its X account: “The air traffic control service is experiencing a technical issue which is impacting departing flights at UK airports. Arriving flights are not currently impacted. We are supporting our local NATS team in their efforts to resolve the issue as quickly as possible.” However, some passengers arriving at Heathrow reported knock-on disruption, including being kept on aircraft after landing. Other airports such as Birmingham Airport and Jersey Airport have also issued statements, but neither NATS nor the airports have given a firm timeline for a return to normal operations. According to the Financial Times, Eurocontrol – the organisation responsible for coordinating air traffic across Europe – warned that disruption to airspace over London, southern England and Wales could continue until 9pm on Tuesday. Passengers should check the status of their flight directly with their airline and monitor the NATS website and X account for further updates. UK airports reporting disruption include: - London Heathrow Airport - London Gatwick Airport - London Luton Airport - London Stansted Airport - Manchester Airport - Birmingham Airport - Belfast City Airport - Edinburgh Airport - East Midlands Airport - Jersey Airport

item.title: Volcano eruption in Indonesia: the latest updates, government guidelines and travel advice
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.08
Late on Friday 4 September, Mount Anak Krakatau, located 150km from Jakarta, erupted continuously for 25 hours, producing fountains of lava and a booming sound that could be heard hundreds of kilometres away from the epicentre. According to Indonesia’s Geological Agency, the continuous eruption began at 11.07pm local time on Friday and ended 25 hours later, at 12.04am on Sunday 6 September. The volcano remains active today, with lighter, intermittent eruptions, prompting school closures and maintaining its Level III alert status. The Geological Agency confirmed that “the probability of additional eruptions in the coming days remains high”. “We continue to evaluate the volcano’s development based on all monitoring data, not solely on the number of eruptions or the height of the ash column,” said Lana Saria, head of the Geological Agency. Mount Anak Krakatau, which means "Child of Krakatoa", is located in the Sunda Strait, separating the islands of Java and Sumatra. Since it emerged from the sea about a century ago in the caldera formed after the 1883 eruption of Mount Krakatoa, it has been sporadically active. In 2018, the collapse of Anak Krakatau triggered a tsunami that killed at least 430 people in Sumatra and Java, but, according to Saria, the most recent series of eruptions does not have the potential to trigger a tsunami. The main hazards for visitors and locals are volcanic ash, high gas concentrations, and the ejection of hot rocks, lava, and other material around the crater area. Indonesia has more than 120 active volcanoes and sits in a seismic area prone to earthquakes and tsunamis. Indonesia lies along the Pacific ‘Ring of Fire’, a belt of seismic activity around the Pacific Ocean that contains around 75 per cent of the world’s active volcanoes. Travel disruption in Indonesia Volcanic ash is present in the airspace around Jakarta and several other cities, which prompted Indonesian authorities to close eight airports until 6pm Monday (local time), including Jakarta's international airports of Soekarno-Hatta and Halim Perdanakusuma, Radin Inten in Lampung on Sumatra, and Husein Sastranegara in West Java. The situation is developing, so airport closures could therefore be extended further, depending on volcanic activity, as confirmed by transport minister Dudy Purwagandhi: “We cannot ascertain when this will end due to the dynamic weather.” So far, the natural disaster has disrupted around 2,300 flights and affected 270,000 passengers, who are now stranded in the country. Which airports are currently closed? - Halim Perdanakusuma Airport (HLP), Jakarta - Soekarno Hatta International Airport (CGK), Tangerang, serving Jakarta - Radin Inten II Airport (TKG), Lampung - Husein Sastranegara Airport (BDO), Bandung - Budiarto Airport (RTO), Curug, Tangerang - Pondok Cabe Airport (PCB), South Tangerang - Muhammad Taufiq Kiemas Airport, Pesisir Barat, Lampung - Atung Bungsu, South Sumatra Is it safe to travel to Indonesia? Air travel has been significantly disrupted in Jakarta and other affected parts of Java and Sumatra, with flights cancelled, delayed or diverted. Travellers should check the latest status of their flight directly with their airline or travel provider before travelling. The FCDO advises against all travel to certain areas but not the country as a whole; you can find the full list on the government website. If you decide to travel to Indonesia during this time, remember to check with your travel insurer to make sure your plan is still valid considering the circumstances.

item.title: Best eSIMs for travellers 2026: How to beat airport Wi-Fi and extortionate roaming fees for good, tried-and-tested by our editors
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 3.90
On the list of additional costs that can trip up travellers, the dreaded roaming data charge is one of the most irritating. While there are usually phone plan kiosks or the odd SIM card vending machine at the airport, by the point you’ve reached the arrivals lounge, you’re a captive audience and beholden to whatever rate is offered. You also might need data before leaving the airport: I’m still scarred by the charge I incurred in the connecting terminal in Singapore when the WiFi wasn’t working and I needed to let my partner know I’d arrived. But there is a way to beat the charges before you’ve even left the country – and that’s by using an eSIM. Often, purchasing a dedicated travel SIM works out cheaper than buying the additional data bundles offered by your UK phone network, especially for frequent fliers and those headed further than Europe. Plus, by using a digital SIM rather than a physical one, there’s no need to wait for it to arrive or worry about losing your regular SIM card while it’s not in use. Below, we’ve outlined the best eSIM services to know in time for your next trip, along with the price for a week’s worth of data for a long-haul flight to Indonesia as a price comparison guide. The best eSims for travellers at a glance: - Best overall: Ubigi - Best for digital nomads: Saily - Best for customisable data top-ups: aloSIM - Best for heavy data users and longer stays: Holafly - Best pay-as-you-go eSIM: Roamless - Best value eSIM: Airhub - Best for app-free setup: easySim - Best for short trips: GoMo World - Best for security and extra perks: Yesim - Best for essential app-only coverage: Honest Mobile - Best for rewards and younger travellers: Global YO - Best for business travel: Maya Mobile Ubigi Best eSIM overall - Pros: Top-up possible without WiFi or data remaining, worldwide data plans, 5G available - Cons: Little pricier than some of the other services on our list for some countries - Price for a 3GB eSIM for Indonesia: £6 - Price for a 3GB eSIM for USA: £6 Ubigi is a comprehensive data service for over 200 countries, with data plans from 500mb to unlimited. There are one-off, monthly and annual services, so digital nomads, business travellers and holidaymakers alike will all be covered. If you run out of data, you can top up without being connected to WiFi even without any remaining data, which is an additional safety boon that other services on this list can't always match. 5G connectivity is also available at no extra cost where possible. You can also save 10 per cent on prices on your first order with the code CNTRAVELLER. Editor review: I used a Ubigi eSim when I travelled to Yellowstone from London recently. I think the tell that a service like this is working well is to realise you don’t think about it at all. My internet in the States was just as speedy as when I’m in the UK, and worked as soon as I landed at Denver airport to await my transfer. I appreciate this as a lot of airports charge for WiFi or make you hunt down one of those tedious booths for a code before you’re granted the privilege to log on – if you can’t find one or it’s out of order, as happened to me in Hong Kong one time, then you’re either stuck internetless or have to suck it up and pay your network’s extortionate roaming fee. By activating my eSim immediately upon landing, I didn’t have to worry about connecting to the airport WiFi at all. But the main boon was being able to top up via the app even without being connected to WiFi. Wyoming is very large, very empty, and free fast WiFi was often in short supply. I was grateful to be able to top up without WiFi on one day trip – I didn’t realise I was running low on data before leaving and would have had a whole day without connectivity otherwise. This would have been anxiety-producing as a solo traveller very far from home! Charley Ward Saily Best eSIM for digital nomads - Pros: Good variety of plans, regional and global plans available - Cons: A little more expensive than some of the others listed - Price for a 3GB eSIM for Indonesia: £6.89 - Price for a 3GB eSIM for USA: £6.89 If you’re looking for data abroad, you’re sorted with Saily, whether you’re going on a quick three-day hop to longer three-month treks. You can buy per country or per region – handy if you’re island hopping across Asia, for example – and there are even worldwide plans for the most intrepid travellers. We like how seamless this service is, especially. You can purchase the data in the UK and when you arrive at your destination, it’ll switch on automatically, so you’re never without data and prevents being hit by accidental roaming charges in the airport. Saily has unlimited data plans in 37 destinations including the US, Japan, France, Spain, Italy and Thailand, plus an unlimited European data plan that works in 36 European countries. The app also has various tours and experiences bookable within the Saily app dependent on where you're headed. New users can use code CNT10 for 10 per cent off all mobile data plans worldwide. aloSIM Best for customisable data top-ups - Pros: Easy-to-use app, transparent pricing, flexible data top-ups without hidden fees - Cons: Data-only plans (no traditional phone calls or SMS) - Price for a 3GB eSIM for Indonesia: Approx. £8.20 - Price for a 3GB eSIM for USA: Approx. £6.70 If you prefer straightforward, data-only coverage without signing up for unnecessary bells and whistles, aloSIM is a reliable contender. It operates across more than 170 countries, is easy to set up via the minimal mobile app – which allows you to calculate and purchase the exact amount of data you’ll need before stepping onto the plane; not something that can be said of all of the brands featured here. Installation is instant via a quick QR code scan and topping up takes mere seconds in the app should you run out of data or your trip is extended. One note: this brand’s eSims don’t support traditional voice minutes or SMS. However, for seamless 4G/5G connectivity for internet-based messaging apps, navigation, and streaming, it’s a worthy choice. Holafly Best for heavy data users and longer stays - Pros: Unlimited data packages in most destinations, 24/7 customer support, customisable plan durations - Cons: Considerably higher price point if you’re taking short trips, limited hotspot capabilities on some plans - Price for 7 days of unlimited data for Indonesia: Approx. £20.40 - Price for 7 days of unlimited data for USA: Approx. £20.40 For travellers who refuse to count megabytes or hunt down hotel WiFi, Holafly is the go-to provider. Rather than capped data tiers, Holafly built its reputation on offering unlimited data plans across 180+ destinations – essentially, wherever you are in the world, this is the eSim for you. You can tailor your package to the exact length of your trip – whether that’s three days or a full month – ensuring you never pay for extra days you don’t need. It is undeniably pricier upfront than fixed-data alternatives, but for remote workers, heavy video streamers, or anyone who relies heavily on maps and ride-hailing apps on the move, should find the peace of mind worth the investment. Roamless Best pay-as-you-go eSim - Pros: Pay-as-you-go data options ensures no wasted data, voice calls available, well priced - Cons: Although potentially more convenient, pay-as-you-go plans can work out more expensive than fixed plans - Price for a 3GB eSIM for Indonesia: £6.70 - Price for a 3GB eSIM for USA: £6.70 It’s a problem I’ve had when travelling a couple of times: you have to top up your eSim a day or so before the end of your trip, but then leave the country without using all the new data, thus wasting it (and, therefore, the money you paid for it). Not so with Roamless, which has pay-as-you-go options that won’t expire after 30 days. That means if you don’t burn through all your data on your trip, you can use it on your next getaway, even if you’re not returning to the same destination. The brand also has regular data packages for over 200 countries worldwide from free 500MB packs up to to 20GB, as well as packages including call-time, all for a very reasonable price point that’s lower than some of our other favourites on this list. You can save 20 per cent on your first purchase with the code CNT20. Airalo - Pros: 200+ destinations, regional and global deals, great connection - Cons: highest prices on our list, most packs are data-only - Price for a 3GB eSIM for Indonesia: £6.50 - Price for a 3GB eSIM for USA: £8.50 Habits are hard to break, and I must admit I was sceptical about using my first eSIM. But after one-too-many surprise phone bills, I finally decided to take the leap during a sunny Croatia break, and where better to start than the world’s first and largest eSIM provider: Airalo. Steady Wi-Fi for around twenty minutes is necessary for installing the eSIM, so I’d recommend doing so before you travel, but you can activate the actual data plan within minutes once you land. Airalo’s easy-to-follow setup guide clearly directed me through the process, and I quickly found myself connected to my new data plan – with noticeably improved connection. I was staying in an off-grid beach village near Dubrovnik, and while my travel buddy struggled for internet access in our hotel room, my connection was fast and reliable at all times. Editor review: The sim is all based around Airalo’s no-frills mobile app, where you can flick through the loaded catalogue of national, regional, and global packs. My 3GB package (priced at £7.50) turned out to be plenty for a five-day trip, but the app also provides instant data top-ups in case you run out. It’s worth noting that almost all Airalo packages are data-only, so text and calls have to be supplied through your original provider, but for me, this feature was ideal. With the eSIM neatly slotting alongside my physical sim, there was no need for the confusing chore of switching phone numbers, and so this eSIM lived up to the hassle-free hype in all areas. Layla Quaedvlieg. Airhub Best value eSIM - Pros: Yearly and monthly subscriptions, unlimited data and voice options available - Cons: None that we can see - Price for a 3GB eSIM for Indonesia: £4.75 - Price for a 3GB eSIM for USA: £2.37 This is our best value eSIM option – Airhub is a great service for frequent travellers and digital nomads especially. The app is intuitive and easy to use, and there are plenty of different plans available for trips of all lengths. One perk this service offers over the others we like is the yearly and monthly subscriptions, which make financially savvy options for those on longer trips – for example if you’re stationed somewhere for work or taking advantage of that post-Covid ‘work from anywhere’ lifestyle. There are also plans that include voice minutes and SMS services, which is an additional boast that the other services here can’t match. Editor review: On a recent work trip, I realised how useful the combined voice and data plans can be when travelling. In the UK I rarely make traditional voice calls, but on this particular trip I needed to connect with a contact that didn’t use WhatsApp, so I couldn’t make a call over the internet. I’ve a spend cap on my regular sim which, as I learned, prevented me from making calls abroad. I was left in a frustrating situation where I wasn’t quite sure how to get hold of the guy. The problem was resolved by downloading this eSim, and also meant I didn’t have to spend time removing and then re-adding the spend cap on my regular plan when I got home. If you travel a business and make a lot of calls, I’d recommend this eSim. Charley Ward EasySim - Pros: Diverse range of data plans, many plans work across multiple countries, no need for an app - Cons: No family feature for managing multiple eSIMS per account - Price for a 3GB eSIM for Indonesia: £8.50 - Price for a 3GB eSIM for USA: £8.50 Editor review: EasySim is part of the EasyJet family of brands, so they know a thing or two about roaming. True to form, it’s one of the most comprehensive services on offer, with a good range of plans at some of the best prices we’ve seen. Some may not like the lack of an app, but the website is easy to use and does the job perfectly well. As a bonus, this service covers a wide range of phones. Not all the options on this list are compatible with my Motorola – an admittedly niche handset – so the compatibility here adds an additional sweetener to this service for me. GoMo World Best eSIM for short trips - Pros: Low starting prices - Cons: Fewer cross-country compatible plans than EasySim, calls, SMS and MMS services aren’t currently provided - Price for a 3GB eSIM for Indonesia: No 3GB plan available; 1.5GB for £3.99 or 15GB for £20 - Price for a 3GB eSIM for USA: No 3GB plan available; 1GB for £3.99 or 15GB for £20 As someone who travels regularly for work, and often only for a few days at a time, I’ve sometimes found myself paying over the odds for week-long data plans when I’m only away a few days. Case in point on a recent trip to the Maldives, where I was beholden to the airport’s singular 10gb data SIM offering despite only being in the country for three days. So, if you’re one for regular short hops, GoMo World’s smaller plans are ones to consider for maximum cost-saving benefits. Yesim - Pros: Coverage in 200+ destinations worldwide and a ‘refer a friend’ rewards system to save money on data plans. - Cons: Connection speeds limited to local carrier availability - Price for a 3GB eSIM for Indonesia: 3GB £9 for 30 days, 5GB £11.70 for 15 days, 10GB £19.80 for 30 days - Price for a 3GB eSIM for USA: 3GB not available, 500MB for 0.45p for 3 days, 10GB £14.40 for 30 days, 15GB £16.20 for 30 days This Swiss-based eSIM provider boasts excellent reviews on Trustpilot and with good reason. The broad, global coverage offers fast, consistent internet activity in over 200 countries, is easy to use and set up, and is reasonably priced with no hidden extras. The built-in VPN technology offers enhanced security and reassurance when travelling, while the fast customer support service is there ready to answer any questions or fix problems, should they arise, with ease. We’re impressed by the virtual phone number rental capability, too – a rare addition among eSIM providers. Honest Mobile - Pros: Perfect if you’re only planning on using apps rather than making calls. - Cons: Doesn’t support internet calling or streaming - Price for a 3GB eSIM for Indonesia: from £3.75 per month for unlimited data roaming - Price for a 3GB eSIM for USA: from £3.75 per month for unlimited data roaming This smart SIM automatically switches to EE, O2, or Three when your main SIM loses signal and provides free, unlimited global roaming for over 200 essential apps, including Google Maps, Skyscanner, and Uber, across 180+ countries. This eliminates the stress of data caps and roaming charges while on your travels. It’s a great idea for keeping costs low, just be careful to stick within the limits of what this eSIM can offer. Maya The best eSIM for business travel - Pros: Money-back guarantee for 180 days, high-speed internet connection, global packages - Cons: None as far as we can see - Price for a 3GB eSIM for Indonesia: From £5.39 - Price for a 3GB eSIM for USA: From £7.19 For a solid choice with no hidden fees, Maya is a good option. No contracts, 24/7 customer service, and a money back guarantee for up to 180 days. This means that if disaster strikes and your trip is cancelled, you can request an immediate refund with no extra charges. The SIMs are compatible with IOS and Android devices, and with at least two (if not more) networks available in each destination, the 4G/5G internet truly is high-speed. We love their new global eSIM package too, which includes across 119 destinations and starts from as low as £4.79, as well as the special business options, revolutionising the company work trip with shared data pooling. FAQs How we tested the best eSims To find the best travel eSIMs, our editors tested a variety of eSims across a range of long-haul and short-haul trips – from quick European city breaks to multi-stop journeys through Asia and North America. We evaluated how straightforward the provider’s app and setup process was, measuring how quickly we could download, install, and activate data profiles before departure. Once on the ground, we put network reliability, download speeds, and signal strength to the test in a variety of locations, including busy airport arrival lounges, remote countryside, and dense city centres. Finally, we compared overall value for money, flexibility, data-top-up ease, and customer support responsiveness. What is an eSIM? In plain English, it’s a virtual sim card that you install via an app rather than by inserting a physical card into your phone. They are activated remotely, so there’s no need to visit your local phone shop or wait for it to arrive. In your phone’s settings, you’ll be able to toggle between your existing physical sim card and the eSim, even being able to use both simultaneously, such as using one for mobile data and the other for calls and texts. This is handy if your eSim plan is data only but you’d still like the phone and SMS capability while away. It means that, if you download and install the eSim before you head off, you can activate it in the airport when you land and beat pricey roaming charges forevermore. The setup is simple. After registering online, all it takes is a quick scan of a QR code and you’re good to go. If you run out of data, you don’t need to download a new one – just top up your existing plan. Each eSIM has its own inclusions, from calls, texts, and internet streaming, to exclusive access to essential apps like Google Maps, so make sure to check in advance which plan best suits your needs. If that’s not enough to convince you, the entirely virtual setup means that they are also kinder to the planet than the plastic chips of traditional SIMs. Is my phone eSim compatible? Most Apple iPhone, Google Pixel, and Samsung Galaxy models released in the UK since 2018 are eSIM compatible. For other smartphones, the quickest way to check eSIM compatibility is by dialing *#06# on your phone's keypad – a screen pop-up including an EID number indicates your device is eSIM-friendly. You will also need to make sure that your device is not locked to a single network. If this is the case, provided you’ve reached the end of your original contract, you can ask your provider to unlock it for free by requesting a Network Unlock Code (NUC). Do I need a different eSIM for each country I visit? No. All eSIMs are suitable for use worldwide, so you’ll only need to install one eSIM. Do check, however, that the eSim provider you select has data plans available for the country you want to visit – all of the brands below have hundreds of countries available, so this shouldn’t be a problem in the vast majority of instances. Some plans are suitable for use in multiple countries, too, which is good if you’re taking a longer trip hopping from place to place – like if taking a cruise, for example. Airalo, for instance, has packages valid for use in up to 137 countries, from Jamaica to Japan.

item.title: Paris could soon be just a train ride away for East London
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 3.62
Stratford International could become a new hub for European rail travel, as Virgin Trains considers stopping in East London when it launches its new cross-Channel services to rival Eurostar. According to the rail regulator, the Office of Rail and Road (ORR), Virgin will be allowed to operate up to 20 daily return services between London and Paris, Brussels or Amsterdam from October 2030, potentially ending Eurostar's monopoly since 1994. The proposed timetable for Paris initially sees six return services per day, increasing to 10 from April 2031 and 13 from October 2031. Following the ORR's decision, there are talks of Virgin’s new international services stopping at Stratford International as well as the usual Eurostar stop at St Pancras International. Sir Stephen Timms, MP for East Ham, has welcomed the possibility of international trains stopping in East London, as it would promote regeneration in the area. Virgin Trains has plans to invest £700m in the project and create hundreds of jobs in the UK, including skilled jobs at the Temple Mills depot in East London. The MP has previously called for more rail services to stop at Stratford International. Responding to his calls for Virgin to consider a stop in East London, a spokeswoman for Virgin Trains said: “We have recently been awarded track access on London St Pancras Highspeed and will be bringing investment and new skilled jobs to the Temple Mills depot in East London.” She added: “Virgin is looking forward to exploring additional stops, including Stratford International.” Virgin is not quite ready to hit the rails yet, as the company still has to secure access to rail tracks through the Channel Tunnel (owned by Eurotunnel) and European rail networks, as well as obtain the necessary safety approvals. If everything goes to plan, Virgin intends to launch services from London to Paris in October 2030, with Brussels and Amsterdam also forming part of its planned European network.

item.title: 11 most beautiful autumn train journeys in Europe that encourage slow travel
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 3.61
Summer is a gorgeous time to enjoy train-hopping on France’s Mediterranean coast (the Train de la Côte Bleue is a journey you must add to your summer 2027 bucket list) or southern Italy on a regional train from Naples to Reggio Calabria – but autumn is arguably the best time to visit Europe by train. While summer sees hordes of tourists travelling from around the world, putting pressure on rail networks and often making a train trip feel like a sauna, autumn – as well as spring – allows you to visit even some of the continent’s most popular destinations with a little more ease and comfort. While Switzerland and Italy may be the ultimate destinations for scenic train travel, there are routes across Europe that combine fabulous scenery with interesting sights and activities at both ends of the journey. We have gathered some of the best train rides across Europe to give you some ideas for your next train adventure. Italy Train line: Vigezzina Centovalli Railway Italians love to complain about their railway system, but the truth is Italy has one of the best – if not the best – train travel offerings in Europe. Simple regional trains often offer fabulous views over the Italian countryside and coastlines – my yearly train from Naples to Paola is one of my favourite summer activities – but there are some specific routes that deserve the detour. The Vigezzina-Centovalli Railway connects Domodossola in Italy to Locarno in Switzerland in around two hours, passing through the striking Vigezzo Valley and the Centovalli (Hundred Valleys) and allows travellers to stop and visit charming villages such as Santa Maria Maggiore or impressive sites like the Sanctuary of the Madonna del Sangue in Re. In autumn, the service becomes known as the ‘Foliage Train’. Just note that the special foliage ticket allows one intermediate stop on either the outward or return journey, rather than unlimited hopping on and off, so choose wisely. Switzerland Train line: GoldenPass Belle Époque (from Montreux to Zweisimmen) When it comes to scenic train routes, Switzerland always makes it to the top of the list. Out of the many famous routes, the Bernina Express is probably the most popular, but I think that is a route that can wait for winter. Instead, autumn is the perfect time of year to book a GoldenPass Belle Époque train and admire some truly stunning Swiss foliage while sitting in vintage 1930s-style carriages. This route takes travellers from Montreux to Zweisimmen in around two hours through the Gruyère district and the Pays-d’Enhaut. The carriages have panoramic windows, offering uninterrupted views of lakes, mountain peaks and forests along the way.T Greece Train line: Odontotos Rack Railway (Diakopto to Kalavryta) Greece is more popular for boat-powered island hopping than for train travel, but the country has a few gorgeous routes up its sleeve. If finding an unspoiled Greek island is becoming more and more difficult, the Peloponnese region is still fairly under the radar and has a lot to offer year-round. The Odontotos Rack Railway from Diakopto to Kalavryta takes around one hour and shows you a different side of Greece, following the Vouraikos River through its dramatic gorge. Take this opportunity to enjoy a few days in Diakopto, a lovely seaside town usually still sunny and warm in autumn, before getting a complete change of scenery when arriving in the mountain town of Kalavryta. France Train line: Strasbourg to Sélestat via Molsheim, Obernai and Barr (following the Route des Vins d'Alsace) If there is one event that defines autumn in Europe, it is the wine harvest, and France has a fabulous train route to celebrate this time of year by rail. The Route des Vins d’Alsace winds through eastern France and offers a wonderful introduction to the Alsace wine region. There are a few itineraries that can be created following this route but, if it’s your first time in the region, starting from the beautiful city of Strasbourg seems like a good option. From there, take the Strasbourg-Sélestat line that runs through vineyards and allows you to stop in some charming towns such as Molsheim, Obernai and Barr. From early August to mid-October, wine villages across the region host a packed calendar of harvest festivals and events, so make sure you check the calendar and organise your visit to coincide with an event that catches your eye. Portugal Train line: Douro Valley Line (Linha do Douro) The Linha do Douro is a 160-kilometre historic line that connects the city of Porto to the village of Pocinho, running alongside the Douro River, and crossing 35 bridges along the way. The one-way trip is three hours and twenty minutes, but the full journey can still be tackled as a day trip, returning to Porto the same evening. If you don’t feel like committing to a seven-hour train journey in a day, you could stop in the charming town of Pinhão for a wine tasting at Quinta do Bomfim or Quinta das Carvalhas. It cuts one hour off the journey each way and you can still do it in one day if you take the morning train from Porto and make sure you are back in time to take the last train back to the city from Pinhão station. Serbia and Montenegro Train line: Belgrade to Bar If you thought that the Balkans didn’t have great train routes, the trip from Belgrade to Bar will change your mind. With its eleven hours and 476 kilometres, this is a very long train journey that takes travellers from the green hills of Serbia to the rugged mountains of Montenegro. The journey can be made on an overnight service year-round, while a daytime train operates seasonally. In 2026, it runs until 30 September, although it’s worth checking the operator’s website before travelling as timetables can change. Of course, the morning train is the one to take to be able to fully enjoy the views through the Dinaric Alps. The railway crosses 435 bridges – the most spectacular being the 498-metre-long Mala Rijeka Viaduct, which rises almost 200 metres above the valley floor. This is neither the quickest nor the most comfortable train ride you can take in Europe, but it’s definitely worth it if you are passionate about train travel. Norway Train line: Flåm Railway Not only is this one of the most beautiful train journeys in Europe year-round, but in good Norwegian fashion, the route is extremely well organised for tourists who want to enjoy everything that the area has to offer. You can simply book your train tickets and enjoy the ride, or choose a package that includes excursions and accommodation through Norway in a Nutshell. The train journey is twenty kilometres long and lasts around one hour one way, taking you through peaks, valleys, waterfalls and rivers. From cycling, hiking and swimming to ziplining, there is a lot to do along the way so you can spend one day or a full week exploring. Austria Train line: The Arlberg Railway This train route connects the Austrian cities of Innsbruck and Bludenz and is 136 kilometres long, with direct trains completing the journey in around one hour and 45 minutes. During this time, you will speed through charming Alpine villages, rivers and steep-sided valleys framed by mountain peaks. If you are travelling from Innsbruck, this is only one of the many stunning train routes you can take around Austria, to Switzerland or through South Tyrol all the way to Italy, but it’s an ideal option if you want maximum scenery without committing to a full day on the rails. Germany Train line: West Rhine Railway If you are looking for a train journey that will immerse you in nature but want a less obvious alternative to the Alpine railways of Switzerland and Italy, consider Germany’s West Rhine Railway. The route stretches for 185 km, starting from Cologne and arriving at Mainz via Bonn, Koblenz, and Bingen. Cologne makes an excellent starting point, with its Gothic cathedral and lively riverside neighbourhoods worth exploring before you board. The two-hour journey is stunning from beginning to end, but the highlight is the Rhine Gorge, a UNESCO World Heritage Site visible from the train. Bulgaria Train line: Rhodope Narrow Gauge Railway This train from Septemvri to Dobrinishte runs four times a day year-round, takes about five hours for the one-way trip, and costs only a few euros. This route is the closest thing in the Balkans to an Alpine train ride, winding through the valleys and gorges of the Rila, Pirin and Rhodope mountains and stopping at Avramovo, the highest railway station in the Balkans. If you want to stop anywhere during your trip, make it the town of Velingrad, the country’s most popular thermal spa destination.

item.title: 14 best hotel resorts in Mallorca to book for 2026
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 3.48
Mallorca does resorts with more subtlety than most islands its size. The infrastructure is there, of course: beach clubs, sprawling spas, kids’ clubs, adults-only sanctuaries, golf courses curling through the hills. But the best resort stays here do not feel air-dropped in. They tend to grow out of the landscape or the island’s own visual language, whether that means a honey-stone hill village above the northeast coast, a 14th-century finca estate folded into vineyards, or a cliff-hugging hideaway where the Tramuntana mountains drop theatrically into the sea. Even the bigger, shinier properties still feel distinctly Mallorcan rather than generically Mediterranean. The island also makes resort-hopping by mood unusually easy. In the north and northeast, around Formentor, Alcúdia and Playa de Muro, the draw is beach life, family ease and a kind of clean, athletic outdoorsiness shaped by cycling routes, sailing and long pale bays. The southeast, around Porto Petro, softens into quieter coves and low-key fishing villages. Inland and toward the west, the tempo shifts again. Here, resorts become more introspective: monastery estates, adults-only retreats among pine trees, well-being hideaways where the point is not to be entertained but restored. What ties the best of them together is that they know their lane. They do not try to be everything at once. They know whether they are for families, aesthetes, golfers, spa obsessives or people who want to spend a week in linen moving between sea, shade and lunch. Here are the resorts that do it best.
