You can purchase and install a travel eSIM before arriving in the United States, making it convenient for travelers with eSIM-compatible phones. eSIM vs. Physical SIM for USA Travel Physical SIM cards may require travelers to find a retailer after arrival, remove their existing SIM card, and store it safely during the trip. An eSIM removes the need to handle a physical card. If your phone is unlocked and supports eSIM, you can buy and install a plan online before you leave. Travelers who want to prepare mobile data before departure can use providers such as Cinqstella, which offer USA eSIM plans to install before a trip and activate according to the provider's instructions. How To Choose an eSIM for the USA Not all eSIM plans are the same. Before purchasing one, consider the following factors. Coverage Check whether the eSIM provides coverage in all the destinations on your itinerary. This is especially important if you're planning to visit remote national parks, Alaska, or Hawaii. Data allowance Consider how you use your phone while traveling. A 3 GB plan may suffice for a short trip with light data use, but travelers who use social media, navigation, video, or hotspot sharing may need more. Network Check which networks the eSIM uses and whether 4G or 5G connectivity is available. A reliable connection matters more than choosing the fastest advertised network. Cinqstella's U.S. eSIM supports the Verizon and T-Mobile networks. Activation Before departure, understand the difference between installing and activating your eSIM. Most providers offer a QR code for quick scanning, but plan validity start times vary. Hotspot Hotspot sharing is important when evaluating an eSIM operator. If traveling with family or friends, it helps multiple devices stay connected on one data plan. Cinqstella allows hotspot sharing on its U.S. eSIM. Validity Check when the validity period starts (purchase, installation, or activation) and confirm it covers your trip. For Cinqstella, validity begins when you activate it. How To Install an eSIM Before Your USA Trip • Buy your destination eSIM and receive the QR code. • Install the eSIM before traveling while on reliable Wi-Fi, but do not activate it early unless directed by the provider. • Use your device to scan the provided QR code and follow the provider's setup instructions. Once you are ready to use the plan, select the travel eSIM for mobile data. Cinqstella's U.S. service is data-only, which means it does not provide traditional cellular calls or SMS through the eSIM. You can still use internet-based messaging and calling apps over the data connection. Tips for Using Mobile Data While Road-Tripping in the USA A road trip in the United States may pass through areas with limited mobile coverage. Before a long drive, download offline maps and save important travel info. Use hotel or café Wi-Fi for large downloads, updates, and video uploads when possible. A car charger or portable power bank helps keep your phone charged during long drives. When visiting remote areas or national parks, plan your route and avoid depending exclusively on mobile data. Offline maps and saved addresses help when you lose signal. Final Thoughts Choosing the right mobile data solution before your trip can make traveling in the United States much easier. Whether you choose a physical SIM or an eSIM, planning will help you stay connected wherever your travels take you. Cinqstella's eSIM for USA plans use the Verizon and T-Mobile networks, permit hotspot sharing, and provide data only. The plan's validity period begins upon actual activation, so follow the provider's instructions about when to activate it. This article was published in partnership with Cinqstella.

item.title: 7-Day Egypt Itinerary for First-Time Visitors
item.description:
Source: GoBackpacking Score: 3.52
Egypt is too large and historically rich to fully explore in a single week. Still, it is possible to see the highlights if you plan efficiently by combining Nile exploration with your itinerary. A 7-day Egypt itinerary with a Nile cruise lets many travelers explore the country's historical wonders. The three major cities, Cairo, Luxor, and Aswan, are key tourism locations that visitors must see to learn about Egyptian civilization and the Pharaonic Age. To complete the exploration across 7 days, we advise tourists to plan their itinerary day by day. For first-time visitors to Egypt, planning may prove difficult. It's possible to select pre-arranged 7-day itineraries offered by Egypt tour operators such as Nile Cruisen; these itineraries include visits to the pyramids, a cruise on the Nile, tours of major historical sites, and other features like transfer arrangements, entry fees, and meals. Before you begin: Is seven days sufficient for a visit to Egypt? Yes, realistically, in seven days you will explore the following: - Giza Pyramids and Sphinx - Grand Egyptian Museum - Luxor's major temples and tombs - Valley of the Kings - Temple of Hatshepsut - Edfu Temple - Kom Ombo Temple - Aswan-Philae Temple - Nile River scenery and life along the river You might need a 10- to 12-day trip if you are going to visit places such as Alexandria, the Siwa Oasis, the White Desert, and Hurghada. Think carefully and choose your package once you've compared the itineraries. Before you book, make sure you know what is on offer at each location and the kinds of experiences available. If you'd like some assistance, you can look at the Egypt travel guide on Nile Cruisen to get a better understanding of Egyptian tourism. Your 7-Day Egypt Itinerary at a Glance | Day | Destination | Main Experience | | Day 1 | Cairo | Arrival + settle in; can explore the city and markets | | Day 2 | Cairo/Giza | Pyramids, Sphinx & GEM (Grand Egyptian Museum) | | Day 3 | Luxor | Fly to Luxor + East Bank exploration + board cruise | | Day 4 | Luxor ? Nile | West Bank historical site visits + sailing | | Day 5 | Edfu ? Kom Ombo | Temples + Nile cruising | | Day 6 | Aswan | Aswan sightseeing + optional Abu Simbel | | Day 7 | Aswan | Philae + departure | This sample itinerary illustrates one possible seven-day route through Cairo, Luxor, and Aswan. Flight times, cruise schedules, excursions, and the order of activities vary by package, so confirm the final itinerary with the operator before booking. Day-wise: 7-day Egypt itinerary for first-time visitors Day 1: Arrive in Cairo International visitors usually reach Cairo, the capital of Egypt, first. When they arrive, we recommend that they relax and contact the tour company if they are taking a pre-arranged 7-day package. Hotel reservations and excursions are included, which makes arrival easier. On your first day, make it flexible so that you can get used to the culture; if you can manage it, have dinner at a local cafe and then browse the markets. Day 2: Cairo & Giza Begin your journey into history with the Great Giza Pyramids and the Sphinx, which are situated on the Giza Plateau near the western edge of Cairo. Go on and visit the fully open Grand Egyptian Museum if you want to gain a deep understanding of history; it features the Tutankhamun Galleries and the Khufu's Boats Museum, and can serve as a good introduction should you then take a Nile cruise. In the evening, visit Khan el-Khalili and then have Egyptian food at one of the well-known restaurants. It's important to finish early to be ready for the journey the following day. Day 3: Cairo to Luxor-From Capital to Ancient Thebes The day involves a domestic flight from Cairo to Luxor, followed by a transfer to the cruise ship and boarding. On Day 3, the shore excursions will depend on the cruise timetable. They will mostly include the East Bank, with tourists having the opportunity to visit the Karnak Temple, the Luxor Temple, and the Avenue of the Sphinxes if time allows. The East Bank contains the stories of the ancient civilization's New Kingdom, which was known as Thebes during the Pharaonic age. If you embark from Aswan, you first take a domestic flight there. Some Nile Cruisen packages include domestic flights, while others require travelers to arrange them separately. Included domestic flights are a major reason first-time travelers choose packaged deals. Check the stated inclusions before booking. You can check their unique 5- to 12-day itineraries, curated especially for foreign tourists, to ensure comfortable vacations in Egypt. Day 4: Luxor's West Bank-Tombs, Temples & Sailing Visit Hatshepsut's Temple, the Valley of the Kings, and the Colossi of Memnon on the west bank of Luxor. The Valley of the Kings contains more than just tombs; it also offers unique insight into ancient Egyptian beliefs about death and the afterlife. Following their day of sightseeing, the guests relax on the decks of the Nile cruise and observe the small villages, feluccas, riverbanks, and sunsets. The Nile is far more than a scenic feature of Egypt; it links the ancient sites, and a visit to Egypt would be incomplete without it. Day 5: Edfu & Kom Ombo-The Advantage of Cruising The shore trips feature visits to places such as the Edfu Temple and the Kom Ombo Temple. Cruise tours are simpler than road trips since the views of the river around these monuments are peaceful. Visitors can combine sailing with historical investigation. Travelers visiting for the first time go to the double temple dedicated to Sobek and Horus the Elder at Kom Ombo and study the pharaohs' religious and practical lives through the vivid reliefs. The two temples are well-preserved along the Nile. The travel company Nile Cruisen has a team of Egyptologists who have designed the itineraries so that tourists can both investigate and appreciate the story of ancient Egypt. If you want a rewarding experience, you should book their 7-Day Trip Nile Cruise & Cairo or explore the other itineraries on their official website. The Nile has long been regarded as the longest river in the world, even though recent measurements of the Amazon have cast doubt on that status. It served as the lifeblood of ancient Egypt. Day 6: Aswan-A Slower Side of Egypt Southern Egypt offers a noticeably different atmosphere from Cairo and Luxor, with Nile islands, attractive river scenery, and a more relaxed pace. Visit the Aswan High Dam and Unfinished Obelisk, with the option of arranging a separate excursion to Abu Simbel. Some tourists plan an optional trip to Abu Simbel, as it's not included on many standard cruise itineraries. Upon request, Nile Cruisen experts can tailor a package that may include additional charges for transportation to and from the destination. Day 7: Philae, Final Nile Views & Departure After breakfast, disembark and visit Philae Temple. Depending on your travel plans, you can then transfer to Aswan Airport for a domestic flight to Cairo or continue to another destination in Egypt. Since seven days are not sufficient for exploring all of Egypt, you might choose to plan a longer trip of eight or twelve days to visit parts of the great Sahara Desert, the Red Sea, and Alexandria. What is typically included in a seven-day Egypt package? As per the Nile Cruisen packages, if you book the pre-planned itineraries, you enjoy some of the inclusions, which are - Private transfers - Nile cruise accommodation - Cairo hotel accommodation - Meals according to the selected itinerary - Domestic flights on applicable packages - Taxes and service charges - Tour guide support - Monument entrance fees What is included in the package will vary depending on the itinerary or the travel company you select. Before making your booking, you should check what is included. People who are visiting for the first time ought to compare different travel booking companies. If you book through a well-known tour operator based in Egypt, you should have easier access to local assistance and guides while on your trip. Before making your booking, it is necessary to compare different operators, check their qualifications, review recent customer feedback, verify the insurance coverage, examine the cancellation policy, find out about emergency support, and also check exactly what is included in the price. Final Thoughts If you have just one week to spend in Egypt, do not make it a hassle. Book a package tour and travel in comfort; the itineraries have been selected by experienced travel agents who believe a holiday should be relaxing, not tiring. If it's your first time traveling and you have only a week, don't attempt to see everything; instead,, concentrate on Cairo, Giza, Luxor, and Aswan, since you'll manage to see a great deal in seven days. You'll also enjoy the outstanding hospitality available on Nile River cruises. This article was published in partnership with Nile Cruisen.

item.title: How To Turn a Long Flight Into Useful Personal Time
item.description:
Source: GoBackpacking Score: 3.50
A long flight can feel like dead time because it sits between two places and belongs to neither. Yet it is also one of the few stretches in modern-day travel when everyday demands temporarily lose their grip. The trick is not to fill every minute but to offer a small menu of activities that fit different energy levels. A downloaded book, a notebook, a favorite album, and a short game of PlaySolitaire each offer a different way to experience the journey. That compact game loop matters because it creates a clear beginning and ending when the hours ahead feel shapeless. Stop Planning the Flight Like a Workday Travelers often board with an ambitious list. They plan to finish a novel, clear a laptop folder, watch three films, and arrive with a new language skill. This turns a quiet journey into a performance test. Cabin conditions rarely cooperate. Sleep may be broken, concentration can fade, and the person beside you may need to move just as you settle into something demanding. A better plan is flexible. Choose several low-effort options and let your attention decide which fits the moment. Build a Menu Instead of a Timetable A useful flight menu has contrast. Bring something to read, something to listen to, something to write, and something to play. Download what you need before leaving home because a plan that depends on perfect onboard internet is not much of a plan. Keep choices easy to reach. If every activity requires unpacking half your backpack, you will likely return to scrolling through the entertainment screen without choosing anything. Choose Activities With Natural Endings Open-ended entertainment can cause time to feel longer. Endless feeds and large game worlds provide no clear stopping point, so an hour disappears without feeling complete. A chapter, a crossword, a journal page, or a single hand of solitaire has a finish line. PlaySolitaire works well in this role because its rules are familiar and each round stands on its own. You can put it away when the meal arrives without feeling as though you have abandoned a larger mission. Load the game before departure so the cached version can be reopened if your flight lacks reliable Wi-Fi. Alternate Attention With Real Rest Not all quiet moments need an activity. After reading or watching something, close your eyes for a while. Look out the window when the view allows. Stretch when it is safe to move around the cabin and drink water regularly. The aim is not to defeat boredom at all costs. It is to move gently between focus and rest so neither becomes exhausting. A good activity should support that rhythm rather than call for constant attention. Leave Part of the Journey Unclaimed The most memorable travel days are rarely controlled minute by minute, and the journey can follow the same principle. Leave space for a conversation, an unexpected film, or simply doing nothing. Long flights become easier when they stop being a problem to solve. With a few carefully chosen options and permission to change your mind, the cabin becomes a temporary room of your own. You may not use every hour productively, but you can arrive feeling that the time was yours. This article was published in partnership with PlaySolitaire.io.

item.title: The Famous 1983 Plum Torte Gets a Remix
item.description:
Source: NYT > Dining & Wine Score: 5.42
Advertisement First published in September 1983, Marian Burros’s plum torte has become one of the most popular recipes in the history of The Times, and it’s no mystery why. It’s easy, it’s practically no-fail and it’s endlessly adaptable. Here are five ways to make the 43-year-old recipe your own, drawn directly from readers who have done just that. Recipe: The Original Plum Torte 1. Toss in almost any fruit “Made this for the first time using 4 cups of blueberries and raspberries (mixed). It was perfect!” Apricots, halved and pitted; cranberries or any summer berry work beautifully, as do sliced apples, nectarines, peaches and pears. Canned and frozen fruit can happily stand in for fresh. 2. Experiment with spices, herbs and extracts “I added a teaspoon of finely minced fresh rosemary to the batter. Nice, subtle flavor.” Depending on your mood, add vanilla extract, almond extract, nutmeg, ginger, cardamom, rosemary, orange or lemon zest for a subtle twist. 3. Play with flours “Made this last night after tasting the one made by our daughter. Used raspberries and blackberries, one basket each, instead of plums, and ⅓ cup cornmeal and ⅔ cup flour. Fantastic!!! The cornmeal adds a very sophisticated ‘Italian’ character to it, very slight crunch, and amazing flavor.” For a different texture, consider a half-and-half mixture of almond or cornmeal flour and all-purpose flour. (Melissa Clark made a version with whole-wheat flour.) Or swap in gluten-free flour blends, with excellent results. 4. Change up the pan “Make it in any Pyrex, casserole, anything.” The torte can be baked in any dish provided it’s around 8 to 10 inches in diameter and oven-safe, so spring-form pans, skillets, ceramic casserole dishes will all yield happy results. 5. Double, triple, even quadruple it “Think about making two … one is not enough.” The batter scales up like a dream, and the baked cake freezes well. In 2023, Ms. Burros recounted the time she once made two dozen and asked her friend to store 12 in her freezer. She got 10 back. item.title: The Flatiron Steak Is Affordable and Versatile
item.description:
Source: NYT > Dining & Wine Score: 5.35
Advertisement Say flatiron to a New Yorker and a triangular building on lower Fifth Avenue comes to mind. But to a butcher? It’s a prized but underappreciated cut of steak that’s finally having its moment. The flatiron delivers delectably rich beefy flavor and nice marbling to yield a tender bite, less grainy than flank steak, more succulent than hanger. It’s extremely versatile, excellent to sear or grill but also superb slivered and marinated for a Chinese stir-fry or sliced into a taco. It’s rarely recommended for stroganoff, which is a big mistake. And it can also be braised. The really good news, though, is that it’s often half the price, or less, than the marquee filet mignon, rib-eye or strip loin steaks. As for tenderness, it’s generally considered to be second only to the tenderloin, against which it’s also juicier, with more beefy flavor. “With cuts like flatiron you can give people a great meal without it costing a ton of money,” said Joe Carroll, an owner of the St. Anselm steakhouses in Brooklyn and in Washington, D.C. David Lowenberg has been serving it for years for steak frites: “Hanger and skirt have gotten more expensive,” said Mr. Lowenberg, who owns the Beacon and Bell & Anchor in Sag Harbor, N.Y. “Flatiron is delicious and costs less.” Home cooks can expect to pay about $20 to $30 a pound for the cut depending on the market. Costco’s price is a rock-bottom $10 to $12 a pound. Even at Eli’s Market on the Upper East Side, it’s $30 a pound, less than half the price of strip loin. But it comes with quality more typical of costlier choices. It’s so budget friendly because it’s from the shoulder muscle, a part of the animal usually considered better for stewing than for a splurge. A flatiron steak is a boneless rectangle of well-marbled meat, a scant inch thick, sometimes called blade steak. The muscle itself is a hefty hunk, suggesting a chuck roast, and great for pot roast. I have been happily buying flatiron steaks from Hudson & Charles, a nose-to-tail butcher in my neighborhood on the Upper West Side, and also in the West Village, for years. But it was only after discussing the cut with Daniel Boulud, who also has flatiron steak on the lunch menu at Le Pavillon and plans to include it at his new Brasserie Boulud at New York’s Lincoln Center, that I realized I grew up eating braised flatiron, or what Mr. Boulud and the rest of France calls paleron. For stews and pot roast it’s what my mother, for whom the flavor and texture of the more typical brisket wasn’t appealing, called chicken steak. And so did Anthony Bourdain in recommending it for his beef bourguignon. Why chicken steak? No one seems to know. “I have never been able to find out,” said Jake Dickson, another flatiron fan, of Dickson’s Farmstand Meats in Chelsea Market in Manhattan. The singular drawback is that the muscle has a vein of gristle running up the center. Remove the meat on either side and you have two big flatiron steaks. When you slowly braise the whole muscle, or thick slabs of it sliced against the grain as my mother did, or cut it in pieces for stew à la Bourdain, the gristle is less significant. At his new Brasserie, Mr. Boulud’s flatiron steak will come sliced with either a shallot and red wine pan sauce or prepared “au poivre,” a preparation favored at other restaurants, including Vaux Social and Lori Jayne, both in Brooklyn. Marinating first is in order at some. “It takes a marinade very well,” Mr. Lowenberg said. At the new Jack’s All Day on Restaurant Row in Manhattan, it’s treated with herbs, Worcestershire sauce, mustard, olive oil and tamari overnight before grilling. Elsewhere, a swipe of chimichurri or salsa verde is another typical flourish before serving. It’s the signature steak, rubbed with coffee and cocoa and finished with smoked chile butter, at Lazy Dog restaurants, a national chain. At the some places, including St. Anselm and the STK restaurants, salt and pepper is all the steak needs before it hits the grill. Robert Liberato, STK’s executive chef, called it a “rewarding cut” that easily holds its own. Follow New York Times Cooking on Instagram, Facebook, YouTube, TikTok and Pinterest. item.title: A Pistachio-Lemon Snacking Cake That’s Perfect for Rosh Hashana
item.description:
Source: NYT > Dining & Wine Score: 3.25
Advertisement A lemony polenta cake, the kind of thing that’s fancy enough to feel like an occasion, yet simple enough to whip up on a whim, is rooted in Italian tradition. I’ve baked more versions than I can count. But Benjamina Ebuehi’s take, from her latest cookbook, “I’ll Bring Dessert,” made me rethink them all. Because along with the expected shower of lemon zest, she stirs in a hefty dose of minced preserved lemon. Recipe: Pistachio Polenta Cake It was a brilliant twist, and not surprising that it came from Ms. Ebuehi, the British cookbook author and food stylist who got her start as a contestant on “The Great British Bake Off.” She’s got a knack for reworking familiar baked goods. Seasoning polenta cake with preserved lemon, a staple of North African and Middle Eastern kitchens, is a perfect example. Where fresh lemon brings pure brightness, the preserved lemon adds something earthier and more complex: saltiness, depth and a touch of funk from the fermentation. “I typically like pairing pistachios and lemons,” Ms. Ebuehi said when I asked her how she came up with the recipe. “Then I got the idea to try preserved lemons, which makes the flavor more robust. It gives the cake an edge.” (This said, if you don’t have any preserved lemon on hand, you can skip it for a more straightforwardly citrusy cake.) As for the pistachios, she grinds them into the batter in place of the almond flour usually found in gluten-free bakes like this one. They give the crumb a marked richness, while the polenta keeps things rustic, with a gritty, nubby bite. My only change to Ms. Ebuehi’s recipe was to swap in olive oil for the sunflower oil. Olive oil turns up often in polenta cake, and here it underscores the cake’s savory bent, which is balanced by a thick lemon glaze. This crowning touch nods to Ms. Ebuehi’s own baking tradition, a first cousin of the soaking syrup on a classic British lemon drizzle cake, reimagined as a tangy white icing that’s just sweet enough. For Ms. Ebuehi, this is the kind of relaxed cake she’d set out with tea for friends. But I think it’s also an ideal dessert for the upcoming Jewish holidays. And since Rosh Hashana runs two nights, there’s no need to choose between this and Marian Burros’s plum torte. Make both — then revel in the leftovers. item.title: The 3 Exercises That Will Save Your Legs on the Descent
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 5.67
(Photo: Canva) Most hikers think that the ascent up a mountain is the hardest part. But it’s the descent that your legs will remember the next day, especially every time you step down stairs or sit in a chair. As you place your foot on the ground, your quads absorb the impact and act like brakes, slowing your body down. This braking causes the soreness you’ll feel days later. If your quads fatigue early, it causes further stress on the muscles, ligaments, and tendons, which can lead to injury. The remedy for pain-free descents? Don’t think about strengthening certain muscles. Instead, think about preparing your body for the three actions it needs to perform going downhill: absorbing impact, controlling each step, and controlling the foot. Training these qualities three times a week over six to eight weeks leading up to your next backpacking trip can help your descents feel smoother, more controlled, and leave your legs fresher for the miles ahead. This exercise elevates the heels by a couple of inches, allowing the quads to work through a longer range of motion. By taking four seconds to lower into the squat, you can create the time under tension needed for the trail. Descending a trail is really thousands of controlled single-leg stability landings. The terrain, your balance, braking ability, coordination, and confidence will all affect how safely you can navigate a descent. One of the best gym exercises that carries over to hiking is the lateral step-down, which trains balance, eccentric control, and coordination, and boosts knee stability. It’s also a go-to for reducing knee pain during downhill hiking. The tibialis anterior, or shin muscle, works in a couple of ways during each step. One job is to lift the toes to clear obstacles such as rocks or roots. Its other role is to slow your foot down after your heel touches the ground; it’s basically a brake that keeps your foot from slapping the ground with each step. Long descents can leave this muscle sore because the toes land below the heel with each step, increasing the range of motion. This exercise helps strengthen and stabilize the muscles around the foot and ankle so you can descend pain-free. To make the exercise harder: walk your feet farther away from the wall. To make it easier: move your feet closer to the wall. Want more Outside health stories? Sign up for the Bodywork newsletter. And for tips on how to train, fuel, and recover better, sign up for the Sweat Science 101 newsletter.

item.title: Arc’teryx Wants the Sperro SV to Be the Last Jacket You Ever Buy—Seriously
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 4.99
Engineered for versatility across high-stakes mountain environments, the Sperro SV underwent rigorous testing during ski tours and ice climbing ascents. (Photo: Courtesy of Arc'teryx) Tucked alongside the interior chest pocket of a two-toned magenta Arc’teryx jacket is a laser-etched QR code—but instead of pulling up the menu at your local pub, it prompts you to register your new purchase, immediately kicking off a record of the jacket’s materials, origin, and, eventually, repair history. A QR code seems simple enough—after all, you encounter dozens of them weekly—but a QR code on a mountain-grade hardshell requires a different level of engineering than the laminated square on your bartop. The internal placement makes it near-impossible to destroy or remove; the laser etching, adapted from the electronics industry, underwent multiple trials to ensure it left a permanent mark without degrading the fabric. So why spend so much time, money, and engineering on a single square inch of jacket? For Arc’teryx, that QR code is the entry point into System 0™, a new framework that reimagines how products can be designed, manufactured, used, repaired, and ultimately regenerated. In fact, the QR code is just one of many updates and innovations Arc’teryx built into its first System 0 jacket, the Sperro SV. Among the others: an easily repairable zipper, a nylon face fabric and backer engineered for chemical recyclability, and reinforcement at common failure points. System 0 started as a “what if” conversation between Arc’teryx CEO Stuart Haselden and VP of Advanced Concepts, Alex Plante, brainstorming what circularity would look like for the company. At that point, Arc’teryx’s ReBIRD program already existed, with a solid infrastructure for product repairs, resale, trade-in, and upcycling, but the team knew they were still missing an actual process—a viable, repeatable way to create products that can be used for longer and ultimately regenerated into something new. “We landed on what product we wanted to develop within that [circularity] concept, and then, while we were developing the product, realized that we didn’t have all the pieces of the system,” says Andrew Yip, Senior Director of Materials Innovation at Arc’teryx. That meant building capability as they went, bringing in people like Kyle Wood, Vice President of Strategy, to focus on circularity. They also recruited for other supporting roles, like sourcing manager for raw materials. Throughout the circularity initiative, Yip and his colleagues used one principle as their North Star: Sustainability alone isn’t a reason for a product to exist. Anything they created had to live up to Arc’teryx’s sky-high standards for technical excellence and durability. “Most sustainable materials and products are just less bad than their incumbent,” argues Yip. “If you’re just going to make something less bad from a sustainability perspective but make it worse in terms of performance, then there really isn’t a justification for it to exist.” To that end, Arc’teryx prioritized abrasion resistance on both face fabric and backer, while refusing to compromise on tear and tensile strength, waterproofing, and breathability—all the things that determine whether a jacket becomes a one-season purchase or a mainstay in your gear closet. They also intentionally aligned on nylon 6 as the key material instead of polyester; even though polyester has more recycling opportunities, the team knew that nylon 6 fabric would perform best. To find the exact nylon content ratio—the perfect number that would make the fabric functionally and financially recyclable—Arc’teryx worked closely with Aquafil, the manufacturer of ECONYL® regenerated nylon. According to Aquafil, the textile is known for high wear resistance and impact strength (aka extreme durability). Finding the perfect jacket material was one thing. But that wasn’t the hardest problem the Arc’teryx team had to solve, says Yip. You already know Arc’teryx for its insanely technical, single-purpose shells like the Alpha SV—a scalpel, according to Yip. “It’s really a precision tool, and it was designed for ice climbing,” he explains. “It doesn’t have hand pockets for a reason—you don’t need hand pockets when you’re ice climbing.” On the contrary, the Sperro SV had to be a jacket-of-all-trades, working in a variety of environments and use cases. “With the Sperro SV, we wanted to make something that was multi-environment, multifunctional, and multi-activity,” details Yip. They needed a Swiss Army Knife, not a scalpel—but that Swiss Army Knife couldn’t compromise on durability. To ensure the Sperro SV was worth its mettle, Arc’teryx tested the jacket on ski tours, hiking trips, snowshoeing expeditions, and even ice climbing. They also partnered with the North Shore Search and Rescue, a volunteer-led organization and one of Canada’s oldest search-and-rescue teams, to make sure the jacket performed in high-stakes scenarios. All that engineering ultimately serves one purpose: creating a jacket worthy of what Yip refers to as custodianship, rather than ownership. “Hopefully, the person who’s purchasing this jacket is somebody who cares about their stuff and is going to take care of the garment, bring it in for repair, and extend its lifetime as much as possible,” says Yip. “And only after many, many years and many, many repairs, when something is no longer repairable, only then is when we take it back.” Hence, the QR code. Arc’teryx hopes that by making it as seamless as possible for customers to track the Sperro SV’s lifespan, materials, and repair history, customers will view themselves as custodians with a responsibility to their gear—instead of temporary owners of a disposable item. If all goes according to plan, the Sperro SV might be the last jacket Arc’teryx ever sells you. At a gulp-worthy $1,200 retail price, most customers are probably praying that they never have to buy another jacket again, but it’s not exactly a sound business strategy in an industry that counts on customers to replace old gear. Yip is strangely okay with that. “When we’re developing new products and prototypes, we know we have something when our athletes and field testers don’t want to give it back,” he explains. “Similarly, I think we’re onto something if we have a commercial product that people can buy and they don’t want to replace it. So personally, I would have no problem with that.” When asked to comment on the price, Arc’teryx reps note that the Sperro SV is priced in line with their most advanced hard shells, and the price reflects the design effort and materials that went into this sustainable jacket. “Circularity at this level of performance requires significant investment across materials, manufacturing, certification, and end-of-life infrastructure,” Arc’teryx acknowledges. They believe that the price reflects the value of three years of unlimited repairs, a product they’re backing to last for years, and eventually, an end-of-life offramp. “When you factor in the total life of the jacket, the value calculation looks different than a traditional purchase,” reasons the brand. Whether consumers will find the price a fair trade-off for the total package remains to be seen. The Sperro SV is just the first “statement of intent,” as Yip puts it, for what System 0 can do within the Arc’teryx playbook. With the streamlined processes and internal philosophies Arc’teryx has now aligned on, they’re free to explore further iterations of circular gear. “We started with a hardshell because it’s what we know, what we make, and what we’re known for—so you can imagine that the other things we’re known for and make well are coming down the pipeline,” hints Yip. And for the Arc’teryx loyalists who worry this new iteration of a hardshell won’t live up to their high standards—you’ve got nothing to worry about. “If anyone were to put on the jacket and close their eyes, it really shouldn’t be different at all compared to anything that we’ve made before. And I think that’s the point,” says Yip. “It’s everything else around it that we’re trying to change.”

item.title: The High-Altitude Journey of the World’s Most Famous Adventure Cat
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 4.31
Simon the adventure cat (Photo: Courtesy of JJ Yosh) Had JJ Yosh, an adventure content creator based in Boulder, Colorado, simply taken his cat, Simon, on a handful of hikes and posted the videos online, I would have dismissed it as a pet-thetic social media stunt. But a decade after adopting the black Bombay cat, the duo—better known to millions as Backpacking Kitty on Instagram and TikTok—has built something far more remarkable. Together they’ve hiked the Austrian Alps, whitewater rafted California’s Sacramento River, climbed a volcano in Guatemala, and traveled to more than 15 countries and four continents. They’ve flown on over 100 flights, including on a seaplane, and kayaked some of the most remote waterways in the world, taking an audience of 11 million followers along with them, and making Simon less of a novelty and more like a bona fide field companion. Now Yosh has something even more ambitious in mind. He’s preparing to take Simon on a multi-year Seven Summits spree. “I’m positive he’s the only cat who has summited a dozen of Colorado’s 14ers,” Yosh says of Simon who he rescued from euthanasia in 2016. Yet even those accomplishments, and, arguably, the title of one of the most famous cats in the world, pale beside this latest odyssey. Over the next three years, they plan to tackle the tallest mountain on every continent: Denali, Mount Kilimanjaro, Aconcagua, Mount Elbrus, Vinson Massif, Puncak Jaya, and the world’s highest peak, Mount Everest. Before you picture a cat being hauled into Everest’s notorious Death Zone—a place so hostile to life it contains only about a third of the oxygen available at sea level—rest easy. “I’m definitely not taking Simon to the summit. I’m not risking his life,” Yosh says. While Yosh makes his push for the top, Simon will be living the considerably cushier life at Everest Base Camp with a dedicated pet sitter, people he already knows and trusts. Yosh is emphatic that Simon’s health and safety come first. “How high he goes depends entirely on the mountain,” Yosh says. That means, for Everest, Base Camp is his ceiling. “Nothing above it, no exceptions.” For Kilimanjaro and Aconcagua? Those are non-technical walk-ups, so there is more room. “He could go higher than base camp on those, and how much higher gets decided on the ground rather than promised in advance.” As for everywhere else, Yosh will assess each peak one at a time, and veterinary opinions will inform each decision. Yosh says, “ If the answer is that it is too high for a cat, that is the end of it. He does not go.” It’s all part of the careful balance Yosh has spent the past decade striking with his feline partner. Simon may be born for adventure—while he does trek via leash, he’s happiest riding Yosh’s shoulders through forests and across alpine trails, even snowboarding—he’s still a cat, with very real limitations. For example, while Yosh was on a Mount Baker crevasse rescue training ahead of his Seven Summits bid recently, Simon wasn’t practicing self-arrests. Which begs the question: How do you prepare a house cat for extreme altitude? After all, Everest Base Camp sits at a breath-stealing 17,598 feet. The answer starts at home. In Boulder, where the pair live at roughly 6,000 feet above sea level, acclimatization is woven into everyday life. Yosh’s home—playfully known as “the house his cat built”—is tucked into a rocky cliff and outfitted with an indoor climbing wall scaled by both owner and pet. Outside, Colorado’s high country is Simon’s natural conditioning ground, where regular mountaineering outings have gradually exposed him to thinner air—one might say the purrfect conditions—long before the Himalayas come into view. Yosh has even taken Simon on technical rope climbs, securing him a small-dog harness. And when it comes to gear, Simon is just as outfitted as his owner: Yosh has assembled a wardrobe for Simon to rival any serious adventurer’s, with specialized gear for seemingly every climate, condition, and expedition. Add to that the deep relationship these two have built. Even talking about the possibility of something happening to Simon makes Yosh visibly shaken. The depth of that bond was forged early. Not long after Yosh adopted Simon, he left the cat with a friend while filming a commercial in Bolivia. What Yosh didn’t learn until later was that Simon had gone missing for three days. “Thankfully, they didn’t tell me at the time,” Yosh says. “They’d put up missing posters everywhere, but I had no idea.” Even now, the memory rattles him. “If that happened today and I found out while I was on a mountain, I’d turn around. I wouldn’t be able to finish the climb,” he says. “You have to be in a good mental place to climb a mountain, and I wouldn’t be.” “This work can be so taxing and draining. You question why you’re doing it over and over again,” Yosh says. “That’s where having Simon is such a huge emotional pillow. The hardest moments usually aren’t the scary, high-adrenaline ones. They’re when the weight of the whole expedition catches up with you.” Whether he’s just finished an ultrarun or a grueling climb, Yosh knows there’s one constant: Simon, curled up in the tent ready for a cuddle at the end of the day. In a life all about relentless forward motion, that ritual has become the reset that keeps him going. It will be tested during their next challenge. But first, there are the logistics to work through. Namely, the travel concerns of hop-scotching the planet with a cat. Fortunately, this isn’t Simon’s first rodeo. He has a U.S. ID card and an E.U. pet passport that allows him to easily cross borders, and he doesn’t fly cargo. “But of course he has to get all of these health certificates for each country,” Yosh says. Then there’s the tricky reality of lengthy flights and layovers. Naturally, I had to ask, does Simon get jet lag? “Simon gets so excited every time we reach a new hotel or destination,” Yosh says. “He’s like ready to go.” Apparently, when you’re an international adventuring cat of mystery, the only thing tougher than Everest is waiting for room service. That, and then clawing your way into mountaineering history.

item.title: Colorado’s Maroon Bells Are Closed After a Second Climber Has Died in Less Than a Week
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 4.30
Responders with Mountain Aspen Rescue evacuated a deceased climber on September 6 using a technical lowering system (Photo: Photo courtesy of MRA) The U.S. Forest Service temporarily closed all climbing access to Colorado’s Maroon Peak on September 8, 2026, to recover the body of a climber who had fallen off the mountain. The death marked the first of two fatal mountaineering accidents on Colorado’s famed 14er summits in less than a week. Officials have not released the names, sex, or ages of either person. On September 8, authorities embarked on a recovery mission for the body of a climber who went missing six days earlier, on September 2, according to the responding agency, Mountain Rescue Aspen (MRA). To aid the recovery, the U.S. Forest Service closed climbing access to Maroon Peak, including the standard route from West Maroon Creek and the traverse from North Maroon Peak. After the climber was reported missing on September 2, rescuers found notes in their vehicle parked at the trailhead. Based on these notes, responders conducted aerial searches in the Maroon Bells-Snowmass Wilderness, a remote alpine area that contains six peaks over 14,000 feet, including the iconic maroon-colored twin peaks known as the Maroon Bells and Snowmass Mountain. “During the aerial search, the climber was located deceased and tentatively identified in very technical and difficult terrain to access,” MRA wrote in a statement. In an unrelated incident on September 6, a second climber died after falling from the north face of Castle Peak, located about 12 miles south of Aspen. An all-volunteer team of 21 members responded on the ground and by helicopter. Rebecca Rees, a dental anesthesiologist, witnessed the September 6 fall while hiking with a group between Castle and Conundrum Peaks. Rees, 44, lives in a suburb of Denver and has been climbing Colorado 14ers since 2017. She said she had been on this specific climb around five times. “There had been a rockfall all day from Conundrum going into the lake, so we were used to hearing these rocks fall into the lake,” she said. “At 12:25 P.M., we heard the rocks again but it was a different sound. I looked over and I saw this gentleman tumbling down the mountain. It was horrifying because it was not a fall that would be survivable.” Rees estimated that the man initially fell about 30 feet, and then continued to tumble hundreds more down the mountain. It’s not clear how or why he fell, she said. Her group called emergency services, and yelled at the man, but he was unresponsive. Looking up-slope, she said they saw his sunglasses and water bottles in a debris field. “Mountain Rescue Aspen personnel reached the climber at approximately 3:58 P.M. and determined the individual had sustained injuries that were not survivable,” MRA wrote. “Team members then carefully evacuated the climber from the mountain using a technical lowering system.” Located in Colorado’s Elk Range, the Maroon Bells are one of the most photographed destinations in the state, and encompass Maroon Peak and North Maroon Peak. The peaks have earned their nickname “Deadly Bells“—the mountains are highly technical, dangerous, and extremely difficult, according to the nonprofit that does service work on the state’s highest peaks, Colorado Fourteeners Initiative. “These mountains are known for having a lot of loose rock and being fairly dangerous,” Rees told Outside. “Up close, the rock is very loose and unforgiving. Route-finding is difficult, and it’s very easy to take a wrong step or have the wrong handhold and fall,” she said. Incredibly steep terrain also means seemingly innocuous mishaps can quickly become deadly. In May, a hiker slid 200 feet down the Maroon Bells after slipping at an elevation of around 11,300 feet. In August, Colorado hiker Brandon Hinkle was completing the Maroon Bells Traverse when he tumbled 500 feet down a sheer rock face and suffered multiple serious injuries. Rees reiterated the importance of traveling with a buddy, especially in dangerous terrain. “Without even realizing it in the moment, you’re constantly checking in with each other when you’re hiking up,” she said. “Having that constant feedback and another opinion is helpful checks and balances.” And if you’re not feeling it, Rees said known when to turn around can save lives. “The mountain will be there forever, and it’s okay to get to a certain point and realize today is not the day,” she said. MRA also reminds backcountry travelers to leave a detailed itinerary with a trusted person before departing, including the intended route, expected return time, and contingency plans. Anyone traveling in the backcountry should also carry appropriate equipment, be prepared for rapidly changing mountain conditions, and always bring a reliable two-way satellite communication device when traveling in areas without cell service. “We’re not going to stop hiking these peaks,” Rees added. “It’s traumatizing but, just be safe and be prepared. Know when to stop, and know your limits.”

item.title: 2 Men Tried to Bail in Wyoming’s Cirque of the Towers. They Ended Up Staying the Night on Pingora Peak.
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 4.03
With only a few hours to spare before sunset, the rescue had to wait until the next morning to head in (Photo: Courtesy of Tip Top Search and Rescue) Two stranded climbers had to spend the night on Pingora Peak, a nearly 12,000-foot granite mountain in the Wind River Range of Wyoming, before being rescued by lifesaving crews. On August 20, the duo tried to bail on a climbing route when their rope got stuck while rappelling, leaving them unable to descend. It was around 5 P.M. when they hit their SOS button from a ledge, according to responding agency Tip Top Search and Rescue. With only a few hours to spare before sunset, the rescue had to wait until the next morning. Around 7 A.M., a search-and-rescue group set in to rescue the two climbers. Two Lander Search and Rescue (LSAR) high-angle rescue teams, a specialized emergency response unit trained to reach and recover people from steep faces, also took part. “Multiple attempts were made to deliver long-line supplies to the two stranded climbers, but due to the wind and the clearance of the rotor blades, it was aborted,” Tip Top SAR said in a statement. “The two LSAR climbers were deployed. Once LSAR reached the two climbers, they lowered both to the base of Pingora.” One of the climbers was wearing a bright orange jacket, which helped the team spot the duo on their first pass into the Cirque, Tip Top wrote. “Despite spending a chilly night on the side of Pingora, the rescued climbers reported that they were okay, just thirsty and tired,” responders wrote. “Both were uninjured and declined transport. The rescued climbers continued their trip and hiked out.” Pingora Peak is a famed summit that forms the Cirque of the Towers, a granite amphitheater of jagged peaks in the southern part of the Winds. It’s unclear what route the two were on, but Pingora Peak is considered to be a “low-hanging fruit of accessible alpine climbing in the Wind River Range,” Colorado climber Adam McClatchie told Outside. Pingora Peak is included in the 50 Classic Climbs of North America, a list of coveted climbs made famous in the 1979 climbing guidebook by Yosemite climbing pioneers Steve Roper and Allen Steck. Although McClatchie considers Pingora Peak a bucket-list climb and a beginner route, its remote location makes it deceptively difficult. For starters, would-be climbers need to hike about ten miles to reach its base, which requires a certain level of alpine fitness. The routes can also be hard to spot, so climbers need a trained eye, and its steep terrain requires technical skills and proper rope management. McClatchie, 34, has been climbing for over a decade and has climbed routes on Pingora Peak on three occasions between 2020 and 2022. He says that it’s not uncommon for people to get in sticky situations and need rescue. “I have witnessed parties on Pingora very late at night that were very clearly struggling to get down,” McClatchie said. “I don’t think I witnessed a rescue per se, but I’ve seen headlamps on the wall in the wee hours of the night in rainstorms.” “That’s the nature of alpine climbing,” McClatchie added. “Things can turn really quickly.”

item.title: Where to Stay in Moab, From Dirtbag Cheap (and Free) to Desert Luxury
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 2.61
The massage caves inside a sandstone formation at ULUM Moab, glamping at its peak. (Photo: Maya Silver) On my very first trip to Moab at age 10, I stayed at a very memorable hotel called the Gonzo Inn. I formed indelible memories of the hotel sign adorned with a clothed lizard straight out of the 1998 film (and 1972 novel) Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas, and of a sunlit glorious pool—a reprieve from the hot, dry days of Southeastern Utah. This little lodge had just opened in 1998; the town was rather quiet back then. Nearly three decades later, the Gonzo Inn is still there every time I return to Moab, which is approximately twice a year when I can get away from my home in northern Utah a few hours away. In my dozens of pilgrimages to the desert, I’ve stayed just about everywhere you can imagine in the adventure capital of Utah (and arguably the Southwest). I’ve pulled over on the side of BLM roads at dusk, set up my tent in sandy dispersed campsites, started campfires that cast shadows against stone, settled for budget hotel rooms in tighter times, booked Airbnbs and VRBOs for large crews, and splurged on lodges right on the Colorado River. If you’re headed to Moab, I’ve put together my personal guide to where to bed down between adventures. From Free 99 to $1,200, here’s the best places to stay in Moab for every budget, the pros and cons of each spot, and some insider tips. My favorite Moab trips often include a mix of camping with a splurge night or two at a hotel. Keep in mind that availability and rates fluctuate dramatically depending on the season. Though these days, winter (December through February) is just about the only time Moab isn’t busy. During the rest of the year, make reservations well in advance. In winter, rates typically drop 40 percent, and during spring break season, prices tend to rise. If you know where to look, you can find free dispersed camping on BLM land to park your van or pitch your tent around Moab. A popular spot where I used to camp was once along U.S. 191 heading into town. But the new Utahraptor State Park has turned some of the dispersed camping into two campgrounds. You can still access dispersed camping beyond the Dalton Wells Dinosaur Quarry to the east, or further south near the Klonzo and Sovereign trailheads, but you’ll need to enter the state park to get there. If you want to avoid a fee, you can try sweet talking the state park ranger, or entering at odd hours when the entrance is unmanned. You can also find some dispersed camping along La Sal Mountain Loop Road. This is an especially great option in late spring through early fall, when the mountains are the place to escape the heat. Check out this map to see where the BLM land that allows dispersed camping exists—and where camping is explicitly banned. Location: Across the Moab area Pros: Free peace and quiet Cons: May require some questing Local tip: Buy some wag bags at a local gear shop (like Gearheads Outdoor Store) to responsibly dispose of your human waste. It can take 10 or more years to break down in the desert, so digging a deep hole ain’t cutting it. You can dispose of those wag bags in trash receptacles marked accordingly in downtown Moab. If you’re on a dirtbag budget but need a roof over your head—maybe you don’t have camping gear or maybe it’s cold and rainy—head to Moab’s only hostel. In full transparency, I have not stayed at Lazy Lizard Hostel. But I have stayed at many hostels and I included this one in my Moon travel guide to Utah because I’ve heard great things (it also has 4.5 stars on Google with over 700 reviews). This locally owned hostel has been around since 1987 and 40 years later, it’s still a great place to rent a room in Moab for as cheap as possible. If you’d rather not bunk down with strangers, you can pay a bit more ($48) for a two-person guest room, or a log cabin ($53-70; sleeps up to six). Location: 1 mile south of town Pros: Dirt cheap Cons: Not walking distance to town Local tip: Bring coins. If you’re dirtbagging it, chances are your clothes stink as much as you do! Use the coin-operated laundry machines onsite. Devils Garden Campground in Arches National Park is one of my favorite spots to camp anywhere. For one, it positions you to catch sunrises, sunsets, and stars amid the arches—and without the crowds. Humps and hills of slickrock roll upward right from the campsites. And a lovely trail to Broken Arch starts right from the campground. Reserve as far in advance as you can, or come during the first-come, first-served off season (Nov.-Feb.)—and bring a lot of layers. Plan a sunrise or sunset hike to Delicate Arch while you’re sleeping in the area. Bathrooms and potable water are available, but there are no hook-ups and you can’t buy firewood here. Also if you’d rather not cook at camp, it’s easy to pick up takeout or pre-made food at Moonflower Co-op in town and bring it up to your campsite. Location: In the Devils Garden area of Arches National Park, about 22 miles north of Moab Pros: Arches within spitting distance of your tent Cons: Hard to get a reservation Local tip: Reservations may be difficult to come by in peak season, but this campground is first come, first served from November through February. Roll up in the morning and snag a site. If you can’t find a site, Sand Flats Recreation Area on a hill just east of Moab offers similarly scenic campsites—and dinosaur tracks. Aside from camping, hostels, and chain motels, the most reasonable rates and best stay in Moab can be found at The Gonzo Inn, where I first stayed in 1999. This locally owned hotel just a block from Main Street offers standard rooms and condo-style suites, plus a lovely outdoor pool and firepit area. Inspired by the hallucinatory lizards of Fear and Loathing, the vibe is colorful, convivial, and “desert chic,” as Gonzo describes itself. Hunter S. Thompson would surely approve. Location: One block west of Main St. Pros: Rooms include a $14 breakfast voucher per person per day. Cons: The onsite cafe where you can use that voucher was very crowded with long lines the last time I stayed here. Local tip: The hotel offers secure gear storage for your dirty bike; ask at the front desk. Just a few miles drive down the road from Sorrel River Ranch, Red Cliffs Lodge has hosted guests along the Colorado River since the 1980s, but the ranch of the same name has been here since the 19th century. The lodge has changed hands many times; most recently, it was acquired by Marriott and dramatically renovated. In the basement of the lodge, you’ll find the Moab Museum of Film & Western Heritage, which has long housed a collection of memorabilia from Westerns filmed in Moab. In fact, many films have been shot right at Red Cliffs, including Wagon Master, Son of Cochise, Warlock, and the John Wayne film Rio Grande. With its can’t-beat-it location right on the Colorado, one of the best perks about Red Cliffs is that you can book a rafting or SUPing trip through the property. Many of the accommodations are in well-sized and well-appointed cabins, and many come with river views. The decor feels more modern than what you’ll find at Sorrel River Ranch. There is also a New American restaurant onsite called Ember with a swanky (for Moab) lounge and a patio overlooking the Colorado. Red Cliffs is pricey, but if you want to balance a long day of roughing it on the trails or river with a luxury stay, this is my favorite place to do it. It’s cheaper to stay in the main lodge ($225-600), then to get a cabin ($1,000-$1,200 per night). Location: In Grandstaff Canyon along Highway 191, 17 miles northeast of Moab Pros: The sights and sound of the Colorado River right outside your room. Cons: If you want to be in town, it’s a 30-minute drive to Moab. Local tip: Red Cliffs is just a stone’s throw away from Castle Valley. Cool off and take a scenic drive up into the La Sal Mountains, where you can hike, bike, climb, or just bask in the big views. You’ve probably heard of Under Canvas, the network of stargazing-focused glamping across the country, often adjacent to national parks. But you may not have heard of the slightly more luxury-oriented ULUM, which opened in 2023 by the same folks behind Under Canvas. At ULUM Moab, every tent is a “suite” with its own bathroom. But more importantly, the ULUM Moab location is approximately 10 times more lovely than the Under Canvas Moab location, which sits right off Highway 191 amid wind-blown sagebrush lands. By comparison, ULUM Moab is about a 30-minute drive south of Moab, tucked in a wind-protected ring of stunning sandstone cliffs. It’s also within spitting distance of the Looking Glass rock feature—a magnificent arch that offers hiking, scrambling, rock climbing, and rappelling. I’ve stayed at Under Canvas Moab and luckily, had a tent with a bathroom. But as far as I’m concerned, if I’m going to dish out a few hundred dollars to glamp, the setting better be spectacular (rather than windy and shade-less) and I want my own bathroom. Otherwise, I’d rather pitch my own tent. And I don’t want to pay $200-$500 with the sound of said wind rattling the metal bones of the canvas tent, keeping me up all night. ULUM also offers some noteworthy amenities like a literal massage cave, a pretty decent onsite restaurant, and warm/cold plunge pools. ULUM Moab is open late-March through late-October. Location: 25 miles south of Moab, off Highway 191 Pros: In a remote location, the stars here are absolutely next-level. Especially against the backdrop of Looking Glass Rock. Cons: It’s a 30-minute drive from Arches and Moab, with no restaurants or shops nearby. Local tip: ULUM Moab makes for a great basecamp to climb, hike, and explore nearby Indian Creek, the Newspaper Rock Petroglyph Panel, and the Needles District of Canyonlands. It’s also a good spot to stop for a night en route to destinations further south like Bears Ears National Monument or Monument Valley. You can’t beat the setting: Sorrel River Ranch sits right on the Colorado River. I should add that this lodge did have a little drama in the news recently, when the state temporarily shut it down over violations in its onsite water treatment system. The lodge has since reopened and vehemently denied some concerning allegations that restaurant workers were asked to use pool water to wash dishes(!). I stayed at Sorrel River Ranch—a couple months before the water issues bubbled up—for my son’s birthday and thankfully, all of our digestive systems during our stay were fine. All of the rooms here are in big log cabins, some with two floors. The decor is Westerncore with touches like a rodeo lasso passing as art, bull’s horns hanging on the walls, a bed made of logs, and housemade red, white, and blue chips with salsa as a welcome offering. Book a horseback ride, enroll your kids in the junior wrangler program, or just feed the boisterous goats. Location: In Grandstaff Canyon along Highway 191, 20 miles northeast of Moab Pros: Serene location close to trails, climbing, and the Colorado River Local tip: Sorrel Ranch sits 10 minutes away from the trailhead to Fisher Towers. This rollicking hike meanders over rock ledges and through gullies as it takes in stunning rock formations—peep the iconic Ancient Art tower, a classic climbing testpiece. About the author: Maya Silver has been traveling to Moab since 1999. These are only a handful of the places she’s stayed in Moab, but they are her favorites. Even though Moab has become almost unbearably busy at times in the 27 years since she’s been visiting, she still loves this bustling adventure town of Southeastern Utah. When she isn’t acting as editor-in-chief of Climbing Magazine, she also writes Moon travel guides to Utah, including a just-updated edition of her guide to Southern Utah.

item.title: No, You’re Not Imagining It. Bear Encounters Really Are on the Rise.
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 2.51
Between 1990 and 2019, North American black and grizzly bears have killed 150 people (Photo: Scott Suriano/Getty Images) On the evening of August 31, a bear attacked a woman walking with her dog in Columbia Falls, Montana, a small town just outside of Glacier National Park. According to Montana Fish, Wildlife and Parks (FWP), the woman sustained significant injuries and was transferred to a medical facility for treatment. The attack marks the latest in a long list of bear run-ins across North America this summer. Experts say that human-bear encounters have been higher in 2026 than in recent years. “Especially with black bears, we’ve definitely seen an uptick in their activity and subsequent conflict activity across the state,” Dan Thompson, large carnivore biologist with the Wyoming Game and Fish Department, told Outside. Bears have already killed two people this year. Anthony Pollio, 33, died while hiking in Glacier National Park in May. A black bear attacked and killed a New Mexico man in August, marking the state’s second fatal bear attack on record. A grizzly attacked two Yellowstone hikers, a Wyoming woman was bitten in the butt by a black bear, an Alaska woman fended off a grizzly using jiu-jitsu, and a black bear charged a group of students in Washington State. It seems the bears are everywhere. Thompson attributes the heightened bear activity to a one-two punch of weather extremes: an unusually low snowpack across the West last winter, followed by scorching summer temperatures. Together, those conditions have diminished the natural food sources bears rely on, including the berries, fruits, nuts, and grasses that make up the bulk of their diet. With less food available in the wild, more bears are venturing beyond their usual habitat and into neighborhoods in search of an easier meal. “Human-bear conflicts in general tend to increase when there are shortages of natural bear foods,” Frank van Manen, a bear expert and emeritus ecologist with the U.S. Geological Survey, told Outside. “It is possible that conflicts suddenly drop off if high-calorie foods that bears pursue in the fall are abundant. In areas where such foods are in low supply, human-bear conflicts may intensify.” Montana, home to nearly two-thirds of grizzly bears in the Lower 48, has reported 194 grizzly conflicts so far in 2026, and another 250 black bear-related incidents, according to Montana FWP data. “This year is panning out to be one of the worst natural food failure years on record,” Jamie Jonkel, Montana FWP bear conflict specialist, said in a statement. “Our regional bear team is working around the clock, and we are asking the public to be patient and to please be diligent with containing all attractants.” In Colorado, the state confirmed five black bear attacks amid an all-time high of more than 8,600 sightings, more than double the number of sightings in 2025. Connecticut wildlife officials reported that over 50 bears have entered homes. There have been at least 168 black bear incidents this year in Utah—also twice the amount from the previous year—and another 187 in New Mexico. Bear populations in some areas are also rebounding, moving beyond their recovery zones, and this year’s low food supply has only compounded those pressures. “There’s no silver bullet, no divine answer for why exactly,” Thompson said. “It’s a combination of factors: the lack of winter in other areas, moisture turning into a lot of heat, early blooms that froze and reduced the berry crop, and increased human use of these areas.” Vocabulary matters when you’re talking about bear data. Here’s how the experts distinguish between different events. Data suggests that brown bear attacks are rising around the world. According to a 2019 study, between 2000 and 2015 there were 183 attacks in North America, averaging 11 every year. Most of these victims were lone males recreating outside. Research on U.S. bear attacks is consistent with these numbers. Between 1990 and 2019, North American black and grizzly bears have killed at least 150 people, and more people have died in recent decades than a century ago. Scientists involved in the studies concluded that’s partly because far more people may be encountering bears. As remote bear territory diminishes, these encounters are even more likely to rise. Cody Miller, a wildlife scientist at Brigham Young University in Utah, wrote in his 2024 study that human–bear conflicts are still rare, but increasing at a steady rate because more people are hiking, camping, and hunting than ever before. Van Manen adds that more people in the landscape also increases the likelihood that bears encounter and pursue human foods, like garbage left behind at camp. Grizzlies account for more conflicts than black bears and are more likely to injure people, Miller concluded. Interestingly, though, black bear conflicts are more likely to be fatal. Most of these incidents began as surprise encounters, as with Pollio in Glacier. Van Manen cautions that although 2026 appears to be an unusually active year for encounters, it doesn’t necessarily mean that fatal bear attacks are on the rise—such a trend takes years of data to establish. “Because of the rarity of these events, comparisons of a single year with a ten-year average are not meaningful,” van Manen said. “Decadal comparisons for North America do not suggest distinct trends.” According to van Manen, grizzly bears killed 17 people in the United States during the 2010s, and 14 in the 2020s so far. American black bears, by comparison, killed ten people in the 2010s and 13 so far in the 2020s. Since 1892, researchers have documented 20 fatal attacks in the Greater Yellowstone area; some years have more, others less. “This is an example of how unpredictable these events are: there was a fatality in 1986 followed by a 25-year period with no fatal incidents and then several years with multiple incidents,” van Manen said. Nationwide tracking doesn’t exist—states hold the data—and establishing a full, nationwide picture of bear deaths is challenging. Chris Servheen, the former national grizzly bear recovery coordinator for the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, told Outside that statistically speaking, a grizzly kills less than one person annually, on average. Even one death is a tragedy, and most fatal attacks are purely coincidental, van Manen adds. “These are chance events that are driven by human and bear numbers: in areas with increasing and expanding bear populations,” he said. “Combined with increases in recreational visits, the chance of a bear encounter that may end in a physical attack increases as well, however small that may be.” But all that could change as we head into the fall months. As more people move into bear country, and more bears come into towns looking for food, conflicts are sure to increase. Late summer and early autumn bring hyperphagia, a period during which bears spend almost all their time consuming calories to build fat reserves for winter. As more bears spend more time looking for food, the chances of people coming across them during fall hikes or bike rides increase. Nathaniel Bowersock is a biologist who spent nearly a decade working with bears in Yellowstone National Park. He is now a black bear specialist in Missouri and works with BearWise, a national program of the Association of Fish and Wildlife Agencies dedicated to mitigating human-bear conflict. He says the most important thing hikers can do is bring bear spray. “Bear spray continues to be shown to be an effective tool at deterring or lessening an encounter with a bear, both black bears and grizzly bears, and bear spray will work under many conditions, even on a windy day,” Bowersock told Outside. “In addition, bear spray has been found to be more effective than a firearm at deterring a bear encounter, and bear spray is easier to use than a firearm. Therefore, any time someone is looking to recreate in grizzly country, I strongly suggest they carry bear spray.” And if you see something, say something. “We have a lot of bears that don’t get reported until it’s too late, or until their behavior is at a level that we can’t tolerate from a human safety standpoint,” Thompson said. “Don’t let garbage be available. Don’t let food be available. Bring in pet food. When you’re camping, make sure you’re keeping a clean camp.”

item.title: Recent Research Says That Climbing Can Reduce Depression and Anxiety
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 2.48
(Photo: Canva) My eyes shot open two hours before my alarm, again, and the anxiety train that is my postpartum brain pulled out of the station right on schedule. I’m a journalist and Outside‘s former health history columnist, and I work full-time. I’m also a new parent. Naturally, my work hours and personal life are all over the place. Four months into motherhood, I find myself managing everything from moments of crushing anxiety to bouts of depression any time I question my parenting abilities. On top of that, as a runner and someone who loves to ski and do anything outdoors, I’m feeling a bit of cabin fever these days and trying to figure out when the hell I can get back on my workout schedule or do any kind of physical activity at all. That said, you can imagine my surprise—and subsequent elation—when I came across a study, published this year, where people with anxiety and depression climbed rocks to work through it. I interviewed the paper’s lead author and a psychologist who specializes in sports and performance. Here’s what they had to say. The study, published in the scientific journal BMC Medicine, is the latest from a German research team that has spent over a decade testing bouldering as therapy. Bouldering is a type of rock climbing done on small rock formations (or indoor rock walls) sans rope and harness. For safety, rocks are generally no more than 20 feet high. Researchers in this 2026 study randomly assigned 128 adults with diagnosed depression into three groups: one did structured bouldering therapy, another tried a newer talk therapy, and a third received standard care as a comparison. That newer talk therapy is called WISE-T, which stands for What’s Important: Schedule and Engage Therapy, and it focuses on identifying what actually matters to you and following through on it, instead of reacting to whatever feels most urgent. The goal of that therapy is to help combat symptoms that accompany depression, including anhedonia—the inability to feel joy or pleasure. In this study, bouldering involved climbing moderate heights, up to ten feet, without ropes or harnesses. Thick pads at the bottom broke falls. Each bouldering session involved three parts: a mindfulness exercise beforehand, the climbing portion, and a relaxation component at the end of class. The two therapy groups ran for ten weeks, once a week, in real settings: a bouldering gym for the bouldering therapy group and a psychiatric clinic for the WISE-T group, led throughout by trained therapists. Both WISE-T and bouldering therapy cut anxiety scores significantly compared with standard care, which barely changed over the same ten weeks. Depression, the study’s main focus, dropped in both groups. On average, people went from moderate depression to mild. Bouldering’s effect was considered moderate; the talk therapy’s was slightly larger, though the gap is small. What matters most is that two very different approaches, one physical, one purely cognitive, both worked. Self-efficacy also improved, most clearly in the talk therapy group. Self-efficacy refers to people’s belief in their ability to handle hard situations. The bouldering group’s effect on self-efficacy appeared, too, but only after some statistical untangling. As expected, only the bouldering group showed a jump in mindfulness during physical activity, and lead researcher Katharina Luttenberger has a theory as to why. “Thought can never be in the here and now, because thoughts necessarily always deal with the past or the future. Therefore, it makes perfect sense to me that mindfulness is fostered through physical activity rather than through cognitive engagement,” she told Outside. Because the participants were randomly assigned to groups, the results are more than a coincidence, but researchers can’t say that bouldering itself caused every improvement. Scientists can conclude, however, that there is an association between fewer depression symptoms, reduced anxiety, and bouldering therapy. The researchers have a clear explanation for why climbing specifically works: a boulder problem forces total, immediate attention. Every route is a specific puzzle you have to solve with your body, right now, leaving no spare processing power for anything else. That’s different from running or cycling, where your mind can wander for miles. Add real but manageable risk, a fall that’s expected, cushioned, and pretty safe, and you get practice handling uncertainty in a contained space. A 2025 survey on bouldering found that nearly three-quarters of American climbers said the sport had a real, positive effect on their mental health. Over 70 percent of 748 people surveyed said climbing was more effective at improving their mental state than medication, and nearly 65 percent said bouldering was better than therapy. Teresa Behrend Fletcher, a psychologist at Adler University who studies sports and human performance, explained that metaphors work in therapy because clients get stuck rehashing a problem the same way, and a metaphor forces a different angle. Bouldering works especially well for this, she said, because a client isn’t just imagining a solution; they’re finding one in real-time. Standing back and reading a route, then adjusting mid-climb when the first plan fails, mirrors the process of working through anything hard. As she put it, the goal is ensuring that “every problem has a solution,” Fletcher told Outside. A few limitations in Luttenberger’s study are worth noting. This study took place in one city, at one gym, and participants were employed and already getting some kind of treatment for their anxiety or depression. But the appeal here isn’t just the sport itself. It’s finding anything that demands your full attention long enough to interrupt rumination and anxious-thinking loops. Trail running a technical descent might do it. So might reading whitewater, or skiing a double black diamond trail. It’s not the rock that matters. It’s what engaging with the rock or other outdoor entity takes off your plate. When you’re trying to survive, your worries tend to fall away. Now, is bouldering therapy going to be a widespread method for alleviating anxiety and depression? Not quite. Luttenberger said that it depends on therapists’ qualifications and national regulations. “In Germany, for example, where the study took place, group psychotherapy is covered by health insurance, and under certain conditions, certified therapists can offer group sessions in various settings,” she said. One of the biggest hurdles in group bouldering psychotherapy, she said, is that “therapeutic climbing with a group of people with mental health issues is very demanding and should not be underestimated.” For it to be feasible and effective, “thorough training in all three areas—psychotherapy, climbing safety, and therapeutic climbing—is required.” I personally haven’t been bouldering, and I’m not claiming it would fix anything. But a researcher and a psychologist, working independently, landed on the same idea, and it’s got me thinking that heading to a climbing gym or even tackling a small boulder on my own might be that way out of my postpartum fog. Whether I climb or find time to get back on the running trails, my goal is to move my body in a way that pulls me out of my head for a while. Want more Outside health stories? Sign up for the Bodywork newsletter. And for tips on how to train, fuel, and recover better, sign up for the Sweat Science 101 newsletter.

item.title: Gossamer Gear “The Free” Freestanding Tent Review
item.description:
Source: Sectionhiker.com Score: 2.23
The Gossamer Gear The Free is a freestanding, double-wall ultralight tent made with Robic nylon that weighs 29.8 oz. It has a single front vestibule and requires two multi-segment aluminum tent poles for setup. While it is very lightweight, the tent is quite narrow inside, with a tapered footprint and sloping walls that can feel claustrophobic. The designers clearly optimized for weight over livability, with mixed results. - Freestanding (inner tent first) - Trail Weight: 29.8 oz total / 845 g - Total Weight: 33.02 oz / 935.8 g (including stuff sacks, stakes) - Minimum tent stakes to pitch: 1 (door) 5-6 recommended - Interior Dimensions: head end: 34″ / 86.4 cm; foot end: 21.5″ / 54.6 cm; length: 86″ / 218.4 cm; height: 39″ / 99.1 cm - Bathtub floor: 7″ deep / 178 cm - Pockets: 2 – ceiling, corner - Seam-sealed: Yes - Materials: 15D Recycled Robic fabric with a 20D dope-dyed ripstop SIL/PU coating (1200 mm) - Hydrostatic head: 4,923 mm The Free is a freestanding double-wall tent with a separate inner tent and rainfly, where the inner tent must be set up first.
