It has two tent poles joined by a central pivoting hub that hooks onto the inner tent ceiling, while the rest attaches to the poles using plastic clips. When setting up the inner tent, it's easiest to stake out the corners before inserting the pole ends into the corner hardware. Once that's done, you can pick up the inner tent and move it to a different location as desired, but trying to insert the poles without a fixed corner is awkward at best, and downright comical if anyone is watching. The inner tent has a directional pitch, with a wider head end (34″) and a narrower foot end (21.5″). The inner has a high bathtub floor with a D-shaped door. While the foot end is narrower than many non-tapered or wide inflatable sleeping pads, you can still fit one if you don't mind losing some bathtub-floor height. The inner tent is 86″ long, but the wall slopes in noticeably. When I sat up inside (I'm 5'10”), my shoulders touched the inner tent's side walls; I measured the width here at 12″. While you're less likely to experience internal condensation transfer in a double-wall tent, the Free is pretty narrow and feels like the walls are closing in, making the tent feel more like sleeping in a bivy than a tent. This happens because there isn't a horizontal strut keeping the two overhead crossing poles separated, so they sag toward each other and reduce the tent's effective interior space. I tried fashioning a cross brace like this with sticks, as similar tents from other manufacturers do, but the fly fabric is so slippery that they slid right off. I suspect adding an extra pole component would bump the shelter weight up over 2 pounds, but it'd be worth it to improve the tent's livability. There are two pockets on the inside of the tent, one in the door-side corner of the head end and the second in the ceiling. The corner pocket is triangular and should be used with caution. Every time I put my glasses in, they simply slid out, over and over. There's a gear loft overhead and a large plastic hook on the ceiling, and you'd be better off stowing or hanging delicate items from them instead. The rainfly drapes over the inner tent and secures to the corner hardware used to stake out the inner tent. There's no way to attach the fly to the pole set, again using tiny toggles or Velcro as provided in other weather-worthy tents. I didn't test the tent in high winds, but I'd expect some flapping. There's a vestibule zipper with a wide fabric flap over the front vestibule to prevent a deluge of rain (onto you) when you unzip the tent in the pouring rain. You can roll back both halves of the vestibule and secure them with toggles. Many competitive ultralight tents now use magnets instead of toggles. You'll appreciate the difference in ease of use when it starts to rain, and you struggle to undo a toggle while staying inside the inner tent. Assessement I've used and recommended Gossamer Gear products for a long time, but I'd pass on The Free tent. The Free would be more competitive with a perpendicular cross pole between its existing two tent poles to create more vertical sidewalls inside. It's too confining now. Several freestanding double-wall tents in the same weight range offer far better internal livability, like the MSR Freelite 1 (26 oz) or the Big Agnes Copper Spur 1P (32 oz). I'd recommend adding them to your short list instead. Disclosure: Gossamer Gear donated a tent for review. SectionHiker never accepts payment for gear reviews or editorial coverage. When you buy through affiliate links on our site, we may earn a small commission at no extra cost to you. Help us continue to test and write unsponsored and independent gear reviews, hiking and backpacking FAQs, and free hiking guides. I’m a Gossamer Gear fan and have several packs. I was going to get The One until they made it smaller. The Free reminds me of the Exped solo from a few years ago, which passed into the sunset. I don’t know what GG was thinking when this tent was brought to market. Where is the upside? IMHO this tent and the big company tents don’t come close to the Durston X-Dome 1+ on features for a similar price. The fly first pitch is a game changer for me. Yes, you may have to wait a while on an order. But you can choose carbon or aluminum poles. However, the MSR, Big Agnes and Nemo tents can be found on sale several time a year which is a big plus. a short answer and a long answer: 1) Gossamer Gear is a backpack company not a tent company, just a six moon designs is a tent company and not a backpack company. 2) Some of the mid-size cottages like Gossamer Gear and Hyperlite are hell bent on making and selling as many things as possible in their online stores, regardless of quality because it is a gold rush out there for ultralight gear. I think they shipped this despite its flaws because they needed it out before the holiday season, knowing that people would buy the “brand” and not the tent. There may also have been a calculation that are enough large websites and Youtube reviewers out there who think they can make money on affiliate sales by giving it a good review or merely mentioning it, that the dissenting voices will be drowned out. Think Wirecutter. Then, as is Gossamer’s standard pattern of behavior, they’ll fix it in version two. It’s also worth noting that Gossamer Gear has hired a bunch of people who are not original staff and aren’t necessarily experienced backpackers. That may also have dilluted an appreciation for the finer points of livability. How does the new fabric compare to prior versions of the One and Two– any noticeable improvement? more slippery.

item.title: ‘Fabulous museums and no queues’: five of the best under-the-radar city breaks in Europe
item.description:
Source: The Guardian Travel Score: 3.49
Nantes, France As dilemmas go, it’s an unusual one: saddle up a giant squid or board a submersible for a voyage to the bottom of the ocean. In the end, I find myself drawn to a fierce-looking merhorse and tentatively take the reins. High above, my daughter glides by on a flying fish, metallic fins flapping, while her Dad is battling stormy seas at the helm of a huge conch shell. A ride on the Carrousel des Mondes Marins (marine worlds carousel) – a three-storey steampunk merry-go-round inspired by Jules Verne’s novel Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea – is one of the highlights of a visit to Nantes. A surreal fairground ride, a work of art and a homage to the city’s most famous son. It’s also a lot of fun. On the banks of the Loire, 30 miles from the Atlantic ocean, Nantes is a city whose fortunes were built on the sea. As a young boy growing up near the docks in the 1830s, Verne dreamed of being a ship’s captain, but it wasn’t to be. Instead, he embarked on a series of journeys of the imagination, channelling his wanderlust into novels such as Around the World in 80 Days and Journey to the Centre of the Earth. The last of Nantes’ shipyards closed in the 1980s, but Verne’s unique vision provided the inspiration for a radical art and regeneration project, Les Machines de l’Île, that has breathed life into the abandoned quays and warehouses of the Île de Nantes, the river island that was home to the city’s docks. This is now the stomping ground of the Grand Éléphant, a 12m-high mechanical pachyderm that carries passengers on tours of the island, spraying bystanders with water from its trunk. I’d seen photos but nothing prepares you for the thrill of turning a corner and seeing the real thing lumbering towards you. You can learn about the magic behind the machinery at the nearby Galerie des Machines, where the creators bring a mechanical menagerie of strange creatures to life. The Verne connection also inspired the name of the city’s summer arts festival, Le Voyage à Nantes, which transforms streets, parks and public spaces into an open-air art gallery from July to September. Our visit coincides with the festival’s opening weekend, and the squares and avenues of the elegant Graslin district are busy with DJ sets, food stalls and people checking out the new artworks. In the Place Graslin, a beautiful square built – like much of Nantes – from chalky-white tuffeau stone from the Loire valley, some kind of cataclysmic eruption has been conjured up in front of the opera house. Huge ammonites appear to have been forced up from beneath the earth, engulfing cars in a mountain of rubble, their doors wide open, radios playing, as though abandoned in haste. Just yards away, children are playing in the dancing water fountains of the square, while the white-aproned waiters of art nouveau brasserie La Cigale weave through the pavement tables delivering seafood platters to diners unfazed by the apocalyptic scene before them. Titled Fossil Opera, the artwork is a commentary on consumerism and the fleeting nature of human endeavour, and is one of about a dozen site-specific installations that have appeared in the city, as if by magic. Even outside the summer months, there is plenty to discover in France’s sixth largest city. Each year, a handful of the festival installations are selected to become permanent fixtures, which has resulted in an impressive collection of contemporary public art, from Les Anneaux, a series of 18 giant steel rings on the Quai des Antilles, which frame views of the Loire and light up at night, to Tadashi Kawamata’s Belvédère de l’Hermitage, a viewing platform inspired by a swallow’s nest, which juts over a sheer cliff. All of these cultural highlights, old and new, are linked by the Ligne Verte, a 12-mile (20km) green line painted on the pavement. We follow the trail through the Passage Pommeraye, an exquisite 19th century glass-roofed shopping arcade; past the imposing Château des ducs de Bretagne, a moated 15th-century castle; stop off at the excellent Musée d’arts de Nantes, which houses an impressive collection of international art spanning seven centuries; and finish up at the peaceful Jardin des Plantes, a charming (and free) botanical garden which is home to a handful of modern art installations and a good cafe. From here it’s a short stroll to the Lieu Unique, a cultural space and concert venue in the factory that once produced the city’s beloved buttery LU biscuits. And there’s more to come. The Jardin Extraordinaire is a newly created garden and climbing wall in a disused granite quarry in the Bas‑Chantenay district. The exotic planting, waterfall and paddling pools were inspired by descriptions in Verne’s novel, The Mysterious Island. The nearby Chantenay docks have been colonised by studios, music spaces and the Little Atlantique Brewery, housed in a 19th-century former oil mill. Opposite the quarry, a derelict industrial building is being transformed into a new riverside cultural hub, the Cité des Imaginaires, which will eventually provide a home for an expanded Jules Verne museum. It’s an ambitious project: creative, unconventional and looking to the future. I’m sure Jules Verne would approve. Joanne O’Connor The trip was supported by Le Voyage à Nantes. Oceania Hôtel de France, just off the Place Graslin, has air‑conditioned doubles from €101 room-only Winter’s Journey, a seasonal festival of concerts, temporary light installations, artworks and gastronomic events, runs from 21 November to 3 January. Basel, Switzerland Unless you’re a professional who makes their way to the Art Basel fair every year, chances are Switzerland’s third largest city will have passed you by – or rather you will have passed it by. Basel is one stop before Zurich on the fast train from Paris, but to whiz through would be a mistake. For art and design lovers, it is the perfect city to explore on a long weekend. Basel bills itself as “the city of art and culture on the Rhine”, and it lives up to its boast. Stroll around the charming old town and marvel at the cathedral before enjoying a cold beer at one of the many cafes. If temperatures soar, you might want to join local people with a dip in the Rhine. Once you’ve done all that, you need to engage with the area’s art offerings. Within the city, the Kunstmuseum holds more than 300,000 works spanning eight centuries, with big hitters such as Monet, Van Gogh and Warhol, while Museum Tinguely is home to the work of the idiosyncratic Swiss sculptor Jean Tinguely and his dada-esque machines. But the two real draws are on the outskirts of the city. Fondation Beyeler in the suburb of Riehen is home to an impressive collection of modern and contemporary art, and always has a blockbuster exhibition (currently Pierre Huyghe) to check out. A short bus or train ride across the German border in Weil am Rhein is the Vitra Design Museum, home to one of the world’s largest permanent exhibitions of modern furniture design. Before you admire the furniture collection, take a walk around the campus, where you can marvel at the main museum building designed by Frank Gehry; the Vitra Schaudepot – which houses the furniture collection – designed by Herzog & de Meuron; Zaha Hadid’s former fire station; and Tadao Ando’s conference centre. There is a beautiful garden by the Dutch designer Piet Oudolf, and the recently added Doshi Retreat for a moment of quiet reflection designed by the Indian architect Balkrishna Doshi, his first completed project outside India and the last he worked on before he died in 2023. That’s half the day gone, so time to head inside. In lots of ways, exploring the Schaudepot is like walking through a giant doll’s house, with the rooms filled with instantly recognisable furniture icons from the 19th century to today, including works by Verner Panton, Le Corbusier, Alvar Aalto and Charles and Ray Eames. The museum also puts on temporary exhibitions. And if all of that has exhausted you, head to the VitraHaus Café, which serves a delicious lunch. Max Benato The Volkshaus, a boutique hotel in the old town, has doubles from 152 swiss francs (£138) room-only Lübeck, Germany Unless you’ve read Buddenbrooks, Thomas Mann’s epic family saga, you may not have heard of Lübeck. But in the middle ages, this port city in Germany, 70km north-east of Hamburg, was one of the richest and most powerful places on Earth. Today, despite the best efforts of the RAF to destroy it in 1942, it remains a beautifully intact medieval gem. The old town is a Unesco world heritage site. It sits on an island in the centre of the city, encircled by the rivers Trave and Wakenitz, and the water is a good place to start exploring. My boyfriend and I hired an electric boat (€49 for up to six people) and spent an hour circumnavigating and gazing at its distinctive seven church spires. Back on dry land, we set off on a guided walking tour, starting at the imposing – if wonky – Holsten Gate. We took in the five red brick churches the spires belong to (two have doubles), and climbed one of them, St Petri’s viewing tower, for a panoramic view. We also stopped at the 800-year-old town hall on the marketplace. But just as fascinating was what lies behind the gothic splendour. At one time, there were 180 hidden alleyways and courtyards threaded through the old town, and about 80 remain. These labyrinthine lanes were built behind wealthy merchants’ mansions to house the poor. Today, the restored cottages are sought-after and the flower-filled, cobbled alleys are charming to explore. To better understand Lübeck’s past, we visited the European Hansemuseum in the old castle monastery. It tells the story of the Hanseatic League, the powerful trade network that stretched from England to Russia and gave Lübeck (“the Queen of the League”) its wealth in the middle ages and its status as a free city state right up to 1937. In a nearby palace, the Museum Behnhaus Drägerhaus displays 19th- and early 20th-century German and European art, including work by Edvard Munch, who visited Lübeck and painted its salt warehouses. Just round the corner is the Günter Grass-Haus, where the writer regularly stayed (he died in Lübeck in 2015). We visited in June during the HanseKulturFestival, when the quarter around St Jakob’s church was full of live music stages, food stalls and outdoor bars. The next festival isn’t until 2028, but there are annual museum, theatre and literature nights, and popup live music in the summer. Lübeck has three natural open-air swimming areas, one on the island. And the seaside isn’t far away – we had a day trip to Travemünde, a historic resort town with miles of sandy beach, taking a scenic river ferry there (90 minutes) and a 20-minute train back. In town, the medieval Schiffergesellschaft (Seafarers’ Guild) is now a traditional Hanseatic restaurant, with long communal tables. Alongside North Sea fish and Holstein meat dishes are vegetarian versions of labskaus, a sort of hash. Sadly, we couldn’t visit Buddenbrookhaus, the museum dedicated to the novel, as it is being renovated. It is expected to reopen in 2030 – which gives you plenty of time to read Mann’s 864-page doorstopper. Like Lübeck itself, it is worth the effort. Rachel Dixon The trip was provided by germany.travel and luebeck-tourismus.de. Accommodation was provided by Liho Lübeck, doubles from £73 room-only Parma, Italy Parma is just far enough off Italy’s main travel routes to discourage the huge crowds of tourists that flood the likes of Venice and Florence. Most travellers reach this tranquil Italian gem by flying into Milan or Bologna, followed by an hour’s train ride. It is definitely worth that extra effort, as I discover a city that ticks every box for a weekend getaway: fabulous museums and frescoed churches without long queues or the need to book a timeslot in advance; friendly, affordable trattorie and osterie showcasing a feast of local food and wines; and, if you time it right, the chance to catch an opera composed by locally born Giuseppe Verdi in the intimate Teatro Regio. The historic centre of Parma is small and easily explored on foot, taking me past an array of architectural masterpieces. I kick off at the grand Piazza Duomo, dominated by the imposing 900-year-old romanesque cathedral. Everyone’s eyes are drawn up to the ornate cupola, decorated with a captivating illusionist fresco by local Renaissance artist Antonio da Correggio. Next to the cathedral stands the early gothic Battistero, an octagonal baptistery whose bare, minimalist exterior contrasts with an incredible explosion of colours from the 13th- and 14th-century paintings that cover the interior. Then, tucked away behind the Duomo, I come upon the entrance of the medieval Monastero di San Giovanni Evangelista, whose cloisters and garden are a peaceful oasis. Entry to the monastery and cathedral is free. Parma’s big must-see is the monumental Palazzo della Pilotta, a baroque complex of palatial museums, a library and remarkable 400-year-old theatre, all included in a single €18 entry ticket. Just by the Parma river that slices the city into two, the palazzo was built by the Farnese family, whose patronage created most of the city’s Renaissance monuments. The Teatro Farnese, made almost entirely of wood, is rarely used as a venue today, but a visit remains an incredible experience. I leave most sightseeing time, though, for the Pilotta’s landmark Galleria Nazionale di Parma, a treasure trove of old master paintings. It may not quite rival the collection of the Uffizi, but I enjoy the chance to just turn up without booking in advance and quietly appreciate works by Leonardo da Vinci, Fra Angelico, Canaletto and Tintoretto without being surrounded by crowds. Sightseeing is only part of Parma’s attraction, however, as this is one of Italy’s food capitals. I walk into the rustic, raucous OsteMagno bar, where everyone is tucking into tagliere – wooden boards piled with razor-thin slices of cured ham, the famous prosciutto crudo di Parma, artisan salami and crumbly aged parmigiano reggiano cheese, accompanied by a glass of the local’s favourite tipple, fizzy red Lambrusco wine, which is a lot more drinkable than I expect. This is not a city to seek out chic, gourmet restaurants, but rather one of the many traditional trattorie such as Da Antonia, whose eponymous owner has overseen the cucina for more than 50 years, or the 120-year-old Trattoria Corrieri, serving up generous plates of homemade pasta for less than €15. John Brunton Palazzo Dalla Rosa Prati has doubles from €80 room-only Santander, Spain Often dismissed as little more than a ferry terminal – somewhere to stop overnight if you want to take your dog to Europe or lower your carbon footprint – the port city of Santander is undergoing something of a cultural renaissance. It’s already blessed with a spectacular bay facing the Cantabrian mountains, wide sandy beaches, grand, colonnaded plazas and superb food, but the opening of new art spaces and museums in the coming months will put the Cantabrian capital firmly on the weekend-break map. Leading the way on 8 September is Faro Santander – a new cultural centre in a grand historical building housing a 1,000-piece art collection belonging to Banco Santander, including works by Velázquez, Goya, Titian, Rubens and Picasso. Different parts of the collection will be shown at different times. With its ornate white facade facing the bay, the Pereda building was previously the bank’s headquarters, but has been transformed into a striking, 21st-century museum space by Pritzker prize-winning British architect David Chipperfield. Santander’s moment in the spotlight will extend into 2027 when Madrid’s Reina Sofia Museum opens its first outpost, set in a similarly grand neo-Renaissance building just a few metres away from Faro Santander. The museum will house the Archivo Lafuente, with paintings, sculptures and manuscripts, including major collections on dadaism and the Spanish civil war, as well as art from Spain, North America and Latin America. Faro Santander and Archivo Lafuente will form two points on a kind of “art triangle”, along with architect Renzo Piano’s 2017 Centro Botín contemporary art centre just over the road. With a bijou but impressive permanent collection, including works by Matisse, Juan Gris, Joaquín Sorolla and Mark Rothko, the Centro Botín sits on the waterfront like a giant, stilt-mounted, 60s alarm clock sawn in half. Spaniards cottoned on to Santander’s charms long ago, and the seafront is lined with elegant fin-de-siècle villas built when well-heeled Madrileños discovered that the city’s Atlantic breezes were the perfect respite from the Spanish capital’s infernal summer. More than 100 years later, while Britain was experiencing its own heatwave, I followed their lead. Temperatures were in the balmy high 20s as I ambled past toddlers building sand castles and teenagers frolicking in the surf on El Sardinero beach, just 15 minutes by bus from the city centre. The centre itself is wonderfully walkable and there’s an unhurried, laid-back vibe in the streets, grand plazas and narrow alleys near the gothic cathedral, lined with bars serving pinchos – the Cantabrian equivalent to tapas. After tucking into tender, grilled squid, laced with gutsy garlic and olive oil, at Mesón Rampalay on a leafy square, I spent a fascinating couple of hours at Mupac – the Museum of Prehistory and Archaeology of Cantabria, just a few minutes’ walk away from Faro Santander. The museum, which is home to one of Spain’s most important prehistoric collections, features excellent interactive displays, and in 2027 it is moving to a brand new, multimillion-euro building. By next year, it seems, Santander will be not just the capital of Cantabria, but a capital of culture too. Eddi Fiegel The trip was provided by Faro Santander. Abba Santander, near the Centro Botín, has stylish doubles from €66 room-only

item.title: ‘So big and so close’: spotting endangered bears on a trip to northern Spain
item.description:
Source: The Guardian Travel Score: 3.14
Once upon a time, in the woods outside Pola de Somiedo, lived a family of Cantabrian brown bears. The villagers reported sightings of a mother bear who had lost a leg to a hunter’s trap, her two cubs and two adult males, either of which might have been the father. In those days, at the end of the 1980s, they seemed to be the last of their kind in this part of Asturias. Meanwhile, the wider population dropped to about 60 bears across the surrounding Cantabrian mountain range that gave the species its name. They have since clawed their way back from the edge of extinction here in northern Spain, and nature guide Luis Frechilla believes their numbers may now be upwards of 500 again. “They’re still classed as endangered,” he tells me, until the official count hits 1,000. But relative abundance makes them much easier to see today in Somiedo natural park – one of Spain’s first such protected areas, established in 1988. Setting his scope on a tripod in a steep-angled pasture, Frechilla spots a bear almost as soon as we start looking. A juvenile, apparently, which means the animal is old enough to be foraging alone, but it’s still too small, and too far away, for him to tell if it’s a male or female. Another bear-spotter standing near us seems more willing to take a guess. “Ooh, look at his little ears,” she says delightedly, beaming behind binoculars. No expert myself, I watch that distant fuzzy shape move across the viewfinder and along the sharp ridges opposite, blinking in and out of sight like a cursor on the trend line of a graph. I’m not sure that we are close enough to call this an encounter, but it is an experience. The sun drops behind the peaks; the birds sing a dusk chorus in the birches and oaks; cowbells ring through the valley from the dairy herds that help this region of so-called “Green Spain” look and sound like the Swiss Alps. It gets cold at night up here, and it’s been known to snow in summer, though my own visit in late spring sees the mountaintops looking whiter than anyone around here can remember so deep into May. That weather, and the sheer calorific spend of living and working at a median altitude of 1,300 metres, has made the traditional cuisine much sturdier here than elsewhere in Spain. Down at the village inn, Casa Miño, we share a bottle of regional cider and a cachopo (beef fillet topped with serrano ham, peppers and goat cheese, and pounded into a single solid unit the size of a solar panel). I want fabada, too, the famous Asturian stew of white beans, pork belly and blood sausage. Frechilla says it’s a winter dish, customarily eaten for lunch – too heavy for the body to process later in the day. But I would order fabada at midnight in a heatwave, and keep eating it even while they loaded me into the ambulance. The bears, meanwhile, don’t have much to feed on at the moment. They only woke from hibernation a few weeks ago, explains Alicia Madrid the next day, on a forest trail above the century-old hydroelectric power station at La Malva. A biologist with the conservation group Fundación Oso Pardo, Madrid tells me that Cantabrian bears don’t hibernate as long or deeply as other brown bears and are generally smaller and lighter than American grizzlies. “They’re adapted to this terrain, and they can’t be too heavy because they have to climb a lot,” she says. Their paw prints in the mud look big enough to me, and the bite marks where they chewed clumps of long grasses, and the hairs shed where they scratched their backs against trees. Madrid shows us, too, the hefty rocks they overturned looking for insects. Further into the summer, there’ll be plenty of berries, acorns, chestnuts and maybe some meaty carrion to fatten them up. The foundation has played a major role in the regrowth of bear populations, building bio-corridors with strategic placements of trees and bushes full of all the things they like to eat. Another key factor is the hunting ban, introduced in 1973. The trick now, says Madrid, is coaxing isolated cohorts to breed with other groups and boost genetic diversity. Also: managing the tourists who come to see them, and balancing ecological imperatives against financial incentives. Later, after a long hike through the Valley of the Lake to reach the aptly named Lake of the Valley, I overhear Frechilla fielding the related concerns of two local women. Against a backdrop of blue sky, bright wildflowers and silver waters, the women seem to argue that conservation efforts amount to commercial exploitation. Frechilla gently insists that Somiedo natural park is a model of good practice in Spain. Much of the bears’ territory is closed to the public, and spotting expeditions are only permitted in the company of licensed guides. Nature tourism, he says, keeps villagers in jobs where farming culture cannot, and is proving vastly more sustainable than hunting bears for sport. As for protecting humans, there has been only one bear attack in recent memory, on an elderly lady whose evening stroll led her between a mother and cubs. She survived. For now, at least, most residents seem willing to share the bears with outsiders. That evening, a small crowd gather by the side of a winding back road near Saliencia, some sitting comfortably on camping chairs with spotting scopes in their hands. Everyone is watching a large male bear – so big and so close that they don’t need the viewing equipment – as he lopes across a meadow to take a quick splash in the river. Another male is spotted in the treeline above, and the two circle each other at a distance for a while. There is some speculation that they might fight for this turf, and a man with two leashed greyhounds seems ready to take bets on it. Frechilla shakes his head. “Maybe later in the season, when they’ve gained enough weight.” These bears are doing better now, but it’s still a tough life. The reality of their ongoing baby boom is that only 30% of juveniles will survive on their own, after a year of maternal supervision. This is surely why I find it so moving when we follow reports of another sighting in the twilight: a mother and her two young cubs have been seen climbing a slope called El Diente, or “The Tooth”. It’s getting dark and cold, but we can see them through the scopes, about a mile away from us across the high mountain pass at La Peral. I watch the mother bear waiting and cajoling as needed while the siblings struggle up the vertical planes of rock like toddlers trying to climb a baby gate. On the ridgeline, they turn to silhouettes, play-fighting against a white sky. They disappear over the far side, but then a little one comes back, seeming to wave goodbye with both front paws in the air. I remember a story I read to my daughter once, which put a poignant time limit on the usual fairytale ending: “And they all lived happily together, for as long as they could.” The trip was provided by the Spanish Tourist Office, Turismo Asturias and Casa Miño in Pola de Somiedo. Bear-spotting tours with nature guide Luis Frechilla can be organised through Wild Spain Travel. For more information on the Cantabrian brown bear and related conservation efforts, visit Fundación Oso Pardo Comments (…) Sign in or create your Guardian account to join the discussion

item.title: A city break in Łódź, Poland’s capital of cinema and factories
item.description:
Source: The Guardian Travel Score: 2.85
Sometimes travel delivers a real shock. I’m moving along the boulevards in the Polish city of Łódź, enjoying the excellent cafes and warm sunshine, when I spot the vans. They are parked up on the verge, with racks of clothing and heavily laden tables behind. I can’t resist a Sunday morning market and walk towards a group of men huddled around a car that is covered in blankets. And then it happens. They turn – and I see they are weighing pistols in their hands. I recognise the lean profile of a German Luger, and then the bulkier Colt 45. There is a second of doubt. I hesitate. They replace the weapons on the display and walk away laughing. I approach. On the car roof is a row of dusty soldiers’ helmets. “We were repairing a pavement in the centre of town,” says the seller cheerfully, handing me a badge to inspect. “Imagine! For 80 years, all this stuff was just under our feet.” It’s a Wehrmacht shoulder badge from Kuban 1943, a last-ditch post-Stalingrad action on the Crimean peninsula. Who wore this, I wonder? A veteran of the Russian front who almost made it home? Nothing is clear, except that in Łódź, the past is never far away. I arrive the previous night, a little disoriented, whizzing past unlit buildings, huge brick structures like Victorian factories. “Are we in the city yet?” I ask. The taxi driver gives me a quizzical look. “Yes, this is Łódź.” I note the pronunciation, like “wudge”. I glimpse five-storey blocks, tree-lined streets, a tramline. “I could never live anywhere else,” he adds. A huge blue graffito is caught in the headlights, like a monstrous alien creature. “Why?” I ask, but we are already pulling up outside an immense red-brick building, my hotel, and he never answers my question. The reception area is huge, with a strange scalloped ceiling in red brick that hints at a previous incarnation as a factory. This is my first visit to Łódź, a city about 75 miles (120km) south-west of Warsaw. My interest has been piqued by a list of notable people associated with the place. It features an astonishing number of Oscar-winning or nominated film directors connected to the city: Andrzej Wajda (The Promised Land), Roman Polanski (The Pianist), Paweł Pawlikowski (Ida), Agnieszka Holland (Europa Europa), Krzysztof Kieślowski (Three Colours trilogy) and Zbigniew Rybczyński (Tango). But under the bonnet there is a vast array of talent in acting, production and technical excellence. The city’s film school is responsible, of course, but Łódź itself features as a setting, too, notably in David Lynch’s Inland Empire and Wajda’s masterpiece The Promised Land. Łódź, I had decided, must be fascinating. Any visit starts with Piotrkowska Street, the longest shopping street in Europe at about 2½ miles. My guide, Anna, takes me through Plac Wolności (Freedom Square), where a dance festival is in progress, with hooded hip‑hoppers rubbing shoulders with troupes of line dancers and girls in colourfully embroidered traditional dress. This is a city where music and dance are never far away. We dodge down a side alley and emerge in a striking art installation – an entire street, Pasaż Róży (Rosa’s Passage), covered in mirrors by the artist Joanna Rajkowska. Back on the main pedestrianised route, the mix of ancient and modern continues: 19th‑century porticoed palaces adorned with colourful graffiti. I ask Anna how Łódź fared in the second world war. “It was not too badly damaged,” she says. “Both the Germans and the Russians wanted the industry intact.” There is no medieval heart, no ornate houses like in Wrocław or Kraków. What Łódź possesses is an impressive array of 19th-century factories, mostly textiles, built to show off their owners’ power, wealth and architectural aspirations. Now, this heritage has become a stunning example of urban regeneration. We turn into OFF Piotrkowska, a complex of beautiful old textile mills reborn as a hive of small businesses. There are lots of vibrant restaurants and bars, but Anna wants to show me a shop that she likes: Pan Tu Nie Stał. “It was a saying in communist times: ‘You’re not in the queue.’ We said it to people trying to push in,” Anna says. This is the spot to pick up a T-shirt featuring Soviet combine harvesters or some Czas Pokaże (Time Will Tell) socks. The shop says a lot about the Polish attitude to communist times: none of the maudlin ostalgie of East Germany; this nostalgia comes with healthy dashes of colour and humour. It did all start, however, with a disaster. The old mills had survived two world wars, but died in the economic collapse after communism ended in 1989. “Everything closed down,” says Anna. “We call that time the transformacja. It was very hard.” We stroll into the Manufaktura area, once the site of a vast textile business started by a local scrap metal dealer, Izrael Poznański, in 1872, and now another beautifully restored collection of red-brick buildings housing restaurants, bars, shops and the fascinating Museum of the Factory. Next door is the palace that Poznański built, a neo-baroque monstrosity of bulging wealth, now the city museum. After the Congress of Vienna in 1815, Łódź became part of the Russian empire, a melting pot of German, Jewish, Polish and Russian influences. In the 1870s, Poznański was one of a group of men who saw the potential of steam power. They imported looms from England and were soon amassing unimaginable wealth, constructing a city of handsome red-brick factories, the core of which still remains. The Museum of the Factory houses a collection of working looms that date back to the 1880s. Only four machines are ever turned on due to noise pollution laws – in the old days, one factory might have had hundreds. This was the city of the deaf, but the deafest of all were the bosses, oblivious to the terrible hardships of their workforce, from the founders through to their communist successors. When Wajda came to these mills in the early 1970s, planning The Promised Land, he needed to make only minor adjustments to start filming. The tired faces, the crashing looms, the heat and the dust – it was all very much like 1880. Is that your favourite film, I ask Anna? She shakes her head. “Cold War by Pawlikowski,” she says. “I love that film.” This 2018 masterpiece is the story of a tragic love affair conducted across the Iron Curtain in the years following the second world war. Based on the lives of Pawlikowski’s parents, it is dark and sensuous, full of great music and dance. Pawlikowski has used Łodż as a location. We move on to the Museum of Cinematography, a tour de force that warrants some preparation (watch films by Polish directors). They have everything from early working equipment to props from the most recent Oscar triumphs. By the time I get to the end, I have only a few minutes to rush to the Central Museum of Textiles. There I find a technician, Przemysław, about to start up a 1893 Greenwood loom. He’s a former policeman with a few tales to tell, but right now one question is bothering me. “Why did film-making succeed so brilliantly in this city of textiles?” I ask him. He taps the cast iron loom and chuckles. “I’ll show you.” With the flick of a switch, the loom begins to clank and turn. The noise is incredible. Przemysław is moving around, adjusting and calibrating, his face concentrated. I see the spools of thread begin to unwind, the shuttle dashing back and forth, the warp and weft rhythmically rising and falling. The different colours, each no more than a thin line, but magically coming together. And from the lip of the machine spills a beautiful multicoloured cloth. Przemysław looks at me and raises a questioning eyebrow. “Like weaving a story, right?” The trip was provided by the Polish Tourism Organisation, with Holiday Extras lending travel support in car parking, insurance, airport transfers and hotels

item.title: ‘It feels like Italy with the volume turned down’: readers’ favourite (smaller) city breaks in Europe
item.description:
Source: The Guardian Travel Score: 2.51
Renaissance art without the crowds in Italy Ferrara in Emilia-Romagna won me over precisely because it feels like Italy with the volume turned down. I stayed in a small family-run hotel near Via delle Volte, where mornings began with quiet cobbled streets and the smell of fresh pastries. The Palazzo dei Diamanti was almost empty when I visited, giving me space to enjoy its Renaissance art without crowds. Evenings meant cycling past terracotta walls to tiny trattorias serving pumpkin cappellacci, a traditional pasta dish. It’s a city that lets you slow down, breathe and enjoy its beauty. John One of Germany’s greenest cities Next to flashy Munich or cool Berlin, Hanover in northern Germany has a reputation of being boring. It is totally undeserved: there are world-class museums, such as the modern art gallery Sprengel, one of the best-preserved baroque gardens in Europe – the Great Garden at Herrenhausen – impressive Victorian era architecture, 640 hectares (1,680 acres) of city forest (the Eilenriede, nearly double the size of New York’s Central Park) and a large artificial lake just south of the centre that you can travel on with a bus ticket (or hire a boat). Explore the city and its surroundings on more than 600 miles of cycle paths, find independent shops in the well-heeled art nouveau district of List or the multicultural Linden, and relax in a deck chair on Ballhofplatz with tea and cake at the Teestübchen. Ulrike The Algarve’s city of crafts Bursting with Portuguese charm, Loulé is 10 miles inland from Faro, capital of the Algarve. The small city has a rich history of preserving traditional crafts, supported by Loulé Criativo, a network of community-driven artisans that keeps alive and celebrates the identity of Loulé and the Algarve. It includes the House of Weaving (Casa da Empreita) and the Watchmakers (Oficina do Relojoeiro) and Stringed Instrument Workshop (Oficina de Cordofones). In these vibrant spaces – where visitors can interact with artisans – the city’s heritage is preserved and passed down through generations. Sue Unesco sites in northern France Arras, 35 minutes on the train from Lille, has two Unesco world heritage sites: the belfry of the Hotel de Ville and the Vauban Citadel. Exploring the Boves, a 10th-century network of tunnels which played roles in the first and second world wars, is an amazing experience. Above are two magnificent large squares in the Flemish style with a wide variety of alfresco cafes, restaurants and indie shops. Arras also holds one of the biggest Christmas markets north of Paris, noted for its amazing range of international gourmet foods. Bryan Boese Artistry and cake in Sweden’s beautiful south Malmö is easily accessible (being connected by bridge to Copenhagen) and very walkable. We enjoyed the free Malmö Konsthall arts centre with contemporary exhibitions and also the skateboard artistry in the square outside. The Western Harbour contains architectural gems, such as the twisted skyscraper Turning Turso, restaurants and swimming piers in a former industrial area. The cafe Hollandia offered classic Swedish cakes and a lovely atmosphere. The Disgusting Food Museum next door was an interesting cultural experience showing food considered to be delicacies in some countries, not so much in others. A sign shows the number of people who have thrown up (visit Hollandia first)! Elisabeth Brilliant beach and seafood in Sardinia If you can tear yourself away from Poetto – surely one of the prettiest city beaches in Europe – you’ll find a lot more to love in Cagliari, capital of Sardinia. The huge indoor produce market is a riot of glistening seafood, local pecorino and sweet, nutty Sardinian treats. The town centre strides uphill from the port, with the elegant bulwark of Bastione St Remy delineating the ancient Castello district and serving up epic rooftop and coastal views. We missed the renowned archaeological museum, but that just gives us the perfect excuse to go back. Cagliari’s affordable seafood was a definite highlight, and Trattoria Lillicu’s chargrilled bream and calamari is another tempting reason to hurry back. Martha Stained glass wonder in north-west Spain In León, colours grab your attention and take away words. León cathedral completely wrongfooted me. This city seems to be under the British tourist radar. I thought I’d already seen stained glass that was worthy of heaven – this was another level. Coupled with this was how visitors were reacting. Everyone was using the free audio guide. No one was just marching round and ticking off the sights. People were learning and savouring the experience. The humble ninth-century San Isidoro church, one of the most important romanesque buildings in Spain, is a refreshing contrast. Deborah Norway’s art nouveau gem Ålesund is one of Norway’s most beautiful stops on an already spectacular western coast, despite having been devastated by fire in 1904. We reached the small, rebuilt art nouveau city via the breathtaking winding roads of the Trollstigen (the “Troll’s Path”) and had our first sighting from the top of the panoramic Aksla mountain viewpoint. Exactly 418 steps lead down to the historic centre where museums, cafes, restaurants and shops cluster around the Brosundet Canal in renovated warehouses and ornate buildings. Kayaking, a rib boat ride or a trip to the stunning Geirangerfjord? We couldn’t choose so did them all! Teresa Stansby The French city with a bit of everything I spent five days in Saint-Malo this August. It has everything: a beautiful walled city with lots of history, a variety of beaches offering shifts in light and character throughout the day, a modernist tidal pool with a high diving platform. The city has so much pride, and the art inspired by its famous landmarks make for great souvenirs. My favourite thing, though? The wonderful cider at La Passage (on Instagram) with my sister. And despite the heat everywhere else, the temperature never got above 25C. Sophie Amos Winning tip: a watery Dutch master of a city Leiden starts badly. The walk from the station is grim. Scruffy bars and vape shops. And then, suddenly, this watery Dutch gem reveals itself. Canals shoot off from a boat-filled basin, each one lined with grand brick mansions tapering to elegant finials under the sort of blue lowland skies that typify every good (and bad) Flemish painting. Dig deeper into its narrow traffic-free courtyards and squares with cafes spilling out light and chatter, much as they did when Rembrandt trudged to the school that still stands here, just round the corner from his first tutor’s studio. He’d find it mostly unchanged if he walked back. At Christmas, an ice rink spreads across the main canal, and the smell of warm wine, cloves and crepes hovers over the market stalls. Bill Jones Comments (…) Sign in or create your Guardian account to join the discussion

item.title: TSA liquids rule: What to know about 3-1-1 before you head to the airport
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 6.04
TSA liquids rule: What to know about 3-1-1 before you head to the airport Editor's Note It's the rule every passenger has to consider when packing for a flight. For 20 years now, the Transportation Security Administration has enforced rules on the liquids passengers can bring in carry-on bags. This policy is the reason you can't bring a full-size bottle of shampoo or sunscreen through a TSA checkpoint. It's one of the biggest reasons bags get pulled for secondary screening. Last year, the TSA stopped requiring flyers to take off their shoes, but the liquids rule remains one of the biggest hurdles travelers still face when passing through security. But what exactly are the TSA liquid rules, and why do they exist? And, most importantly, what does this mean for packing ahead of your next trip? Here's a quick rundown. TSA liquids rules: Why do they exist? The TSA's restrictions on liquids date back to 2006. In the wake of a thwarted terrorism plot overseas, the agency started restricting the liquids, gels and aerosols passengers could bring in their carry-on baggage. Scores of other countries around the world put similar policies in place in the name of aviation security. What is the TSA's 3-1-1 rule? The TSA's ban on liquids — or at least large quantities of them — is governed by what's known as the "3-1-1 rule." The decades-old policy states that: - Liquids must be in containers no larger than 3.4 ounces, or roughly 100 milliliters (that's the "3"). - All containers must be placed in one clear, quart-size plastic bag ("1"). - Each passenger is only allowed one such plastic bag ("1"). These rules govern liquids, gels and aerosol products ranging from toothpaste to shampoo, conditioner, mouthwash and sunscreen — among other products. Liquid products larger than 3.4 ounces must be placed in a checked bag. That applies even to those large shampoo containers with just a tiny bit of shampoo left, per TSA policy. Exceptions to the TSA's 3-1-1 policy There are a few exceptions, though. The TSA will allow you to bring "medically necessary" liquids, gels and aerosols in reasonable quantities for your flight. However, you must declare those items to security officers at the checkpoint for inspection. The agency asks travelers with larger amounts of medically necessary liquids to remove them from the carry-on bag and place them in a bin or bowl. The TSA has a variety of alternative screening methods it can use. What can you bring through a TSA checkpoint? You can bring creamy cheeses, liquid chocolate, liquid coffee, creamy dips and spreads, gravy, honey, hummus, ice cream, jam, jelly, juice, syrup, peanut butter, salad dressing, sauce, salsa, soda, soup and yogurt as long as they are in a container of less than 3.4 ounces, according to the TSA. You can bring your water bottle with you — as long as it's empty. This can also be a great way to save money at the airport, since many now have postsecurity filling stations for reusable water bottles. When in doubt, consult the TSA's list of what you can carry through the airport and check with your airline. Or, better yet, download the MyTSA app. It contains a "Can I Bring?" section, allowing you to look up items and find out whether they're allowed outright, restricted to 3.4 ounces, permitted only in a checked bag, permitted only in a carry-on bag or prohibited altogether. Could 3-1-1 finally go away? While the TSA's 3-1-1 liquids rules remain in place, there's reason to wonder how long they'll be around. The U.K. has begun a long-planned rollback of its liquids rules. And after the TSA ended its long-standing "shoes-off" policy in 2025, the Trump administration signaled that the liquids restrictions could be next ... someday. "We're exploring technologies that might allow us to bring water bottles again through checkpoints," newly appointed TSA administrator David Cummins told Congress during his summer 2026 confirmation hearing. So, abide by the rules for now. But stay tuned. Learn more: Citi / AAdvantage Business World Elite Mastercard Application restrictions Citi has some strict application restrictions. Citi doesn't limit the number of cards you can have, but it will limit your overall credit. Citi is also sensitive to recent inquiries, so for the best results, wait a few months from your last card application before applying for a Citi card. Additionally, Citi has the 8/65 rule, which means: - You can apply for only one card (personal or business) every eight days and no more than two cards in a 65-day window. - You can only apply for one business card every 90 days. There are exceptions to this rule, but this is general guidance for optimal results. You'll generally want a good credit score of at least 670 before applying for either card. Additionally, if you have previously earned a welcome bonus on a Citi / AAdvantage card, it's possible to earn another. According to the Citi / AA Executive's terms, "New account bonus is not available if you have received a new account bonus for a Citi® / AAdvantage® Executive account in the past 48 months or if you converted another Citi credit card account on which you earned a new account bonus in the last 48 months into a Citi® / AAdvantage® Executive account." These terms apply only to individual cards, not to the whole family of cards. You can also hold multiple Citi / AA cards at the same time. You can even earn multiple welcome bonuses as long as they are different card products and it's outside the 48-month window. It's important to note that the 48-month period starts when you receive the welcome bonus, not when you're approved for the card. For example, if you switch to the Citi / AAdvantage Platinum Select World Elite Mastercard after earning the welcome bonus on the Citi / AAdvantage Executive World Elite Mastercard, you'd still have to wait 48 months from when you earned your welcome bonus on the Citi / AAdvantage Executive to earn another Citi / AAdvantage Executive welcome bonus. item.title: Who are the Chase Ultimate Rewards airline and hotel transfer partners?
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 5.64
Who are the Chase Ultimate Rewards airline and hotel transfer partners? Editor's Note Chase Ultimate Rewards is one of the most valuable rewards currencies you can have in your wallet. Aside from possibly earning 1 to 10 points per dollar spent on select Chase-branded credit cards, you can maximize their value by transferring your hard-earned Ultimate Rewards points to one of the issuer's 14 loyalty partners. Whether you want to book a flight to Europe, save on a domestic trip or stay at a high-end hotel, redeeming your Ultimate Rewards points via transfer partners can be a lucrative way to spend (and even save) your Chase points. Here is everything to know about Chase Ultimate Rewards' transfer partners. Who are the Chase Ultimate Rewards transfer partners? You can transfer Ultimate Rewards points to 10 airline programs: - Aer Lingus AerClub - Air Canada Aeroplan - Air France-KLM Flying Blue - British Airways Club - Iberia Club - JetBlue TrueBlue - Singapore KrisFlyer - Southwest Rapid Rewards - United MileagePlus - Virgin Atlantic Flying Club Chase also partners with four hotel programs: Chase points transfer to partners at a 1:1 ratio, with one exception. New Chase Sapphire Preferred® Card (see rates and fees) cardholders who applied on or after June 15 can transfer Chase points to World of Hyatt at a 4:3 rate. Existing Sapphire Preferred cardholders can continue transferring points to Hyatt at a 1:1 rate through Sept. 30, before moving to a 4:3 rate on Oct. 1. For Ink Business Preferred® Credit Card (see rates and fees) cardholders, transfers to World of Hyatt remain 1:1 through Sept. 30. Beginning Oct. 1, both existing cardholders and new applicants will transfer Chase points to Hyatt at a 4:3 rate. Transfers must be made in increments of 1,000. However, Chase occasionally offers transfer bonuses to partners, which can yield even higher value for your redemptions. How long do Chase Ultimate Rewards transfers take? Most transfers from Chase Ultimate Rewards to its partner programs are instantaneous. However, in our most recent testing, transfers to Singapore KrisFlyer took about 48 hours. Delays can happen when transferring your points for some simple reasons as well. To facilitate the transfer process, ensure that the name on your Ultimate Rewards account matches the one on your loyalty program account. Additionally, make sure you have signed up for a loyalty program in advance, as transferring to a new account may also cause a delay. How do you transfer Chase Ultimate Rewards points to partners? You can easily transfer Chase points online. First, log in to your Chase account and navigate to the Ultimate Rewards portal. In the "Travel" drop-down menu, select "Transfer points to partners" to access the main transfer page. You will then see the list of transfer partners and any current transfer bonuses. Select your desired transfer partner, link your external account if you have not already done so, select the number of Ultimate Rewards points you wish to transfer and then submit the transfer. Remember, Ultimate Rewards transfers cannot be reversed, so it's best to wait until you have a specific redemption in mind before transferring points. Related: Chase Ultimate Rewards points: How to redeem for maximum value What are the best Chase Ultimate Rewards transfer partners? If you prefer to transfer your points to one of the 10 airline program partners, the best redemption options for you may vary depending on factors such as which airlines fly to and from the destinations you wish to visit and which airlines you prefer to fly. However, there are notable sweet spots with certain airline transfer options, especially those programs that have retained award charts. Here are some of our favorite partners to book using Chase points. Book a round-trip flight to Madrid via Iberia Club Flying from the U.S. to Spain doesn't have to set you back thousands of dollars. Round-trip, off-peak flights from New York's John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) and Boston Logan International Airport (BOS) to Adolfo Suárez Madrid-Barajas Airport (MAD) will only set you back 32,000 Avios in basic economy, 59,000 Avios in premium economy and 81,000 Avios in business class (plus applicable taxes and fees) when you transfer your Chase points to Iberia Club, though the airline sometimes runs award discounts that can mean even cheaper seats. Considering that most airlines charge at least 60,000 miles for a one-way business-class award to Europe, an off-peak business-class flight to and from Madrid booked via Iberia Club for just 32,000 Avios round-trip is excellent value. Book flights to Hawaii via British Airways Club Did you know that you can book American Airlines and Alaska Airlines flights with Chase points? Though the carriers' loyalty programs are not direct transfer partners of Chase, you can book flights on these airlines by transferring your Ultimate Rewards points to British Airways Club and then redeem British Airways Avios for award flights on its Oneworld partners. Typically, you can find saver-level award space from American's and Alaska's West Coast gateways to various airports in Hawaii in economy for 44,000 Avios round-trip, or 22,000 Avios one-way, plus minimal taxes and fees. Book lie-flat business-class seats to London via Virgin Atlantic Flying Club Is London calling? Though Virgin Atlantic Flying Club prices its award seats dynamically, the loyalty program offers saver fares for low-demand travel dates. If you're flexible and come across availability, you could score lie-flat business-class seats from JFK to London's Heathrow Airport (LHR) for as few as 29,000 points with one recent deal, though note that taxes, fees and carrier-imposed surcharges of around $700 one-way are also payable. If you're looking to be more thrifty with your hard-earned points, you can fly the exact same route in economy for as few as 6,000 points (plus about $165 in taxes and fees), depending on the direction. You can use Virgin Atlantic's reward seat checker to find saver fares or an award booking platform like Seats.aero to search dates and prices. However, be sure to confirm award availability with the airline prior to booking a seat. Book a stay at a top-tier Hyatt hotel via World of Hyatt You can also get great value from your Chase Ultimate Rewards points by transferring them to World of Hyatt. The hotel loyalty program offers a very appealing award chart, broken into 8 hotel categories and 5 rate tiers from Lowest to Top. By transferring your Chase points to Hyatt, you can book some of the most luxurious Park Hyatt properties in the entire portfolio, including the Park Hyatt London River Thames, starting at 35,000 points per night during the Lowest dates. Just remember that after the 4:3 rate for Chase to Hyatt transfers goes into effect, you'll need to transfer 47,000 Chase points to World of Hyatt to make that 35,000 point booking. What are Chase Ultimate Rewards points worth? TPG values Ultimate Rewards points at 2.05 cents apiece, per our September 2026 valuations, but you can find even more value by transferring points to airline and hotel partners. However, you'll get different values for Chase points when you pursue other redemption options. For example, since the addition of Points Boost, Ultimate Rewards points can be worth up to 2.5 cents per point on select Chase Travel℠ bookings if you hold the Chase Sapphire Reserve® (see rates and fees) or the Chase Sapphire Reserve for Business℠ (see rates and fees). You can receive up to 1.5 cents per point through the portal if you hold the Chase Sapphire Preferred or the Ink Business Preferred. How can you earn Chase Ultimate Rewards points? You can earn Chase points depending on the specific Chase credit card you carry. The following cards earn fully transferable Ultimate Rewards points: - Chase Sapphire Reserve: Earn 100,000 bonus points after spending $6,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. - Chase Sapphire Reserve for Business: Earn 200,000 bonus points after spending $30,000 on purchases in the first six months from account opening. - Chase Sapphire Preferred Card: Earn 75,000 bonus points after spending $5,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. - Ink Business Preferred Credit Card: Earn 100,000 bonus points after spending $8,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. However, if you have an Ultimate Rewards points-earning card, you can effectively convert your cash-back rewards into Ultimate Rewards points, too. For this reason, having more than one Chase card can make sense to maximize your earning and redeeming potential. Here are the four cash-back Chase cards that offer the opportunity to convert the cash-back rewards you earn into fully transferable Ultimate Rewards points as a cardholder of one of the above points-earning Chase cards: - Chase Freedom Flex® (see rates and fees): Earn $200 cash back after spending $500 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. - Chase Freedom Unlimited® (see rates and fees): Earn $200 cash back after spending $500 on purchases in the first three months from account opening. - Ink Business Cash® Credit Card (see rates and fees): Earn $1,000 cash back after spending $8,000 on purchases in the first four months from account opening. - Ink Business Unlimited® Credit Card (see rates and fees): Earn $1,000 cash back after spending $8,000 on purchases in the first four months from account opening. Bottom line If you value the flexibility of choosing from 10 airline partners and four hotel partners, Chase Ultimate Rewards is one of the best points programs out there. In the age of no-notice devaluations by some loyalty programs, it is smart to earn Ultimate Rewards points via credit card welcome offers, category bonuses and everyday spending and then keep your points until you are ready to transfer and book with an airline or hotel partner, which is why earning Chase Ultimate Rewards points is an exceptionally savvy travel strategy. Related: The power of the Chase Trifecta: Maximize your earnings with 3 cards TPG featured card | 5x | Earn 5x on travel purchased through Chase Travel℠. | | 3x | Earn 3x on dining, vacation homes, gas & EV charging, top streaming services and online groceries (excluding Walmart, Target, and wholesale clubs). | | 2x | Earn 2x on all other travel purchases. | | 1x | Earn 1x on all other purchases. |

item.title: How to access American Airlines Admirals Club lounges
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 5.62
How to access American Airlines Admirals Club lounges Editor's Note The American Airlines Admirals Club airport lounge is a great place to relax and recharge before a flight on American Airlines or its partners. Inside the lounge, you can expect complimentary refreshments, Wi-Fi and a place to sit away from the hustle and bustle of the airport terminal. You'll find nearly 50 Admirals Clubs in airports worldwide, including major American Airlines hubs. There are a handful of ways to access the Admirals Club before your next flight — here are your options. Citi® / AAdvantage® Executive World Legend Mastercard® (see rates and fees): For a limited time, earn 125,000 bonus miles after spending $15,000 on purchases in the first five months from account opening. Access the Admirals Club on same-day flights Regardless of how you gain access to the Admirals Club — through a membership, class of service or American Airlines AAdvantage elite status — know that you must present a same-day boarding pass for an eligible departing or arriving flight. The eligibility requirements vary slightly depending on how you're accessing the lounge. For example, one-day passes require a same-day flight marketed or operated by American Airlines or a Oneworld airline. The same is true for Admirals Club members, except that flights marketed or operated by Aer Lingus also qualify. Lifetime Admirals Club members are subject to the same-day eligible-flight requirement as well. Access the Admirals Club with a credit card An easy way to access the Admirals Club is by opening the Citi / AAdvantage Executive World Legend Mastercard, which, for a limited time, earns 125,000 bonus miles after spending $15,000 on purchases in the first five months from account opening. Cardholders also receive a complimentary Admirals Club membership, which can provide substantial value compared with purchasing an annual membership separately. The card has a $695 annual fee. With this membership, you get access for up to two guests or immediate family members traveling with you. Guests must present a boarding pass for same-day travel on American Airlines or a Oneworld airline. The card remains the only credit card that includes an Admirals Club membership. The real hidden gem of this card is its generous authorized-user policy. You can add up to three authorized users to your account for $175, then additional authorized users for $175 each. Authorized users get Admirals Club access when they hold a same-day boarding pass for a flight marketed or operated by American Airlines or marketed and operated by a Oneworld airline. Because of this, some may even consider splitting the annual fee among several authorized users to lower everyone's lounge costs. Be aware that authorized users do not receive a full membership; they only have access. They must present their physical Citi / AAdvantage Executive World Legend Mastercard and may bring immediate family members or up to two guests. Authorized users do not have access to partner lounges. You can also access Admirals Club lounges with four single-visit Admirals Club passes each year for the primary cardmember with either of the following cards: - Citi Strata Elite℠ Card (see rates and fees) - Citi® / AAdvantage® Globe™ Mastercard® (see rates and fees) To use them, you must present a same-day boarding pass for an eligible American Airlines or Oneworld flight. These passes cannot be shared or gifted. Each accompanying adult 18 or older requires their own pass, though up to three children under 18 traveling with an adult passholder may enter without additional passes. The primary cardmember may redeem all four passes in a single visit to bring in up to three adult guests. Any passes not redeemed at the end of the calendar year will be forfeited. Related: Best credit cards for American Airlines flyers Access the Admirals Club with a paid membership If opening a credit card is not appealing, you can always purchase a membership. American Airlines significantly changed its Admirals Club membership structure and pricing on Aug. 23. There are now two main paid membership options. A standard Admirals Club membership includes guest privileges and access to eligible partner lounges, while the less expensive single membership provides Admirals Club access only for the member and does not include guests or third-party partner lounge access. Here's how much a standard annual Admirals Club membership costs: - AAdvantage member: $1,400 or 140,000 miles - AAdvantage Gold: $1,350 or 135,000 miles - AAdvantage Platinum: $1,300 or 130,000 miles - AAdvantage Platinum Pro: $1,250 or 125,000 miles - AAdvantage Executive Platinum: $1,200 or 120,000 miles ConciergeKey members receive complimentary Admirals Club access. Alternatively, the single membership costs $750 or 75,000 miles per year, regardless of AAdvantage elite status. It is intended for travelers who only need access for themselves and does not include guest privileges or access to third-party partner lounges. American is also discontinuing household memberships. Existing household memberships remain valid through their current membership year. Members eligible to renew before Oct. 3 can do so at the household rate one final time; those renewing on or after Oct. 3 must select one of the new membership options. You can also use miles to purchase an Admirals Club membership at 1 cent apiece. Per TPG's September 2026 valuations, American Airlines miles are worth 1.45 cents apiece, so we generally don't recommend redeeming American miles this way. Related: Best credit cards for airport lounge access Admirals Club one-day pass You can use one-day passes at some Admirals Club locations. These are available for purchase for $79 or 7,900 AAdvantage miles. During peak hours, however, be prepared to be turned away with a one-day pass. A one‑day passholder may bring up to three children under 18 at no extra charge, subject to lounge capacity. One-day passes can be activated within 12 months of purchase and, once activated, are valid for 24 hours. You'll need a same-day boarding pass for a departing or arriving flight marketed or operated by American Airlines or marketed and operated by a Oneworld airline. Access the Admirals Club with elite status Admirals Club and Flagship Lounge access rules overlap, but they aren't identical. Flagship Lounges generally have more restrictive eligibility requirements for American Airlines AAdvantage and Alaska Airlines Atmos Rewards elite members, although qualifying Oneworld Sapphire and Emerald members from other programs can also receive access regardless of cabin. If you have a choice between the two, head to the superior Flagship Lounge. American Airlines AAdvantage and Alaska Airlines Atmos Rewards elite members If you hold Oneworld Sapphire or Emerald status through American Airlines AAdvantage (via AAdvantage Platinum, Platinum Pro or Executive Platinum status), you and a guest can access Admirals Clubs when traveling on qualifying international itineraries marketed and operated by American Airlines, a Oneworld airline or Aer Lingus, even in economy class. Qualifying AAdvantage itineraries include flights between the U.S. and Asia, Australia, Canada, the Caribbean, Central America, Europe, Mexico, the Middle East, New Zealand and South America. However, on Alaska Airlines-operated flights, access is not granted when flying from the U.S. to Canada, the Caribbean or Mexico. Alaska Airlines Atmos Rewards Gold, Platinum and Titanium members have separate Admirals Club eligibility rules. When traveling on flights marketed and operated by American Airlines or a Oneworld airline, they can access Admirals Clubs on qualifying flights between the U.S. and Asia, Australia, Central America, Europe, New Zealand and South America, as well as on eligible Flagship transcontinental routes. Unlike qualifying AAdvantage elite members, Atmos Rewards members do not receive status-based Admirals Club access for travel between the U.S. and Canada, the Caribbean or Mexico. Other Oneworld elite members If you are a Oneworld Sapphire or Emerald member with a program other than AAdvantage or Atmos Rewards, you and a guest can access an Admirals Club or Flagship Lounge when traveling on American Airlines or another Oneworld carrier. Flagship Lounge access is a generous benefit for Sapphire-level members of foreign programs. Related: Why I earn status with foreign airlines — and whether you should, too Loyalty Point Rewards The following Loyalty Point Rewards are available to help you get into an Admirals Club. When you reach the following point thresholds, you can choose a reward once per year: - 250,000 Loyalty Points: An Admirals Club membership (remember, when you achieve this tier, you can select from two Loyalty Point Rewards, but the Admirals Club membership requires both of your selections) - 400,000 Loyalty Points: An Admirals Club membership (requires two choices) - 550,000 Loyalty Points: An Admirals Club membership (requires two choices) - 750,000 Loyalty Points: An Admirals Club membership (requires two choices) One-day passes are no longer offered as a Loyalty Point Reward. Access the Admirals Club with a certain fare class While standard domestic first-class tickets won't get you access to Admirals Clubs, the following types of tickets will: - Business- and first-class tickets on qualifying international flights marketed and operated by American Airlines, a Oneworld airline or Aer Lingus - Domestic Flagship-ticketed flights, including nonstop flights between: - New York's John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) and Los Angeles International Airport (LAX), John Wayne Airport (SNA) in Orange County, California, or San Francisco International Airport (SFO) - Boston Logan International Airport (BOS) and LAX - Miami International Airport (MIA) and LAX - Dallas Fort Worth International Airport (DFW) and Honolulu's Daniel K. Inouye International Airport (HNL), Hawaii Island's Ellison Onizuka Kona International Airport at Keahole (KOA) or Maui's Kahului Airport (OGG) - Chicago's O'Hare International Airport (ORD) and HNL or OGG - Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport (PHX) and HNL (seasonally) Again, if you're flying through LAX, MIA, DFW, ORD or Philadelphia International Airport (PHL), you should seek out a Flagship Lounge if you're eligible for access. At JFK, American Airlines and British Airways instead operate three joint premium lounges in Terminal 8: Chelsea, Soho and Greenwich. Which one you can access depends on your cabin, status and itinerary. Still, Admirals Club access can be a benefit for premium transcontinental passengers originating in Boston or San Francisco. You won't be able to bring in a guest if you're getting lounge access this way unless you're flying in international first class, in which case you're allowed one guest. The guest must be traveling on a departing or arriving Oneworld flight; they do not have to be booked on the same flight as you. Military access to the Admirals Club With a valid military ID and a boarding pass for a same-day flight operated by American Airlines, U.S. military personnel traveling in uniform can access the Admirals Club and most partner club locations. You can bring in your immediate family or up to two guests. However, uniformed U.S. military personnel can't access these two partner lounges: - Aspire Lounge at San Diego International Airport (SAN) - Japan Airlines Sakura Lounge at HNL Related: The best military travel deals for service members Bottom line There are numerous ways to access American Airlines' Admirals Clubs. While the creature comforts of the Admirals Clubs vary significantly, these lounges are still better than sitting in a crowded terminal and spending more than $5 on a bottle of water. Ensure you're well versed in the ins and outs of accessing Flagship Lounges and, at JFK, American Airlines and British Airways' joint premium lounges. After all, if you have access to Flagship Lounges, which are significantly nicer, you wouldn't want to visit the Admirals Club mistakenly. If you're like many TPG staffers who value an Admirals Club membership, an American Airlines cobranded credit card that provides you with membership and access for your guests may be the way to go, particularly now that a standard paid Admirals Club membership costs between $1,200 and $1,400 per year, while the Citi / AAdvantage Executive World Legend Mastercard has a $695 annual fee.

item.title: 11 ways to use points and miles for an incredible trip to Costa Rica right now
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 5.13
11 ways to use points and miles for an incredible trip to Costa Rica right now Editor's Note Gorgeous beaches, lush rainforests, dramatic volcanoes, incredible biodiversity and phenomenal hotels ranging from sprawling seaside resorts to intimate jungle lodges … Costa Rica is truly one of the most unique, welcoming destinations in the world. The coffee is pretty phenomenal, too, if you're into that (and I am!). To travel there is to fall in love with its natural wonders and cultural riches — I have yet to meet anyone who has visited and not wanted to return. Costa Rica pioneered the ecotourism trend, protecting over a quarter of its territory as national reserves and parks, both on land and in the ocean. It's also a beacon of stability in a region that has been volatile at times, making it a safe bet for a hassle-free vacation. While many folks flock to its Pacific and Caribbean beaches, its world-class surf breaks and golf courses, others are enchanted by its teeming forests, where you can spot unique fauna like snuffly tapirs foraging for food, dazzlingly colorful resplendent quetzals, quizzical toucans and languorous sloths sunning themselves in the canopy. Just to name a few. So, if this little Central American nation has been on your travel to-do list, now might just be the right time to plan your visit, especially once the summer heat has dissipated and the days turn dry and sunny. Here are some of our best tips to make the most of your trip to Costa Rica, and how to get the most out of your points and miles while doing so. What's the best part of Costa Rica for a trip? Although it's the third-smallest country in Central America (and that's not saying much!), Costa Rica still clocks in at over 19,000 square miles, which means most travelers will likely want to stick to one or two spots during their visit. The capital of San José offers plenty of flights to and from U.S. hubs, but for many vacationgoers, the main arrival point is Liberia on the country's west coast thanks to its proximity to the beach resorts of Guanacaste, the rainforests of the interior and the national parks to the south. For the purposes of this guide, we'll just stick to the regions around Liberia, though if you're interested in exploring other parts of the country, let us know in a comment and we'll write up guides to those as well. Related: The 13 best all-inclusive resorts in Costa Rica Mix and match Alaska Airlines and American Airlines awards One of the best ways to fly from the U.S. to Costa Rica is to take either American Airlines or Alaska Airlines, two U.S.-based Oneworld airline partners that, between them, fly to Liberia from the following airports (though note some of these are seasonal): - Chicago O'Hare International Airport (ORD) - Dallas Fort Worth International Airport (DFW) - Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) - Miami International Airport (MIA) - New York's John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) That gives flyers a lot of choices when it comes to redeeming miles. In some cases, you're better off redeeming Alaska Airlines Atmos Rewards points for shorter American Airlines flights, but in others, redeeming American Airlines AAdvantage miles for its own flights as well as those on Alaska is the better choice. So … you have to do a little homework, but it can be worth it to save thousands of points or miles. For instance, you can book American Airlines' flights from Miami to Liberia for as few as 7,500 Alaska points plus $44 (or $76 in the other direction), while American's award rates start at 9,000 miles plus slightly lower taxes and fees. However, Alaska will charge you 17,500 points and the same taxes and fees from other hubs like DFW, JFK and LAX ... Whereas American AAdvantage rates tend to start at around 10,000-11,500 miles each way plus $24 in taxes and fees (or $56 coming from Costa Rica). Use a tool like seats.aero to compare rates quickly and determine which is best. So that you're stocked up and ready with the specific types of points or miles you need when you're ready: Alaska is a 1:1 transfer partner of Bilt.
